claims.text: On Defects4J, GPT-3.5 AutoFL beats the external SBFL/MBFL baselines at acc@1; its improvement over Ochiai is 19.7%.
claims.quote: For the Defects4J dataset (Fig. 3a), the graph shows that AutoFL, when using GPT-3.5 as the language model, outperforms SBFL and MBFL, which were the best-performing standalone FL techniques from Zou et al. [ 53], on the acc@1 measure.

claims.text: GPT-3.5 AutoFL outperforms external SmartFL on the same 222 Defects4J bugs excluding Closure.
claims.quote: On the same bug dataset, AutoFL still outperformed SmartFL, as shown in the square marker graphs of Fig. 3a.

claims.text: On BugsInPy, GPT-3.5 AutoFL improves acc@1 over external Ochiai by 166.7%.
claims.quote: AutoFL-GPT3.5 and AutoFL-GPT4 improved method-level acc@1 by 166.7% and 233.3% when compared with Ochiai.

claims.text: On BugsInPy, GPT-4 AutoFL improves acc@1 over external Ochiai by 233.3%.
claims.quote: AutoFL-GPT3.5 and AutoFL-GPT4 improved method-level acc@1 by 166.7% and 233.3% when compared with Ochiai.

claims.text: GPT-4 AutoFL achieves better acc@1–5 than the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks.
claims.quote: AutoFL-GPT4 overcomes the limitations of GPT-3.5 to consistently achieve better performance relative to all baselines up to acc@5.

claims.text: Repository function interaction improves FL over the author-constructed Test-GPT3.5 control on both benchmarks.
claims.quote: Comparing against the Test-GPT3.5 baseline, which prompts GPT-3.5 to predict the fault location without any function interaction, AutoFL consistently outperforms it, demonstrating that the function interactions improve the performance ofAutoFL.

claims.text: Aggregating more AutoFL runs substantially improves FL on both benchmarks.
claims.quote: Meanwhile, merging more AutoFL runs to get an aggregate result helps improve performance by a large margin in both Defects4J and BugsInPy, as shown in Fig. 4.

claims.text: Confidence positively correlates with FL performance: Defects4J rho=0.57/0.67/0.70 and BugsInPy rho=0.52/0.50/0.49 for P@1/RR/AP, respectively.

metrics.name: Spearman rho: confidence versus P@1, RR and AP

claims.quote: In both benchmark datasets, Defects4J and BugsInPy, we observe statistically significant positive correlations between the AutoFL confidence values and the FL performance metrics.

claims.text: Confidence can help filter potentially inaccurate FL results.
claims.quote: Consequently, the confidence value of AutoFL can be used to filter out potentially inaccurate results.

claims.text: 20.0% of the 300 sampled explanation slots accurately describe the bug's root cause.
claims.quote: Regarding the other measure, among all 300 individual explanations generated by AutoFL, 20% of them contained correct descriptions about what was causing the bug (Accurate).

claims.text: At least one accurate explanation is generated for 56.7% of the 60 sampled bugs.

metrics.name: Bugs with at least one Accurate explanation

claims.quote: When explanations are aggregated by bug rather than evaluated individually, at least one accurate explanation was generated for 56.7% of all bugs, suggesting that with an appropriate selection of explanations, developers could benefit from the explanations of AutoFL more often.

claims.text: Higher-confidence bugs have more accurate explanations: individual accuracy rises from 10.0% in the lowest bin to 34.3% in the highest, and per-bug accuracy from 37.5% to 85.7%.
claims.quote: Interestingly, helpful explanations are more common for bugs when AutoFL is confident.

claims.text: Twelve of sixteen developers wanted FL explanations: four called them necessary and eight useful.
claims.quote: Four developers described explanations for FL as necessary, while eight additionally described explanations as useful; in total, twelve developers suggested that they would want explanations when using FL.

claims.text: Developers valued AutoFL's explanations of the intention of functions under test.
claims.quote: Developers appreciated that the explanations described the intention of the function(s) under test, and (when fixes were provided) generally liked the fixes suggested by AutoFL.

claims.text: Developers generally liked the fixes suggested in AutoFL explanations.
claims.quote: Developers appreciated that the explanations described the intention of the function(s) under test, and (when fixes were provided) generally liked the fixes suggested by AutoFL.

claims.text: Five developers liked the natural-language explanation of error messages.

claims.quote: The most common theme was that developers liked a natural language explanation of the error message, with five developers liking this aspect

claims.text: Developers disliked overlapping content within and across AutoFL explanations and wanted summaries.
claims.quote: most said that the overlapping content in the explanations (both between the ten explanations that we provided per bug, and within each explanation) was unnecessary, and that it would be helpful to summarize explanations with the same content.

claims.text: Four developers found suggestions to fix tests confusing.
claims.quote: four others thought that the suggestions of the explanations to fix tests were confusing,

claims.text: Two developers reported insufficient patch or fault-location suggestions causing confusion and wasted time.
claims.quote: two developers noted that the patches or fault locations suggested by the explanations were insufficient to fix the bug, leading to confusion and wasting their time.

claims.text: Eleven developers thought ten explanations per bug were too many and wanted a summary.
claims.quote: Finally, when asked about the ideal number of explanations presented to the developer, 11 developers thought that the ten explanations presented in the experiment were too much, and wanted a summary.

claims.text: Thirteen of sixteen developers agreed, sometimes conditionally, that FL locations would help debugging.

claims.text: Developers regarded FL as more helpful when unfamiliar with a project and less helpful when knowledgeable about it.

claims.text: Developers said explanations help navigation of unfamiliar code and reasoning about fixes.

claims.text: Four developers considered explanations unnecessary for easy code; one worried about explanation accuracy on difficult bugs.

claims.text: Two developers thought explaining the error message did not improve bug understanding.

claims.text: Ten developers found no other content to remove and considered unnecessary material easy to skip.

claims.text: Four developers wanted the original intention of the code/test in an ideal explanation.

claims.text: Thirteen developers wanted a suggested patch, the most popular ideal explanation feature.

claims.text: Four developers wanted actual dynamic values incorporated into explanations.

claims.text: Manual Essentials mappings increased PostgreSQL query acceptance from the no-mapping control's 0% to 35.5%.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 4, essential mappings raise the PostgreSQL success rate
from 0% to 35.5%, short of practical testing needs (query generation combines clauses to obtain a
test query).

claims.text: All four LLM configurations surpassed the 35.5% Essentials acceptance baseline: at 10/50 attempts GPT-5.2 achieved 64.8%/69.9%, GPT-4o 56.0%/60.0%, Qwen3-Coder-30B 40.6%/62.9%, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 36.6%/51.5%.
claims.quote:
Integrating LLMs intoACME yields large gains: GPT-5.2 reaches 64.8% at 10 attempts
and 69.9% at 50 attempts, nearly doubling the heuristic baseline, while even the smallest model
(Qwen2.5-Coder-7B) surpasses the heuristic at 50 attempts (51.5%).

claims.text: Increasing the attempt cap from 10 to 50 improved PostgreSQL acceptance for every model, with the largest gain for Qwen3-Coder-30B, 22.3 percentage points.
claims.quote: Increasing the attempt budget consistently improves performance across all models, most notably for Qwen3-Coder-30B (+22.3%), though at the cost of greater token consumption.

claims.text: Increasing the attempt cap from 10 to 50 increased token use: GPT-5.2 7.5K→33.2K, GPT-4o 10.0K→41.8K, Qwen3-Coder-30B 10.2K→60.4K, and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 20.7K→75.5K.
claims.quote: Increasing the attempt budget consistently improves performance across all models, most notably for Qwen3-Coder-30B (+22.3%), though at the cost of greater token consumption.

claims.text: At 50 attempts, open-weight Qwen3-Coder-30B achieved competitive PostgreSQL acceptance relative to GPT-4o: 62.9% versus 60.0%.
claims.quote:
Results demonstrate that mid-tier
open-weight models such as Qwen3-Coder-30B (62.9% at 50 attempts) can achieve competitive
performance relative to GPT-4o (60.0%), at a fraction of the API cost since open-weight models can
be run using local compute resources.

claims.text: Smaller models required more tokens to obtain mappings; at 50 attempts Qwen2.5-Coder-7B used 75.5K tokens versus GPT-5.2's 33.2K.
claims.quote: Although smaller models consume more tokens to arrive at valid mappings (e.g., 75.5K tokens for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B versus 33.2K for GPT-5.2 at 50 attempts, owing to more frequent re-validation cycles)

claims.text: Open-weight models are claimed to deliver competitive testing support at a fraction of proprietary API cost by running locally.
claims.quote:
Results demonstrate that mid-tier
open-weight models such as Qwen3-Coder-30B (62.9% at 50 attempts) can achieve competitive
performance relative to GPT-4o (60.0%), at a fraction of the API cost since open-weight models can
be run using local compute resources.

claims.text: ACME is claimed to enable effective differential testing across deployment environments, including local models without online API dependence.
claims.quote:
These results confirm thatACME is broadly
applicable across deployment environments, enabling effective differential testing locally without
prohibitive token costs or dependence on online LLM APIs.

claims.text: With Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, validation and re-prompting increased PostgreSQL query acceptance from 34.8% to 42.9%; the disabled condition fell below the 35.5% heuristic baseline.
claims.quote:
Disabling both validation and re-prompting causes the PostgreSQL query success rate to drop
from 42.9% to 34.8%, falling below even the heuristic baseline; this degradation is primarily due to
invalid SQL syntax in unvalidated mappings.

claims.text: The authors attribute improved mapping precision and LLM reliability to the validation/re-prompting pipeline.
claims.quote:
In contrast, retaining the validation pipeline allows
even lightweight models to consistently exceed the heuristic baseline, confirming the contribution
of the re-prompting to ensuring mapping precision.

claims.text: A few valid mappings, exemplified by 10 interaction rounds, are claimed sufficient to significantly expand differential-testing coverage.
claims.quote:
In practice, we find that obtaining a few valid mappings (e.g., 10 rounds of
interaction in Table 4) is sufficient to significantly expand differential testing coverage, incurring
only minimal token costs in LLM usage.

claims.text: ACME is claimed to avoid prohibitive token costs, with minimal costs at ten rounds; the ten-round settings consume 7.5K–20.7K tokens.
claims.quote:
In practice, we find that obtaining a few valid mappings (e.g., 10 rounds of
interaction in Table 4) is sufficient to significantly expand differential testing coverage, incurring
only minimal token costs in LLM usage.

claims.text: ACME could detect every confirmed or fixed bug within six hours on the reported personal workstation; most bugs took only a few hours.
claims.quote:
ACME can detect all confirmed or fixed bugs within six hours of running on personal
computing resources.

claims.text: ACME's focused SQL-engine instruction coverage reached 19,863 by one hour and then remained at that value through one day.
claims.quote: Both tools saturate quickly on the SQL engine (SQLancer reaches 17,122 instructions by 10h and ACME reaches 19,863 by 1h)

claims.text: QuestDB query acceptance remained approximately 72%–73% across the mapping configurations, unaffected by mapping changes.
claims.quote: The QuestDB success rate remains stable at∼72–73% across all configurations and is not affected by clause mapping.

claims.text: The discussion reports only 3 false alarms alongside 55 confirmed bugs during ACME development and use; this denominator differs from the 57 confirmed/fixed bugs elsewhere.
claims.quote:
We encountered only 3 false alarms out of 55 confirmed bugs while developing and
runningACME.

claims.text: Automatic LLM clause-mapping discovery is claimed to require minimal manual effort.
claims.quote:
We initially designed clause mappings manually; however, our current approach
can automatically discover them with the help of LLMs, requiring only minimal manual effort.

claims.text: Human work remains necessary for query generation, result analysis and complex mapping validation.
claims.quote:
Although LLMs can automate clause mappings, we still require some human
effort in query generation, result analysis, and validation of complex clause mappings.

claims.text: Fragile mappings can survive validation, especially when combined with untested clauses, and require further re-prompting.
claims.quote:
Nevertheless, some fragile mappings may persist, especially when interacting
with untested clauses, requiringACME to re-prompt the LLM for alternative mappings.

claims.text: The authors attribute mitigation of mapping-induced false alarms to runtime validation.
claims.quote: While LLM-generated clause mappings can introduce additional false alarms in differential testing, these are largely mitigated byACME’s validation process

claims.text: Manual inspection is claimed necessary to maintain a low false-alarm rate, particularly with small-to-medium models.
claims.quote: however, manual inspection is still necessary to maintain a minimal false-alarm rate, particularly when using small-to-medium-scale models.

claims.text: Effectiveness with lightweight local models is claimed to make ACME practical for continuous integration.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, our experiments confirm
thatACME remains effective even under a lightweight LLM budget using local models, making it a
practical solution for continuous integration.

claims.text: QuestDB developer acknowledgments are presented as evidence of ACME's real-world utility.

evidence.description: The paper reports an official QuestDB blog acknowledgment; the linked material was not consulted.

claims.quote:
The real-world utility of our work is underscored by
acknowledgments from industry developers, such as QuestDB, highlighting the effectiveness of
LLM-driven reasoning in building a unified, scalable, and robust testing framework for the next
generation of new database systems.

claims.text: The 35.5% acceptance achieved by Essentials is characterized as insufficient for practical testing.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 4, essential mappings raise the PostgreSQL success rate
from 0% to 35.5%, short of practical testing needs (query generation combines clauses to obtain a
test query).

claims.text: Query execution success remained stable when new features were only infrequently included in generated queries.
claims.page: p. 15, §5.2, Higher query execution success rate
claims.quote:
The success rate remained stable when new features were infre-
quently incorporated into query generations.

matched_comparisons.metric: PostgreSQL query success rate after clause mapping

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Thunder Brawl, BNB Chain, 1887 lines of code
ecs.protocol: Comparative user study: three experienced auditors, one per assistance condition; AdvSCanner-assisted exploit development versus expert-only and static-analysis assistance; completion time and usefulness of generated framework; case-specific temperature, feedback limit and repetitions not_reported
ecs.quote:
The subject of our study wasThunder Brawl[56], a real-world vul-
nerable project on the BNB Chain, consisting of 1887 lines of code.

claims.text: AdvSCanner achieves 76.41% mean ASC-generation success, exceeding the author-built LLM_C (6.92%) and LLM_CS (18.97%) controls; it exceeds both on all six benchmark subsets.
claims.quote:
Answer to RQ1:AdvSCanner outperforms the two baselines
with a success rate of 76.41% compared to 6.92% and 18.97%,
demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in generating
adversarial smart contracts.

claims.text: AdvSCanner reduces compilation failures to 10/390 (2.56%), versus LLM_C 32/390 (8.21%) and LLM_CS 67/390 (17.18%).
claims.quote:
Conversely, AdvSCanner experiments
resulted in 92 failures (23.59%), with 10 compilation failures (2.56%)
and 82 triggering failures (21.03%).

claims.text: AdvSCanner reduces triggering failures to 82/390 (21.03%), versus the paper's reported rates of 84.87% for LLM_C and 63.85% for LLM_CS.
claims.quote:
Conversely, AdvSCanner experiments
resulted in 92 failures (23.59%), with 10 compilation failures (2.56%)
and 82 triggering failures (21.03%).

claims.text: Attack-flow guidance raises mean success from 1.03% without the attack-flow component to 76.41% with it.
claims.quote:
In𝐴𝑁𝑜𝐴𝐹 experiments, the success rate is
merely1.03%anditsvarianceis9.20 ×10−5,emphasizingthepivotal
role of attack flow in adversarial contract generation.

claims.text: Self-reflection raises mean success from 44.87% without it to 76.41% with it.
claims.quote:
Compared to the AdvSCanner, removing the attack
flow reduces the success rate to 1.03%, while omitting the self-
reflection component to 44.87%.

claims.text: Temperature changes success: 0.3, 0.7, 1, 1.3 and 1.7 yield 73.33%, 72.31%, 76.41%, 67.18% and 0%, respectively; lower-to-moderate settings perform best in the tested range.
claims.quote:
Within the 0.3 to 1.3 range, the success rates were
73.33%,72.31%,76.41%,and67.18%,respectively.

claims.text: Increasing the feedback limit from 1 to 5 to 10 raises mean success from 55.64% to 76.41% to 83.85%.
claims.quote:
Specifically, Ad-
vSCanner yielded a success rate of 55.64% with one feedback time,
whereas 5 and 10 feedback times yielded higher success rates of
76.41% and 83.85%, respectively.

claims.text: GPT-4o gives the highest aggregate success (81.54%), followed by GPT-4 (80.26%) and GPT-3.5-turbo (76.41%), at temperature 1 and feedback limit 5.
claims.quote:
AsillustratedinTable 7,GPT-4oachieveidenti-
calperformance,yieldingasuccessrateof81.54%,whilesurpassing
GPT-4, which achieves a success rate of 80.26%.

claims.text: In the Thunder Brawl user study, the AdvSCanner-assisted auditor completed exploit development in about 3 hours, versus 24 hours unassisted and 6 hours with static-analysis assistance; different auditors performed the three conditions.

metrics.name: Auditor time to implement a successful adversarial contract

claims.quote:
Furthermore, a case study illustrates that AdvSCanner can
greatly reduce auditing time from 24 hours (without assistance) to
approximately 3 hours when used during the auditing process.

claims.text: The generated Thunder Brawl framework and its callback/attack-flow guidance helped the assisted auditor develop an effective exploit.

metrics.name: One auditor's successful development using the generated framework

claims.quote:
Despite the adversarial contract generated by AdvSCanner
couldn’t successfully exploit the complex reentrancy vulnerability,
it provided a fundamental framework and valuable insights into
callback mechanisms and attack flows.

claims.text: AdvSCanner did not autonomously produce an ASC that successfully exploited the complex Thunder Brawl project.

metrics.name: Automated exploit-generation success: unsuccessful in this case

claims.quote:
AlthoughAdvSCannerdidnotsuccessfullygenerateanadversarial
contract that exploited the reentrancy vulnerability in this compli-
catedproject,itdidproduceanadversarialcontractframeworkthat
significantly aided auditors in developing effective exploits.

claims.text: Across the reported trials, AdvSCanner and LLM_C are more stable than LLM_CS: variances are 3.02e-4, 2.37e-4 and 4.50e-3, respectively.

metrics.name: Variance of generation success across trials

claims.quote:
Furthermore, the corresponding statistical variance
in results for𝐿𝐿𝑀𝐶,𝐿𝐿𝑀𝐶𝑆, and AdvSCanner were 2.37×10−4,
4.50×10−3, and 3.02×10−4, respectively.

claims.text: Mean phase times are judged acceptable: static analysis 0.98 s, LLM response 39.47 s per iteration, and validation 16.62 s.
claims.quote:
After the analysis, we found that the average times for static
analysis, LLM responses (per iteration), and the validation process
are 0.98s, 39.47s, and 16.62s, respectively, which are acceptable.

claims.text: At temperature 1.7, internal API errors, typically invalid Unicode output, cause all attempts to fail.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table5, a temperature of 1.7 resulted in failures
due to internal errors, leading to a 0% success rate.

claims.text: On ATR, self-reflection reduces success: the full configuration obtains 40%, versus 48% without self-reflection.
Increasing feedback iterations is said to increase computational overhead, motivating the choice of five iterations; overhead is not quantified by iteration setting.

metrics.name: Configured feedback iteration limit; setting-specific elapsed time/cost not_reported

claims.quote:
These findings underscore the piv-
otal role of iterative feedback in augmenting the effectiveness of
adversarial contract generation, notwithstanding the heightened
computational overhead.

claims.text: Lower-to-moderate temperatures, especially near 1, are claimed to favor compilable code that executes the intended attack.

metrics.name: ASC success rate requiring compilation and attack triggering

claims.quote:
lower tempera-
tures, particularly those close to 1 (≤1) are preferable, producing
less diverse but more precise and reliable outputs, ensuring the
generated smart contract code compiles successfully and executes
the intended attack effectively.

claims.text: Lower-to-moderate temperatures are claimed to produce more reliable outputs; reported variances are 2.24e-4, 4.34e-4, 3.02e-4 and 1.42e-3 at temperatures 0.3, 0.7, 1 and 1.3.
claims.quote:
lower tempera-
tures, particularly those close to 1 (≤1) are preferable, producing
less diverse but more precise and reliable outputs, ensuring the
generated smart contract code compiles successfully and executes
the intended attack effectively.

claims.text: Without attack-flow information, exploring possible attack flows is proposed to make generation inefficient; no ablation-specific time or search-work measurement is reported.
claims.quote:
Without such
insight, LLM would attempt to explore all conceivable attack flows
to exploit reentrancy vulnerabilities, rendering the process ineffi-
cient.

claims.text: Self-reflection is proposed to reduce repeated error iterations and improve success within a limited number of attempts; error-iteration counts are not reported.
claims.quote:
Integrating self-reflection into the analysis process can
mitigate error iterations, thereby enhancing the likelihood of suc-
cess within a restricted number of attempts.

claims.text: Static-analysis limitations, LLM understanding and token limits are proposed as sources of difficulty with complex real-world vulnerabilities.

metrics.name: Failure to generate a working autonomous exploit in the case study

claims.quote:
The potential challenges in handling real-world complex vul-
nerabilities include the constraints of static analysis, the LLMs’
understanding, and token limits.

claims.text: The paper argues that the relative effectiveness result remains informative even if data leakage occurred because the controls use the same base model; leakage itself is not measured.

metrics.name: Relative ASC-generation success under a shared base model

claims.quote:
Even if data leakage occurred, Table2still demonstrates
theeffectivenessofAdvScannerasthesamebasemodelisalsoused
in baselines.

claims.text: At N=3, EnAgent outperforms Augment, Augment with pruning, DeiBase and DeiBase with pruning, with reported relative Pass@1 improvements of 5.01%–12.86%; its four model-setting scores are 62.27%, 66.40%, 59.00% and 65.67%.

evidence.type: statistical test: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<8.00×10^-6
evidence.quote:
The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test [56]
(at a significance level of 0.05) yields p-values below 8.00× 10−6,
confirming that EnAgent significantly outperforms all baselines
in terms of Pass@1.

claims.quote:
Specifically, it demonstrates
an improvement of 5.01%∼12.86% compared to the baselines in
terms of Pass@1.

claims.text: Across the evaluated ensemble sizes, EnAgent outperforms the four external ensemble comparators, with reported average relative improvements of 5.83%–14.60%; the abstract summarizes an overall average improvement of 10.22%.

evidence.type: statistical test: paired Wilcoxon signed-rank, p<3.74×10^-12
evidence.quote:

Rank Test [56] (at a significance level of 0.05) yields p-values below
3.74× 10−12, validating that EnAgent significantly outperforms all
baselines across different ensemble sizes in terms of Pass@1.

claims.quote:
Experimental results demonstrate
that EnAgent consistently achieves superior performance, with
an average improvement of 10.22% over all baselines in terms of
Pass@1.

claims.text: EnAgent has lower mean time overhead than DeiBase and DeiBase with pruning, but higher overhead than Augment and Augment with pruning; its means are 22.73, 22.01, 22.73 and 23.27 seconds.
claims.quote:
While
prompting-based Augment and Augment w/ Pruning demonstrate
better efficiency than EnAgent, the notable performance gains of
EnAgent justify its additional computational cost, indicating a fa-
vorable trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency.

claims.text: EnAgent uses fewer tokens than DeiBase and DeiBase with pruning, but more than Augment and Augment with pruning; its mean overheads are 25.00K, 26.81K, 22.32K and 26.46K tokens.
claims.quote:
While
prompting-based Augment and Augment w/ Pruning demonstrate
better efficiency than EnAgent, the notable performance gains of
EnAgent justify its additional computational cost, indicating a fa-
vorable trade-off between effectiveness and efficiency.

claims.text: EnAgent's Pass@1 increases as ensemble size grows from 1 to 10, unlike the eventual degradation reported for the external ensemble comparators.
claims.quote:
In contrast, EnAgent
consistently demonstrates an upward trajectory in terms of Pass@1
with increasing ensemble size, demonstrating superior effectiveness
and scalability.

deviating from the intended plan.

claims.text: The Action Model became stuck in loops in 11/57 correct-plan cases (19.30%).
claims.quote:
The ”Stuck in Loop” failures
further illustrated these challenges, manifesting as ”Menu
Loops” (14.04%), ”Command Loops” (3.51%), and even a
”Death Loop” (1.75%).

claims.text: Menu loops affected 8/57 correct-plan cases (14.04%), particularly during Create World navigation.
claims.quote:
”Menu Loops,” particularly within
the ”Create World” screen, indicated difficulties in reliably
navigating complex GUI structures.

claims.text: Command loops affected 2/57 correct-plan cases (3.51%), with repeated unparseable or ineffective commands.
claims.quote:
”Command Loops” arose
from issues in command parsing or execution, with the agent
repeatedly attempting unparseable or ineffective commands.

claims.text: A death loop affected 1/57 correct-plan cases (1.75%), caused by hostile mobs repeatedly killing the player.
claims.quote:
The single ”Death Loop” instance was caused by hostile mobs
continuously killing the player, preventing progress.

claims.text: Framework incapability affected 4/57 correct-plan cases (7.02%), with limitations in precise mouse control, rapid actions and specific UI interactions.
claims.quote:
Limitations in precise mouse control, rapid action execution, or
interaction with specific UI elements within the game hindered
the Action Model’s ability.

claims.text: The authors attribute 24/29 faulty-plan cases (82.76%) to unrecovered failures caused by incorrect steps.
claims.quote:
In scenarios where the Step Syn-
thesizer provided faulty plans and the Action Model did not
recover, the overwhelming majority of failures (82.76%) were
attributed to these incorrect steps.

claims.text: Four of 86 GPT-4o attempts ended in errors (4.65%): three internal JSON-schema failures and one potential-bug-related technical issue.

metrics.name: Internal JSON-schema errors: 3; bug-related technical errors: 1

claims.quote:
Three errors were from internal crashes (LLM failed to give
the output in correct JSON schema) and one error was from
the technical issues that the potential bug could cause.

claims.text: Average reproduction time was 10.00 minutes with GPT-4.1 and 15.56 with GPT-4o, slower than external CUA (6.37) and UI-TARS (3.27), reflecting an effectiveness/time trade-off.

metrics.name: Average reported reproduction time: GPT-4.1 10.00 min, GPT-4o 15.56 min, CUA 6.37 min, UI-TARS 3.27 min

claims.quote:
Regarding execution efficiency, BugCraft com-
pleted reproductions in 10.00 minutes on average with GPT-
4.1 (15.56 minutes with GPT-4o), showing a trade-off between
success rate and speed compared to CUA’s 6.37 minutes
and UI-TARS’s 3.27 minutes.

claims.text: Reported cost per attempt was $1.16 with GPT-4.1 and $1.45 with GPT-4o, above external CUA's $0.65 and UI-TARS's $0.02.

metrics.name: Cost per attempt: GPT-4.1 $1.16, GPT-4o $1.45, CUA $0.65, UI-TARS $0.02

claims.quote:
The cost analysis shows that
BugCraft operates at $1.16 per attempt (GPT-4.1), placing it
between the more economical CUA ($0.65) and the low-cost
UI-TARS ($0.02), which reflects the computational demands
of its two-stage approach.

claims.text: GPT-4.1 BugCraft's 34.9% success rate was below the reported human-expert rate of 83%.
claims.quote:
While BugCraft’s 34.9% success rate is lower than the 83%
achieved by human experts, this overlooks crucial operational
advantages.

claims.text: The authors report faster operational reproduction for GPT-4.1 BugCraft: 10 minutes versus human confirmation turnaround of 3.41 days; human active work was 20 minutes.

metrics.name: Reported turnaround: BugCraft 10 min, human 3.41 days

claims.quote:
BugCraft demon-
strates remarkable time efficiency, completing a reproduction
in 10 minutes compared to a human’s 3.41 day turnaround,
which is often delayed by organizational overhead.

claims.text: The discussion claims a tenfold reduction in cost per successful reproduction: $3.44 for BugCraft versus $35.25 for a human.

metrics.name: Reported cost per successful reproduction: BugCraft $3.44, human $35.25

claims.quote:
Financially, the system offers a 10-fold cost reduction
per successful reproduction-$3.44 for BugCraft versus $35.25
for a human - and its success with crash bugs is definitively
verifiable.

claims.text: The authors argue BugCraft's shorter turnaround makes it suitable for rapid triage.

metrics.name: Reported reproduction turnaround: 10 min versus human 3.41 days

claims.quote:
This vast
reduction in time allows our system to be suitable for rapid
triage.

claims.text: The authors claim parallel BugCraft instances enable scalable throughput beyond sequential human reproduction; no throughput experiment is reported.
claims.quote:
Finally, unlike human experts who work sequen-
tially, the framework processes bugs in parallel across multiple
instances.

claims.text: Wrong-command errors were often attributed to outdated pretrained syntax, especially for newer Minecraft versions.
claims.quote:
”Wrong Command” errors often stemmed
from the LLM relying on outdated command syntax from its
pre-training data, especially for newer Minecraft versions.

claims.text: The Step Synthesizer sometimes generated hallucinated commands that never existed in Minecraft.

metrics.name: Qualitative identification of nonexistent generated commands

claims.quote:
Additionally, some hallucinated
commands were generated that never existed in the game.

claims.text: Missing-step errors reflected incomplete capture of crucial details, especially for complex bugs and recent mechanics.
claims.quote:
”Missing Step” errors indicated that the Step Synthesizer
sometimes failed to capture all the crucial details needed
for successful reproduction, particularly for complex bugs or
those involving recent game mechanics.

claims.text: Execution-log inspection found GPT-4.1 followed prescribed step clusters more closely, while GPT-4o made more off-plan attempts.

metrics.name: Qualitative adherence to prescribed step clusters

claims.quote:
A qualitative execution-log analysis
indicates GPT-4.1 followed the prescribed step clusters more
closely, whereas GPT-4o exhibited more off-plan attempts.

claims.text: External CUA navigated menus better than BugCraft's Action Model in the qualitative analysis.
claims.page: p. 11, §V-C4; BugCraft model for this observation not_reported
claims.quote:
OpenAI-CUA nav-
igates menus better than our Action Model, but its poorer
solution choices reveal the value of our Step Synthesizer’s
bug analysis.

claims.text: The authors claim cross-version adaptability from processing reports across over 70 Minecraft versions and more than six years; version-stratified success rates are not reported.

metrics.name: Reported versions processed: over 70; span: more than six years

claims.quote:
Moreover, BugCraft demonstrated its adaptability by suc-
cessfully processing reports from over 70 different Minecraft
versions, spanning more than six years of the game’s devel-
opment.

claims.text: In the MC-161902 case, BugCraft placed water through a command while external CUA's physical placement failed; the case-study BugCraft model is not_reported.

metrics.name: Case-study water placement: BugCraft success, CUA failure

claims.quote:
Case study analysis of MC-161902 comparing how our framework
successfully places the water block whereas OpenAI-CUA fails.

claims.text: The models had complementary successful reports: 20 shared, 10 only GPT-4.1, six only GPT-4o, yielding oracle coverage of 36/86 (41.9%).
claims.quote:
The models’ successes only partially overlapped (20 both; 10
only GPT-4.1; 6 only GPT-4o; McNemar p=0.45), yielding
an oracle coverage of 36/86 (41.9%).

claims.text: The authors infer that mixing agent strategies could increase reproduction coverage, without evaluating a mixed-strategy harness.

metrics.name: Oracle union coverage: 41.9%, versus 34.9% and 30.2% individually

claims.quote:
This complementarity
implies that mixing agent strategies can increase coverage in
bug reproduction.

claims.text: BLAST outperforms external AutoTDD and ZeroShot with all three models: gpt-4o 151/426 (35.4%), llama3.3 131/426 (30.8%), DeepSeek 114/426 (26.8%).

evidence.quote:
We find that all of them
target the core issue, so for LLM-generated tests we assume
F → P ∗ = F → P .

claims.quote:
Table I presents the results: BLAST outperforms previous
methods across all underlying LLMs evaluated.

claims.text: C1 produces F→P tests for 84/426 issues (19.7%) in the simulated pre-patch/TDD condition.
claims.quote:
For the TDD scenario ( C1), BLAST generates a F →P test
in 19.7% of the cases even though it was not designed
for TDD.

claims.text: Providing the issue description instead of only its title increases gpt-4o F→P rate from 20.2% (86) to 29.1% (124), an 8.9-point gain.
claims.quote:
When only the issue title is given instead of the
description ( C2), BLAST performs significantly worse (8.9%)
than when the description is added ( C3).

claims.text: Focal context increases gpt-4o F→P rate from 29.1% (124) to 32.2% (137), a 3.1-point gain.
claims.quote:
By adding focal context (C4), the performance increases
by another 3.1%.

claims.text: Adding retrieved existing tests increases gpt-4o F→P rate by 0.7 points (137 to 140) and llama3.3 by 6.3 points.
claims.quote:
The retrieved test case ( C5) yields small
increase (0.7%) in gpt-4o, but yields the largest increase for
llama3.3 (6.3%).

claims.text: Pynguin-test prompt context gives the best gpt-4o LLM-branch result: C6 reaches 145/426 (34.1%), versus C5's 140 (32.9%); C7 reaches 143 (33.6%).
claims.quote:
Incorporating Pynguin-generated tests into
the prompt ( C6, C7) yields the best performance (+1.2), even
though Pynguin-generated tests were only available for113 out
of the 426 cases.

claims.text: gpt-4o outperforms DeepSeek and llama3.3 across all seven input combinations.
claims.quote:
DeepSeek and llama3.3 follow a similar trend
with small differentiations that we analyze in our replication
package [17], with gpt-4o outperforming them across all Ci.

claims.text: Cumulative union F→P rates across C1–C7 are 19.7%, 32.6%, 42.3%, 45.1%, 48.8%, 49.3% and 49.5%; the final union exceeds the best individual run's 34.1% by 15.4 percentage points.
claims.quote:
Unexpectedly, the cumulative number of F →P tests gener-
ated by the union of all combinations (last column of Table II)
is 15.4% higher than the best-performing individual run.

claims.text: Seeded SBST performs best at 60 seconds: 10/113 verified successes (8.8%), versus 7 (6.2%) at 6 seconds and 9 (7.9%) at 600 seconds.
claims.quote:
Surprisingly, extend-
ing the time budget to 600 seconds results in one less F →P
test.

claims.text: At 60 seconds, LLM seeding increases SBST's verified issue-reproducing successes from 4/113 (3.5%) to 10/113 (8.8%).
claims.quote:
In this setting, only four F →P tests are generated, high-
lighting the critical role of our seeding approach in aligning
Pynguin’s search with the issue description and the patch.

claims.text: SBST supplies successes missed by the LLM branch: Table III reports 4, 6 and 5 unique cases at 6, 60 and 600 seconds, and 3 without seeding; Finding 2 instead says 5 at the selected setting.
claims.quote:
BLAST ’s SBST Component generates
an issue-reproducing test in 10 cases, 5 of which
missed by the LLM Component.

claims.text: SBST contributes 11/151 (7.3%) of BLAST's successful benchmark cases, combining direct SBST successes and improvements from SBST prompt context.
claims.quote:
Hence, Pynguin contributes
in 7.3% (11/151) of the generated issue-reproducing tests of
BLAST .

claims.text: Finding 2 attributes 151/426 issue-reproducing successes to the LLM Component, conflicting with Table II's 143 for C7 and 145 for C6.
claims.quote:
Finding 2 BLAST ’s LLM Component generates an
issue-reproducing test in 151/ 426 cases, with the focal
context and the SBST tests being the most important
prompt context.

claims.text: In vivo, llama3.3 yields the most LLM-branch F→P tests: 8/32 (25.0%), versus gpt-4o's 7/32 (21.9%) and DeepSeek's 4/32 (12.5%).
claims.quote:
In contrast to our benchmark-based evaluation, llama3.3
achieves the highest number of F →P tests (8/32, 25.0%), fol-
lowed by gpt-4o (7/32, 21.9%) and DeepSeek (4/32, 12.5%).

claims.text: BLAST can generate genuine issue-reproducing tests beyond historical benchmarks; the discussion summarizes real-world performance as 25.0%.

evidence.quote:
The developer considered 6/11 (55%) tests as valid issue-
reproducing tests, two of which were successfully included
in the projects’ test suite, one without any changes and the
other after inserting it in a different test file.

claims.quote:
While improving upon
the SOTA, BLAST manages to generate an issue-reproducing
test for 35.4% of the issue-patch pairs in the benchmark and
for 25.0% in the real-world evaluation, which leaves ample
room for future improvement.

claims.text: Developers judge 6/11 proposed F→P tests (55%) to reproduce the issue.
claims.quote:
The developer considered 6/11 (55%) tests as valid issue-
reproducing tests, two of which were successfully included
in the projects’ test suite, one without any changes and the
other after inserting it in a different test file.

claims.quote:

reproducing tests, two of which were successfully included

claims.text: BLAST and external AutoTDD have complementary successes: BLAST alone succeeds on 67 issues, AutoTDD alone on 16.
claims.quote:
Regarding overlap,
BLAST generates issue-reproducing tests for 67 issues that
AutoTDD misses, while AutoTDD does so for 16 issues that
BLAST misses.

claims.text: BLAST's successful tests cover 94% of patch lines versus external ZeroShot's 91%; the difference is not statistically significant.
claims.quote:
The coverage ranges from
91% for ZeroShot to 94% for BLAST but the difference is not
statistically significant.

claims.text: Under the paper's zero-overhead assumption for LLM/context operations, BLAST uses two LLM queries plus 60 seconds of SBST, versus external AutoTDD's three queries without SBST overhead.
claims.quote:
Under these assumptions, BLAST requires two
LLM queries and 60 seconds time overhead, while AutoTDD
requires three LLM queries with no time overhead.

claims.text: BLAST's selected test file matches the developer's file in 86% of cases, versus external AutoTDD's 61%.
claims.quote:
BLAST ’s name-
and git-based heuristic matches the developer file in 86% of
the cases, compared to AutoTDD’s LLM-based retrieval which
only matches the developer’s file in 61% of the cases.

claims.text: F→P alone does not establish genuine issue reproduction: verified/raw SBST counts are 7/10, 10/13 and 9/12 at 6, 60 and 600 seconds, and 4/8 without seeding; live judgments accept 6/11 proposals and 0/2 SBST tests.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, as a community we should reflect on evaluation
metrics like F →P, which, while widely used, do not always
correspond to issue-reproducing tests.

claims.text: Pynguin runs successfully on only 113/426 benchmark instances (26%), limiting SBST's contribution.
claims.quote:
The first limitation
is the inability of SBST tools to run in arbitrary code, e.g.,
Pynguin runs successfully in 113/426 (26%) dataset instances.

claims.text: In vivo, Pynguin runs on 11/32 PRs and produces two F→P tests.
claims.quote:
Pynguin successfully ran in 11/32 PRs and generated two
F→P tests, but our bot did not propose them to the developer
because gpt-4o-generated tests had precedence.

claims.text: Neither of the two in-vivo SBST F→P tests genuinely reproduces its issue on manual inspection.
claims.quote:
After inspect-
ing the tests ourselves, we found that they were not issue-
reproducing tests.

claims.text: Real-world performance is lower than benchmark performance; different repositories prevent attributing the drop solely to memorization.
claims.quote:
The accuracy of
BLAST in the real-world setting is lower than in TDD-Bench-
Verified, but we cannot attribute the drop to memorization
only, since the repositories are also different.

claims.text: LLM-code mistakes account for 22/30 analyzed LLM-branch failures: 12 logical/assertion failures and 10 syntactic/setup failures.
claims.quote:
Regarding the LLM Component, the failure is due to
mistakes in the LLM code in 22/30 cases, which we categorize
in logical (12), caused by an assertion error (or lack thereof),
and syntactic (10)

claims.text: Additional context could help only two of ten syntactic failures; eight have no missing context.
claims.quote:
In
only two of the syntactic failures further context could help,
while for the other eight cases no context is missing: in two
such examples, the LLM defines a helper function with two
arguments and calls it later without arguments.

claims.text: Five of 30 analyzed LLM failures involve noncompliance with the requested raw-function output format.
claims.quote:
In five of the other eight cases, the LLM does not comply
with requested output format .

claims.text: Ten of 20 analyzed SBST failures do not cover the patch, reflecting module-level rather than changed-method targeting.
claims.quote:
Regarding the SBST Component, the most common issue
(10/20) is that the tests do not cover the changes, because
Pynguin generates tests for whole modules and not classes
or methods.

claims.text: Five of 20 analyzed SBST failures require unsupported setup, such as decorators.
claims.quote:
In 5/20 cases, the test requires setup currently
unsupported by Pynguin, e.g., the patch only adds decorators
to methods, and Pynguin does not support decorators.

claims.text: In three of 20 analyzed SBST failures, generated tests cover the changes without triggering them.
claims.quote:
In 3/20
cases, the changes are covered but not triggered, while in 2/20
cases Pynguin generates tests that require additional setup to
run, leading to errors.

claims.text: Two of 20 analyzed SBST failures result from missing execution setup and consequent errors.
claims.quote:
In 3/20
cases, the changes are covered but not triggered, while in 2/20
cases Pynguin generates tests that require additional setup to
run, leading to errors.

code, because the LLM considers -oo to be a singleton that,

Finally,
in two cases the developer deemed the test to be reproducing

claims.text: Two proposed tests for renaming changes are considered unnecessary.

the issue was a renaming of a component from Fenix

claims.text: Two proposed tests for new features are judged unhelpful for those particular changes.

Upon a follow-up question, the maintainer clarified
that tests for new features are generally useful, but for these
specific two they were not that useful.

claims.text: One proposed test merely asserts changed query parameters instead of reproducing the issue.

In the lack of context for
a proper issue-reproducing test, BLAST asserts that the query

Another developer explained that the proposed tests become
obsolete when new commits are pushed to the PR, and
suggested triggering the bot on each new commit, which we
implemented.

We
attribute this to the fact that LLMs have been shown to
prioritize content towards the end of the prompt, known as
recency bias [48].

hcs.name: ChatRepair
hcs.quote:
Each generated patch by the
model is followed immediately by a patch validation step to compile
and run the patch on the test suite.

hcs.name: BaseChatGPT
hcs.removed: Initial test-failure information, failed-attempt conversations, and patch-conditioned alternative generation; independently samples the initial prompt.
hcs.quote:
Moreover, we also evaluate against a baseline of di-
rectly sampling using the ChatGPT model to perform repair without
any conversation or feedback information.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with BasePrompt
hcs.removed: Test-failure information from the initial prompt; conversational validation and subsequent feedback remain active.
hcs.quote:
First, we observe that the base initial prompt of only providing
with the buggy code and asking it to generate a patch performs the
worst in terms of the number of bugs fixed.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with TestName+ErrMsg initial context
hcs.removed: Relevant failing-test code line from initial context; retains failing-test name and error message.
hcs.quote:
We see that by adding
auxiliary information such as failing test name and error message,
we can further improve the repair performance.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with TestName+ErrMsg+TestBody initial context
hcs.removed: Replaces extraction of the failing-test code line with inclusion of the entire failing-test function body.
hcs.quote:
Moreover, we observe that the prompt which includes
the entire test function code also performs well in terms of the num-
ber of bugs fixed.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with BaseFeedback
hcs.removed: Detailed and dynamic failure feedback; retains validation and a generic incorrect-patch response.
hcs.quote:
RowBaseFeedback
means we only tell the model that the generated patch is not correct
without any additional feedback.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with TestName+ErrMsg feedback
hcs.removed: Failing-test code line and dynamic original-failure reference policy; uses static test-name/error feedback.
hcs.quote:
Similar to the initial prompt con-
struction, TestName+ErrMsg includes both the failing test name
and test failure error message,TestName+ErrMsg+FailLine ad-
ditionally includes the exact line where the failure occurred within
the test.

hcs.name: ChatRepair with static TestName+ErrMsg+FailLine feedback
hcs.removed: Dynamic policy that refers back to the original failure instead of repeating its details; retains detailed static feedback and validation.
hcs.quote:
Different from initial prompt construction,Dynamic is our
default approach where we only provide the test name/error/line
if the new generated patch has a different failure than the original
(Section 3.2).

hcs.name: ChatRepair with maximum conversation length 1
hcs.removed: Failed-attempt conversation history and feedback between initial repair attempts; the plausible-patch generation stage remains in Algorithm 1.
hcs.quote:
Recall from Sec-
tion 3.2 that the maximum conversation length dictates the amount of
history/feedback within each individual repair conversation, where
length = 1 is equivalent to sampling using the initial prompt without
any feedback.

hcs.name: ChatRepair under Ochiai top-40 fault-localization eligibility

ing widely adopted fault localization (Ochiai [86]) and assumed that

the top-40 suspicious locations.

claims.text: Across five Android hosts, MemoDroid raises activity coverage by 79%-96% over the respective unmodified external tools.
claims.quote:
Specifically, activity coverage increases by 79% - 96%,
and code coverage improves by 81% - 97%, indicating that
MemoDroidenables more effective activity and code ex-
ploration.

claims.text: Across five Android hosts, MemoDroid raises code coverage by 81%-97% over the respective unmodified external tools.
claims.quote:
Specifically, activity coverage increases by 79% - 96%,
and code coverage improves by 81% - 97%, indicating that
MemoDroidenables more effective activity and code ex-
ploration.

claims.text: MemoDroid increases bugs detected by 57%-198% over the respective unmodified GPTDroid, DroidAgent, AUITestAgent, VisionDroid and Guardian tools.
claims.quote:
In terms of bug detection, the number of bugs
discovered increases by 57% - 198%.

claims.text: The performance benefit applies to both text-based and vision-based Android testing hosts.
claims.quote:
The performance gains hold across both
text-based and vision-based baselines, confirming the general
applicability ofMemoDroid.

claims.text: Removing episodic memory lowers activity coverage by 23%-26%.

activity coverage and a 29% - 22% drop in code coverage.

claims.text: Removing episodic memory lowers code coverage by 22%-29%.

activity coverage and a 29% - 22% drop in code coverage.

claims.text: Removing episodic memory lowers bugs detected by 14%-24% across the five hosts.
claims.quote:

to a notable drop in performance, confirming that all three
components are essential.

claims.text: Reflective-memory removal produces the largest activity-coverage loss among layer ablations, 25%-38%.

reduction in activity coverage, 37% - 25% in code coverage,
and 39% - 19% fewer bugs detected.

claims.text: BICSleuth outperforms FONTE, Bug2Commit, FBL-BERT and HMCBL in BIC ranking across the three evaluated discriminator models; GPT-4o achieves MRR 0.786, 48.9% above FONTE and 407.1% above Bug2Commit.
claims.quote:
To be speciﬁc, BICSleuth_4o achieves
an MRR that is 48.9% higher than the best baseline, FONTE,
and a 407.1% improvement over the best IR-based baseline,
Bug2Commit.

claims.text: The abstract reports top-one success of 70.0% and top-five success of 84.6%; the latter conflicts with Table I's 117 of 130 top-five successes.
claims.quote:
Additionally, BICSleuth
ranks the BIC ﬁrst in 70.0% of projects and within the top ﬁve
in 84.6%.

claims.text: BICSleuth remains effective across GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini and DeepSeek-V3, with MRRs 0.786, 0.748 and 0.707; the mini model remains competitive with GPT-4o.
claims.quote:
BICSleuthdoes not depend on a speciﬁc LLM agent, the agent
based on GPT-4o mini can achieve a competitive performance
compared to the agent based on GPT-4o.

claims.text: The authors attribute effectiveness primarily to the framework architecture and design rather than overfitting to a particular LLM.
claims.quote:
These results across
three different LLMs demonstrate that the effectiveness of BIC-
Sleuth largely stems from its architecture and design, rather than
overﬁtting to a particular LLM.

and BICSleuth_4om i n iW/Otest , with the MRR reducing to
0.726/0.717 and A ccuracy@1 falling to 78/77.

to 0.701, and Accuracy@1 falls to 75.

W/Ocm
and BICSleuth_4om i n iW/Otest , with the MRR reducing to
0.726/0.717 and A ccuracy@1 falling to 78/77.

The MRR decreases to 0.667, and Accuracy@1 drops to 75,
indicating that the custom re-ranking strategy is more effective
than the LLM-based approach in the speciﬁc task of locating
BICs.

claims.quote:

from 0.660 to 0.577, and Accuracy@1 drops from 76 to 64.

claims.text: The ranking training objective materially improves Stage 1 performance; removing it produces the largest Table III degradation among the objective and stack-trace removals, with MRR 0.522 and Accuracy@1 52.
claims.quote:

drops to 0.522, and Accuracy@1 decreases sharply to 52.

claims.quote:

replacing our small model in the ranker, this variant achieves
an MRR of 0.452 and Accuracy@1 decreases sharply to 36,
respectively.

claims.quote:

test time for BICSleuth_ 4o and BICSleuth_4om i n iis 52.1
and 49.3 seconds, closely matching FONTE’s 54.2 seconds.

claims.text: BICSleuth is slower end to end than the evaluated IR-based comparators, whose mean times are 17.2 seconds for Bug2Commit, 2.4 for FBL-BERT and 3.1 for HMCBL.

metrics.name: Mean execution-inclusive localization time in seconds

claims.quote:
In contrast, IR-based methods such as
Bug2Commit (17.2 seconds), FBL-BERT (2.4 seconds), and
HMCBL (3.1 seconds) are substantially faster.

claims.text: Excluding test execution, BICSleuth takes 11.6 seconds with GPT-4o and 8.8 seconds with GPT-4o mini, below FONTE's 13.7 seconds.

metrics.name: Mean localization time excluding execution in seconds

claims.quote:
As shown in Table V, the execution-free test time for
BICSleuth_4o and BICSleuth_4om i n iis 11.6 and 8.8 seconds,
which is lower than FONTE’s 13.7 seconds.

claims.text: Mean LLM API cost per BIC localization falls from USD 1.50 with GPT-4o to USD 0.06 with GPT-4o mini.

metrics.name: Mean LLM API cost in USD per localization

claims.quote:
By replacing the agent in the pipeline with GPT-4o mini,
the call cost for per item is reduced to 0.06 USD, resulting in
a signiﬁcantly lower expense.

claims.text: The authors characterize BICSleuth's monetary cost as minimal compared with human labor, but report no measured human-labor cost comparator.

metrics.name: Mean LLM API cost in USD per localization

claims.quote:
This monetary cost
is minimal when compared to the costs associated with human
labor.

claims.text: The GPT-4o mini setting is presented as a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off suitable for resource-constrained use.
claims.quote:
This suggests that BICSleuth_ 4om i n imay offer a
favorable trade-off between performance and computational
efﬁciency, making it suitable for scenarios where resource
constraints are a concern.

claims.text: Execution is the main source of BICSleuth's additional end-to-end overhead; the execution component is reported as 40.5 seconds.
claims.quote:
The additional overhead incurred by
BICSleuth and FONTE is primarily due to the requirement for
executing test cases.

claims.text: LLM discriminator calls dominate the reported execution-free computation: GPT-4o uses 9.2 seconds, compared with 2.3 seconds for ranking and 0.1 seconds for re-ranking.
claims.quote:
The majority of BICSleuth ’s time overhead
is spent on large model calls, reﬂecting the cost of utilizing
LLMs in the localization process.

claims.text: Replacing GPT-4o with GPT-4o mini reduces discriminator calling time from 9.2 to 6.4 seconds.
claims.quote:
When replacing GPT-4o with
GPT-4o mini, the calling time is reduced from 9.2 seconds to
6.4 seconds.

claims.text: GPT-4o mini uses fewer retrieval calls per candidate than GPT-4o: 2.1 versus 2.7, with full-content/failing-test breakdowns of 1.5/0.6 versus 1.8/0.9.

claims.quote:

is used as the discriminator, the average number of function
calls decreases to 2.1 (1.5 for get_full_content and 0.6
forget_failing_test), reducing the total time to 3.4 sec-
onds.

claims.text: Reported retrieval overhead is 5.7 seconds with GPT-4o and 3.4 seconds with GPT-4o mini; GPT-4o's full-content and failing-test retrievals account for 3.8 and 1.9 seconds.
claims.quote:

hcs.name: TestPrune-Additional: issue-based regression-test minimization
hcs.quote:
Since the greedy-additional algorithm demonstrates higher
performance than greedy-total, we use the regression tests fromTestPrune-Additional in the
following experiments, and refer toTestPrune-Additional asTestPrunethroughout.

hcs.quote:

tests remain in the loop.

hcs.name: Top-ten-file test sets before greedy minimization

test sets, yielding test suites that range from tens to hundreds of tests, with an overall average of
117across all models and datasets.

hcs.name: TestPrune-supported Otter planner reproduction-test generator
hcs.quote:

drops it from the context to avoid duplication and reduce the false-positive rate (§4.5).

hcs.name: TestPrune-supported heterogeneous-prompt Otter reproduction-test ensemble
hcs.quote:
TestPruneimproves the 𝐹→𝑃@ 1 rate, but for patch ranking the more meaningful metric is

test selection step withTestPrune.

hcs.quote:

claims.text: Average suite size falls from 9,012/11,769 tests on Lite/Verified to 117 after ten-file selection and to 9 with greedy-additional or 11 with greedy-total; final pruning is over 1,000× smaller than full suites and about 13× smaller than ten-file sets.
claims.quote:
TestPrunereduces the size of tests by over a thousand times
relative to the full test suites and by around13times relative to the ten-file test sets.

claims.text: Minimized tests execute in 52 seconds on average versus 23m49s for full suites, about 27× faster.
claims.quote: Running the full test suite takes 23m49s on average across all datasets and models.

claims.text: Greedy-additional has the highest mean relevance precision, 0.63, followed by greedy-total at 0.60; external Agentless and BM25 achieve 0.28 and 0.10.
claims.quote:
Finding 2.TestPruneachieves the highest precision with an average of0 .63and the highest coverage
recall of0.71, further confirming the effectiveness ofTestPrune.

claims.text: Greedy-additional achieves mean buggy-line coverage recall 0.71 and median 0.98, versus greedy-total 0.67, external Agentless 0.66 and BM25 0.13, despite its smaller suite.
claims.quote:
For coverage recall,TestPrune-Additional also outperforms all other methods, achieving an
average of0.71with a median of0 .98across all datasets and models.

claims.text: TestPrune-supported Otter improves F→P@1 over external planner by 6.2–9.0% relatively: Claude/Verified 31.2→34.0%, GPT-4o/Verified 29.0→30.8%, Claude/Lite 27.0→29.3%, GPT-4o/Lite 23.7→25.3%.

evidence.description: Selected examples describe modifying existing tests to overcome incorrect test localization.
evidence.quote:
When we provided theTestPrune-selected tests, the model
chose to modify an existing test instead of writing a new one, which enabled Otter to generate a
proper fail-to-pass test.

claims.quote:
We repeat the process with another model (GPT-4o) and on another benchmark
(SWE-Bench Lite), and observe a similar performance improvement.

claims.text: The six-candidate ensemble attains F→P@6 of 49.8%, 43.8%, 43.7%, 36.3% for Claude/Verified, GPT-4o/Verified, Claude/Lite, GPT-4o/Lite; TestPrune uniquely contributes 20, 15, 8, 8 successes, the largest contribution among candidates.

claims.quote: We find that removing TestPrune has the largest negative impact.

claims.text: Every tested five-candidate ensemble retaining TestPrune beats original five-prompt Otter++: F→P@5 ranges are 47.8–49.2% versus 45.8% for Claude/Verified, 41.8–43.4% versus 40.8% for GPT-4o/Verified, 41.3–42.3% versus 41.0% for Claude/Lite, 34.3–35.7% versus 33.7% for GPT-4o/Lite.
claims.quote:
In this experiment, we remove one variant at a time
and measure 𝐹→𝑃@ 5 .

claims.text: Replacing Agentless regression tests with TestPrune tests while keeping default reproduction tests improves resolution by 2.4–4.1% relatively: 260/500 Claude/Verified, 202/500 GPT-4o/Verified, 127/300 Claude/Lite, 99/300 GPT-4o/Lite.

evidence.description: django__django-11964 illustrates relevant tests rejecting the incorrect patch selected by Agentless.

claims.quote:

tests can improve the issue resolution rate.

claims.text: TestPrune regression tests plus Otter reproduction tests replacing default reproduction tests improve Agentless resolution by 3.3–7.3% relative to original Agentless: 268/500 Claude/Verified, 204/500 GPT-4o/Verified, 126/300 Claude/Lite, 103/300 GPT-4o/Lite.
claims.quote:
If we use Otter-generated tests
instead of Agentless’s default tests withTestPrune, performance improves by 3.3%–7.3%.

claims.text: Combining TestPrune regression tests with both default and Otter reproduction tests gives the best Agentless resolution: 278/500 (55.6%), 219/500 (43.8%), 135/300 (45.0%), 105/300 (35.0%) for Claude/Verified, GPT-4o/Verified, Claude/Lite, GPT-4o/Lite; relative gains over Agentless are 9.4%, 12.9%, 10.7%, 9.4%.

When we consider our two primary variants—planner and
TestPrune—their combined𝐹→𝑃@ 2 is 205.

claims.text: For the two-test Claude/Verified combination, reported golden-patch coverage rises from planner's 0.74 to 0.78; combination coverage uses the higher of the two individual test coverages.
claims.quote:
However, if we apply both tests (discussed in Section 4.5), both the 𝐹→𝑃 rate (156→ 205) and
coverage go up (0.74→ 0.78).

claims.text: For Claude/Verified, TestPrune-supported planner uniquely reproduces 49 issues while original planner uniquely reproduces 35, so the context change both helps and hurts individual issues.
claims.quote:
This means TestPrune helps in 49 instances but also hurts performance in 35
cases.

claims.text: The full TestPrune-assisted Agentless pipeline gains 30/33 previously unresolved issues on Verified and 15/11 on Lite for Claude/GPT-4o, while losing 6/8 on Verified and 2/2 on Lite.

On the SWE-Bench Lite dataset,TestPruneexclusively fixes15instances with Claude
and11with GPT-4o, while on the SWE-Bench Verified dataset, it exclusively fixes30and33
instances, respectively.

claims.text: SWE-agent gains 24 previously unresolved Lite issues but loses 8 formerly resolved ones; Trae Agent gains 43 Verified issues but loses 17.

Integrating minimized regression tests also caused some previously resolved instances to fail—8
for SWE-agent and 17 for Trae Agent.

claims.text: Coverage generation fails for fewer than 1% of samples in the pre-built Docker environment.

Since we use a pre-built Docker container, we did not encounter many
dependency issues, and coverage failed for fewer than 1% of samples.

claims.text: Observed agent-resolution improvements suggest that minimized regression-test benefits generalize across agents with different models, though only two agent/model/benchmark combinations are tested.

The McNemar test also shows statistical significance for both
agent–benchmark pairs at the 99% confidence level (𝑝< 0.01):

claims.quote:
These improvements hold across different agents with different underlying models,
suggesting that the benefit of minimized regression tests generalizes across diverse agents.

claims.text: Test-file detection@10 accuracy is reported as approximately 95%; model, subset and denominator are unspecified.

Additionally,
the test file detection @ 10 accuracy is very high in our case (around 95%).

but did not see noticeable changes in the output.

itize the wrong patch.

claims.text: On the balanced benchmark, full Cascade has the highest precision, 0.88, and specificity, 0.97, among the evaluated direct LLM controls, voting controls, DocChecker and C4RLLaMA.
claims.quote: In this evaluation,Cascadeachieves the highest precision(0.88) andspecificity(0.97).

claims.text: On the 10%/90% benchmark, Cascade retains the highest reported precision, 0.39, and specificity, 0.96, compared with the author controls, DocChecker and C4RLLaMA.
claims.quote: Although recall is limited, the low false positive rate prevents an excess of incorrect reports.

claims.text: Cascade has the highest precision throughout the five evaluated class distributions compared with Voting≥3, DocChecker-single and C4RLLaMA-single.
claims.quote: Cascadeachieves the highest precision across all class distributions.

claims.text: Cascade's F1 changes comparatively little as consistent samples become more prevalent, while the selected voting and external comparator curves decline more substantially.
claims.quote: Cascaderemains comparatively stable and achieves the highest𝐹1-score for the 10%/90% split.

claims.text: Cascade reaches F1 approximately 0.28 at the 10%/90% split, highest among the Figure 3 methods and tied with LLM-A_c after Table 2 rounding.
claims.quote: Only one additional approach (LLM-A𝑐) achieves a comparable𝐹1-score; however, it exhibits lower precision, lower specificity, and a worsePFP-rate.

claims.text: Cascade's precision-first design has low recall, reported as 0.21 on both benchmark splits.
claims.quote: Cascadeexcels in precision and specificity, with expectedly lower recall; which aligns with our design goals.

claims.text: Adding the basic Phase 2 cross-check reduces false alarms: Table 3 changes precision from 0.60 to 0.85, specificity from 0.63 to 0.96, and false positives from 27 to 3.
claims.quote: Overall, Phase 2 accounts for the bulk of the precision improvement by discarding spurious failures, while the additional requirement p2f=0 prunes misclassifications from wrong generated code.

claims.text: Phase 2 sacrifices inconsistency detection: Table 3 reports recall falling from 0.59 to 0.24 and true positives from 41 to 17; the prose describes Phase 1 as finding 41 of 71 inconsistencies.
claims.quote: This configuration catches 41 out of 71 real inconsistencies (recall of 0.59) but at the cost of 27 false positives, which drags precision down to 0.60 and specificity to 0.63.

claims.text: The final p2f=0 check further improves false-alarm avoidance: Table 3 reports precision 0.85→0.88, specificity 0.96→0.97 and false positives 3→2; the prose instead reports precision 0.82→0.88 and one remaining false positive.
claims.quote: This step removes one of the two remaining false positives, slightly improving precision (0.82 to 0.88) with only a marginal decrease in recall (0.26 to 0.21).

claims.text: The final p2f=0 check slightly reduces recall: 0.24→0.21 in Table 3, versus 0.26→0.21 in the prose.
claims.quote: This step removes one of the two remaining false positives, slightly improving precision (0.82 to 0.88) with only a marginal decrease in recall (0.26 to 0.21).

claims.text: Cascade better distinguishes inconsistent methods from their corrected counterparts than DocChecker and C4RLLaMA; Table 2 reports Cascade PFP 0.87 versus their lower PFP values.
claims.quote: In contrast,Cascade’s test-case-based approach should handle this problem more effectively.

claims.text: Cascade's precision varies more across sampled negative subsets than the selected comparator methods, because inclusion of individual false positives has greater relative impact.
claims.quote: Consequently, whether specific false positives are included or excluded in a randomly sampled subset has a relatively large impact on precision.

claims.text: Precision declines monotonically with increasing class imbalance for Cascade, Voting≥3 and the selected external comparators.
claims.quote: Since all evaluated approaches produce false positives, precision declines monotonically across splits.

claims.text: The authors recommend Cascade as the most effective evaluated choice when false alarms are costly and developers need trustworthy reports.
claims.quote: For settings where false alarms are costly and the trustworthiness of each predicted sample is important,Cascade represents the most effective choice among the evaluated techniques.

claims.quote: This stricter threshold explains why both ‘inconsistency’ prompts have higher precision but lower recall than the repsective ‘consistency’ prompts.

claims.text: Full-class context substantially reduces recall: 0.67→0.46 for consistency-direction prompts and 0.54→0.29 for inconsistency-direction prompts.
claims.quote: Adding more context in the advanced prompts (LLM-A𝑖 and LLM-A𝑐) generally shows only a small improvement accross both prompting directions and dataset splits, however, the recal drops strongly indicating that the extra information leads to less reported cases in general.

claims.text: Manual examination of explanations suggests consistency questions elicit broad style or missing-error-handling concerns, whereas inconsistency questions demand a specific erroneous word or line.
claims.quote: When queried for consistency, the model often focuses on general style or potentially missing things like error handling, and thus more eagerly reports an inconsistency.

claims.text: Ensemble voting is claimed to mitigate the volatility of individual LLM queries; no repeated-run stability metric is reported.
claims.quote: Ensembling mitigates the volatility of individual LLMs.

claims.text: Voting≥3 is selected as the best voting configuration by balanced-split precision; Table 2 gives precision 0.61, versus 0.54 for each other threshold.
claims.quote: Voting≥3 as the best of the four variants surpassesCascade’sPFPscore (0.92 vs. 0.86) but still has lower precision and specificity.

claims.text: The prose claims Voting≥3 surpasses Cascade in PFP, 0.92 versus 0.86; Table 2 instead reports 0.69 versus 0.87, contradicting that ranking.
claims.quote: Voting≥3 as the best of the four variants surpassesCascade’sPFPscore (0.92 vs. 0.86) but still has lower precision and specificity.

claims.text: The permissive Voting≥1 ensemble finds more true inconsistencies than any individual direct-query baseline, with recall 0.81.
claims.quote: It is also interesting to see that the different baselines report different samples as inconsistent; otherwise, the voting could not return more true positives (and false positives) than any single baseline does.

claims.text: The permissive Voting≥1 ensemble also produces more false positives than the individual queries; specificity is 0.32 balanced and 0.34 imbalanced.
claims.quote: It is also interesting to see that the different baselines report different samples as inconsistent; otherwise, the voting could not return more true positives (and false positives) than any single baseline does.

claims.text: Several unfine-tuned direct LLM controls exceed C4RLLaMA-single's balanced precision of 0.53: LLM-S_i reaches 0.56, LLM-A_c 0.55 and LLM-A_i 0.59.
claims.quote: However, a precision of .53 is still well below the results achieved byCascadeor even basic, non-fine-tuned LLMs.

claims.text: Manual review attributes the two curated-benchmark Cascade false positives to generated code and tests sharing the same incorrect assumption about underspecified documentation.
claims.quote: We manually evaluated the two single false positives predicted byCascade. and they both came from cases wehre the generated code and tests made the same false asumption over something underspecified in the documentation.

claims.text: False negatives mostly arise from non-compiling tests or failure to generate a discriminating case.
claims.quote:
False negatives, by contrast, mostly arise from tests that do not compile or from missing discrimi-
nating cases.

claims.text: Cascade generates roughly 5–20 tests per method, averaging 8.4.
claims.quote: An analysis of the different classification types reveals that for a given method, roughly 5-20 tests are generated (average of 8.4).

claims.text: The reported average transition counts are p2p=5.9, f2f=2, p2f=0.3 and f2p=0.4.
claims.quote: The average numbers for the results classes are: p2p:5.9; f2f:2; p2f:0.3 and f2p:0.4.

claims.text: At most three f2p tests, usually one or two, target the specific documented behavior that is wrong.
claims.quote: At most, three f2p (usually 1-2) cases exist which are testing exactly the one thing that is wrong in the documentation.

claims.text: The authors identify uncaught declared exceptions and hallucinated functions or fields as the two main reasons for non-compiling generated tests.
claims.quote: DuringCascade’s development, we found two main reasons for non-compiling tests: uncaught declared exceptions and the LLM hallucinating non-existent functions or fields.

claims.text: Precision drops in the real-world evaluation compared with the curated RQ1/RQ2 evaluations; the paper does not report a single aggregate field precision value.
claims.quote: The observed drop in precision compared to the results of RQ1 and RQ2 can likely be attributed to two main factors.

claims.text: Field false positives primarily arise when generated tests and generated implementations both make incorrect assumptions; manual inspection filters these cases.
claims.quote: These primarily resulted from cases in which both the generated tests and the generated code assumptions were incorrect.

viously undocumented inconsistencies in widely used open-source projects, of which 10 were subsequently acknowledged by maintainers and fixed.

metrics.name: manually identified false-positive count by repository

claims.quote: Such cases were identified and filtered out through manual inspection.

claims.text: Some field findings reflect unspecified exception behavior or deviations without observable semantic impact and are judged too minor to report.
claims.quote: Although technically inconsistent, such cases reflect underspecification rather than clear semantic contradictions and were therefore not considered substantial enough to be reported.

claims.text: One reported hash-function case was reclassified as minor after maintainers disputed whether the behavior constituted an inconsistency.
claims.quote: In one instance, maintainers argued that the reported behavior did not constitute a genuine inconsistency.

claims.quote: Cascadediscovered that the method consistently crashes with an arithmetic overflow when min is close to the max value of long, due to a floating point rounding error.

claims.quote: With its proposed code, the tool assisted us in identifying the root cause of the problem, highlighting its potential as a valuable developer assistant.

claims.text: The RustQuant finding led to a documentation improvement that the authors characterize as meaningful.
claims.quote: This is a notable case, because our approach revealed an omitted aspect of correct behavior, leading to a meaningful documentation improvement rather than identifying a blatantly incorrect claim.

claims.text: Cascade can expose both erroneous documentation and erroneous implementations, as illustrated by the field cases.

evidence.type: developer confirmation through fixes of documented examples

claims.quote: Showing thatCascade’s test-generation strategy can detect both faulty documentation and buggy code.

claims.text: In the introductory startsWithAny experiment, direct inconsistency questions usually miss the known case-sensitivity mismatch.
claims.quote: Most of the time, it returned a clearno, completely missing the point in its explanation and focusing only on the general structure and the usage examples in the documentation.

claims.text: Reversing the startsWithAny question to consistency sometimes changes the answer and once elicits the correct case-sensitivity explanation.

metrics.name: qualitative answer and explanation changes under reversed question polarity

claims.quote: When asked the semantically similar, but oppositely framed, question of whether the method and documentation were consistent, it sometimes returned anoand in one cases gave the correct explanation by (correctly) guessing that the underlying startsWith method was case-sensitive.

claims.text: The authors suggest poor or underspecified field documentation limits precision by making genuine contradictions harder to distinguish.
claims.quote: Since our approach targets inconsistencies between documentation and implementation, poorly specified or low-quality documentation inherently limits the achievable precision, as it becomes difficult to determine whether deviations constitute genuine inconsistencies.

claims.text: The authors hypothesize that additional class context distracts direct LLM classifiers toward general issues, explaining fewer reported cases.

claims.quote: Presumably because, the model sometimes gets distracted and drifts into more general issues.
