claims.text: ChainDelta generated working exploits for 16/25 benchmark vulnerabilities (64%).
claims.quote:
ChainDeltasuccessfully generated exploits for 16 out of 25 vulnerabilities, achieving an 64%
success rate.

claims.text: ChainDelta outperformed EtherDiffer, hive, AFL++ and PatchFuzz in benchmark vulnerability success; the comparator acceptance criterion was confirmed bug identification rather than generation of a working exploit.
claims.quote:
It is convincing thatChainDelta
outperforms state-of-the-art tools.

claims.text: ChainDelta's reported benchmark false-positive rate was 15.8%.
claims.quote:
ChainDeltasuccessfully generated exploits for Ethereum patches, achieving
a success rate of 64% with a false positive rate of only 15.8%.

claims.text: Environment-agent removal reduced exploit success from 64% to 16% (four true-positive cases); the full system's success rate was four times higher.
claims.quote:
While the ablated variant was able to trigger
inconsistencies in 14 cases, only four were true positives.

claims.text: Environment-agent removal increased the reported false-positive rate from 15.8% to 71.4%.
claims.quote:
This represents a dramatic drop in the
success rate from 64% to 16% and an increase in the false positive rate from 15.8% to 71.4%.

claims.text: Agent-driven environment setup enables exploration of state-dependent, deeper vulnerabilities that the directed fuzzer alone cannot reach.
claims.quote:
The analysis shows that without the agent, the directed fuzzer is unable to perform the necessary
on-chain setup (e.g., deploying specific contracts) to create the preconditions for the more complex
vulnerabilities.

claims.text: State-aware filtering improves precision over a raw-output differential oracle, whose alarms have an extremely low true-positive rate.
claims.quote:
This demonstrates that a naive differential oracle is insufficient and that state-aware
filtering is essential for precision.

claims.text: Table 3 reports a 1.8-times exploit-success-rate advantage for the full system over the state-aware-filtering ablation.
claims.quote: Success Rate Improvement 4× 1.8×

claims.text: Reusing generated exploits uncovered four previously undisclosed findings across Reth, BSC, Celo Network and AntChain, primarily resource-exhaustion denial-of-service vectors; three were developer-confirmed vulnerabilities.

evidence.quote:
Three of these vulnerabilities were confirmed by the respective
development teams, and we were awarded a total of $2,000 in bug bounties for our responsible
disclosure.

claims.quote:
This process led to the discovery of four previously undisclosed vulnerabilities in four blockchain
implementations, including Reth, BSC, Celo Network, and AntChain.

claims.text: ChainDelta exposed an incomplete B2 patch: crafted concurrent accesses triggered data races and panic errors in the patched client through paths lacking the new lock.

evidence.type: root cause analysis of missing locking on additional code paths
evidence.quote:
Our root cause analysis
revealed that while the developers had correctly protected the primary GetTransactionLookup
function, several other code paths also accessed the same sensitive data structures but did not
acquire the new lock.

claims.quote:
However, when we ranChainDeltaon this benchmark, it consistently triggered numerous panic
errors in the patched version of the client, not the original vulnerable one.

claims.text: ChainDelta's state-aware treatment reduces transient-state false alarms relative to the external comparison tools.
claims.quote:
In contrast, baselines
suffer from high false alarms due to their inability to filter false alarms caused by transient states.

claims.text: Environment agents slow detection of simple bugs B4/B6/B7 versus the no-LLM ablation: ablated TTF is under 10 s; Table 3 full-system TTF is 44 s/5 min 47 s/51 s, while prose instead says one to 20 minutes.
claims.quote:
For the simple vulnerabilities that both systems could find (i.e., B4, B6, B7), the
ablated variant found them much faster, with a Time to First Exploit (TTF) of under 10 seconds.

claims.text: Removing state-aware filtering did not generally improve TTF according to the authors; B1 became slower (43 min 25 s versus 27 min 8 s), although Table 3 also contains faster ablated cases.
claims.quote:
One might expect the
simpler oracle to be faster, but the TTF was comparable to the fullChainDeltaframework, and
even slower in complex cases like B1.

claims.text: The auditing findings demonstrate practical ecosystem-wide security value from automatically generated patch exploits.

evidence.quote:
Three of these vulnerabilities were confirmed by the respective
development teams, and we were awarded a total of $2,000 in bug bounties for our responsible
disclosure.

claims.quote: This experiment underscores the practical value ofChainDeltafor ecosystem-wide security.

claims.text: Responsible disclosure of the auditing findings yielded $2,000 in bug bounties.
claims.quote:
Three of these vulnerabilities were confirmed by the respective
development teams, and we were awarded a total of $2,000 in bug bounties for our responsible
disclosure.

claims.text: Slight target-interface differences required only minimal manual API-payload adaptation during exploit reuse; effort was not quantified.
claims.quote:
In cases of slight
interface divergence, minimal manual effort was required to align the API payload with the target’s
specific specification.

claims.text: Generated exploits are portable across Ethereum-compatible implementations because they use standard RPC/API interfaces.
claims.quote:
As these exploits target standard RPC and API interfaces, they are inherently portable to other
Ethereum compatible implementations.

claims.text: The authors attribute six benchmark cases without generated exploits to limitations in environment interaction and oracle capabilities.
claims.quote:
ChainDeltafailed to generate exploits for six cases, due to limitations in its
environment interaction and oracle capabilities.

claims.text: B8 remained unexploited because the required unsupported legacy-transaction deployment was outside the agent's standard-endpoint interaction capability.
claims.quote:
This action was outside the scope of the current agent implementation, which is
limited to interacting with the client via standard endpoints.

claims.text: B9 remained unexploited because its symptom requires a client-side timeout, while timing-based oracles were deliberately absent.
claims.quote:
We deliberately did not implement timing-based
oracles, as they are notoriously prone to false positives caused by test environment fluctuations,
making them unreliable for our automated framework.

claims.text: Handling pending-block vulnerabilities entails a trade-off between bug detection and avoidance of benign nondeterministic divergences.
claims.quote:
While our state-aware sanitizer is designed to handle this, it
represents a fundamental trade-off between detecting vulnerabilities that are related to pending
blocks (e.g., B2) and avoiding false positives from benign non-determinism.

claims.text: The fourth auditing finding was acknowledged as RPC denial of service but rejected as a security flaw by its developers, who assigned prevention to node operators.

metrics.name: acknowledged findings with disputed security classification

claims.quote:
The fourth vulnerability, a denial-of-service (DoS) vector via an RPC endpoint, was
acknowledged by the developers but not classified as a security flaw, as they argued that DoS
prevention is the responsibility of node operators.

claims.text: The authors judge the additional environment-fuzzing overhead acceptable because it enables complex vulnerabilities requiring deep state manipulation.
claims.quote: However, we argue this overhead is an acceptable and necessary trade-off.

claims.text: hive's manually designed tests identify some vulnerabilities missed by ChainDelta, despite ChainDelta's stronger overall benchmark result.
claims.quote:
Note that hive is capable of identifying
some vulnerabilities omitted byChainDelta, as its detection relies on manually designed test suites.

claims.text: The authors attribute environment-agent latency to additional inter-module communication, including shared-memory writes; no isolated communication-cost measurement is reported.
claims.quote:
This overhead is expected and stems from the extra inter-module communication (e.g., writing
to shared memory).

claims.text: The authors attribute the raw-oracle variant's indirect inefficiency to false alarms flooding the corpus and misguiding exploration; the sanitizer's direct tracing cost is judged worthwhile.
claims.quote:
The constant stream of false alarms spams the corpus in the directed
patch fuzzer and can misguide the system into pursuing useless exploration paths based on benign
inconsistencies.

claims.text: ChaCo generates passing tests at rates of 32.9% for SciPy (274/832), 24.7% for Qiskit (170/689), and 21.8% for Pandas (161/737).
claims.quote:
Table 2 shows the test pass
rate of the tests generated by ChaCo on the 145 benchmark PRs.

claims.text: ChaCo adds 189 covered lines: SciPy 112 across 27/50 PRs, Qiskit 57 across 21/50, and Pandas 20 across 17/45; mean fractions of missing coverage filled are 40.0%, 34.0%, and 33.5%, respectively.
claims.quote:
ChaCo reliably generates passing tests that add high-quality
regression test coverage (189 lines) to complex, real-world
projects, showing the benefit of integrating LLM-based test
generation into CI workflows.

claims.text: The results prose reports 43 PRs reaching full patch coverage, approximately 30%; Table 3 instead lists 15 SciPy, 13 Qiskit, and 14 Pandas PRs, totaling 42.

metrics.name: number/proportion of PRs reaching 100% patch coverage

claims.quote:
ChaCo fully covers 43 PRs
with 100% patch coverage.

claims.text: LLM expenditure averages $0.11 per PR, ranging from $0.08 for Qiskit/Pandas to $0.17 for SciPy.

metrics.name: LLM monetary cost, USD per PR

claims.quote:
Studying the costs of running ChaCo, we find
that augmenting one PR costs between $0.08 and $0.17, depending
on the project, with an overall average of $0.11 per PR.

claims.text: Coverage added by ChaCo represents readable, regression-quality tests.

by ChaCorepresents a readable, regression-quality test, and should
not be compared with coverage obtained from approaches, such as
fuzzing or search-based software testing (SBST).

test context outperforms two variants (i) purely LLM-generated
test context, (ii) no text context, by the same 100% in coverage
increment, highlighting the importance of precise retrieval of test
context thanks to dynamic analysis.

claims.quote:
Iterative feedback signifi-
cantly improves the test pass rate by 312% and coverage by
460%.

claims.quote:

cantly improves the test pass rate by 312% and coverage by

chance of increasing coverage by 100%, compared to using
(i) no test context and (ii) LLM-generated test context.

claims.text: Some Python responses pursued a promising diagnosis without reaching an actionable fix.
claims.quote: In some cases, it was on the right track but did not converge on an actionable fix.

claims.text: Some suggested Python changes would introduce additional bugs.

metrics.name: Qualitative inspection of harmful suggested changes; frequency not_reported

claims.quote: In others, it suggested changes that would introduce other bugs.

claims.text: Python reasoning occasionally confused proportions with percentages.
claims.quote: It also occasionally made mistakes, such as conflating proportions and percentages or failing to handle unusual corner cases.

claims.text: Python responses occasionally failed to handle unusual corner cases.

metrics.name: Qualitative corner-case failure observations; frequency not_reported

claims.quote: It also occasionally made mistakes, such as conflating proportions and percentages or failing to handle unusual corner cases.

claims.text: For BC, GZIP, NCOM and POLY, common buffer-overflow suggestions prevented overflow through truncation but silently truncated inputs and required additional measures for robust fixes.

metrics.name: Qualitative inspection of bounded-copy fix behavior

claims.quote: While correct, this change truncates the input silently.

claims.text: For BC’s generated code, clangd could not provide the definitions needed by ChatDBG.

metrics.name: Qualitative observation of failed definition retrieval

claims.quote: The clangd language server does not handle this case in a way that would let ChatDBG answer the LLM’s definition requests properly.

claims.text: For PEG, ChatDBG correctly identified the null pointer.
claims.quote: In the case of PEG, ChatDBG correctly identifies which pointer is null but typically suggests ignoring it instead of failing immediately.

claims.text: For PEG, ChatDBG typically proposed ignoring the null pointer instead of failing immediately.

metrics.name: Qualitative assessment of proposed error handling

claims.quote: In the case of PEG, ChatDBG correctly identifies which pointer is null but typically suggests ignoring it instead of failing immediately.

claims.text: For YAML2, ChatDBG favored replacing the assertion with an internal check rather than checking the callee’s preconditions at the client.

metrics.name: Qualitative comparison of suggested fix with Table 5 root-cause criterion

claims.quote: This is similar to YAML2, where ChatDBG recommends replacing the assertion with a check inside a function rather than recommending that the client check that the function’s preconditions are met prior to the call.

claims.text: For YAML1, ChatDBG often proposed correct recursion-depth guards and had a relatively high root-cause fix rate.

metrics.name: Manually assessed root-cause fix success rate; numeric value not_reported in text

claims.quote: It often correctly suggests fixes to limit recursion depth (YAML1) and to validate input parameters (TIFF).

claims.text: For TIFF, ChatDBG often proposed correct input-parameter validation and had a relatively high root-cause fix rate.

metrics.name: Manually assessed root-cause fix success rate; numeric value not_reported in text

claims.quote: It often correctly suggests fixes to limit recursion depth (YAML1) and to validate input parameters (TIFF).

claims.text: Repeated experiments produced stable results with small aggregate variation.

metrics.name: Aggregate variation across repeated trials; numeric dispersion not_reported

claims.quote: To mitigate this threat, our evaluation runs ChatDBG on each test program at least ten times, which produced stable and repeatable results with only small variation in aggregate.

claims.text: The authors infer that response-length constraints may prevent sufficient reasoning in a single exchange.

metrics.name: Success-rate improvement after a fixed continuation query

claims.quote: This phenom indicates that constraints on the underlying LLM’s response lengths may prevent it from conducting the amount of reasoning necessary to develop a fix in a single step.

claims.text: Greater distance between root cause and observable failure generally made diagnosis harder.

metrics.name: Qualitative association between causal distance and diagnosis difficulty; quantified distance analysis not_reported

claims.quote: In general, the further the distance between the root cause of a bug and observable effect, the more challenging it was for ChatDBG (and people [47, p. 243]) to find it.

claims.text: The authors attribute occasional feature-related regressions to longer and more complex prompts.

metrics.name: Per-program success-rate regressions after enabling features

claims.quote: We attribute this result to the fact that longer and more complex prompts can occasionally degrade the effectiveness of LLMs [22].

claims.text: The authors attribute most Python completion time to OpenAI service performance.

metrics.name: Completion time; service-versus-harness timing breakdown not_reported

claims.quote: Time was highly variable and dominated by the performance of OpenAI’s service.

claims.quote: The most common sub-category of compilation errors isAccess Error, which occurs when LLMs frequently generate test code that attempts to invalidly access private variables or methods.

claims.text: Test setup errors are the most frequent execution-error subcategory, linked to mock configuration and input construction.
claims.quote: The most common sub-category of execution errors is Test Setup Error, primarily due to LLMs facing challenges in accurately inferring the mock object configurations, as well as generating valid test data inputs.

claims.text: CITYWALK detects many artificial faults: 5088/6272 tinyxml2 mutants (81.12%) and 754/844 json.cpp mutants (89.34%).

evidence.detail: Separate real-bug analysis associates two generated tinyxml2 tests with issues #323/#825; evidence for the second reproduction is limited.

claims.quote: These results indicate that CITYW ALKis highly effective in generating test cases that detect a substantial proportion of artificial bugs introduced into the code, validating its capability to uncover potential bugs.

claims.text: CITYWALK's mutation scores exceed literature values for external EvoSuite (34.1%) and universalmutator (35%), measured on different benchmarks.

evidence.detail: Comparator scores come from other studies and benchmarks; no common-benchmark within-paper evaluation is reported.

claims.quote: In comparison, the mutation scores achieved by CITYW ALKare notably higher, further emphasizing the effectiveness of CITYW ALK-generated test cases.

claims.text: Two generated tinyxml2 tests are associated with human-reported issues #323 and #825, suggesting real-bug detection potential.

evidence.detail: Existing human issue reports corroborate issue identities; no developer confirmation of the generated tests is reported, and Figure 11(b) shows a warning rather than a failing assertion.

claims.quote: In summary, the test cases generated by CITYW ALKdemonstrate the potential to detect real bugs in open-source projects.

claims.text: Dependency context and fixed mocking knowledge guide basic GPT-4o to an executable mock-based decode test.
claims.quote: Furthermore, Figure 4(c) presents a working example of how cross-file data dependencies can guide LLMs in generating executable test code for Failed Test Case ➌ shown in Figure 1.

claims.text: Cross-file dependency guidance prevents the non-existent setNumber call and produces a compiling Json::setNull test.
claims.quote: By providing the key Depd (i.e., the initialization constructor of Json) from the json.h file, LLMs can prevent compilation errors that would otherwise arise due to invoking the non-existent function setNumber.

claims.text: Retrieved invocation and initialization examples enable corrected assertions in the illustrated yaml-cpp test.
claims.quote: These examples significantly aid LLMs in understanding the usage patterns of the focal method, contributing to the generation of functionally correct assertions and enhancing code coverage.

claims.text: Runtime-output-guided assertion revision can produce an executable false positive, illustrated by copying observed 'str' into the expected result.
claims.quote: As illustrated in Figure 12, when provided with the error message, GPT-4o directly uses the expected value“str” as the input for assertions, resulting in a passing test case that is, in reality, a false positive.

claims.text: External I/O and synchronization features are proposed explanations for CITYWALK's poor leveldb results.

evidence.detail: Authors attribute multiple-definition/undefined-symbol failures to I/O-related redefinition and undefined calls.

claims.quote: Additionally,leveldb involves advanced features like synchronization locks, which significantly increase the complexity and challenge the test generation process.

claims.text: The absence of post-hoc assertion fixing is proposed as a cause of remaining assertion failures.
claims.quote: The most frequently occurring assertion errors can be traced back to the lack of supplementary post-processing techniques (e.g., post-hoc fix), which could help prompt LLMs to rectify incorrect assertions in the generated test cases.

claims.text: The paper attributes quality gains primarily to harness guidance rather than memorization; post-cutoff json.cpp's mutation score exceeds tinyxml2's by 8.22 points.

evidence.detail: Four projects postdate the stated GPT-4o cutoff; training membership is unverified, and cross-project mutation differences do not isolate memorization.

claims.quote: This provides additional evidence that CITYW ALK’s ability to generate high-quality test cases is primarily driven by the designed components as guidance, rather than relying on GPT-4o’s memorization of training data.

claims.text: The 1,000 generated fix attempts comprise 520 single-line, 444 multi-line and 36 multi-file changes.
claims.quote:
Out of1,000fixes,
520 affect only a single line, 444 are multi-line fixes, and 36 are multi-file fixes.

claims.text: False-positive suppressions are 95.1% single-line and 4.9% multi-line, with no multi-file changes; true-positive fixes are 33.2% single-line, 61.6% multi-line and 5.2% multi-file.
claims.quote:
For warnings classified
as FPs, almost all fixes are single-line (95.1%).

claims.text: Plausibility decreases with fix complexity: 99.4% for single-line, 95.5% for multi-line and 75.0% for multi-file fixes.
claims.quote:
As
shown in the last column of the table, less complex fixes are more likely to be plausible: 99.4% of
all single-line fixes are plausible, compared to 95.5% for multi-line fixes and an even lower 75.0%
for multi-file fixes.

claims.text: CodeCureAgent produces plausible fixes across all four rule categories: 849/877 code smells (96.8%), 90/92 bugs (97.8%), 17/19 security hotspots (89.5%) and 12/12 vulnerabilities (100%).
claims.quote:
When breaking down the results by rule-category (see Section 4.1.1),
we find that CodeCureAgent performs robustly across all categories, generating plausible fixes
for 849 code smells (96.8%), 90 bugs (97.8%), 17 security hotspots (89.5%), and all 12 vulnerabilities
(100.0%).

claims.text: Warnings left unfixed take 14.0 minutes on average, compared with 4.4 minutes over all warnings.

metrics.name: Mean processing time by repair outcome

claims.quote: For unfixed warnings, the mean is higher at 14.0 minutes.

claims.text: Unfixed warnings consume the full 40-cycle repair cap, whereas fixed warnings use eight repair cycles on average.
claims.quote:
This is expected, as warnings
that the agent fails to fix consume the full repair budget of 40 cycles, compared to an average of
only 8 repair cycles for fixed warnings.

claims.text: Build, test and static-analysis execution account for 41.1% of runtime, and LLM querying accounts for another 39.2%.
claims.quote:
On average, 41.1% of the time is attributed to building
and testing the target project, and to running the static analysis.

claims.text: Mean LLM token consumption is 139K tokens per warning.

metrics.name: Mean total LLM tokens per warning

claims.quote:
The LLM usage of CodeCureAgent incurs a mean token consumption
of 139K tokens per warning.

claims.text: Output tokens account for only 3.0% of total token consumption.
claims.quote:
Only 3.0% of these tokens are output tokens (which are usually the
more expensive tokens).

claims.text: Cached input tokens account for 78.8% of input tokens because prompts largely persist across cycles.
claims.quote:
Of the input tokens, 78.8% are cached input tokens, since large parts of the
prompts created by CodeCureAgent are unchanged from previous cycles.

claims.text: Unfixed warnings incur a mean LLM cost of 21 cents, compared with 2.9 cents over all warnings.

metrics.name: Mean LLM cost by repair outcome

claims.quote:
Unfixed warnings have a mean cost of 21
cents.

claims.text: CodeCureAgent specifies a patch using 73 lines on average, including 32 changed-code lines, compared with CORE's 255 output code lines per patch; the paper links this compact output to lower LLM cost.

metrics.name: Mean lines used to specify a patch

claims.quote:
In contrast, our approach requires only 73 lines on
average for specifying edits, of which only 32 lines indicate changed code lines.

claims.text: Every provided tool is invoked during the evaluation.
claims.quote: CodeCureAgent invokes all the provided tools at varying rates.

claims.text: Read lines is the most frequently used information-gathering tool.
claims.quote:
Among the information-
gathering tools,Read linesis used most frequently.

claims.text: Answer classification questions is called three times and Give final verdict once on average.
claims.quote:
TheAnswer classification questionstool is called three times and theGive final verdicttool once
on average.

claims.text: Write fix is called 1.52 times per fixed warning and 14.25 times per unfixed warning.

metrics.name: Mean patch-proposal tool calls by repair outcome

claims.quote: TheWrite fixtool is called 1.52 times for fixed warnings and 14.25 times for unfixed warnings.

claims.text: The conclusion claims that automated warning handling significantly reduces developer manual effort, although developer workflow impact and acceptance were not assessed.

evidence.details: A single author inspected 291 distinct-rule cases; correctness was assessed only for correctly classified warnings, with 251 correct fixes and eight incorrect plausible fixes.
evidence.quote:
Specifically, CodeCureAgent proposes plausible fixes for 259
warnings (89.0%), of which 251 are confirmed as correct, yielding an overall accuracy of 86.3%.

claims.quote:
By addressing multi-line and multi-file fixes, and
by filtering FPs, CodeCureAgent significantly reduces the manual effort needed to maintain clean
codebases for a cost of only a few cents and a couple of minutes per warning.

claims.text: Classification is the principal reported source of manual-sample errors: 24/291 classifications are wrong (8.2%), including 19 warnings incorrectly labeled false positive.
claims.quote:
In the 291 inspected warnings, we find 24 misclassified warn-
ings, which represent 8.2% of all inspected warnings; 19 wrongly classified as FP.

claims.text: Manual diagnosis attributes the 24 classification errors to hallucination in 11 cases, insufficient context in 11 (nine documentation issues and two shallow-context cases), and disagreement with developer conventions in two.
claims.quote:
(1) LLM hallucination (11/24): The LLM ignores given context and outputs a decision that is
contradictory to indications available in the context.

claims.text: Of 32 repair failures, 26 involve inability to correct code-breaking modifications, four involve addressing multiple warnings and two involve unsupported file creation, renaming or deletion.
claims.quote: The repair sub-agent fails to (plausibly) fix 32 warnings.

claims.text: Eight inspected plausible fixes are semantically incorrect, showing that passing the approval checks does not establish correctness.
claims.quote:
Fur-
thermore, 8 inspected plausible fixes are incorrect.

claims.text: In the weblogic-monitoring-exporter example, CodeCureAgent fixes S3457 and also repairs a faulty platform-specific line-separator test.

metrics.name: Successful warning repair and test correction in the reported case

claims.quote:
In this
way, CodeCureAgent not only resolves the warning but also corrects the faulty test.

claims.text: For the OpenTripPlanner S5042 example, successive build, static-analysis and test feedback enable the agent to improve its patch until approval.

metrics.name: Approval of the reported security-warning fix

claims.quote:
This example illustrates how CodeCureAgent can address challenging warnings by using
the change approver checks and feedback to iteratively improve fixes.

claims.text: For Amidst S2234, on-demand documentation, local code and reference retrieval enable the agent to identify intentional argument inversion and suppress the false positive.

metrics.name: Correct classification/suppression in the reported case

claims.quote:
This example demonstrates how the agent can collect
various types of context on demand to make informed decisions and avoid incorrect fixes for FPs.

claims.text: In the MsgViewer S2885 example, the agent recognizes a duplicated closing bracket from feedback but cannot repair it within its cycle budget.

metrics.name: Failure to produce an accepted patch within the cycle cap

claims.quote:
From the failure feedback provided by the change approver, Code-
CureAgent identifies the issue but still fails to correct it within the allotted cycle budget.

ecs.quote:

claims.text: ContrastRepair correctly repairs 103/255 Defects4j 1.2 and 40/82 Defects4j 2.0 bugs, exceeding CHATREPAIR (90/34), BaseChatGPT (68/28), and the evaluated non-LLM baselines; the combined 143/337 exceeds the best comparator's 124.
claims.quote:
Specifically, ContrastRepair can repair 103 out of 255 bugs
and 40 out of 82 bugs in Defects4j 1.2 and Defects4j 2.0, respec-
tively.

claims.text: For Defects4j 1.2 SL/SH/SF, ContrastRepair yields 56/69/75 correct fixes versus CHATREPAIR's 45/53/52 and BaseChatGPT's 38/50/37.
claims.quote:
In the three repair scenarios of Defects4j 1.2, ContrastRepair
significantly outperforms CHATREPAIR by repairing 11, 16, and 23
more bugs respectively.

claims.text: Across localization scenarios ContrastRepair repairs all 40 QuixBugs programs in each language, versus CHATREPAIR's 38 Python and 37 Java programs.
claims.quote:
Notably, ContrastRepair successfully rectified all
bugs within the QuixBugs-Java and QuixBugs-Python datasets,
demonstrating its marked superiority over other methods.

claims.text: ContrastRepair exceeds CHATREPAIR and BaseChatGPT in every QuixBugs localization setting: Python SL/SH/SF correct fixes 36/36/37 versus 33/35/34 and 31/32/30; Java 34/35/37 versus 32/33/34 and 29/30/33.
claims.quote:
Specifically, ContrastRepair outperforms CHATREPAIR
among three scenarios in both QuixBugs-Python and QuixBugs-
Java.

claims.text: ContrastRepair needs fewer API queries on Defects4j 1.2 SL/SH/SF: 44.38/55.24/77.36 versus CHATREPAIR's 62.36/79.14/82.27 (28.83%/30.20%/5.97% reductions) and BaseChatGPT's 66.88/79.89/96.16.
claims.quote:
Furthermore,ContrastRepair requires fewer
API queries than CHATREPAIR.

claims.text: ContrastRepair fixes 13 Defects4j 1.2 bugs that none of the evaluated prior tools fixes.
claims.quote:
We can see thatContrastRepair fixes
13 unique bugs not addressed by any other prior tools.

claims.text: On the purportedly unseen HumanEval-Java benchmark, ContrastRepair achieves 137 correct fixes versus CHATREPAIR's 130 and BaseChatGPT's 126 (reported relative improvements 5.38% and 8.73%).
claims.quote:
As illustrated in Table 5, ContrastRepair achieves the best results
among the three tools, successfully fixing 137 out of 164 total bugs.

claims.text: On HumanEval-Java, ContrastRepair averages 17.44 API queries versus CHATREPAIR's 24.68 and BaseChatGPT's 28.90, reductions of 29.34% and 39.66%.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, ContrastRepair significantly outperforms the other
two methods in terms of efficiency, as indicated by the average
number of ChatGPT queries on each bug ( #𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦 ).

claims.text: On the 106-bug pair-count study, correct fixes increase from basic prompting's 31 to 32/33 with one/two failed tests, and to 35/37 with one/two contrastive pairs.
claims.quote:
Crucially, using test case pairs
consistently outperformed merely submitting the same quantity of
failed test cases.

claims.text: In the pair-count study, two pairs yield the most suite-passing patches (60), followed by one pair (58), two failures (55), one failure (53), and BaseChatGPT (48).
claims.quote:
Offering just a single test case pair led to the second-
highest fix effectiveness (35/58).

claims.text: Two pairs minimize mean API queries (63.09), versus one pair 66.14, two failures 68.57, one failure 69.23, BaseChatGPT 76.16, and external CHATREPAIR 69.09.
claims.quote:
Notably, ContrastRepair,
when fed with two test case pairs, demanded the fewest #𝑄𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦
(63.09).

claims.text: With the same 120-attempt budget, the balanced m=40,n=3 configuration gives 21 correct fixes versus restart-only m=120,n=1's 18 and deeper m=12,n=10's 15.
claims.quote:
An analysis of the outcomes in Table 7 reveals that the40× 3 con-
figuration excels in terms of the number of correct/plausible fixes
(21/33).

claims.text: The balanced lifecycle gives 33 plausible fixes versus 31 for restart-only and 23 for m=12,n=10.
claims.quote:
An analysis of the outcomes in Table 7 reveals that the40× 3 con-
figuration excels in terms of the number of correct/plausible fixes
(21/33).

claims.text: The balanced lifecycle also uses the fewest API queries (70.53), versus restart-only 74.78 and m=12,n=10 88.48.
claims.quote:
Each configuration adheres to the same overall budget limit,
totaling 120 tries.

claims.text: With three runs on 106 bugs, contrastive-pair feedback improves average correct fixes from 30.67 without pairs to 37.00.
claims.quote:
ContrastRe-
pair w/o Pair only has 48.00 plausible fixes and 30.67 correct fixes
on average.

claims.text: Contrastive-pair feedback improves average plausible fixes from 48.00 without pairs to 60.33.

claims.quote:

claims.quote:
For the 106 bugs, ContrastRepair generates

claims.text: Similarity-guided selection reduces mean API queries from random selection's 72.62 to 63.09 (the ablation's reported increase is 15.11%).
claims.quote:
Fur-
thermore, the incorporation of similarity-based pair selection and
contextual information contributes to a reduction in the number of

claims.quote:

claims.quote:
Fur-
thermore, the incorporation of similarity-based pair selection and
contextual information contributes to a reduction in the number of
queries made to ChatGPT API.

claims.text: On CM, CoverUp has higher overall coverage than CodaMosa (codex) and CodaMosa (gpt4o): line 63.8% versus 53.5%/50.6%, branch 49.2% versus 33.6%/28.6%, and line+branch 60.3% versus 48.7%/45.2%.
claims.quote: Across the entire benchmark suite, CoverUp achieves 64% (vs. 54% and 51%) line coverage, 49% (vs. 34% and 29%) branch coverage, and 60% (vs. 49% and 45%) line+branch coverage.

claims.text: On CM, CoverUp has higher median per-module coverage than both CodaMosa versions: line 82.4% versus 62.9%/54.2%, branch 66.7% versus 35.6%/19.0%, and line+branch 79.6% versus 55.1%/47.2%; the authors report statistically significant per-module comparisons.

claims.quote: On a per-module basis, CoverUp achieves 82% (vs. 63% and 54%) line coverage, 67% (vs. 36% and 19%) branch coverage, and 80% (vs. 55% and 47%) line+branch coverage.

claims.text: Keeping the page reaching scorer increases reproduced crashes from CT_wp's 42 to CrashTranslator's 46.
claims.quote:
Overall,
CT𝑤𝑝 can only successfully reproduce 42 crash reports, 4 fewer
than CrashTranslator.

claims.text: Keeping the page reaching scorer reduces common-success mean reproduction time from 127.1 to 69.7 seconds; CT_wp is reported 82% slower.

metrics.name: Mean reproduction time on common successful reports

claims.quote:
Meanwhile, the average reproducing time of
CT𝑤𝑝 is 127.1 seconds, which is 82% slower than CrashTranslator
(69.7s vs. 127.1s) considering the reports both can reproduce.

claims.text: Keeping the widget hitting scorer increases reproduced crashes from CT_ww's 44 to CrashTranslator's 46.
claims.quote:
For
CT𝑤𝑤 , it can successfully reproduce 44 crashes (2 fewer than Crash-
Translator), and the average reproducing time is 113.2s (63% slower
than CrashTranslator).

claims.text: Without the widget hitting scorer, successful reproduction averages 113.2 seconds, reported as 63% slower than CrashTranslator.
claims.quote:
For
CT𝑤𝑤 , it can successfully reproduce 44 crashes (2 fewer than Crash-
Translator), and the average reproducing time is 113.2s (63% slower
than CrashTranslator).

claims.text: Generated steps let at least two participants reproduce all 46 reports (100%), versus 29/46 (63%) with stack traces alone; six stack-trace-only reports are reproduced by no participant.

metrics.name: Reports reproduced by at least two of three participants

claims.quote:
Following the re-
producing steps generated by CrashTranslator, 100% of reports are
successfully reproduced by at least two participants.

claims.text: Manual reproduction from generated steps averages 66.7 seconds overall; on reports with success in both conditions, it averages 57.3 versus 180.5 seconds from stack traces, reported as 215% faster.
claims.quote:
Besides, the average reproducing time with CrashTrans-
lator is 66.7 seconds, which is 215% faster than reproducing from
stack traces (57.3s vs. 180.5s) considering the reports that both have
at least one participant can reproduce.

claims.text: Automatic reproduction is faster than mean manual stack-trace reproduction on 42/46 reports (91.3%).

metrics.name: Proportion of reports with shorter automatic reproduction time

claims.quote:
This further implies the usefulness of CrashTranslator which
provides an automatic solution and can be faster than humans.

claims.text: Generated reproduction steps make stack-trace-only reports easier for developers to reproduce within the studied participant group.

evidence.detail: Post-task interviews report agreement that CrashTranslator can automate tedious app exploration and finding crash paths/widgets.
evidence.quote:
By comparison, they agree that CrashTranslator can automatically
conduct the tedious process of exploring the app and finding paths
to crash-occurring pages and crash-triggering widgets.

claims.quote:
This indicates the usefulness
of our proposed CrashTranslator, whose generated reproducing
steps can supplement the stack-trace-only crash reports and make
the crashes easily to be reproduced.

claims.text: Interview participants agree that CrashTranslator can automate tedious exploration and finding paths and widgets that trigger crashes.
claims.quote:
By comparison, they agree that CrashTranslator can automatically
conduct the tedious process of exploring the app and finding paths
to crash-occurring pages and crash-triggering widgets.

claims.text: Removing either scorer has little effect on short-sequence cases; R-10 FastAdapter-394 takes 8 seconds under all three configurations.
claims.quote:
For the reports which involve shorter exploration sequences for
reaching the crash-occurring page, e.g., R-10 FastAdapter-394, we
find that excluding the page reaching scorer or widget hitting scorer
would not largely influence the reproduction.

claims.text: Page reaching guidance helps crowded-entry cases: R-5 AnyMemo-18 is reproduced by CrashTranslator but not CT_wp.
claims.quote:
In this case, the page reaching scorer which is
accomplished by LLM contributes significantly to the crash repro-
duction by providing step-by-step guidance to the crash-occurring
page.

claims.text: Page reaching guidance speeds longer exploration sequences; A-5 andOTP-500 takes 120 seconds with CrashTranslator versus 425 seconds without that scorer.
claims.quote:
In this case, the page reaching scorer which is
accomplished by LLM contributes significantly to the crash repro-
duction by providing step-by-step guidance to the crash-occurring
page.

claims.text: Widget hitting guidance improves efficiency on pages with many candidate widgets; R-14 SMSsync-464 takes 118 seconds with CrashTranslator versus 254 seconds without that scorer.
claims.quote:
The inferior performance of CT𝑤𝑝 /CT𝑤𝑤
indicates that the two scorers can significantly improve the effec-
tiveness and efficiency of crash reproducing.

claims.text: Scorer guidance sometimes hurts reproduction efficiency; R-11 LibreNews-22 takes 93 seconds with CrashTranslator versus 31 seconds without page reaching.
claims.quote:
Still, we need to admit that on some reports like R-11 LibreNews-
22, removing the scorer would improve the crash reproduction
efficiency.

claims.text: Widget hitting also has report-specific time costs: CrashTranslator versus CT_ww takes 71 versus 51 seconds on R-12 LibreNews-23 and 23 versus 21 seconds on R-28 FlashCards-13.
claims.quote:
If the above approach successfully reproduces the crash,
we record the reproduction time (in seconds) in the table, and if it fails, we record ×.

claims.text: The authors tentatively attribute lower success on AndroR2 and their GitHub dataset to longer required exploration sequences; this explanation is not separately tested.
claims.quote:
While on the An-
droR2 dataset and the CrashTranslator’s dataset, CrashTranslator
can achieve a success rate of 40.9%-45%.

claims.text: Environment failures prevent reproduction in three ReCDroid apps and one AndroR2 app.
claims.quote:
1) Some
apps (3 from the ReCDroid’s dataset, 1 from the AndroR2 dataset)
could not run in our environment, e.g., the server is down, incom-
patibility with our emulator.

claims.text: Unsupported GUI actions hinder reproduction, illustrated by C-4 Alarmio-47 requiring scrolling.

metrics.name: Report-level reproduction failure under unsupported actions

claims.quote:
2) CrashTranslator does not cover all
the interactive GUI actions.

claims.text: A reported limitation is failure when stack traces lack the crash-occurring page or crash-involved APIs.
claims.quote:
First, CrashTranslator may fail to reproduce crashes that do
not contain crash-occurring pages or crash-involved APIs in stack
traces.

claims.text: A reported limitation is inability to autonomously reproduce crashes requiring valid input such as login credentials.
claims.quote:
Second, CrashTranslator cannot reproduce crashes requiring
valid input contents, e.g., performing a crash-triggering log-in re-
quires a valid username and password.

claims.text: A reported limitation is inability to capture special triggering preconditions, such as switching to a dark theme before reaching the crash page.
claims.quote:
Third, CrashTranslator cannot capture special preconditions that
trigger crashes.

claims.text: Reproducing one crash with CrashTranslator requires on average about 42.6 prompts (4,939.7 tokens) at an estimated cost of about US$0.01.

three models.

claims.text: On Python, ungated Debug2Fix improves GPT-5 from 31.2% to 36.2%, Haiku from 34.3% to 38.5%, and Sonnet from 39.6% to 40.4% pass rate (reported relative gains 16.0%, 12.2%, 2.0%).
claims.quote:
GPT-5 shows the highest call rate of>60%
and has the corresponding largest improvement (16%).

claims.text: Direct tools leave Java GPT-5 nearly flat (60.8% versus 60.2%), decrease Haiku (70.4% versus 71.0%), and substantially decrease Sonnet (64.5% versus 75.7%; table −14.8%, prose ∼18%).
claims.quote:
We see negligible change for GPT-5
and Claude Haiku, but for Claude Sonnet we see a drop of
∼18% over baseline.

claims.text: The subagent wrapper improves Java pass rates over direct tools for all models (64.0% versus 60.8%, 76.1% versus 70.4%, 78.0% versus 64.5%); the authors call the architecture necessary.

evidence.description: Only 17 direct-tool instances used the debugger; this supports the adoption explanation rather than independently validating fixes.
evidence.quote:
Manual inspection of the trajectories re-
vealed that the main agent rarely leverages the debug tools,
calling at least one debug tool in only 17 (9%) of the instances.

claims.quote:
Through an ablation study we find that ex-
posing debug tools directly to the main agent is ineffective
and can even degrade performance i.e. subagent architecture
is necessary.

claims.text: The editing gate improves Java pass rates over ungated Debug2Fix: GPT-5 73.1% versus 64.0%, Haiku 82.3% versus 76.1%, Sonnet 85.5% versus 78.0%.
claims.quote:
For GitBug-Java, by enforcing debugging before editing, our
approach was able to raise the call rates to∼99% for all models
and produce performance gains across the models.

claims.text: The editing gate raises Java subagent call rates from 64.5%, 69.4%, 70.4% to 99.5%, 98.9%, 98.9% for GPT-5, Haiku and Sonnet respectively.
claims.quote:
For GitBug-Java, by enforcing debugging before editing, our
approach was able to raise the call rates to∼99% for all models
and produce performance gains across the models.

claims.text: Tool-limited GPT-5 nearly matches baseline Sonnet on Java (73.1% versus 75.7%), narrowing the model gap.
claims.page: 8, §6.2, Better tooling closes the gap between models; Table 1
claims.quote:
As
one can see for GitBug-Java,GPT-5 with Debug2Fix scores
(73.1%) nearly the same as baseline Sonnet (75.7%), de-
spite the 15% gap in their respective baselines.

claims.text: Tool-limited Haiku exceeds baseline Sonnet on Java by 6.6 percentage points (82.3% versus 75.7%).
claims.page: 8, §6.2, Better tooling closes the gap between models; Table 1
claims.quote:
Similarly,De-
bug2Fix helps Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform baseline
Sonnet 4.5 by 6.6%.

claims.text: Question categories and debugging trajectories resemble expert developers' workflows; no measured expert-workflow comparison is provided.
claims.quote:
These categories mirror the core use cases
developers use debuggers for in the real life and also what the
main agent was asked to use the Debug Subagent for (Figure 4).

claims.text: The approach generalizes from Java/JDB to Python/PDB within the two evaluated benchmarks despite differing debugger interfaces.
claims.quote:
Further, this example also shows our approach
generalizing to Python despite there being differences between
the interfaces of JDB and PDB and how they’re used.

claims.text: Across Java debugger configurations, main-agent steps and tokens increase for GPT-5 and Haiku but decrease for Sonnet; gated Sonnet uses 33.7 versus 35.7 main steps and 978k versus 1.22M main tokens.
claims.quote:
Examining the steps taken by each model, we can
see that they also go up in most cases except for Claude Sonnet.

claims.text: The Java subagent adds work: ungated GPT-5/Haiku/Sonnet average 33.7/52.1/39.8 subagent steps and 479k/760k/478k tokens; gated runs average 25.9/44.5/33.1 steps and 350k/619k/396k tokens.
claims.quote:
We also show the breakdown of steps and tokens used by
the main agent and the Debug Subagent within each of our configurations.

claims.text: The authors describe GPT-5 and Haiku total-token increases from adding the subagent as modest; Table 1 reports higher main tokens plus additional subagent tokens for both.

metrics.name: mean main-agent and subagent input+output tokens

claims.quote:
For GPT-5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, the total tokens increases
modestly.

claims.text: On Python, Debug2Fix increases main steps (21.9/57.5/54.4 versus 20.0/55.4/53.0) and main tokens (630k/2.08M/1.97M versus 550k/1.97M/1.96M), adding subagent steps (24.6/28.6/31.4) and tokens (350k/371k/281k).

metrics.name: mean main-agent and subagent input+output tokens

claims.quote:
Comparing the performances, token usages and steps used by Debug2Fix and Baseline agent on the Python
subset of SWE-Bench Live dataset.

claims.text: Ungated call rates cluster at 64.5–70.4% on Java but diverge on Python: GPT-5 61.4%, Haiku 33.2%, Sonnet 8.1%.
claims.page: 7, §6.2, New tool’s call-rate can vary by language; 8, Tables 1–2
claims.quote:
However, for Python
the call rates diverge dramatically between the models.

claims.text: On Python, higher adoption accompanies larger pass-rate gains: GPT-5 61.4% calls/16.0% relative gain, Haiku 33.2%/12.2%, Sonnet 8.1%/2.0%; causation is not established.
claims.quote:
However, this reluctance to adopt the Debug Subagent also
reflects the smaller improvements seen in their performance
(Table 2).

claims.text: The prose calls GPT-5 most suggestible and Sonnet most unwilling to adopt the subagent on Java, although Table 1 reports 64.5% calls for GPT-5 and 70.4% for Sonnet.
claims.page: 7, §6.2, The subagent alone is often insufficient; 8, Table 1
claims.quote:
Based on our results on GitBug-Java
(Table 1), GPT-5 seems to be the most suggestible when it
comes to adding a new tool for the agent to call, while Claude
Sonnet 4.5 seems the most unwilling.

claims.text: Inspection of a direct-tools run found debugger calls in only 17 instances (9%); the model is not explicitly identified.

metrics.name: instances with a debugger call (count and %)

claims.quote:
Manual inspection of the trajectories re-
vealed that the main agent rarely leverages the debug tools,
calling at least one debug tool in only 17 (9%) of the instances.

claims.text: Direct-tool debugging subsequences contain at most four calls; in the gated GPT-5 trace analysis, most subagent trajectories finish within 10–15 steps, while many reach the 25-step limit.
claims.quote:
Most trajectories finish within 10-15 steps, though many still
go on until Debug Subagent trajectory limit of 25 steps.

claims.text: On the 17 instances selected for direct debugger use, Debug Tools Only succeeds on 14 (∼82%) versus baseline on 11 (∼64%).

metrics.name: test-based successes on selected subset (count and %)

claims.quote:
Interestingly, it resolves 14 (∼82%) of those instances, while
in the baseline only 11 (∼64%) of those instances succeed.

claims.text: In the 50-trajectory usage sample, exception diagnosis is the most common question category: 27.8% of questions, appearing in 17 instances.
claims.quote:
The most common use case is notably Exception Diagno-
sis, which covers ∼28% of the questions asked.

claims.text: Root cause analysis is the second most common question category: 25.3% of questions and 15 sampled instances.
claims.quote:
The second most com-
mon category is Root Cause Analysis, where the agent asks
prying questions about the underlying behavior behind the
bug.

claims.text: Local variable inspection accounts for 15.2% of questions and appears in 11 sampled instances.
claims.quote:
Local Variable Inspection and Attribute Value Inspection
make up ∼30% of the cases, where the main agent asks the
subagent to observe runtime state and get values of variables
and expressions.

claims.text: Attribute value inspection accounts for 15.2% of questions and appears in nine sampled instances.
claims.quote:
Local Variable Inspection and Attribute Value Inspection
make up ∼30% of the cases, where the main agent asks the
subagent to observe runtime state and get values of variables
and expressions.

claims.text: Assertion-failure investigation accounts for 6.3% of questions and appears in five sampled instances.
claims.quote:
Categorization of the kinds of questions we observed the main agent posing to the Debug Subagent in a sample
of 50 instances.

claims.text: Code-reachability investigation accounts for 5.1% of questions and appears in four sampled instances.
claims.quote:
Categorization of the kinds of questions we observed the main agent posing to the Debug Subagent in a sample
of 50 instances.

claims.text: Post-fix verification accounts for 5.1% of questions and appears in three sampled instances.
claims.quote:
Categorization of the kinds of questions we observed the main agent posing to the Debug Subagent in a sample
of 50 instances.

claims.text: Aggregated gated GPT-5 subagent trajectories always begin with Debug Start Session; subsequent steps are dominated by inspection and execution control.
claims.quote:
We can
see that the first step is always Debug Start Session.

claims.text: Source-file reading, grep, and breakpoint-setting occur in subagent trajectories but become less frequent in later steps.
claims.quote:
We also see
the subagent reading files, grepping and setting breakpoints,
which becomes less frequent in the later portion of the plot.

claims.text: Debugger-session/build-or-test infrastructure failures are the largest failure category (18/50, 36%), limiting runtime diagnosis to buildable projects with executable tests.

metrics.name: manually classified failure-category count and percentage

claims.quote:
We observe that the most preva-
lent failure mode is due to the debug session failing, which
manifests as Debug Start Session tool call timing out in the
trajectory.

claims.text: Incorrect or incomplete main-agent fixes despite correct subagent diagnostics account for 17/50 failures (34%).

metrics.name: manually classified failure-category count and percentage

claims.quote:
The second largest category
is the main agent implementing the wrong fix despite correct
answer from Debug Subagent.

claims.text: Complex bugs requiring more than three debug sessions without convergence account for 8/50 failures (16%).

metrics.name: manually classified failure-category count and percentage

claims.quote:
Bug required >3 debug sessions, yet the agent could not converge on the
correct fix despite these multiple attempts.

claims.text: Subagent server/API errors returning an empty response account for 4/50 failures (8%).

metrics.name: manually classified failure-category count and percentage

claims.quote:
Debug Subagent request failed due to server errors, which results in an
empty response.

claims.text: Subagent fallback to static analysis without actual runtime values accounts for 3/50 failures (6%).

metrics.name: manually classified failure-category count and percentage

claims.quote:
Debug Subagent ends up doing static code analysis, providing incomplete
information without actual runtime values.

claims.text: The authors hypothesize that greater confidence in static or print debugging explains some models' lower Python subagent adoption; confidence and training history are not measured.
claims.page: 7, §6.2, New tool’s call-rate can vary by language
claims.quote:
We hypothesize that this may be be-
cause certain models are more confident in their ability to
fix Python issues statically or via print-debugging without
needing a debugger, which is what they were likely trained to
do.

claims.text: The authors generalize from the model-gap results that better tool design can be as impactful as switching to a more expensive model.
claims.quote: This suggests that equipping agents with better tooling can be just as, if not more impactful than simply upgrading to a more capable model, which has been the belief in Coding Agent community.

claims.text: DeepK systematically improves repair accuracy over the corresponding original ThinkRepair and Self-Repair systems across the 20 model/dataset/workflow comparisons.

evidence.detail: Table 4: Wilcoxon signed-rank across 20 dataset/transition pairs; W=1.0; one-sided p=1.9e-6, two-sided p=3.8e-6; tests original-system comparisons, not every state-of-the-art comparator.

claims.quote:
Across 20 paired observations (5 datasets× 4 transitions), the test indicated a significant positive
median improvement (one-sided p < 0.001 as shown in Table 4), supporting the conclusion that
debugging knowledge systematically enhances APR performance.

claims.text: The paper claims consistent repair-accuracy superiority over state-of-the-art comparators ThinkRepair, Self-Repair, LDB, AgentCoder and AutoCodeRover; Table 2 contains exceptions, including AgentCoder on DeepSeek-v3 ARC/AGC and LDB on GPT-4o AGC.

evidence.detail: Table 4: Wilcoxon signed-rank across 20 dataset/transition pairs; W=1.0; one-sided p=1.9e-6, two-sided p=3.8e-6; tests original-system comparisons, not every state-of-the-art comparator.

claims.quote:
Results
show that DeepK consistently surpasses state-of-the-art APR systems in repair accuracy.

claims.text: DeepK-T has the highest in-distribution repair accuracy among evaluated methods: GPT-4o ACPR/Hard 76.53%/58.17%, DeepSeek-v3 90.56%/76.75%, exceeding ThinkRepair, Self-Repair, LDB, AgentCoder and AutoCodeRover.
claims.quote:
With GPT-4o, DeepK-T achieves the highest accuracy on ACPR
(76.5%), surpassing ThinkRepair (74.7%) and Self-Repair (70.4%).

claims.text: DeepK-S achieves the highest Atcoder-ABC accuracy with both GPT-4o (29.0%) and DeepSeek-v3 (42.5%), exceeding ThinkRepair, Self-Repair, LDB, AgentCoder and AutoCodeRover.
claims.quote:
With GPT-4o, DeepK-S achieves the best accuracy on Atcoder-ABC (29.0%), representing a 5-point
improvement over Self-Repair (24.0%).

claims.text: On DeepSeek-v3 Atcoder-ARC/AGC, DeepK-T exceeds ThinkRepair, Self-Repair, LDB and AutoCodeRover, but AgentCoder is better.
claims.quote:
Excluding this case,
DeepK-T consistently surpasses all other baselines.

claims.text: Knowledge gains depend on workflow and model: DeepK-T versus ThinkRepair averages +7.6±3.1 pp with DeepSeek-v3 and +1.9±2.0 pp with GPT-4o; DeepK-S versus Self-Repair averages +2.3±0.9 and +3.3±1.0 pp respectively.

suggest that debugging knowledge is particularly beneficial under distributional shift, where

claims.text: Diffploit migrates a reported 580/689 version tasks (84.2%).

metrics.name: Successfully migrated versions and migration success rate

claims.quote: Diffploitsuccessfully migrates 580 of them, achieving an overall success rate of 84.2%.

claims.text: Diffploit outperforms external TaRGET: reported success rates are 84.2% versus 32.2%; prose inconsistently reports 51.0% or 52.0% improvement.
claims.quote: Compared to the baseline methodTaRGET,Diffploitachieves a relative improvement of 51.0%, demonstrating its robustness in handling critical challenges in exploit migration, such as adapt- ing to non-function-level edits like import adjustments and build configuration updates.

claims.text: Diffploit outperforms external IDEA: 84.2% versus 22.6% success, with a reported 61.6% improvement.
claims.quote: When compared withIDEAthat combines IntelliJ IDEA’s Quick Fix and Auto Import features,Diffploitout- performs significantly in 61.6%.

claims.text: Diffploit's 580 reported migrations exceed direct GPT-4o's 243/689 (35.2%).

metrics.name: Successfully migrated versions and migration success rate

claims.quote: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 can migrate 243 (35.2%) and 263 (38.1%) cases respectively, which, while competitive in some straightforward scenarios, underperform due to lack of migration context.

claims.text: Diffploit's 580 reported migrations exceed direct DeepSeek-V3's 263/689 (38.1%); the introduction reports a 46.1% improvement over the base model.

metrics.name: Successfully migrated versions and migration success rate

claims.quote: We demonstrate the rationality ofDiffploit’s design through ablation studies, where it achieves a 46.1% improvement over the base model.

claims.text: Migration succeeds for 23/30 CVEs, which the authors interpret as generality across vulnerability classes and library ecosystems.

metrics.name: Number of CVEs with at least one successful migration

claims.quote: In the context of 30 representative CVEs,Diffploitsuccessfully performs exploit migration for 23 cases, covering a diverse range of vulnerability types and affected libraries.

claims.text: The results prose reports complete migration for every required version in 20 CVEs.

metrics.name: Number of CVEs with all migration versions successful

claims.quote: Notably, for 20 CVEs, all associated versions requiring migration are successfully repaired, highlighting the potential ofDiffploitto serve as a re- liable component in automated vulnerability validation pipelines.

claims.text: Every removed component reduces migration success: full Diffploit achieves 84.2%, versus 68.2%, 71.0%, 67.1% and 73.3% for the four ablations.
claims.quote: We observe from Table 2 thatDiffploitachieves the highest success rate, outperforming the best ablated variant by over 10.9%.

claims.text: Full Diffploit requires fewer adaptation steps than every ablation: 8.28 versus 12.71, 11.15, 15.02 and 13.35; reported overheads are 277.15%, 159.09%, 444.69% and 400.92%.

metrics.name: Average adaptation steps, assigning 30 to failures

claims.quote: In terms of cost,Diffploitnot only achieves the highest success rate but also requires the fewest steps on average (8.28), demonstrating that each component ofDiffploit contributes effectively to the overall performance.

claims.text: All four component ablations still migrate more versions than the direct base model.
claims.quote: This confirms that each component in our design contributes to the overall success.

claims.text: Migrated exploits reveal five NVD entries with missing or unclear affected-version ranges; three cases receive CNA confirmation.

metrics.name: CVE entries with missing or unclear affected-version ranges

evidence.detail: CNAs confirmed three of five CVE-range cases and incorporated migrated exploits into references.
evidence.quote: Among them, three cases are confirmed, with our submitted exploit links incorporated into the reference links.

claims.quote: As illustrated in Table 3, our mi- grated exploits uncover five NVD entries with missing or unclear specifications of affected version ranges, as well as 111 affected versions omitted from the GitHub Advisory Database.

claims.text: Migrated exploits reveal 111 affected versions omitted from the GitHub Advisory Database; 82 are accepted according to Table 3.

evidence.detail: Table 3 and the introduction/conclusion report 82 accepted additions; §5.3.1 prose instead reports 57.
evidence.quote: Meanwhile, we submit six pull requests to the GitHub Advisory Database to include a total of 111 missing versions detected byDiffploit, of which 82 versions are accepted.

claims.quote: As illustrated in Table 3, our mi- grated exploits uncover five NVD entries with missing or unclear specifications of affected version ranges, as well as 111 affected versions omitted from the GitHub Advisory Database.

claims.text: CNA confirmations and accepted advisory updates demonstrate practical feasibility, with three confirmed CVEs and 82 accepted versions reported in Table 3 and the conclusion.
claims.quote: The addition of our ex- ploits to the CVE reference links and the update of affected versions identified by migrated exploits demonstrate our practical feasibility.

claims.text: Successful migrations have low estimated financial cost: 7,029 input tokens, 831 output tokens and $0.0014 on average at July 2025 prices.
claims.quote: According to the pricing details provided by DeepSeek as of July 2025, this corresponds to an average cost of $0.0014 per successful migration.

claims.text: Failed migrations average 12,977 input tokens, 997 output tokens and an estimated $0.0020.
claims.quote: Similarly, for failed migrations, the average token consumption is 12,977 input tokens and 997 output tokens, resulting in an average cost of $0.0020 per failed attempt.

claims.text: Diffploit remains effective on post-cutoff vulnerabilities: 19/19, 71/71, 190/192, 28/28 and 2/2 migrations, supporting robustness to unseen CVEs.
claims.quote: As illustrated in Table 4,Diffploitsuccessfully migrates ex- ploits for all affected versions of four unseen CVEs, with only two versions of CVE-2025-53864 failing to produce valid exploits.

claims.text: Environment repairs reproduce 128 previously failing versions across seven exploits without changing exploit code, demonstrating environment-level repair capability.

metrics.name: Successfully reproduced versions without exploit-code changes

claims.quote: These migrations enabledDiffploitto successfully reproduce 128 previously fail- ing versions, suggesting that many failures of origin exploits are not rooted in the exploit logic but rather caused by external or environmental factors.

claims.text: Diffploit performs nontrivial migrations, with original-to-migrated token AED of 176.00 over the reported 22-CVE analysis subset.
claims.quote: On the 22 CVEs where exploit migration is successful byDiff- ploit, the average edit distance between the migrated exploits and the original exploits is 176.00, indicating that the required modifica- tions are non-trivial and reflect substantial structural or semantic changes.

claims.text: The authors estimate roughly 80% less manual migration effort than using external IDEA; IDEA-edited exploits remain 59.69 token edits from Diffploit outputs on average.
claims.quote: Based on these observations, we estimate thatDiffploitreduces manual effort by approximately 80%, as measured by the total edit distance required for the exploit migration compared toIDEA.

claims.text: Diffploit handles edits outside function bodies, including imports and build configuration, more adaptably than external TaRGET.
claims.quote: Compared to the baseline methodTaRGET,Diff- ploitdemonstrates superior adaptability in handling test changes that are not confined to the function level.

claims.text: Diffploit can adapt silently passing exploits that should fail to expose the vulnerability; separate quantified results are not reported.
claims.quote: Diffploitis also capable of addressing scenarios where an ex- ploit test should fail but instead passes silently in the target version.

claims.text: Fixed original assertions limit migration when vulnerability manifestations change; representative failures include exceptions, remote connections and VM crashes.

metrics.name: Migration failures under the fixed assertion criterion

claims.quote: First, it struggles to handle cases where the vulnerability manifests differently across versions.

claims.text: Diffploit cannot reliably synthesize specialized byte- or format-sensitive payload changes, illustrated by crafted PDF, token and cookie cases.
claims.quote: These artifacts often need pre- cise byte-level or format-aware modification, which is outside the current capabilities ofDiffploit.

claims.text: Large API gaps can leave migration incomplete, as in CVE-2022-34662 where only part of the required class/API replacement is performed.
claims.quote: For example, CVE-2022-34662 required replacing a service class and finding an appropriate replacement API (fromResourcesServiceImpl.verifyFile toResourcesService.updateResource); Diffploit is only able to perform part of the migration, leaving the exploit nonfunctional.

claims.text: The authors attribute effectiveness to diff-based design rather than potential training-data leakage, using the drop in base-model performance.
claims.quote: This result suggests that the effectiveness ofDiffploitdoes not stem from potential data leakage but from its diff-based design.

claims.text: Accepted version additions and working migrated exploits improve CVE record completeness and quality.

metrics.name: New affected-version information added to records

evidence.detail: Red Hat acknowledges changed version information and added exploit references.
evidence.quote: The changes for version infor- mation were made, and the references you sent added.

claims.quote: Diffploitcontributed to improving the quality of the CVE re- ports by identifying additional affected versions and providing a working exploit.

claims.text: The migrated protocols-imap exploit for CVE-2021-40111 is a flaky test; flakiness frequency is not reported.
claims.quote: The exploit is a flaky test.

claims.text: The motivating CVE-2024-22257 exploit is migrated in nine steps despite 2,555 candidate version diffs.
claims.quote: Diffploittakes nine steps to migrate the exploit for CVE-2024-22257, despite the significant challenge of identifying relevant information from the 2,555 diffs between the two versions.

claims.text: Removing diff annealing produces the highest reproduction cost among ablations (15.02 average steps, 444.69% overhead), which the authors take as evidence that annealing is the most important component for prioritizing helpful diffs.

This highlights the importance of the anneal-
ing process in filtering and prioritizing diffs that are most helpful
to migration.

claims.text: Diffploit-Combining has the highest success among ablations but needs 13.35 versus 8.28 steps, which the authors read as the combination strategy substantially improving efficiency of finding valid exploits.

est success rate among all variants, it requires significantly more

kill all the mutants (MS = 100%) or there is no surviving
mutant that is not used in the augmentation process (Line

FramePilotautomates

patch implementation.

𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑠, and𝑟𝑒𝑡 ) to form the fullFramePilot.

a patch.

the Verified benchmark, the ADI-enabled agent achieves a 63.8% resolved rate.

a top-performing 50.7% resolved rate.

two tasks on the entire SWE-bench leaderboard [49] which none of the rest baselines could.

claims.text: The headline Claude-Sonnet-3.7 FramePilot result costs an average $1.28 per task.

Verified set, even slightly outperforming the highly-optimized and high-investmentClaude-Toolsagent, at
an average cost of $1.28 per task with Claude-Sonnet-3.7.

capability boosts the number of resolved tasks by 10.6% with Claude-Sonnet-3.7 and 18.5% with

claims.text: DLLens synthesizes 1,401 validated API counterparts, 1.84 times TensorScope's 762: 689/1,862 TensorFlow APIs (37.00%; 126.64% more than 304) and 712/1,121 PyTorch APIs (63.51%; 55.46% more than 458).

The manual verification reveals that most counterparts
(i.e., 81 out of 100) implement the same functionalities as their target APIs.

claims.quote:
Our evaluation shows that
DLLens synthesizes counterparts for 1.84 times as many APIs as those found by state-of-the-art techniques on
these libraries.

claims.text: DLLens supports differential testing for 1,055 APIs whose counterparts TensorScope does not find: 533 TensorFlow and 522 PyTorch APIs.
claims.quote:
In particular,DLLens col-
lects counterparts for 1,055 (533+522) APIs where TensorScope fails.

metrics.name: Unique argument-property values in validation inputs

unique property values for each argument.

claims.text: In the 100-counterpart manual sample, 81 counterparts fully implement the target functionality; 19 are only partially valid for particular input conditions.

The manual verification reveals that most counterparts
(i.e., 81 out of 100) implement the same functionalities as their target APIs.

2,161) more property constraints.

18.14 path constraints for each TensorFlow API and 38.76 for each PyTorch API, including path
constraints extracted from their counterparts.

claims.text: The authors interpret the increase from 1.78 to 3.18 input constraints/path for TensorFlow and from 1.57 to 3.91 for PyTorch as more complete path constraints and improved guidance toward target paths.

accuracy of inferred constraints, our manual validation confirmed that 348 out of 694 (50.14%)

claims.quote:
The more input constraints included in a
path constraint, the more complete the path constraint is likely to be.

claims.text: Manual checking finds 348/694 inferred constraints correct (50.14%): TensorFlow yields 223 inferences, averaging 8.92 inferred and 4.56 correct/API; PyTorch yields 471, averaging 18.84 inferred and 9.36 correct/API.

metrics.name: Manually correct inferred constraints and accuracy

claims.quote:
Regarding the
accuracy of inferred constraints, our manual validation confirmed that 348 out of 694 (50.14%)
inferred constraints are correct.

claims.text: LLM inference substantially increases the available correct input constraints in the 50-API sample, supplying 348 manually correct inferences where the no-ICF version extracts only 79 constraints in total.

inference significantly increases the number of accurate input constraints compared to DLLens
(w/o ICF).

claims.text: With the same five-hour input-generation budget, ICF increases covered branches by 6.10%, from 14,975 to 15,889; beyond about 12,800 initially covered branches, the corresponding additional coverage is 2,175 versus 3,089.
claims.quote:
After running our test input generation for five hours, inputs generated following
path constraints from DLLens outperforms those from DLLens (w/o ICF) by covering 6.10% more
branches (15,889 v.s. 14,975, considering branches in both TensorFlow and PyTorch).

claims.text: After five hours per library, DLLens exceeds the best external baseline FreeFuzz by 7.23% in total branch coverage: 15,889 versus 14,817; TensorFlow improves 6.78% (9,393 versus 8,797), and PyTorch 7.91% (6,496 versus 6,020).
claims.quote:

baseline by covering 7.23% (15,889 v.s. 14,817) more branches, including 6.78% more branches (9393
v.s. 8797) in TensorFlow and 7.91% more branches (6496 v.s. 6020) in PyTorch.
