claims.text: PSG correctly extracts the evaluated protocols' message formats: 82 BGP, 32 CoAP, 86 DNS, 171 HTTP, 43 RTSP, 63 FTP and 132 SSH.

metrics.name: Correctly extracted formats, manually checked against RFCs and IANA

claims.quote:
By manual inspection against
RFCs and IANA registries, we conﬁrmed that PSG accurately
extracted the formats for evaluated protocols, with format
numbers shown in Table II.

claims.text: PSG reaches 100% format coverage for all seven protocols by five generation attempts, versus 32.7% average coverage for the external basic seed corpus.
claims.quote:
The results show that PSG
can generate syntactically and semantically correct inputs for
all desired formats.

claims.text: PSG can generate syntactically and semantically correct inputs for every desired format.

metrics.name: Format coverage of syntactically and semantically correct inputs

claims.quote:
The results show that PSG
can generate syntactically and semantically correct inputs for
all desired formats.

claims.text: Full PSG covers 2.9 times as many unique formats as the authors' LLM-only PSG° control: 100% versus 34% mean format coverage.
claims.quote:
It covers 2.9× more unique formats than
a method relying solely on the internal knowledge of the
LLM without augmentation, and 1.7× more than a method
employing the knowledge base to directly generate messages
without optimization and guidance.

claims.text: Full PSG covers 1.7 times as many unique formats as PSGm1 with direct hex generation: 100% versus 58% mean format coverage; code generation and refinement are evaluated together.
claims.quote:
It covers 2.9× more unique formats than
a method relying solely on the internal knowledge of the
LLM without augmentation, and 1.7× more than a method
employing the knowledge base to directly generate messages
without optimization and guidance.

claims.text: Knowledge-base planning and augmentation increase mean format coverage from PSG°'s 34% to PSGm1's 58%, with notable HTTP and RTSP improvements.
claims.quote:
After providing
augmentation, PSG m1’s result increases to 58%, with par-
ticularly notable improvements on textual protocols: HTTP
and RTSP.

claims.text: The first generation attempt already covers 51–98% of formats across protocols, including 97% HTTP, 98% RTSP and 97% FTP.

metrics.name: Format coverage after one generation attempt

claims.quote:
Nevertheless,
empowered by the reﬁnement process, PSG still achieved high
format coverage in the initial attempt across all protocols.

claims.text: BGP and CoAP require four generation attempts and SSH five to achieve full format coverage.
claims.quote:
In contrast, BGP, CoAP, and SSH require
4, 4, and 5 attempts , respectively, to achieve 100% coverage
due to their more intricate formats involving complex ﬁeld re-
lationships and message assembly requirements.

claims.text: PSG requires an average of 1.39 generation attempts per message format.
claims.quote:
On
average, PSG requires only 1.39 attempts per message format,
showcasing both efﬁciency and accuracy.

claims.text: PSG seeds increase AFLNet's mean branch coverage by 11.2% and line coverage by 9.4% over external unenhanced AFLNet across twelve measured implementations.

evidence.description: Mann–Whitney U test reported significant for all coverage results; p-values and thresholds not_reported.
evidence.quote:
All results are statistically signiﬁcant per the Mann-
Whitney U test [40].

claims.quote:
On average, AFLNet PSG , ChatAFL PSG , and Snipuzz PSG
achieve (11.2%, 9.4%), (9.5%, 8.6%), and (10.3%, 8.4%)
higher (branch, line) coverage than their respective base-
lines.

claims.text: Replacing ChatAFL's seed enrichment with PSG improves coverage across all measured subjects, averaging 9.5% more branches and 8.6% more lines than external ChatAFL.

evidence.description: Mann–Whitney U test reported significant for all coverage results; p-values and thresholds not_reported.
evidence.quote:
All results are statistically signiﬁcant per the Mann-
Whitney U test [40].

claims.quote:
On average, AFLNet PSG , ChatAFL PSG , and Snipuzz PSG
achieve (11.2%, 9.4%), (9.5%, 8.6%), and (10.3%, 8.4%)
higher (branch, line) coverage than their respective base-
lines.

claims.text: PSG seeds increase black-box Snipuzz's mean branch coverage by 10.3% and line coverage by 8.4% over external unenhanced Snipuzz.

evidence.description: Mann–Whitney U test reported significant for all coverage results; p-values and thresholds not_reported.
evidence.quote:
All results are statistically signiﬁcant per the Mann-
Whitney U test [40].

claims.quote:
On average, AFLNet PSG , ChatAFL PSG , and Snipuzz PSG
achieve (11.2%, 9.4%), (9.5%, 8.6%), and (10.3%, 8.4%)
higher (branch, line) coverage than their respective base-
lines.

claims.text: AFLNetPSG and ChatAFLPSG jointly discover ten previously unknown bugs: four FreeCoAP, two GoBGP, and one each in OpenBGPD, FRR, SmartDNS and GStreamer; external unenhanced fuzzers find only bugs 3, 5 and 6.

evidence.description: Eight of ten discoveries received CVE identifiers, corroborating a subset; a developer-confirmation procedure is not_reported.
evidence.quote:
Eight of them have been assigned CVE identiﬁers,
all of which received CVSS scores of High or Critical,
highlighting their severity.

claims.quote:
AFLNetPSG and ChatAFL PSG found 10 new bugs in the
widely-used implementations of evaluated protocols (see Ta-
ble V).

claims.text: Eight discovered bugs receive CVE identifiers and all eight have High or Critical CVSS ratings.
claims.quote:
Eight of them have been assigned CVE identiﬁers,
all of which received CVSS scores of High or Critical,
highlighting their severity.

claims.text: A corpus generated using one server implementation transfers to other implementations of the same protocol and enhances downstream fuzzing across grey-box and black-box paradigms.

metrics.name: Coverage improvement across implementations and fuzzing paradigms

claims.quote:
In the following fuzzing phase, all
corresponding implementations are tested, e.g., cpp-httplib and
Lighttpd are tested based on the generated seed corpus.

claims.text: PSG-generated seeds enable continuing branch-coverage growth where external basic-corpus fuzzers plateau early.
claims.quote:
In
contrast, the diverse seed inputs generated by PSG activate
varied program logic, enabling fuzzers to further explore
more code branches and continuously increase code cover-
age.

claims.text: ChatAFL's usual coverage advantage over AFLNet diminishes when both use PSG-generated seeds.

metrics.name: Between-fuzzer coverage difference with and without PSG seeds

claims.quote:
While ChatAFL—a state-of-the-art protocol fuzzer with
advanced strategies—outperforms AFLNet on most subjects,
this advantage diminishes when using PSG-generated seeds,

=== PAGE 14 ===
TRANSACTION OF SOFTW ARE ENGINEERING 14
highlighting the critical role of a diverse seed corpus in
fuzzing.

claims.text: PSG-generated messages generally have smaller data payloads than real-world traffic messages.
claims.quote:
PSG-generated messages typ-
ically contain concise data ﬁelds, whereas real-world trafﬁc
often carries extensive payload data to fulﬁll actual com-
munication needs.

claims.text: PSG-generated messages contain fewer optional-field combinations within individual messages than real-world traffic.
claims.quote:
PSG-generated
messages typically contain fewer combinations of optional
ﬁelds within individual messages.

claims.text: For formats shared with real-world traffic, PSG messages are broadly similar, particularly in key-field validity.
claims.quote:
To better understand the charac-
teristics of PSG-generated messages, we compare them with
those from real-world trafﬁc.

claims.text: PSG may still generate invalid inputs despite validation and refinement; an invalid-input rate is not reported.
claims.page: 14, §V, Validation of the Generated Seed Corpus
claims.quote:
As shown in
Section IV-C in the evaluation, the inputs generated by PSG
may sometimes be invalid due to protocol complexity and the
unpredictable nature of the LLM.

claims.text: Some bugs revealed by PSG-enhanced fuzzing had persisted for up to nine years.
claims.quote:
Some bugs persisted for up to 9 years
due to inaccessible code paths caused by inadequate initial
seed corpus.

claims.text: Concise PSG payloads may improve fuzzing efficiency by reducing mutations spent on low-complexity data content; no runtime or cost comparison isolates this effect.
claims.quote:
This characteristic can enhance fuzzing
efﬁciency because data-related ﬁelds typically trigger less
complex parsing logic than other structural ﬁelds.

claims.text: Generating optional fields separately may impair fuzzing efficiency when combinations activate complex paths; this effect is not measured separately.
claims.quote:
Conversely, when different optional ﬁelds
interact and their combinations activate more complex code
paths, fuzzing efﬁciency may be impacted.

claims.text: ErrorPrism achieves 97.0% exact-path accuracy on 102 error events, exceeding Internal Code Agent (87.1%), CoReQA (57.4%) and Pure LLM (50.5%).
claims.quote:
With a total accuracy of 97.0%, ErrorPrism significantly
outperforms all baselines.

claims.text: The paper claims LLM-guided reconstruction improves static-analysis performance from 90.7% candidate-function precision to 97.0% exact-path accuracy, although these measure different outcomes.
claims.quote:
ErrorPrism
improves this result to a final accuracy of 97.0%, which
showcases the LLM’s indispensable role in analyzing, ranking,
and selecting the single correct path from the statically-
generated candidates.

claims.text: ErrorPrism maintains high accuracy across path complexity: 100%, 100%, 95.2%, 100% and 85.7% for 0, 1, 2, 3 and ≥4 hops respectively.

metrics.name: Exact-match path accuracy stratified by hop count

claims.quote:
This high level of accuracy is
consistently maintained even on complex error paths with
multiple hops, a scenario where other approaches begin to
degrade.

dates (reflected in its 90.7% precision score), it cannot by itself

metrics.name: Exact-match path accuracy stratified by hop count

claims.quote:

claims.text: The paper attributes the 97.0% versus 50.5% accuracy gap over Pure LLM to candidate generation being essential; the control also removes tools and iterative guidance.
claims.quote:
The results first show that a candidate generation phase
is essential for enabling LLMs to reason effectively in this
domain.

claims.text: For ≥4-hop paths, the paper claims ErrorPrism is substantially more accurate (85.7%) than Static Analysis (66.1%); the static result is candidate-function precision.
claims.quote:
For example, on paths of four or more hops, ErrorPrism
(85.7%) is substantially more accurate than the Static Analysis
baseline (66.1%), proving that its reasoning capability is vital
for solving the long-tail and complex diagnostic challenges.

claims.text: ErrorPrism averages 5.93 seconds per template, approximately 8.4 times faster than Internal Code Agent's 49.75 seconds.
claims.quote:
With an average
inference time of5.93 s, ErrorPrism is approximately 8.4x
faster than the Internal Code Agent (49.75 s).

claims.text: The paper attributes ErrorPrism's inference-time advantage over Internal Code Agent to static pruning and focused context, without an isolated pruning-only timing experiment.
claims.quote:
In contrast, ErrorPrism uses static
analysis to massively prune the search space before engaging
the LLM agent, providing it with a highly focused context.

claims.text: ErrorPrism is claimed to be a practical tool for industrial microservice root-cause analysis.

convention, providing a complete and actionable diagnosis.

claims.quote:
ErrorPrism provides
an effective and practical tool for root cause analysis in industrial
microservice systems.

claims.quote:
As a result, the ambiguous template
prevents ErrorPrism from accurately reconstructing the error
propagation paths, constituting the primary source of the 3%
of the failed cases in our evaluation.

claims.text: ErrorPrism inference time has a long tail, attributed to long, complex paths with weaker candidate pruning and more agent iterations.
claims.quote:
The
box plot also reveals a long tail in ErrorPrism’s performance
distribution, indicating that some cases have longer inference
times.

claims.text: Pure LLM's inference-time distribution lacks the long tail observed for ErrorPrism; CoReQA is reported similarly.

baselines may have a lower median inference time, their
efficiency is achieved at the expense of accuracy, severely

claims.text: Almost all basic-prompt ChatGPT tests are syntactically correct, with one malformed-parenthesis exception.
claims.quote:
For example, almost all the tests generated by ChatGPT (except the one has an incorrect parenthesis
generated) are syntactically correct, but nearly a half of the tests generated by AthenaTest are
syntactically incorrect.

claims.text: Only 42.1% of basic-prompt ChatGPT tests compile successfully.
claims.quote:
Overall, we could observe that a large portion of tests generated by ChatGPT suffer from correctness
issues, i.e., 42.1% of the generated tests are successfully compiled while only 24.8% of the generated
tests are executed successfully without any execution errors.

claims.text: Only 24.8% of basic-prompt ChatGPT tests pass execution.

evidence.detail: Failing generated tests were attributed to improper test code rather than focal-method bugs.
evidence.quote:
We further manually inspect the failed
tests to check whether they actually reveal bugs in the focal method under test, but we find that all
of them are caused by the improper test code itself.

claims.quote:
Overall, we could observe that a large portion of tests generated by ChatGPT suffer from correctness
issues, i.e., 42.1% of the generated tests are successfully compiled while only 24.8% of the generated
tests are executed successfully without any execution errors.

claims.text: Basic-prompt ChatGPT outperforms external AthenaTest in syntactic, compilation and execution correctness.

metrics.name: syntax ≈100% vs 54.8%; compilation 42.1% vs 18.8%; passing 24.8% vs 14.4%

claims.quote:
As for the learning-based baseline AthenaTest, ChatGPT has a substantial improvement over
AthenaTest in terms of syntactic correctness, compilation correctness, and executable correctness.

claims.text: Basic-prompt ChatGPT has lower compilation and execution passing rates than external EvoSuite.
claims.quote:
As for the traditional
search-based baseline Evosuite, we could observe a higher compilable rate and passing rate in its
generated tests.

claims.text: ChatGPT compilation errors are diverse, dominated by unresolved symbols, with type, access, abstract-instantiation and unsupported-operator errors also observed.

metrics.name: error frequencies: unresolved class 1,934, method 471, variable 466, unspecified symbol 169; type 73/46/11; private access 75; abstract instantiation 33; unsupported diamond operator 15

claims.quote:
Finding 2: The ChatGPT-generated tests encounter diverse compilation errors, such as symbol
resolution errors, type errors, and access errors; the majority of failed executions are caused by
the incorrectly-generated assertions.

claims.text: Assertion errors account for 85.5% of ChatGPT's failed executions and are attributed to incorrect generated assertions.

evidence.detail: Failing generated tests were attributed to improper test code rather than focal-method bugs.
evidence.quote:
We further manually inspect the failed
tests to check whether they actually reveal bugs in the focal method under test, but we find that all
of them are caused by the improper test code itself.

claims.quote:
As shown in the table, the majority of failed executions (85.5%)
are caused by assertion errors, i.e., the assertions generated by ChatGPT consider the behavior
of the program under test violates the specification.

claims.text: On the common executable subset, ChatGPT tests achieve coverage comparable to developer-written tests.
claims.quote:
As shown in the table, we could observe that the tests generated ChatGPT achieve the highest
coverage compared to existing learning-based and search-based techniques and it also achieve
comparable coverage as manually-written tests.

claims.text: The paper claims the highest coverage over external AthenaTest and EvoSuite; Table 5 supports statement coverage superiority but EvoSuite union branch coverage exceeds ChatGPT's.

metrics.name: statement coverage: ChatGPT 82.3%, AthenaTest 65.5%, EvoSuite union 81.1%
branch coverage: ChatGPT 65.6%, AthenaTest 56.2%, EvoSuite union 77.3%

claims.quote:
As shown in the table, we could observe that the tests generated ChatGPT achieve the highest
coverage compared to existing learning-based and search-based techniques and it also achieve
comparable coverage as manually-written tests.

claims.text: ChatGPT tests most closely resemble manual tests in assertion-count distribution, compared with external AthenaTest and EvoSuite.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, we observe that ChatGPT-generated tests exhibit most similar
distribution as manually-written tests in the number of assertions per test.

claims.text: Passing ChatGPT tests have reasonable readability comparable to, and sometimes better than, manual tests.

metrics.name: five participants' readability scores (2–6): naming intuitiveness and code layout

claims.quote:
Overall,
most ChatGPT-generated tests are assessed with decent readability, and they are also considered
with comparable and sometimes even better readability compared to manually-written tests.

claims.text: Passing ChatGPT tests have usability comparable to manual tests.

metrics.name: five participants' usability scores (2–6): assertion quality and adoption effort

claims.quote:
Interestingly,
we find the ChatGPT -generated tests exhibit comparable usability compared to manually-written
ones.

claims.text: Participants are willing to directly adopt ChatGPT-generated tests in a considerable proportion of cases.

metrics.name: adoption-effort ratings / willingness to directly adopt

claims.quote:
In a consider-
able portion of cases, participants are willing to directly adopt ChatGPT-generated tests.

claims.text: ChatTester raises compilation success from 39.0% to 73.3%, a 34.3 percentage-point gain over basic ChatGPT.
claims.quote:
For example, additional 34.3% tests (= 73.3% - 39.0%) can be successfully compiled and
additional 18.7% tests (= 41.0% - 22.3%) can pass the execution.

claims.text: ChatTester raises execution success from 22.3% to 41.0%, an 18.7 percentage-point gain over basic ChatGPT.
claims.quote:
For example, additional 34.3% tests (= 73.3% - 39.0%) can be successfully compiled and
additional 18.7% tests (= 41.0% - 22.3%) can pass the execution.

claims.text: The paper interprets the 18.7-point execution gain as more tests with correct assertions.
claims.quote:
Our evaluation demonstrates the effective-
ness of ChatTester by generating 34.3% more compilable tests and 18.7% more tests with correct assertions
than the default ChatGPT.

claims.text: The intention-based initial generator alone raises compilation success from 39.0% to 50.7%.
claims.quote:
In addition, we could observe that the variantChatTester-Ite outperforms the default ChatGPT
by achieving 11.7% and 7.4% improvements in the compilation rate and passing rate.

claims.text: The intention-based initial generator alone raises execution success from 22.3% to 29.7%.
claims.quote:
In addition, we could observe that the variantChatTester-Ite outperforms the default ChatGPT
by achieving 11.7% and 7.4% improvements in the compilation rate and passing rate.

claims.text: ChatTester-Ite corrects 12.5% of assertions that were incorrect in basic ChatGPT outputs.
claims.quote:
In particular,
we find that among the ChatGPT-generated tests with incorrect assertions, 12.5% of them are fixed
into correct assertions in ChatTester-Ite, indicating the effectiveness of the initial test generator.

claims.text: Keeping the intention-based initial generator improves compilation by 12.7 points over ChatTester-Ini.
claims.quote:
In addition, when comparing ChatTester against the variant ChatTester-Ini, we can
find that removing the initial test generator would decrease 12.7% compilation rate and 7.0% passing
rate, further confirming the contribution of the initial test generator.

claims.text: Keeping the intention-based initial generator improves execution passing by 7.0 points over ChatTester-Ini.
claims.quote:
In addition, when comparing ChatTester against the variant ChatTester-Ini, we can
find that removing the initial test generator would decrease 12.7% compilation rate and 7.0% passing
rate, further confirming the contribution of the initial test generator.

claims.text: Adding the iterative refiner to the initial generator improves compilation by 22.6 points.
claims.quote:
Moreover, we could observe a
further improvement from ChatTester-Ite to ChatTester, i.e., additional 22.6% tests and 11.3%
tests are fixed by the iterative test refiner into compilable tests and passing tests.

claims.text: Adding the iterative refiner to the initial generator improves execution passing by 11.3 points.
claims.quote:
Moreover, we could observe a
further improvement from ChatTester-Ite to ChatTester, i.e., additional 22.6% tests and 11.3%
tests are fixed by the iterative test refiner into compilable tests and passing tests.

claims.text: ChatTester generalizes to both open models in compilation success: CodeLlama 22% to 43%, CodeFuse 1% to 24%.

metrics.name: successful compilation across models: +21 and +23 points

claims.quote:
For the studied LLMs
CodeLlama-Instruct-34B and CodeFuse-34B, ChatTester achieves 21.0%/ 23.0% improvement in
compilation rate and 11.0% /18.0% improvement in passing execution rate.

claims.text: ChatTester improves execution success for both open models: Table 9 gives CodeLlama 3% to 21% and CodeFuse 0% to 11%; prose reverses the gain order.

metrics.name: passing execution across models: CodeLlama +18 points; CodeFuse +11 points

claims.quote:
Overall, ChatTester can consistently improve the quality (e.g., syntactical, compilation,
or execution correctness) of the tests generated by different open-source LLMs.

claims.text: The paper claims consistent project-level coverage superiority over basic ChatGPT, AthenaTest and EvoSuite; Table 10 has EvoSuite exceptions for tabula-java branch coverage and jInstagram statement coverage.

metrics.name: EvoSuite exceptions: tabula-java BC 9.9% > 9.2%; jInstagram SC 45.3% > 41.8%

claims.quote:
Project-level Evaluation Summary: ChatTester consistently outperforms baselines in
coverage, readability, and usability in the project-level evaluation setting.

claims.text: All five participants rate more ChatTester project-level tests as readable than baseline tests.
claims.quote:
As shown in the figure, all the participants find that ChatTester
generate more tests with better readability and usability than baselines.

claims.text: All five participants rate more ChatTester project-level tests as usable than baseline tests.
claims.quote:
As shown in the figure, all the participants find that ChatTester
generate more tests with better readability and usability than baselines.

claims.text: Manual inspection finds no real focal-method bugs among failed empirical-study ChatGPT tests; failures originate in generated test code.

metrics.name: manual attribution: all failed tests reflect improper test code; no revealed focal-method bugs

claims.quote:
We further manually inspect the failed
tests to check whether they actually reveal bugs in the focal method under test, but we find that all
of them are caused by the improper test code itself.

claims.text: Iterative refinement is reported to continuously improve generated-test quality across refinement iterations.

metrics.name: per-iteration successfully compiled and passing test counts, iterations 0–10

claims.quote:
Based on the table, we find that the iterative refinement
continuously improves the quality of the generated tests.

claims.text: ChatTester averages about 99 seconds per test, with 15 seconds for initial generation and 30 seconds per refinement iteration.

metrics.name: mean total time 99.0 s; initial generator 15.0 s; refinement iteration 30.0 s

claims.quote:
The average time cost of ChatTester
is around 99.0 seconds, where the initial test generator takes 15.0 seconds while each iteration
in the iterative refiner takes 30.0 seconds on average.

claims.text: API latency and compilation/execution account for most ChatTester time costs.
claims.quote:
In fact, the majority of the costs come
from the latency of querying the ChatGPT API (i.e., around 10s in our environment) and the test
compilation/execution.

claims.text: ChatTester improves CodeFuse syntactic correctness from 72% to 89%, while CodeLlama remains at 93%.

metrics.name: syntactic correctness: CodeFuse 72% to 89%; CodeLlama 93% to 93%

claims.quote:
Overall, ChatTester can consistently improve the quality (e.g., syntactical, compilation,
or execution correctness) of the tests generated by different open-source LLMs.

claims.text: ChatTester increases average generation time from 5 to 105 seconds with CodeLlama and from 5 to 90 seconds with CodeFuse.

metrics.name: mean time: CodeLlama basic/ChatTester 5/105 s; CodeFuse basic/ChatTester 5/90 s

claims.quote:
The average time costs of CodeLlama-Instruct,𝐶𝑜𝑑𝑒𝐿𝑙𝑎𝑚𝑎 ChatTester,
CodeFuse and𝐶𝑜𝑑𝑒𝐹𝑢𝑠𝑒 ChatTester are 5s, 105s, 5s and 90s.

claims.text: Basic ChatGPT correctness is similar across the empirical-study and separate ChatTester evaluation datasets, suggesting consistency.
claims.quote:
However, we actually observe similar correctness results of
the tests generated by ChatGPT on two different datasets (Table 2 and Table 7), indicating the
consistency of our results.

claims.text: ChatTester also improves successful execution on Python HumanEval, from 31.7% to 43.2%.
claims.quote:
We observed the consistent effectiveness of ChatTester by improving the successful execution
rate of ChatGPT-generated tests from 31.7% to 43.2%.

claims.text: Project-level ChatTester tests are judged to have more intuitive names than baseline tests.
claims.quote:
we find that participants consider the ChatTester-generated tests with more intuitive naming
styles and more structured code (thus with better readability)

claims.text: AutoSD has substantially higher patch-generation time than LLM-Base: a reported average 4.66-fold increase, with mean times of 9 minutes 22 seconds versus 1 minute 59 seconds for ten patches.

claims.quote: Speciﬁcally, to generate ten patches for a single bug, AutoSDwould on average take 9 minutes and 22 seconds, while LLM- Base would take 1 minutes and 59 seconds.

metrics.name: Execution time with versus without bug-report context

claims.quote: when removing the bug report, the execution time was practically the same, while the performance dropped by 39%, indicating that providing additional information can help without signiﬁcant execution cost.

claims.text: The paper attributes the extra repair time mainly to external-tool interaction rather than prompt length.
claims.quote: when removing the bug report, the execution time was practically the same, while the performance dropped by 39%, indicating that providing additional information can help without signiﬁcant execution cost.

claims.text: The paper argues that participant demand for explanations justifies their additional generation cost.
claims.quote: Nonetheless, given the signiﬁcant developer demand for explanations of automatically generated patches as shown in Fig. 7, we believe that the additional cost needed to build explanations for patches is justiﬁed.

claims.text: The paper suggests filtering patches without <DONE> could reduce developer inspection cost, but does not measure inspection effort for that filtering policy.
claims.quote: These results indicate that AutoSDcan indicate when its output is likely to help developers based on its interaction, and thus aid developer decision-making and potentially reduce developer inspection cost when processing automated debugging results.

claims.text: The paper claims execution-grounded observations prevent misleading hallucinated explanations; no hallucination or misleading-explanation rate is measured.
claims.quote: incorporation improved developer trust in the explanations (80% of developers responded positively that the incorporation of execution results enhanced their trust in the explanation) while preventing the LLM from hallucinating explanations that may mislead developers.

claims.text: The two illustrated BugsInPy explanations receive sharply different helpfulness ratings: BIP006 75% liked versus BIP002 16%.
claims.quote: In addition to the example embed- ded in Fig. 1, we provide two reasoning traces generated by AutoSDthat were liked (BIP006 - 75% liked) and disliked (BIP002 - 16% liked) in the human study from the real-world BugsInPy problems.

claims.text: Even the weak BIP002 explanation can aid assessment by exposing weak foundations for its incorrect patch; participants shown it judge the patch more accurately.
claims.quote: In this context, it is noteworthy that developers who saw the explanation of BIP002 more accurately assessed it (Fig. 6).

claims.text: CosFL localizes 324/835 bugs at Top1, 532 at Top5 and 566 at Top10.
claims.page: p. 14, §5.1 and Table 2; pp. 1, 3, 15, 19, repeated summaries
claims.quote: Overall, CosFL achieves the best performance, which localizes 324, 532, and 566 bugs in the top 1, 5, and 10 positions, respectively.

claims.text: CosFL improves Top1 recall over external comparators AutoFL and AgentFL by 57.3% and 26.6%, respectively.
claims.quote: CosFL shows 57.3% and 26.6% increases in Top1 compared to AutoFL and AgentFL, respectively.

claims.text: CosFL improves Top5 recall over external comparators AutoFL and AgentFL by 110.3% and 38.5%, respectively.
claims.quote: For the Top5 accuracy, the increases are even more significant, reaching 110.3% and 38.5%.

claims.text: CosFL ranks buggy methods relatively highly: MFR 14.15 and MAR 14.97, lower than both external navigation-based comparators.
claims.quote: The MFR is 14.15 and the MAR is 14.97, indicating that CosFL can rank the buggy methods at relatively high positions.

claims.text: Module context increases Top1 recall by 80 bugs, with almost unchanged Top5 recall and slightly better MFR/MAR.
claims.quote: Interestingly, after removing the module context, the Top1 value drops sharply by 80, while the Top5 remains relatively unchanged and the Top10 even increases slightly by 32.

claims.text: Module context decreases Top10 recall by 32 bugs: 566 versus 598 without module context.
claims.quote: Interestingly, after removing the module context, the Top1 value drops sharply by 80, while the Top5 remains relatively unchanged and the Top10 even increases slightly by 32.

claims.text: Module-level retrieval improves Top1/Top5/Top10 recall by 12/13/9 bugs and lowers MFR/MAR by 0.53/0.40.
claims.quote: From rows 2 to 3, we can see that both module- and chunk-granularity retrieval enhance the effectiveness of CosFL, contributing respectively to Top1 improvements of 12 and 19, and Top10 improvements of 9 and 23.

claims.text: Chunk-level retrieval improves Top1/Top5/Top10 recall by 19/23/23 bugs and lowers MFR/MAR by 1.00/1.02.
claims.quote: From rows 2 to 3, we can see that both module- and chunk-granularity retrieval enhance the effectiveness of CosFL, contributing respectively to Top1 improvements of 12 and 19, and Top10 improvements of 9 and 23.

claims.text: Chunk retrieval contributes more than module retrieval to rank improvement: MAR reductions 1.02 versus 0.40; the prose mislabels this metric MRR.
claims.quote: Notably, the chunk-level retrieval plays a more critical role, offering an MRR contribution of 1.02, in contrast to 0.40 from module retrieval.

claims.text: The gpt-4o backend improves CosFL over gpt-3.5-turbo by 29 Top1 and 56 Top5 localizations; gpt-3.5-turbo achieves 290 and 471.

claims.text: Increasing retrieval λ from 50 to 75 yields nearly plateaued performance; a moderate retrieval amount suffices.

claims.quote: However, as𝜆 further increases from 50 to 75, the performance nearly plateaued.

claims.text: CosFL's Top5 results cover 80.7% of AgentFL's localized bugs (310/384) and 87.7% of AutoFL's (222/253).
claims.quote: As shown in the figure, we observe that the results of CosFL substantially cover the other two, identifying 80.7% (310 out of 384) of the bugs localized by AgentFL and 87.7% (222 out of 253) of AutoFL.

claims.text: CosFL uniquely localizes 176 bugs at Top5 relative to external comparators AgentFL and AutoFL.
claims.quote: Moreover, CosFL indepen- dently finds 176 bugs, which illustrates the effectiveness of boosting FL through semantic code search.

claims.text: The authors interpret the comparative results as fault-localization performance increasing with the amount of exploitable software information.
claims.quote: Such results are consistent with our expectation that the performance of FL techniques is proportional to the amount of software information they can exploit.

claims.text: Module knowledge reduces LLM confusion and improves the precision of generated faulty-functionality descriptions.
claims.quote: On the one hand, additional information reduces the confusion of the LLM, leading to more precise descriptions of faulty functionalities, thereby positioning the buggy methods higher in the list.

claims.text: The authors attribute the module-context Top10 loss to reduced ambiguity narrowing the search scope.
claims.quote: On the other hand, the reduction in ambiguity somewhat narrows the search scope, decreasing the likelihood of a small fraction of bugs being localized.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER exceeds DAppFL overall: recall@1/@3/@5 is 50.43/73.91/76.52% versus 6.09/12.17/14.78%.
claims.quote:
Finding 1: FAULTSEEKER consistently outperforms
DAppFL across complexity levels and ranking positions,
with overall top-1 recall of 50.43% versus 6.09%.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER maintains comparatively robust localization across complexity strata; top-1 recall is 71.43%, 58.82% and 36.00%, exceeding DAppFL in each stratum.
claims.quote:
Additionally, FAULTSEEKER demonstrates consistent per-
formance across complexity levels, maintaining effective-
ness from moderate cases (71.43%) through complex cases
(58.82%) to extreme cases (36.00%).

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER reportedly localizes faults in all 52 source-unavailable cases, where DAppFL cannot operate.
claims.quote:
While DAppFL fails to operate in such
scenarios due to its reliance on source code access for fault
predictions, FAULTSEEKER successfully localizes faults in all
52 cases where source code is unavailable.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER outperforms every native LLM in each complexity stratum, succeeding on 8/10 moderate, 10/10 complex and 6/10 extreme transactions.
claims.quote:
The results reveal
that FAULTSEEKER achieves superior performance across all
complexity categories, demonstrating resilience to increasing
analytical complexity.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER is more resilient to increasing analytical complexity than the native LLM controls.

metrics.name: top-5 success counts across complexity strata

claims.quote:
Finding 3: FAULTSEEKER consistently outperforms all
native LLMs across complexity levels, demonstrating
superior resilience while LLMs show significant perfor-
mance degradation with increased complexity.

claims.text: Removing forensic scoping reduces successful localizations from 93 to 2, a 97.8% drop, making it the most consequential ablation.
claims.quote:
Variant 1 removes the transaction-level forensics
stage, demonstrates catastrophic performance degradation with
a 97.8% drop in successful localizations.

claims.text: Removing the information organizer reduces successes from 93 to 38, a 59.1% drop, the smallest ablation impact.
claims.quote:
The information organizer agent (Variant 2) exhibits the
smallest individual impact with a 59.1% performance reduc-
tion.

claims.text: Removing the task coordinator reduces successes from 93 to 32, a 65.6% drop.
claims.quote:
The task coordinator agent (Variant 3) contributes mean-
ingfully to systematic analysis, with its removal resulting in
a 65.6% performance drop, though the framework retains
moderate effectiveness in complex scenarios.

claims.text: Replacing specialist workers with a monolithic agent reduces successes from 93 to 21, a 77.4% drop.
claims.quote:
The specialized workers (Variant 4) prove essential for
maintaining the effectiveness of analysis, showing a substantial
77.4% performance reduction when replaced by monolithic
execution.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER completes localization in approximately 4.4–8.6 minutes; moderate/complex/extreme totals are 265.49/454.40/517.98 seconds.
claims.quote:
Our framework demonstrates reasonable execution times rang-
ing from 265 seconds (4.4 minutes) for moderate cases to 518
seconds (8.6 minutes) for extreme complexity transactions.

claims.text: Estimated per-transaction costs are $1.55/$3.04/$4.53 for moderate/complex/extreme cases.
claims.quote:
Finding 6: FAULTSEEKER completes fault localization
within 4.4-8.6 minutes at $1.55-$4.53 per transaction,
which is suitable for routine security assessments.

claims.text: Interpretable intermediate analysis enables security teams to validate findings and understand the process.
claims.quote:
Finding 7: FAULTSEEKER provides interpretable analy-
sis that enables security teams to validate findings and
understand the analysis process.

claims.text: The Orion case study localizes depositAsset's missing reentrancy protection as the exploitable fault.
claims.quote:
The orchestrator synthesizes findings
to identify the fault: depositAssetlacks reentrancy pro-
tection and becomes exploitable when invoked during swap
execution through malicious token callbacks.

claims.text: Reported execution time and estimated cost make FAULTSEEKER suitable for routine security assessments and practical deployment.
claims.quote:
Finding 6: FAULTSEEKER completes fault localization
within 4.4-8.6 minutes at $1.55-$4.53 per transaction,
which is suitable for routine security assessments.

claims.text: Native controls repeatedly flag correctly implemented asset functions: withdraw 48 times, transfer 40 and approve 33.
claims.quote:
Figure 7 summarizes the frequency of func-
tion names flagged across all models, showing that LLMs con-
sistently generate false positives for:withdraw(48 times),
transfer (40 times), and approve (33 times).

claims.text: Expanding FAULTSEEKER's ranking from top 1 to top 3 adds 23.48 percentage points of recall, while top 3 to top 5 adds only 2.61.
claims.quote:
FAULTSEEKER improves by 23.48% from top-1 to top-
3, then by 2.61% to top-5.

claims.text: GPT-4o performs best among the three native LLM controls.
claims.quote:
Among the native LLMs, GPT-4o per-
forms best but degrades substantially with complexity, Claude
3.7 maintains consistent limited performance before sharp
decline with extreme cases, while DeepSeek R1 shows the
most constrained results, failing entirely in moderate cases.

claims.text: Claude 3.7 has similarly limited success on moderate and complex cases, followed by a sharp decline on extreme cases.
claims.quote:
Among the native LLMs, GPT-4o per-
forms best but degrades substantially with complexity, Claude
3.7 maintains consistent limited performance before sharp
decline with extreme cases, while DeepSeek R1 shows the
most constrained results, failing entirely in moderate cases.

claims.text: DeepSeek R1 is the weakest native control overall and fails on every moderate case.
claims.quote:
Among the native LLMs, GPT-4o per-
forms best but degrades substantially with complexity, Claude
3.7 maintains consistent limited performance before sharp
decline with extreme cases, while DeepSeek R1 shows the
most constrained results, failing entirely in moderate cases.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER's failures require bytecode-level understanding beyond execution semantics, exemplified by storage-collision attacks.
claims.quote:
These cases share a common characteristic: they require
analysis capabilities extending beyond transaction execution
to bytecode-level understanding.

claims.text: Stage 1 adds little time while stage 2 dominates execution: 2.72/262.77, 7.87/446.53 and 33.58/484.40 seconds across the three strata.
claims.quote:
Stage 1 exhibits
minimal overhead, while Stage 2 dominates execution time,
reflecting the intensive multi-agent coordination required for
thorough vulnerability investigation.

claims.text: The authors describe cost as scaling linearly with transaction complexity.

metrics.name: estimated cost across three ordered complexity categories

claims.quote:
Cost analysis reveals a linear scaling pattern from $1.55
for moderate to $4.53 for extreme complexity cases, demon-
strating the economic feasibility.

claims.text: Retrieval agents have the highest average input-token consumption, 10,178 tokens.
claims.quote:
Retrieval agents consume
the highest input tokens in average (10,178), reflecting the
extensive data gathering required for comprehensive vulner-
ability investigation.

claims.text: Task-selector agents incur substantial token use: 8,126 input and 4,123 output tokens on average.
claims.quote:
Task selector agents demonstrate sub-
stantial computational demands with both high input (8,126)
and output (4,123) token consumption, reflecting the resource-
intensive nature of adaptive task prioritization in multi-agent
coordination.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER is faster than cited manual expert analysis, which takes 30–60 minutes for moderate cases and hours or days for complex exploits.

metrics.name: manual expert duration cited from DAppFL [41]

claims.quote:
These execution times compare favorably to manual expert
analysis, which typically requires 30-60 minutes for moderate
cases and several hours or days for complex multi-contract
exploits [41], representing a significant efficiency gain while
maintaining comprehensive analytical depth.

claims.text: Without centralized knowledge integration, workers retain substantial analytical capacity, including 20 successful complex cases.
claims.quote:
This indicates that while centralized knowledge manage-
ment provides valuable system coherence, individual workers
retain considerable autonomous analytical capacity.

claims.text: Without the task coordinator, analytical capabilities remain partially functional, particularly for complex cases with 23 successes.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, this
variant performs competitively in complex cases, suggesting
that while coordination enhances overall efficiency, the under-
lying analytical capabilities remain partially functional without
centralized workflow management.

claims.text: FAULTSEEKER is asserted to preserve comprehensive analytical depth during its rapid analysis.
claims.quote:
These execution times compare favorably to manual expert
analysis, which typically requires 30-60 minutes for moderate
cases and several hours or days for complex multi-contract
exploits [41], representing a significant efficiency gain while
maintaining comprehensive analytical depth.

claims.text: The native controls' complexity-related decline is attributed to memory and attention limitations.
claims.quote:
The performance decline observed across all native LLMs
can be attributed to fundamental limitations in their memory
and attention mechanisms when processing lengthy, multi-
contract transaction sequences.

claims.text: Recurring false positives are interpreted as reliance on surface-level function-name patterns rather than transaction/code semantics.
claims.quote:
This demonstrates that native LLMs rely on
surface-level pattern matching rather than semantic analysis
of transaction flows and code implementation.

claims.text: Without forensic scoping, an unfiltered search space overwhelms analysis.
claims.quote:
Without proper scoping, the framework becomes overwhelmed
by the unfiltered search space when forced to analyze all
function calls without prioritization.

claims.text: Task coordination is asserted to improve overall efficiency, although the ablation reports localization counts rather than efficiency measurements.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, this
variant performs competitively in complex cases, suggesting
that while coordination enhances overall efficiency, the under-
lying analytical capabilities remain partially functional without
centralized workflow management.

claims.text: Source-unavailable attacks are said to expose more explicit behavioral evidence through publicly visible interfaces.
claims.quote:
In
fact, without access to code implementation details, attackers
tend to exploit publicly visible contract interfaces, resulting in
more explicit behavioral evidence for analysis.

claims.text: Orchestrator memory and specialist attention are claimed to sustain analytical focus without context loss as complexity rises.
claims.quote:
In contrast, our
multi-agent framework addresses these limitations through
persistent memory management via orchestrator agents and
specialized attention allocation through coordinated worker
agents, enabling sustained analytical focus without losing
contextual information as complexity increases.

claims.text: The native controls' naming biases are used to argue that the multi-agent framework is necessary for investigation beyond function-name patterns.
claims.quote:
This limitation
validates the necessity of our multi-agent framework, which
enables investigation beyond function name patterns through
systematic analysis of transaction execution flows.

metrics.name: Incremental correctly fixed bugs per stage

claims.quote: Subsequent rounds progressively improve performance, with Round 1 contributing the largest gain of 33 fixes, followed by Round 2 with 21 fixes, Round 3 with 8 fixes, and a final arbitration stage adding 4 fixes, reaching a total of 392.

claims.text: Trace-guided single-pass generation is slightly more effective than static debate alone, with 158 versus 154 correct fixes.
claims.quote: In contrast, removing the debate mechanism (TraceRepair𝑁𝐷 ) results in 158 correct fixes, suggesting that trace-guided single-pass generation is slightly more effective than static debate alone.

claims.text: The MF results are attributed to execution traces exposing interprocedural state and data flow, enabling globally consistent cross-method repairs.
claims.quote: In contrast, execution traces explicitly model inter-procedural data flow and state transitions, enabling the model to produce globally consistent repairs across affected methods.

claims.text: The GPT-3.5 comparison is interpreted as showing that improvements primarily arise from the framework rather than backbone choice.

metrics.name: Correctly fixed bugs under a common GPT-3.5 backbone

claims.quote: This result suggests that the observed improvements primarily stem from the proposed framework rather than the choice of backbone model.

claims.text: Repair agents dominate token usage: 78.9k/92.9% for GPT-3.5 and 70.1k/91.1% for DeepSeek-V3.2; probing uses 4.2k/4.9% and 5.2k/6.7%, and judging uses 1.9k and 1.7k, both 2.2%.
claims.quote: In both settings, more than 90% of the tokens are consumed by the Repair Agents, while the Judge Agent accounts for only 2.2%.

claims.text: Successfully fixed bugs finish relatively quickly, averaging 119.8s with GPT-3.5 and 259.3s with DeepSeek-V3.2; unsuccessful DeepSeek-V3.2 runs reach 898.3s while exhausting the iteration budget.

metrics.name: Mean runtime for successfully fixed bugs

claims.quote: In contrast, unsuccessful runs are significantly longer, reaching up to 898.3s for DeepSeek-V3.2, as the framework exhausts its iteration budget.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.2 TraceRepair's monetary efficiency is attributed jointly to lower token consumption and lower model pricing.
claims.quote:
The cost efficiency ofTrac-
eRepair𝐷𝑆𝑉3.2 is attributed to both reduced token consumption and the lower pricing of the underlying model, making it particularly suitable for large-scale deployment.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.2's higher runtime relative to GPT-3.5 is attributed mainly to API response characteristics rather than the repair process.
claims.quote:
The higher latency of the DeepSeek-V3.2 variant is primarily due to differences in API re-
sponse characteristics rather than the repair process.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.2 TraceRepair is presented as particularly suitable for large-scale deployment because of its low cost.
claims.quote:
The cost efficiency ofTrac-
eRepair𝐷𝑆𝑉3.2 is attributed to both reduced token consumption and the lower pricing of the underlying model, making it particularly suitable for large-scale deployment.

claims.text: Bugs uniquely fixed by DeepSeek-V3.2 TraceRepair are characterized as predominantly logic-dependent failures for which static signals are insufficient.
claims.quote: These uniquely resolved cases predominantly involve logic-dependent failures, where static signals are often insufficient to characterize the underlying issue.

claims.text: Diminishing stage gains are interpreted as earlier iterations handling easier errors and later rounds refining harder cases.

metrics.name: Incremental correct fixes by debate stage

claims.quote: The diminishing gains across later rounds suggest that earlier iterations capture the majority of easily correctable errors, while subsequent rounds focus on refining more challenging cases.

claims.text: GPT-3.5 instrumentation failures are reported as occurring more frequently in complex methods.
claims.quote:
TraceRepair𝐺𝑃𝑇3.5 attains 79.3%, with fail-
ures more frequently occurring in complex methods.

claims.text: The coarse-localization experiments are interpreted as evidence of resilience to noisy trace data, although trace noise is not directly manipulated or measured.

metrics.name: Repair performance under PFL versus MFL

claims.quote: Our experiments with coarse-grained fault localization suggest that the multi-agent debate mechanism retains reasonable resilience under noisy trace data, though improving robustness under low coverage conditions remains future work.

claims.text: Long unsuccessful runs are interpreted as indicating insufficient diagnostic evidence in the collected traces.
claims.quote:
This disparity sug-
gests that when runtime traces provide sufficient diagnostic signal, the repair process converges quickly, whereas prolonged runs typi-
cally indicate that the available execution evidence is insufficient to resolve the defect.

claims.text: Lower token overhead is attributed to runtime evidence reducing the need for extended conversational reasoning.
claims.quote: In contrast,TraceRepairreduces this overhead by providing repair agents with concrete runtime evidence prior to patch generation, thereby limiting the need for extended dialogue.

claims.text: Initial LegaTest generates runnable tests for 376/403 classes (93.3%), versus ChatUniTest 37.97% and EvoSuite 33.75%.
claims.quote:
Overall,LegaTest
consistently achieves the highest test generation capability, successfully producing tests for 376 out of 403 classes
(93.3%), whereas ChatUniTest and EvoSuite succeed on only 153 (37.97%) and 136 (33.75%) classes, respectively.

claims.text: Initial LegaTest has 91.52% successful executions, above ChatUniTest's 88.76% and below EvoSuite's 99.29%.
claims.quote:
In contrast,LegaTest achieves
a much broader generation scope while still maintaining strong executability (91.52% successful executions),
demonstrating that the generated tests are not only broadly applicable but also robust in practice.

claims.text: Initial LegaTest has fewer assertion errors than ChatUniTest (5.44% versus 9.60%).
claims.quote:
Compared to
ChatUniTest,LegaTest yields both significantly higher generation success (93.3% vs. 37.97%) and lower error
rates.

claims.text: The paper claims lower runtime failures than the baselines, although Table 2 gives LegaTest 3.04%, ChatUniTest 1.64%, and EvoSuite 0.35%.
claims.quote:
Compared to the baselines,LegaTest
achieves higher generation coverage and lower runtime failures, establishing its superiority in correctness
and executability.

claims.text: Initial LegaTest attains the highest pooled line/branch/method coverage on 403 classes (66.95/54.37/74.16%), exceeding ChatUniTest and EvoSuite.
claims.quote:
When aggregated across the full 403-class benchmark, the initial version ofLegaTest already attains the
highest overall averages: line coverage (66.95%), branch coverage (54.37%), and method coverage (74.16%).

claims.text: Initial LegaTest produces the smallest pooled suites: 11.94 tests, 39% fewer than EvoSuite and 55% fewer than ChatUniTest.
claims.quote:
Importantly, this superior coverage is reached with the smallest test suites on average (11.94 cases),
which is 39% fewer tests than EvoSuite (19.60) and 55% fewer than ChatUniTest (26.82).

claims.text: Evolution improves coverage over Initial across the selected projects under both models: pooled line/branch/method coverage rises 62.11/49.38/70.61→79.91/67.75/86.11% with DeepSeek and 73.21/62.74/79.20→84.05/72.90/89.82% with GPT.
claims.quote:
The
comparison between the initial and optimized versions reveals consistent and substantial improvements across
all projects for both backends.

claims.text: Full LegaTest has significantly higher per-class line, branch and method coverage than ChatUniTest and UTGen under both backends.

evidence.detail: Paired per-class t-tests versus ChatUniTest and UTGen, with failed generations scored zero; all line/branch/method p-values <0.001 under both backends.
evidence.quote:
Under both DeepSeek and GPT backends,LegaTest achieves significantly higher
line, branch, and method coverage than both baselines, with all p-values below 0.001.

claims.quote:
Under both DeepSeek and GPT backends,LegaTest achieves significantly higher
line, branch, and method coverage than both baselines, with all p-values below 0.001.

claims.text: Full LegaTest more often produces class-level coverage results than ChatUniTest and UTGen on the selected 100 classes under both backends.

evidence.detail: McNemar exact tests: DeepSeek discordant pairs 16/2 versus ChatUniTest (p=1.31e-3), 58/1 versus UTGen (p=2.08e-16); GPT 42/0 (p=4.55e-13), 53/0 (p=2.22e-16).
evidence.quote:
These results indicate thatLegaTest significantly outperforms both
baselines in successful class-level result generation.

claims.quote:
These results indicate thatLegaTest significantly outperforms both
baselines in successful class-level result generation.

claims.text: Evolution raises fitness from 0.62 to 0.87 with DeepSeek and 0.79 to 0.95 with GPT between Gen1 and Gen10.
claims.quote:
With DeepSeek, the
fitness increases from 0.62 at Gen1 to 0.87 at Gen10, while GPT exhibits a similar trend, improving from 0.79 to
0.95.

claims.text: Line, branch and method coverage improve monotonically over generations under both backends.
claims.quote: All three coverage metrics demonstrate monotonic improvement as evolution proceeds.

claims.text: The paper generalizes the consistent two-backend improvements as effectiveness largely independent of the underlying LLM.

Fitness improvements across DeepSeek and GPT

claims.quote:
These results confirm
that the genetic algorithm–based refinement improves the quality and adequacy of test suites, and that the
effectiveness of our approach is largely independent of the underlying LLM.

claims.text: The paper attributes high coverage to crossover–mutation synergy and calls the complete evolutionary strategy essential; the operators are not separately ablated.
claims.quote:
This continuous improvement
validates the synergy between the global exploration of crossover and the local refinement of mutation,
confirming that the complete evolutionary strategy is essential for achieving high coverage.

niTest (15.5%) and EvoSuite (2.2%).

claims.text: The paper interprets increasing fitness as enhanced adaptability of the generated suites.

genetic algorithms effectively enhances the adaptability of the generated test suites, with evolutionary refinement
maintaining its positive impact throughout the process.

claims.quote:

(basic) and Level 2 (property) assertions improves test robustness and executability during evolution.

claims.text: The paper interprets the greater repair-token share during evolution as increased difficulty repairing synthesized tests.

claims.text: LegaTest adds LLM-related computational cost relative to fixed-budget EvoSuite.

claims.text: The paper calls LegaTest practical for iterative coverage-driven testing, based on its coverage/cost trade-off without a user study.

practical for iterative, coverage-driven unit test generation.

claims.text: The conclusion claims improved test diversity through feedback-driven evolution without a direct diversity evaluation.
claims.quote:
By coordinating LLMs and genetic algorithms during optimization,LegaTest shifts unit test generation
from static prompts to a feedback-driven evolutionary process, improving accuracy, diversity, and adaptability.

claims.text: The conclusion claims reduced redundancy from optimization without a measured duplicate-test rate.
claims.quote:
This enables broader exploration,
reduces redundancy, enhances structural and semantic coherence through LLM-guided crossover, and supports
fine-grained, goal-directed mutation with adaptive control.

claims.text: Raw zero-shot GPT outperforms some external baselines on several projects, demonstrating nontrivial test-generation capability.

claims.text: Fuzz4All improves final coverage over GrayC on GCC (+18.8%), YARPGen on G++ (+26.5%), TypeFuzz on CVC5 (+24.9%), go-fuzz on Go (+13.7%), Hephaestus on javac (+60.9%) and MorphQ on Qiskit (+75.6%); mean improvement over the best baselines is 36.8%.

evidence.detail: All six RQ1 coverage improvements are marked significant using Mann–Whitney U, p<0.05.
evidence.quote:
Following prior work [36], we use the Mann-Whitney U-test [52]
to compute statistical significance and indicate significant (p < 0.05)
coverage results in applicable tables (Tables 2 and 4) with *.

claims.quote:
We observe thatFuzz4All achieves
the highest coverage by the end of the fuzzing campaign across all
targets, with an average improvement of 36.8% compared to the top
performing baselines.

claims.text: Feature-specific documentation achieves 83.0% mean target-feature hit rate; general fuzzing is reported to have 96.0% lower hit rate.
claims.quote:
We observe that targeting a specific feature yields a high amount
of fuzzing inputs that directly use the feature, with an average
hit rate of 83.0%.

claims.text: General fuzzing achieves higher overall line coverage than each targeted feature campaign in every language.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 3, a general fuzzing approach,
while achieving the highest overall code coverage, can be extremely
inefficient in targeting a specific feature (average 96.0% reduction in
hit rate compared with Fuzz4All’s targeted fuzzing).

claims.text: Autoprompting increases coverage over raw documentation for all six languages under the generate-new-with-examples workflow.
claims.quote:
However, we can further
improve both the code coverage and the validity rate by using our
autoprompting stage to distill the user input into a concise but in-
formative prompt (autoprompt), instead of using the raw user input.

claims.text: Autoprompting increases valid-input rate over raw documentation for all six languages.
claims.quote:
However, we can further
improve both the code coverage and the validity rate by using our
autoprompting stage to distill the user input into a concise but in-
formative prompt (autoprompt), instead of using the raw user input.

claims.text: Automatically including a previous valid input example increases coverage in all six languages.
claims.quote:
Adding an example to the input prompt ( w/ example )
avoids sampling from the same distribution and improves both the
coverage and the validity rate.

claims.text: Automatically including a previous valid input example increases validity in all six languages.
claims.quote:
Adding an example to the input prompt ( w/ example )
avoids sampling from the same distribution and improves both the
coverage and the validity rate.

claims.text: The full three-strategy workflow achieves the highest ablation-study coverage on every SUT; five of six improvements over generate-new with examples are marked significant.

evidence.detail: Table 4 marks full-versus-second-best coverage improvements significant for C++, SMT, Go, Java and Qiskit, but not C.
evidence.quote:
Following prior work [36], we use the Mann-Whitney U-test [52]
to compute statistical significance and indicate significant (p < 0.05)
coverage results in applicable tables (Tables 2 and 4) with *.

claims.quote:
Finally, the full Fuzz4All approach
achieves the highest coverage across all SUTs.

claims.text: Fuzz4All reports 98 bugs: GCC 30, Clang 27, CVC5 9, Z3 14, Go 4, Java 3 and Qiskit 11.

evidence.detail: Table 5 lists 64 previously unknown and 26 known confirmed bugs; six pending and two won't-fix reports remain outside those confirmed columns.
evidence.quote:
In total, Fuzz4All detects 98 bugs, with 64 bugs already
confirmed by the developers as previously unknown.

claims.quote:
In total, Fuzz4All detects 98 bugs, with 64 bugs already
confirmed by the developers as previously unknown.

claims.text: Developers confirm 64 Fuzz4All-detected bugs as previously unknown.
claims.quote:
In total, Fuzz4All detects 98 bugs, with 64 bugs already
confirmed by the developers as previously unknown.

claims.text: Fuzz4All surpasses generation-based YARPGen and MorphQ in coverage almost immediately.
claims.quote:
Contrasting with generation-based fuzzers
(i.e., YARPGen and MorphQ), Fuzz4All is able to almost immedi-
ately achieve higher coverage, demonstrating the powerful genera-
tive ability of LLMs in producing diverse code snippets compared to
traditional program generation techniques.

claims.text: Fuzz4All eventually overtakes mutation-based GrayC and go-fuzz after their initial seed advantage.
claims.quote: Figure 4: Coverage trend of Fuzz4All against state-of-the-art fuzzers in a 24-hour fuzzing campaign.

claims.text: Fuzz4All continues covering new code near 24 hours while GrayC, Csmith, YARPGen, TypeFuzz, go-fuzz, Hephaestus and MorphQ plateau.
claims.quote:
Unlike the baseline fuzzers, which reach a coverage plateau by
the end of the 24-hour period, Fuzz4All keeps finding inputs that
cover new code, even near the end of the fuzzing campaign.

claims.text: Autoprompting adds only 2.3 minutes per campaign on average, included in the 24-hour budget.
claims.quote:
Note that we include
the autoprompting time as part of the fuzzing budget for a fair
comparison, which incurs negligible overhead (avg. 2.3 minutes per
fuzzing campaign).

claims.text: Fuzz4All has 56.0% lower validity on average than the external baseline set: GrayC, Csmith, YARPGen, TypeFuzz, go-fuzz, Hephaestus and MorphQ.
claims.quote:
In
contrast, Fuzz4All has a lower percentage of valid fuzzing inputs
generated (56.0% average reduction compared to baseline tools).

claims.text: Fuzz4All produces 43.0% fewer inputs on average than the external baseline set (GrayC, Csmith, YARPGen, TypeFuzz, go-fuzz, Hephaestus and MorphQ) in fixed-duration campaigns.

metrics.name: unique generated input count per 24 hours

claims.quote:
By using an LLM as the generation
engine, Fuzz4All is bottlenecked by GPU inference, leading to
43.0% fewer fuzzing inputs compared to traditional fuzzers.

claims.text: The narrative states that no initial prompt gives the lowest coverage across all languages; Table 4 instead has lower SMT coverage for raw prompting (49,697 versus 50,838).
claims.quote:
We observe that across all studied languages, the
no input variant achieves the lowest coverage.

claims.text: Raw documentation improves coverage over no initial documentation in five languages; the narrative's unqualified boost has an SMT exception.
claims.quote:
We observe a cover-
age boost as we use the raw prompt variant, where we provide the
raw documentation as the initial prompt.

claims.text: The no-input variant has higher validity than raw prompting and autoprompting in all six languages.
claims.quote:
As such,
the LLM can only generate simple code snippets with high validity
rate but is less effective in covering the SUT.

claims.text: Repeated inputs fall from 8.0% without examples to 4.7% with the full workflow.
claims.quote:
On average, 8.0% of the fuzzing inputs generated are repeated in
w/o example compared to only 4.7% when using the full Fuzz4All
approach.

claims.text: Related targeted features show greater cross-feature hit rates, exemplified by typedef and union compared with goto.
claims.quote:
Furthermore,
we observe that fuzzing on features that are related can lead to a
moderately high cross-feature hit rate (i.e., hit rate of feature X on
fuzzing run for feature Y).

claims.text: Validity varies by language: C 37.26%, C++ 40.74%, SMT2 47.63%, Go 23.02%, Java 49.05% and Qiskit 24.90%.
claims.quote:
Regarding
validity rate, a general-purpose programming language, such as C,
has a relatively lower validity rate compared to domain-specific
languages, such as the SMT2 language used for SMT solvers.

claims.text: Generated-input counts vary across SUTs, from 22,817 for Go to 44,324 for GCC in 24 hours.

metrics.name: unique generated input count per 24 hours

claims.quote:
We note that Fuzz4All achieves a wide range of validity rates
and numbers of fuzzing inputs across different SUTs.

claims.text: A valid std::optional/noexcept program exposes a GCC internal compiler error; prior techniques lack the required noexcept support (comparator names not_reported for this example).

evidence.detail: The GCC example was confirmed, fixed and incorporated into the GCC regression suite.
evidence.quote: The developers have already confirmed and fixed this bug.

claims.quote:
While this
code is valid and should compile correctly, this combination of dif-
ficult runtime dependencies cause GCC to crash with an internal
compiler error .

claims.text: An invalid decltype/throw declaration exposes a developer-confirmed Clang crash that valid-only, feature-limited prior fuzzers struggle to find (comparator names not_reported for this example).

evidence.detail: Developers confirmed that the invalid program reveals a Clang frontend bug.
evidence.quote:
This code, while invalid, is still
useful to reveal a bug in the Clang frontend as confirmed by the
developers.

claims.quote:
This code, while invalid, is still
useful to reveal a bug in the Clang frontend as confirmed by the
developers.

claims.text: Targeting Go runtime documentation exposes a ReadMemStats(nil) segmentation fault, confirmed and fixed by developers; go-fuzz lacks a runtime template.

evidence.detail: The targeted runtime-library example was confirmed and fixed by Go developers.
evidence.quote:
The bug has been confirmed and
fixed by the developers.

claims.quote:
Figure 5c shows a bug found in Go where a nil input causes a
segmentation fault instead of producing a useful failure message.

claims.text: Fuzz4All finds a Qiskit QASM export/reimport crash caused by a named register colliding with an operation name; MorphQ's anonymous-register templates miss this case.
claims.quote:
A quan-
tum program, represented by the qc variable, is exported to QASM,
a low level representation, silently generating an invalid output file,
which leads to a crash when being reimported.

claims.text: GCC developers add a modified Fuzz4All bug-triggering program to the official regression suite.
claims.quote:
Interest-
ingly, they even added a slightly modified version of our submitted
code snippet to the official test suite of GCC.

claims.text: Adding mutation and semantic-equivalence strategies improves validity on five SUTs but reduces Qiskit validity from 29.12% to 27.45%.
claims.quote:
Table 4
shows the coverage and validity rate of our studied variants.

claims.text: Targeted fuzzing reaches recently added Qiskit features at 71.76%, 75.97% and 54.79% hit rates, while general fuzzing reaches none of them.
claims.quote:
Table 3 shows the results of targeted fuzzing
as well as the default general fuzzing used in RQ1.

claims.text: Fuzz4All generates more diverse programs than GrayC, Csmith, YARPGen, TypeFuzz, go-fuzz, Hephaestus and MorphQ, inferred from higher coverage.
claims.quote:
In spite of the lower validity rate and number of fuzzing inputs,
Fuzz4All generates much more diverse programs compared to
traditional fuzzing tools, as evidenced by the high coverage obtained
(+36.8% average increase).

claims.text: Updating examples and generation strategies sustains generation diversity and thereby late coverage growth.
claims.quote:
We hypothesize that this allows Fuzz4All to effectively
generate new and diverse fuzzing inputs even after a long period
of fuzzing, leading to sustained coverage increase.

claims.text: GPU inference is the bottleneck responsible for lower fuzzing-input throughput.

metrics.name: unique generated input count per 24 hours

claims.quote:
By using an LLM as the generation
engine, Fuzz4All is bottlenecked by GPU inference, leading to
43.0% fewer fuzzing inputs compared to traditional fuzzers.

claims.text: Differences in SUT invocation cost explain the differing generated-input counts across targets.

metrics.name: unique generated input count per 24 hours

claims.quote:
The number of
fuzzing inputs varies across targets due to the varying cost to invoke
the SUT after each fuzzing iteration for bug detection.

claims.text: Fewer quantum-program training examples may explain Qiskit's low validity.
claims.quote:
As
quantum computing is an emerging area with its own set of library
APIs, the generation LLM may not have seen as many examples
of quantum programs during its training as for more established
languages.

claims.text: Without initial documentation the model generates only simple snippets, explaining high validity but weaker coverage.
claims.quote:
As such,

hcs.name: GadgetHunter: Java deserialization gadget-chain detection
hcs.quote:
To address these challenges, GadgetHunter integrates static analysis with LLM-guided reasoning
in a three-stage hybrid analysis pipeline (Figure 2).

hcs.name: SA (Static Analysis Only)
hcs.removed: LLM semantic reachability and LLM/SMT path-feasibility analysis; retains interprocedural taint propagation
hcs.quote: SA (Static Analysis Only): Performs only interprocedural taint propagation.

hcs.name: SA_SemReach (Static Analysis + Semantic Reachability)
hcs.removed: JDV constraint extraction, SMT feasibility checking and associated script-repair loop
hcs.quote: SA_SemReach (Static Analysis + Semantic Reachability): removes the feasibility analysis.

hcs.name: SA_LLMD (Static Analysis + LLM Direct)
hcs.removed: Replaces region-based semantic validation and solver-backed feasibility with direct black-box LLM validation of SA candidate chains
hcs.quote:
SA_LLMD (Static Analysis + LLM Direct): Builds on SA by letting an LLM directly validate
candidate chains in a black-box manner.

hcs.name: SA_LLMC (Static Analysis + LLM Constraint)
hcs.removed: Replaces solver-backed feasibility analysis with LLM end-to-end constraint extraction and feasibility judgment
hcs.quote:
SA_LLMC (Static Analysis + LLM Constraint): Inspired by BugLens [25], replaces the feasibility
analysis by using LLMs conduct end-to-end constraint extraction and analysis to decide feasibility.
