GadgetHunter analyzes 2,662 chains in about 62.7k seconds, with an average of 23.53s per chain
and an average cost of $0.04 per chain.

claims.text: Total ysoserial expenditure is $95.24, averaging about $0.04 per chain.
claims.quote:
The total expenditure across
the entire benchmark is $95.24, averaging only $0.04 per chain.

claims.text: Across the four CVEs, GadgetHunter recovers six of eight known chains, missing one SnakeYaml and one Dubbo chain; FNR is 25%.
claims.quote:
Counting against
the ground truth, we matched 6 known chains and missed 2 (one in SnakeYaml and one in Dubbo),
yielding an FNR of 25% (2/8).

claims.text: GadgetHunter reports 18 exploitable chains across the four CVEs; practical exploitability remains unconfirmed by end-to-end PoCs.

evidence.quote:
Manual analysis
confirms that this RCE leveragesCommonsCollections 3.2.1 , and GadgetHunter systematically
enumerates feasible edge substitutions within the same chain schema, thereby producing multiple
valid variants beyond the CVE’s minimal record.
evidence.description: Manual analysis identifies CommonsCollections 3.2.1 and feasible edge substitutions in the Tomcat chain schema; no end-to-end PoCs.

claims.quote: Across the four CVEs, GadgetHunter detected 18 exploitable chains overall.

claims.text: For Tomcat CVE-2025-24813, GadgetHunter finds 12 additional exploitable chain variants beyond the advisory's one chain (13 total in Table 6).

evidence.quote:
Manual analysis
confirms that this RCE leveragesCommonsCollections 3.2.1 , and GadgetHunter systematically
enumerates feasible edge substitutions within the same chain schema, thereby producing multiple
valid variants beyond the CVE’s minimal record.
evidence.description: Manual analysis identifies CommonsCollections 3.2.1 and feasible edge substitutions in the Tomcat chain schema; no end-to-end PoCs.

claims.quote:
Especially, for Tomcat (CVE-2025-24813), although the advisory
documents only a single chain, GadgetHunter uncovered 12 exploitable variants.

claims.text: The authors conclude GadgetHunter is practical for real-world audits (generalization across Tomcat variants is covered by K31).
claims.quote:
This confirms its
practicality in real-world audits, while the Tomcat case illustrates its ability to generalize across
semantically equivalent chain variants.

claims.text: Measured overhead is claimed to make GadgetHunter practical at the scale of thousands of candidate chains.
claims.quote:
These findings show that
GadgetHunter scales to thousands of gadget chains with manageable overhead.

claims.text: Increasing collection time raises Gleipner Depth recovery from 14/20 to 16/20.
claims.quote:
Experiments with extended
collection time recovered additional chains (16/20 and 15/20, respectively), confirming that these
gaps stem from configuration trade-offs rather than fundamental limitations of the approach.

claims.text: Increasing collection time raises Gleipner Polymorphism recovery from 13/20 to 15/20.
claims.quote:
Experiments with extended
collection time recovered additional chains (16/20 and 15/20, respectively), confirming that these
gaps stem from configuration trade-offs rather than fundamental limitations of the approach.

claims.text: Six missed Depth and seven missed Polymorphism cases are attributed to missing call-graph paths caused by time-bounded collection and nondeterministic DFS, rather than fundamental reasoning limits.

evidence.quote:
Experiments with extended
collection time recovered additional chains (16/20 and 15/20, respectively), confirming that these
gaps stem from configuration trade-offs rather than fundamental limitations of the approach.
evidence.description: Additional runs with longer collection recover two more chains in each category, corroborating part of the configuration explanation.

claims.quote:
Regarding the Depth and Polymorphism, the six missing Depth cases and seven missing Polymor-
phism cases are absent from GadgetHunter’s call graph due to its time-bounded path collection
and non-deterministic DFS traversal order inherited from Flash [46].

claims.text: Method-summary-based taint analysis collapses all ten Gleipner Multipath paths into one output chain, sacrificing path sensitivity.
claims.quote:
Consequently, all 10 paths reduce to one identical chain inGadgetH-
unter’s output.

claims.text: Mined ysoserial chains average 10.3 gadgets and 9.1 regions.
claims.quote:
Across all 2,662 mined gadget chains on the ysoserial bench-
mark, we observed an average of 10.3 gadgets and 9.1 regions per chain, with only 14.7% of regions
being fully resolved by static analysis.

claims.text: Only 14.7% of regions are fully resolved by static analysis, motivating LLM reasoning at the remaining boundaries.
claims.quote:
Across all 2,662 mined gadget chains on the ysoserial bench-
mark, we observed an average of 10.3 gadgets and 9.1 regions per chain, with only 14.7% of regions
being fully resolved by static analysis.

claims.text: Region counts are said to correlate strongly with gadget counts and therefore reflect inherent program complexity; no correlation coefficient or test is reported.
claims.quote:
This distribution indicates that region partitioning is not an
artificial decomposition: the number of regions strongly correlates with gadget counts, reflecting
inherent program complexity.

claims.text: Runtime varies substantially by application: Click and Spring take seconds per chain, while Jython reaches 152 seconds per chain.
claims.quote:
Smaller-scale projects such as Click and
Spring complete within seconds per chain, while reflection-heavy frameworks like Clojure and
Jython require significantly longer times (up to 152s per chain).

claims.text: The authors attribute higher runtime in reflection-heavy projects to more dynamic boundaries, LLM queries and larger SMT constraint systems.
claims.quote:
This discrepancy aligns with the
proportion of dynamic regions: projects dominated by reflection or dynamic dispatch involve more
ambiguous edges, triggering more LLM queries and larger constraint systems for SMT solving.

claims.text: The authors describe mostly static FileUpload and Wicket chains as lightweight; Table 7 reports 39.52 and 107.29 seconds per chain respectively.
claims.quote:
In
contrast, projects with mostly static gadget flows (e.g., FileUpload, Wicket) remain lightweight.

claims.text: Region partitioning is claimed to limit LLM invocations by restricting reasoning to ambiguous edges; no separate query-count comparison is reported.
claims.quote:
Runtime variation across
projects aligns with the proportion of dynamic regions, underscoring the role of region partitioning
in limiting LLM invocations.

claims.text: Compact gadget summaries are claimed to control execution time and API expenditure; token savings are not separately measured.
claims.quote:
By summarizing gadgets into compact constraints before SMT
solving, GadgetHunter controls both execution time and API expenditure, supporting scalable
use in real-world audits.

claims.text: Sofa-RPC CVE-2024-23636: one known chain and one detected chain.
claims.quote:
As shown
in Table 6, GadgetHunter successfully rediscovered the known gadget chains in all four CVEs
and additionally surfaced several variants.

claims.text: Tomcat CVE-2025-24813: one known chain and 13 detected chains.
claims.quote:
As shown
in Table 6, GadgetHunter successfully rediscovered the known gadget chains in all four CVEs
and additionally surfaced several variants.

claims.text: SnakeYaml CVE-2022-1471: one of two known chains detected.
claims.quote:
As shown
in Table 6, GadgetHunter successfully rediscovered the known gadget chains in all four CVEs
and additionally surfaced several variants.

claims.text: Dubbo CVE-2023-23638: three of four known chains detected.
claims.quote:
As shown
in Table 6, GadgetHunter successfully rediscovered the known gadget chains in all four CVEs
and additionally surfaced several variants.

claims.text: The reported feasibility results establish theoretical semantic validity, while practical exploitability lacks end-to-end PoC confirmation.
claims.quote:
The feasibility checks conducted
by Z3 constraint solving ensure that the discovered chains are semantically valid, but we have
not yet generated end-to-end PoC exploits to confirm practical exploitability.

claims.text: The authors infer from SA_LLMD's inferior performance that GadgetHunter's improvement cannot be attributed to memorization; these accuracy metrics do not directly test memorization.

evidence.quote:
Second, we evaluated two
CVEs (i.e., CVE-2024-23636 and CVE-2025-24813) disclosed after the presumed cutoff date of LLM
training data, which further reduces the likelihood that data leakage explains our results.
evidence.description: Two CVEs were disclosed after a presumed, unverified training-data cutoff; this does not establish absence of memorization.

claims.quote:
First, ablation studies showed that
direct LLM reasoning (SA_LLMD) is substantially less effective than our integrated framework,
indicating that the improvements cannot be attributed to memorization.

claims.text: Combining static analysis, LLM reachability and path-feasibility analysis achieves a recall-precision trade-off that neither pure static analysis (SA) nor direct LLM validation (SA_LLMD) achieves alone.
claims.quote:
Together, these components achieve
a principled trade-off between recall and precision, which neither pure static analysis nor direct
LLM validation can achieve alone.

claims.text: o4-mini TestGeneralizer averages 77.25% mutation-based and 73.41% LLM-assessed scenario coverage, above Vanilla by 37.44/32.82 points, ChatTester by 31.66/23.08 points, and EvoSuite by 57.67/59.62 points; EvoSuite's average excludes two projects.
claims.quote:
Overall, TestGeneralizer achieves 77.25% mutation-based scenario
coverage and 73.41% LLM-assessed scenario coverage, improving over Vanilla by 37.44% and 32.82%,
and over ChatTester by 31.66% and 23.08%, respectively.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.1 TestGeneralizer averages 80.41% mutation-based and 70.24% LLM-assessed scenario coverage, exceeding the reported Vanilla, ChatTester and EvoSuite averages.
claims.quote:
As we can see, TestGeneralizer still consistently outperforms all baselines across all metrics,
demonstrating its robustness and practicality for deployment in the industry.

claims.text: TestGeneralizer has the highest average branch and line coverage, 17.92% and 21.54%, exceeding ChatTester by 3.51 and 4.13 points.
claims.quote:
TestGeneralizer achieves the highest average branch coverage, line coverage, and
mutation score, with gains of 3.51%, 4.13%, and 9.87% over the best baseline, ChatTester.

claims.text: TestGeneralizer has the highest average whole-project mutation score, 51.31%, exceeding ChatTester by 9.87 points.
claims.quote:
TestGeneralizer achieves the highest average branch coverage, line coverage, and
mutation score, with gains of 3.51%, 4.13%, and 9.87% over the best baseline, ChatTester.

claims.text: Adding generated tests to existing suites increases average mutation score by 7.07 points, from 57.93% to 65.00%, suggesting additional fault-detection capability.
claims.quote:
Across all projects, augmenting the existing tests with TestGeneralizer yields an average increase
of 7.07% (57.93% to 65.00%) in mutation score, 2.46% (17.47% to 19.93%) in branch coverage, and 2.05%
(21.45% to 23.50%) in line coverage.

claims.text: Adding generated tests increases average branch coverage by 2.46 points (17.47% to 19.93%) and line coverage by 2.05 points (21.45% to 23.50%).
claims.quote:
Across all projects, augmenting the existing tests with TestGeneralizer yields an average increase
of 7.07% (57.93% to 65.00%) in mutation score, 2.46% (17.47% to 19.93%) in branch coverage, and 2.05%
(21.45% to 23.50%) in line coverage.

claims.text: Auto-tuned prompting achieves the best VP-identification precision/recall/F1 (81.21/86.39/83.72%), exceeding zero-shot by 31.66/10.90/23.89 points and also exceeding few-shot and hand-crafted prompts.
claims.quote:
In contrast, prompt auto-tuning can synthesize and reconcile rules from diverse samples into a
unified, conflict-resolved rule set, achieving the best results across all metrics with improvements
of 31.66%, 10.90%, and 23.89% in precision, recall, and F1-score over zero-shot prompting.

claims.text: Retaining retrieved knowledge in Stage 2/3 prompts raises average mutation-based/LLM-assessed scenario coverage from 75.35/68.60% to 80.12/74.05%, gains of 4.77/5.45 points.

evidence.description: The ofdrw worked example links retrieved paint subtypes to broader scenario inference.
evidence.quote: This knowledge guides the LLM to infer comprehensive test scenarios.

claims.quote:
As shown in the “w/o knowledge” column, compared to
TestGeneralizer, scenario coverage drops by 4.77% and 5.45% on average in mutation-based and
LLM-assessed metrics, respectively.

claims.text: Including auto-tuned rule text raises average mutation-based/LLM-assessed scenario coverage from 73.23/66.31% to 80.12/74.05%, gains of 6.89/7.74 points.

evidence.description: The Spark worked example attributes spurious VPs and redundant/missing scenarios to the prompt without rules.
evidence.quote:
As a
result, the template includes eight meaningless variation points and only two actual ones, resulting
in four redundant scenarios and missing one of the three intended scenarios.

claims.quote:
Comparing the column “w/o rules” with the column “Test-
Generalizer”, we observe that scenario coverage decreases by 6.89% and 7.74% on average in
mutation-based and LLM-assessed metrics, respectively.

claims.text: Removing input-test oracles causes a moderate decrease from 77.2/73.4% to 65.1/67.4% scenario coverage, indicating useful scenario information remains in setup and invocations.
claims.quote:
L1 (oracle re-
moved) achieves 65.1% / 67.4%, corresponding
to a decrease of 12.1% / 6.0%.

claims.text: Minimal smoke-test inputs retain 60.9/63.7% average scenario coverage, decreases of 16.3/9.7 points from L0, supporting graceful degradation.
claims.quote:
Even when provided with a minimal smoke test, TestGeneralizer maintains over 60% scenario
coverage, indicating the pipeline remains highly effective without requiring rich initial tests.

claims.text: Sixteen of 27 submitted additional tests were accepted and merged, with 11 pending and none rejected, demonstrating practical value within the four-project field study.
claims.quote: Among them, 16 tests have been accepted, 11 tests remain pending, and none are rejected.

claims.text: TestGeneralizer generated 10 of the 27 submitted tests that ChatTester failed to generate (37.0%).
claims.quote: ChatTester failed to generate 37.0% (10/27) of the generalized tests.

claims.text: Six developer-accepted TestGeneralizer tests were missed by ChatTester, representing 37.5% of the 16 accepted tests.

evidence.description: Project maintainers accepted the six tests that the external comparator missed.
evidence.quote:
Importantly,
among the 16 tests accepted by developers, ChatTester missed 37.5% (6/16).

claims.quote:
Importantly,
among the 16 tests accepted by developers, ChatTester missed 37.5% (6/16).

claims.text: The scenario-coverage advantage persists with both the commercial o4-mini and open-source DeepSeek-V3.1 backends.
claims.quote:
As we can see, TestGeneralizer still consistently outperforms all baselines across all metrics,
demonstrating its robustness and practicality for deployment in the industry.

claims.text: Two-example few-shot prompting has lower recall/F1 (70.24/59.52%) than zero-shot (75.49/59.83%); the three-example condition performs worse again, without numerical scores.
claims.quote:
Zero-shot and few-shot
prompting yield the worst performance across all metrics.

claims.text: Hand-crafted prompting outperforms zero-shot and few-shot VP identification, with precision/recall/F1 of 68.47/77.29/72.61%.
claims.quote:
Hand-crafted prompting outperforms zero- and few-shot prompting but remains limited,
as designing comprehensive and non-conflicting rules for complex scenarios is difficult for humans.

claims.text: For ofdrw setClip, TestGeneralizer correctly creates three separate tests for the scenarios in one ground-truth test; LLM-assessed coverage is 1 versus 0.33 mutation-based coverage.
claims.page: p.14 §4.1.4, Mutation-based vs. LLM-Assessed Scenario Coverage
claims.quote:
TestGen-
eralizer correctly generalized these into
three separate tests.

claims.text: Some baselines' higher project-level coverage is inflated by tests exercising extra classes or methods unnecessary for meaningful scenarios, according to case inspection.
claims.quote:
We manually inspected these cases and found that the baseline tests often
exercise additional classes or methods that are unnecessary for testing the meaningful scenarios,
thereby inflating project-level coverage.

claims.text: The unstratified RQ1 generation average is 12K tokens per generated test; a per-model breakdown is not_reported.
claims.quote:
Across all generations, TestGeneralizer consumes on average 12K tokens per
test.

claims.text: The unstratified RQ1 average end-to-end processing time is two minutes per test; a per-model breakdown is not_reported.
claims.quote: The average end-to-end processing time per test is 2 minutes.

claims.text: In Spark EmbeddedJettyFactory.create, omitting rules produces eight meaningless VPs alongside two genuine VPs and four redundant scenarios.
claims.quote:
As a
result, the template includes eight meaningless variation points and only two actual ones, resulting
in four redundant scenarios and missing one of the three intended scenarios.

claims.text: In the same Spark example, the prompt without rules misses one of three intended scenarios.
claims.quote:
As a
result, the template includes eight meaningless variation points and only two actual ones, resulting
in four redundant scenarios and missing one of the three intended scenarios.

claims.text: Stage 1 retrieval in Spark supplies matchPath information needed to infer four path scenarios that are missed without that definition.
claims.quote:
For this example, TestGeneralizer proactively queries
the implementation of matchPath in Stage 1, as it recognizes that it is crucial for determining the
oracle and answering the exam correctly.

claims.text: Stage 2 retrieval of related Paint types guides comprehensive ofdrw setPaint scenarios when the assertion-free initial test causes Stage 1 to be skipped.
claims.quote: This knowledge guides the LLM to infer comprehensive test scenarios.

claims.text: The paper infers practicality for industrial deployment from TestGeneralizer's benchmark performance with DeepSeek-V3.1.
claims.quote:
As we can see, TestGeneralizer still consistently outperforms all baselines across all metrics,
demonstrating its robustness and practicality for deployment in the industry.

claims.text: The author-constructed Vanilla o4-mini control has 39.81% average mutation-based scenario coverage, 20.23 points above EvoSuite's reported average; EvoSuite excludes two projects.
claims.quote:
For
example, its mutation-based scenario coverage is lower by 20.23% than Vanilla and by 57.67% than
TestGeneralizer.

claims.text: A preliminary experiment reports a 72.98% probability of generating at least one alternative oracle exposing the same synthetic bugs as ground-truth tests.

metrics.name: Probability of a synthetic-bug-revealing alternative oracle

claims.quote:
In a preliminary experiment, we found that TestGeneralizer has a 72.98% probability
of generating at least one alternative oracle capable of revealing the same synthetic bugs as the
ground-truth tests.

claims.text: The pending ofdrw texture-paint test may expose a new requirement because complete texture-paint functionality is absent; maintainer confirmation is not_reported.
claims.quote:
Because the project currently does not provide
complete functionality for texture paint, the pending test may have uncovered a new requirement,
which may be under consideration by the maintainers.

claims.text: A mutation-based scenario coverage close to 80% is argued to show that the generalized scenarios are sufficiently close to the ground truth, given 82.1 mutants per ground-truth scenario on average.
claims.quote: A mutation-based scenario coverage close to 80% indicates that the generalized scenarios are sufficiently close to the ground truth, given the large number of mutants per ground-truth scenario on average (82.1).

claims.text: With o1-mini, successful-pass rates exceed TELPA, ChatTester and DA: 92.00% on LLM-Inferred and 94.81% on Human-Written intentions.
claims.quote:
IntentionTest significantly
outperforms TELPA, ChatTester, and DA in success pass rate by 27.88%, 23.66%, and 49.00% on
“LLM-Inferred” dataset.

claims.text: IntentionTest is reported to outperform LLM baselines and perform comparably to EvoSuite on general test validity outcomes.
claims.quote:
Overall,
IntentionTest outperforms the LLM-based baselines and performs on par with EvoSuite in general
metrics (i.e., compilation failure, execution failure, assertion failure, and successful pass).

claims.text: IntentionTest generates tests more faithful to validation intentions than the external baselines, including comparisons restricted to shared passing tests.

metrics.name: Project-specific API invocation count; up to 62.9% more reported in introduction

evidence.description: The hash128 example examines UTF-8 setup and getLongArray assertions; it reports CMS 100% for IntentionTest versus 8% for ChatTester.
evidence.quote:
The intended
test scenario is to validate that the focal method hash128() correctly hashes a UTF-8-encoded
string.

claims.quote:
IntentionTest consistently outperforms all baselines in validation intention alignment—for example,
IntentionTest outperforms TELPA by 6.85% (81.11% vs. 74.26%) and 4.22% (73.63% vs. 69.41%) on
“Human-Written” and “LLM-Inferred” dataset, respectively.

claims.text: The authors report better line-coverage overlap than baselines, highlighting 87.56% exact match and 93.40% common coverage on LLM-Inferred intentions; on Human-Written intentions TELPA's exact match (72.09%) exceeds IntentionTest's (70.42%).
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 3, IntentionTest outperforms the
baselines regarding line coverage overlap (including exact match and common coverage ratio) and
common mutation score.

claims.text: The approach maintains useful generation performance with both commercial o1-mini and open-source DeepSeek-V3.2 models.
claims.quote:
Moreover, IntentionTest maintains its performance
across both commercial LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT) and open-source LLMs (e.g., DeepSeek-V3.2).

claims.text: Adding any tested intention-description content, including an objective of at most 50 words, improves intention alignment relative to providing no description.

evidence.description: The blade example compares objective-only and full-description generated tests with Unicode/ASCII cross-check requirements.
evidence.quote:
We also observed that the test generated with the full description aligns even
more closely, as the Preconditions and Expected Results provide complementary details reflecting
the personalized intention.

claims.quote:
As shown in Table 4, providing any component can improve performance (excluding
metrics related to successful pass), indicating the effectiveness of the three components.

claims.text: IntentionTest is claimed to maintain performance with only a test objective within 50 words.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, we analyze the performance of
validation intention across five levels of detail, demonstrating that it can still maintain the
performance even when limited to a concise description of the test objective within 50 words.

claims.text: Full descriptions capture personalized validation requirements more closely than objective-only descriptions in the illustrated Unicode-password example.
claims.quote:
We also observed that the test generated with the full description aligns even
more closely, as the Preconditions and Expected Results provide complementary details reflecting
the personalized intention.

claims.text: Even without intention descriptions, IntentionTest exceeds ChatTester's CMS by 29.54 and 35.27 percentage points on the two intention datasets.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, even without a validation intention description, IntentionTest still outperforms
the state-of-the-art ChatTester—showing, for example, 29.54% and 35.27% gains in CMS (see the
columns “ChatTester” in Table 3 and the columns “none” in Table 4).

claims.text: Removing intention descriptions slightly increases successful-pass rates: 92.00% to 92.79% and 94.81% to 98.70%.
claims.quote: We also observe a small increase in successful passes when descriptions are removed.

claims.text: Retaining referable-test context increases CMS by 2.45 and 11.00 percentage points relative to No Ref on LLM-Inferred and Human-Written intentions.
claims.quote:
For example, the performance in CMS drops by 2.45% and 11.00% on “LLM-Inferred”
and “Human-Written” datasets, respectively.

claims.text: Retaining referable-test context raises successful-pass rates from 87.41% to 92.00% and from 85.71% to 94.81%.
claims.quote:
Compared to IntentionTest, the test generation performance
declines sharply.

claims.text: Retaining crucial facts increases CMS by 3.91 and 6.38 percentage points over No Fact; additional DeepSeek experiments are said to support this conclusion.
claims.quote:
As for the contribution of crucial facts, the column “No Fact” shows that removing facts from
prompts likewise impairs performance, e.g., 3.91% and 6.38% of degradation in CMS on the two
datasets.

claims.text: Retaining crucial facts raises successful-pass rates from 90.74% to 92.00% and from 90.91% to 94.81%.
claims.quote: This confirms the effectiveness of the discriminator.

claims.text: IntentionTest remains effective across reference-similarity bins, including low similarity, and consistently exceeds No Ref; its pass rates are 92.68%, 95.83%, 97.06% and 96.15%.
claims.quote:
We observed that, while higher similarity
correlates with improved generation quality, IntentionTest maintains robust performance even
in low-similarity regimes, consistently outperforming the“No Ref”variant.

claims.text: IntentionTest generates more practical tests than the external state-of-the-art comparators.

evidence.description: The hash128 example examines UTF-8 setup and getLongArray assertions; it reports CMS 100% for IntentionTest versus 8% for ChatTester.
evidence.quote:
The intended
test scenario is to validate that the focal method hash128() correctly hashes a UTF-8-encoded
string.

evidence.description: The blade example compares objective-only and full-description generated tests with Unicode/ASCII cross-check requirements.
evidence.quote:
We also observed that the test generated with the full description aligns even
more closely, as the Preconditions and Expected Results provide complementary details reflecting
the personalized intention.

claims.quote:
The results show that, compared to the state-of-the-art approaches, IntentionTest generates far
more practical tests with better alignment to developers’ validation intention.

claims.text: With DeepSeek-V3.2, IntentionTest still has higher successful-pass rates than ChatTester, DA and TELPA on both intention datasets.
claims.quote:
The column “Ours (DS)” in Table 3 shows that IntentionTest
powered by DeepSeek-V3.2 still outperforms the baselines.

claims.text: With DeepSeek-V3.2, IntentionTest has higher CMS than EvoSuite, ChatTester, DA and TELPA on both intention datasets.
claims.quote:
The column “Ours (DS)” in Table 3 shows that IntentionTest
powered by DeepSeek-V3.2 still outperforms the baselines.

claims.text: A referable test is found in 69.01% of LLM-Inferred cases and 75.32% of Human-Written cases.
claims.quote:
In the experiment, IntentionTest can find a referable test in 69.01% and
75.32% of cases of test generation on “LLM-Inferred” and “Human-Written” datasets, respectively.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.2 produces fewer passing tests than o1-mini: 89.72% versus 92.00%, and 88.31% versus 94.81%.
claims.quote:
We also observe that IntentionTest (DS)
underperforms IntentionTest (O1), caused by its limited inference performance of adopting crucial
code facts in editing the referable test.

claims.text: DeepSeek-V3.2 has lower CMS than o1-mini: 55.30% versus 76.35%, and 60.53% versus 85.18%.
claims.quote:
We also observe that IntentionTest (DS)
underperforms IntentionTest (O1), caused by its limited inference performance of adopting crucial
code facts in editing the referable test.

claims.text: IntentionTest's CodeBLEU is substantially below DA's, by approximately 30 percentage points in the authors' summary.
claims.quote:
As for CodeBLEU, the results of IntentionTest, ChatTester, and TELPA are much smaller than
DA’s result by about 30%.

claims.text: Many IntentionTest outputs are semantically correct despite being syntactically different from the ground-truth tests.

evidence.description: The hash128 example examines UTF-8 setup and getLongArray assertions; it reports CMS 100% for IntentionTest versus 8% for ChatTester.
evidence.quote:
The intended
test scenario is to validate that the focal method hash128() correctly hashes a UTF-8-encoded
string.

claims.quote:
Moreover, we find that many generated tests by IntentionTest are semantically correct but
syntactically different from the ground-truth.

claims.text: The unlearning prompt is reported to prevent generation of program elements absent from the supplied context.
claims.quote:
Experimental observations confirm its effectiveness in preventing the generation of
program elements (e.g., method invocations) that do not appear in the input context.

claims.text: Overly general intentions can yield tests that miss intended project-specific API behavior, as illustrated by yavi's CodePoints.Range.of() case.
claims.quote:
While the generated test executes
successfully, it partially misaligns with the target test.

claims.text: Higher target/reference similarity is associated with better generated-test quality.
claims.quote:
We observed that, while higher similarity
correlates with improved generation quality, IntentionTest maintains robust performance even
in low-similarity regimes, consistently outperforming the“No Ref”variant.

claims.text: Restricting descriptions to objective and expected-results sections is claimed to require minimal programmer effort.
claims.quote:
Note that, the performance of IntentionTest is stable if we only keep the section of
test objective and expected results in Table 1, which enables the programmers to spend minimal
effort on writing the validation intention.

claims.text: The unlearning strategy is interpreted as mitigating target-test memorization.
claims.quote:
Our results show that DA achieves a significant fit to the distribution of the
12 projects, and also imply the effectiveness of the strategy for mitigating the LLM’s memorization
effect.

claims.text: Retrieved references and crucial facts are proposed as the reason generation depends less on the foundation model's capabilities.
claims.quote:
Generally, the retrieved test reference
and crucial code facts provide useful and enriched external knowledge, making our approach
less dependent on the capability of foundation models.

claims.text: DeepSeek's lower performance is attributed to weaker inference when applying crucial facts to edit reference tests.
claims.quote:
We also observe that IntentionTest (DS)
underperforms IntentionTest (O1), caused by its limited inference performance of adopting crucial
code facts in editing the referable test.

claims.text: Referable tests are interpreted as exposing project-specific idioms and scenarios that the LLM alone cannot infer.

evidence.description: The hash128 example examines UTF-8 setup and getLongArray assertions; it reports CMS 100% for IntentionTest versus 8% for ChatTester.
evidence.quote:
The intended
test scenario is to validate that the focal method hash128() correctly hashes a UTF-8-encoded
string.

claims.quote:
This suggests that (1) even low-similarity references could provide useful structural scaffolds and
project-specific idioms and (2) LLM is relatively robust to irrelevant information.

claims.text: Even low-similarity references are interpreted as useful sources of structural scaffolds and project-specific idioms.
claims.quote:
This suggests that (1) even low-similarity references could provide useful structural scaffolds and
project-specific idioms and (2) LLM is relatively robust to irrelevant information.

claims.text: The similarity-bin results are interpreted as showing LLM robustness to irrelevant information.
claims.quote:
This suggests that (1) even low-similarity references could provide useful structural scaffolds and
project-specific idioms and (2) LLM is relatively robust to irrelevant information.

claims.text: Fact discrimination is identified as insufficient for some fine-grained semantic distinctions between code and intention descriptions.
claims.quote:
This result
exposes a limitation of IntentionTest—the suboptimal ability of fact discrimination component to
capture fine-grained semantic distinctions between codes and intention descriptions.

claims.text: The fine-grained fact-discrimination failure is partly attributed to limited semantic understanding in the lightweight CodeT5 embedding model.
claims.quote:
We attribute
this limitation partly to the weaker semantic understanding of the lightweight embedding model
used (i.e., CodeT5 Embedding).

claims.text: The increased pass rate without intention descriptions is attributed to generation facing fewer constraints.
claims.quote:
This occurs
because the generation now faces fewer constraints, making it easier for to generate.

hcs.page: 4–12, §§4.1–4.6, Algorithm 1; 6, Table 2; 7, graph-completeness check; 8, event constraints
hcs.quote:
In step ⑧, GPT-Monkey sends the
instruction and conﬁguration ﬁle to a Monkey-based testing ker-
nel to conduct automated testing on the target function.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Click-Only
hcs.removed: All permitted event types except clicks
hcs.quote:
Speci ﬁcally,
on the Themis benchmark containing 52 known crashes, we con-
structed four event con ﬁguration strategies: Click-Only, Swipe-
Only, Long Press-Only, and All Events (baseline).

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Swipe-Only
hcs.removed: All permitted event types except swipes
hcs.quote:
Speci ﬁcally,
on the Themis benchmark containing 52 known crashes, we con-

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Long Press-Only
hcs.removed: All permitted event types except long presses
hcs.quote:
Speci ﬁcally,
on the Themis benchmark containing 52 known crashes, we con-
structed four event con ﬁguration strategies: Click-Only, Swipe-
Only, Long Press-Only, and All Events (baseline).

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Activity-Only input
hcs.removed: Layout, screenshots and interface associations; retain target activity name
hcs.quote:
Results show that when provided only with activity names as input,
GPT-Monkey’s accuracy in the function segmentation task drops to
42.6%, and its crash detection rate drops to 36.5 %.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Layout-Only input
hcs.removed: Screenshots and interface association input; retain XML tree and control attributes
hcs.quote:
Under the
Layout-Only and Screenshot-Only con ﬁgurations, GPT-Monkey
retains over 80% function segmentation accuracy and over 42% crash
detection capability, demonstrating the signiﬁcant support provided
by structured controls and visual information for LLM reasoning.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Screenshot-Only input
hcs.removed: Layout and interface association input; retain screenshots
hcs.quote:
Under the
Layout-Only and Screenshot-Only con ﬁgurations, GPT-Monkey
retains over 80% function segmentation accuracy and over 42% crash
detection capability, demonstrating the signiﬁcant support provided
by structured controls and visual information for LLM reasoning.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey Association-Only input
hcs.removed: Specific layout and visual input; retain function transition path
hcs.quote:
The Association-Only conﬁguration, which relies on modeling inter-
face transition links and similarly lacks entry context, achieves only
48.5% segmentation accuracy and 38.5% detection capability.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey without cross-modal alignment
hcs.removed: Layout input; retain screenshots and other unablated modules
hcs.quote: Do not provide the layout and retain only the screenshot.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey without interface association
hcs.removed: Global interface association graph; retain current interface
hcs.quote:
Remove the global interface graph and retain the current
interface.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey without parameter-RAG
hcs.removed: Parameter knowledge-base retrieval; parameters generated solely from prompt
hcs.quote:
Do not call the parameter knowledge base, and LLM generates
parameters solely from the prompt.

hcs.name: GPT-Monkey without user interaction feedback / G2

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Omni-Notes 6.1.0, Text note function; Themis case study
ecs.protocol: Targeted case: touch 70%, motion 15%, syskeys/nav/anyevent 5% each, throttle 300; instruction specifies 500 events; crash and root-cause analysis; repetitions not_reported
ecs.quote:
To illustrate how GPT-Monkey works in practice, we present a
detailed case study of crash detection in Omni-Notes (version
6.1.0), a note-taking application.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey correctly segments all 68 Themis functions (100%).
claims.quote:
From Table 5, GPT-Monkey successfully segmented all 68 critical
functions and achieved 100 % accuracy.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey correctly segments 3168/3337 real-world functions, reported as 95%.
claims.quote:
The testing
results, as presented in Table 6, reveal a 95% accuracy in function
segmentation, with GPT-Monkey correctly segmenting 3168 func-
tions of all 3337 critical functions.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey detects 28/52 Themis crashes versus Monkey 22, APE 24, ComboDroid 21, TimeMachine 15, Stoat 19 and Q-testing 10; only the last three differences are statistically significant at 0.05.

evidence.detail: McNemar exact tests: p=0.0703 Monkey, 0.2891 APE, 0.0654 ComboDroid, 0.0023 TimeMachine, 0.0117 Stoat, <0.0001 Q-testing.
evidence.quote:
To evaluate the statistical
signiﬁcance of these differences, we performed McNemar ’s exact
test [34] for each pairwise comparison between GPT-Monkey and
each baseline, where each of the 52 known crashes constitutes a
paired binary observation (detected or not).

claims.quote:
GPT-Monkey achieves statistically signiﬁcant improve-
ments over Q-testing (p<0:0001), TimeMachine (p ¼ 0:0023), and
Stoat ( p ¼ 0:0117).

claims.text: Mean Themis crash-trigger time is 28.57 min, versus Monkey 76.18, APE 47.25, ComboDroid 43.62, TimeMachine 88.67, Stoat 97.37 and Q-testing 87.90; pairwise differences are significant except against APE and ComboDroid.

metrics.name: Mean time until first crash trigger

evidence.detail: ANOVA F(6,132)=6.70, p≈0.000004; Dunnett post-hoc p=0.0023 Monkey, 0.5377 APE, 0.7717 ComboDroid, 0.0004 TimeMachine, <0.0001 Stoat, 0.0036 Q-testing.
evidence.quote:
The differences compared to APE ( p ¼ 0:5377) and Com-
boDroid ( p ¼ 0:7717) do not reach statistical signi ﬁcance at the
0.05 level.

claims.quote:
GPT-Monkey triggers
crashes signi ﬁcantly faster than Monkey ( p ¼ 0:0023), Stoat
(p<0:0001), TimeMachine ( p ¼ 0:0004), and Q-testing ( p ¼
0:0036).

claims.text: GPT-Monkey finds 397 crashes across 1000 Google Play apps.

evidence.detail: Crash timing, exception-stack location and log/exception semantics assessed configuration versus logic causes; developer confirmation and independent reproduction not_reported.
evidence.quote:
Speci ﬁcally, the post-hoc crash analysis strat-
egy jointly considers the crash timing, the exception call stack
location of a crash, and the crash ’s semantic signals from logs
and exception messages.

claims.quote:
Through the proposed post-hoc crash analysis strategy, we ana-
lyzed that 397 crashes GPT-Monkey found in the top 1000 popular
apps of Google Play stem from app logic bugs rather than con ﬁg-
uration bugs.

claims.text: All Events detects 28 known crashes, exceeding Click-Only 23, Swipe-Only 4 and Long Press-Only 3 under equal event counts.
claims.quote:
In terms of crash detection capabilities, as shown in Figure 9a, the
baseline strategy performs best, detecting a total of 28 crashes.

claims.text: Full contextual input achieves 100% segmentation accuracy, versus Activity-Only 42.6%, Layout-Only 85.3%, Screenshot-Only 80.9% and Association-Only 48.5%.
claims.quote:
In summary, complete
contextual information is crucial for LLM-driven analysis strategies,
especially in function semantic understanding and complex interac-
tion path judgment.

claims.text: Full contextual input detects 28/52 crashes (53.8%), versus Activity-Only 19 (36.5%), Layout-Only 24 (46.2%), Screenshot-Only 22 (42.3%) and Association-Only 20 (38.5%).
claims.quote:
Results show that when provided only with activity names as input,
GPT-Monkey’s accuracy in the function segmentation task drops to
42.6%, and its crash detection rate drops to 36.5 %.

claims.text: Full-system entry-area accuracy is 100%; removing cross-modal alignment, interface association, parameter-RAG or user feedback yields 68.2%, 82.3%, 93.1% or 90.5%, while removing log feedback leaves 100%.
claims.quote:
Removing the cross-modal alignment module signi ﬁcantly
reduces the accuracy of entry area segmentation, indicating that
screenshots cannot support LLM’s accurate reasoning and layout
information is crucial for understanding the interface.

claims.text: Full-system function segmentation is 100%; without cross-modal alignment, interface association, parameter-RAG or user feedback it is 81.3%, 79.4%, 88.2% or 90.1%; without log feedback it remains 100%.
claims.quote:
Removing
the interface association graph signi ﬁcantly reduces the accuracy
of function segmentation, which causes GPT-Monkey to fail to
identify the relevant interfaces of the target function, thus affect-
ing subsequent crash detection.

claims.text: Full-system crash detection is 53.8%; removing cross-modal alignment, interface association, parameter-RAG, user feedback or log feedback reduces it to 36.5%, 38.5%, 40.4%, 44.2% or 44.2%.
claims.quote:
Removing parameter-RAG
increases the reliance of parameter generation on LLM reasoning,
reducing the crash detection rate from 53.8 % to 40.4 % due to
invalid or unreasonable parameter generation.

claims.text: Full-system mean time-to-crash is 28.6 min; removing cross-modal alignment, interface association, parameter-RAG, user feedback or log feedback increases it to 41.3, 39.6, 37.7, 35.8 or 33.9 min.
claims.quote:
Removing the user interaction feedback mechanism reduces
users’ ability to adjust testing parameters, decreasing the crash
detection rate from 53.8 % to 44.2 % and increasing the average
time-to-crash from 28.6 to 35.8 min.

claims.text: Parameter validity is 100% in the full system and without log feedback, versus 98.1% without cross-modal alignment, 99.2% without interface association, 85.3% without parameter-RAG and 89.6% without user feedback.
claims.quote:
Removing parameter-RAG
increases the reliance of parameter generation on LLM reasoning,
reducing the crash detection rate from 53.8 % to 40.4 % due to
invalid or unreasonable parameter generation.

claims.text: User feedback preserves segmentation under ambiguity: G1/G2 are both 100% with explicit requirements, but 93%/62% with ambiguous requirements.

metrics.name: Function segmentation accuracy under explicit/ambiguous inputs

claims.quote:
The ablation experiment results
show that incorporating user interaction feedback can mitigate
the impact of ambiguous user requirements on system test perfor-
mance, enhancing GPT-Monkey’s robustness under ambiguous
natural language input.

claims.text: User feedback preserves crash detection under ambiguity: G1/G2 both detect 28 crashes with explicit requirements, versus 25/17 with ambiguous requirements.

metrics.name: Known crashes detected under explicit/ambiguous requirements

claims.quote:
The ablation experiment results
show that incorporating user interaction feedback can mitigate
the impact of ambiguous user requirements on system test perfor-
mance, enhancing GPT-Monkey’s robustness under ambiguous
natural language input.

claims.text: With ambiguous requirements, user feedback reduces mean time-to-crash from 49.8 to 32.4 min; explicit-requirement times are similar, 29.1 versus 28.6 min.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 16, under explicit requirements, G1 and G2
perform similarly, indicating that user interaction feedback does
not introduce additional interference to explicit test requirements.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey segments functions more accurately than Monkey-TextFocus (100% versus 69.1%); entry-area accuracy is 100% versus 82.4% and associated-interface coverage 100% versus 76%.
claims.quote:
Speciﬁcally, GPT-Monkey maintained 100 % FS-Acc on the 68
target functions in Themis, whereas Monkey-TextFocus
achieved an FS-Acc of 69.1 %.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey detects more Themis crashes than Monkey-TextFocus: 28 (53.8%) versus 23 (44.2%); TextFocus is also above external Monkey's 22 (42.3%).
claims.quote:
For crash detection, Monkey-TextFocus detected 23
crashes among the 52 known crashes, achieving a detection
rate of 44.2 %, which lies between GPT-Monkey’ s
 53.8% and the
traditional Monkey ’s4 2 . 3%.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey detects crashes faster than Monkey-TextFocus: mean 28.57 versus 59.73 min.
claims.quote:
For detection ef ﬁciency, Monkey-
TextFocus achieved an average T-DC of 59.73 min, which is lon-
ger than GPT-Monkey ’s 28.57 min.

claims.text: Automatic function segmentation averages 1 min/function, versus 3–5 min/function for manual annotation; this excludes traversal and manual verification.
claims.quote:
Then, GPT-Monkey used LLM to perform automatic
function segmentation, taking an average of 1 min per function.

claims.text: Entry-interface extraction and global-graph construction average 10 min/app.
claims.quote:
First, the
extraction of the entry interface and the establishment of the
global interface association were performed through the auto-
mated tools UIAutomator and DroidBot, with each app traversal
taking an average of 10 min.

claims.text: Manual verification of automated segmentation costs 2–3 min/function.
claims.quote:
Finally, manual veri ﬁcation was conducted on the automated
segmentation results, taking an average of 2 –3 min per function.

claims.text: The authors interpret the mean 1.2 user-feedback iterations/function as substantially reduced manual intervention, with most functions confirmed in one or two interactions.
claims.quote:
The experimental results show that the average iterative number
of the user interaction feedback is 1.2, and of the log analysis
feedback is 1.3.

claims.text: Log feedback generally completes corrections in one or two iterations, averaging 1.3 iterations/function.
claims.quote:
We also
observed that log analysis feedback can assist LLM to complete
corrections within one or two iterations in most cases.

claims.text: The paper interprets repeated Monkey executions under feedback as addressing LLM randomness; Table 10 totals 158 executions for 68 function tasks, without a variability measure.
claims.quote:
The last
column of Table 10 shows the number of Monkey kernel execu-
tions for each test task, quantitatively demonstrating the effective-
ness of this feedback mechanism in addressing the randomness
of LLM.

claims.text: User feedback requires more interaction under ambiguous than explicit requirements (1.6 versus 1.0 iterations); no-feedback controls require zero.
claims.quote:
Evaluation metrics
included function segmentation accuracy (FS-Acc), the number
of known crashes detected (C-Det), the average time until the
crash is triggered (T-DC, in minutes), and the number of user
interaction iterations (I-Count).

claims.text: The authors attribute all 397 real-world crashes to application logic rather than configuration bugs, although Table 12 describes InflateException causes as often configuration-related.
claims.quote:
Through the proposed post-hoc crash analysis strategy, we ana-
lyzed that 397 crashes GPT-Monkey found in the top 1000 popular
apps of Google Play stem from app logic bugs rather than con ﬁg-
uration bugs.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey triggers an UnsupportedOperationException in Omni-Notes 6.1.0 after 42 min of targeted testing; the case analysis links it to an unsupported Glide fitCenter API.

evidence.detail: A Glide API/version incompatibility is identified; developer confirmation and independent reproduction not_reported.
evidence.quote:
The ﬁtCenter() API
was introduced in a newer version of Glide than the one packaged
in Omni-Notes 6.1.0, causing an UnsupportedOperationException
when the user attempts to view an attached image in the gallery
viewer.

claims.quote:
After 42 min of targeted testing, GPT-Monkey
triggered an UnsupportedOperationExceptioncrash.

claims.text: The authors claim crash discovery can enhance application stability; stability after fixes is not evaluated.

evidence.detail: Log/stack attribution supports observed faults but does not measure improved application stability.
evidence.quote:
Through the proposed post-hoc crash analysis strategy, we ana-
lyzed that 397 crashes GPT-Monkey found in the top 1000 popular
apps of Google Play stem from app logic bugs rather than con ﬁg-
uration bugs.

claims.quote:
GPT-Monkey can achieve a high detection rate and detection
efﬁciency, which is capable of enhancing the application stability
by detecting critical crashes.

claims.text: The authors claim dual feedback mitigates LLM segmentation failures and improves segmentation robustness.

metrics.name: Function segmentation accuracy across feedback/input conditions

claims.quote:
Notably, the dual-feedback mechanism introduced by GPT-Mon-
key can mitigate the segmentation failure that may be caused by
LLM and further enhance the robustness of function segmenta-
tion.

claims.text: The authors describe GPT-Monkey as a simple practical testing workflow driven by natural-language requirements, without a usability study.
claims.quote:
Regarding the implications for practitioners, this study provides a
simple and ef ﬁcient solution for GUI testing of Android apps.

claims.text: The authors claim infrequent LLM interaction reduces resource expenditure because one generated instruction supports continuous operations; monetary and token costs are not_reported.
claims.quote:
Moreover, GPT-
Monkey minimizes the frequency of interaction with LLM in
which the test instruction generated by running GPT-Monkey
once supports continuous operations, improving testing efﬁciency
and reducing resource expenditures.

claims.text: Single-event strategies have broadly similar mean event execution overhead: All Events 287 ms, Click-Only 227 ms, Swipe-Only 254 ms, Long Press-Only 296 ms.
claims.quote:
In terms of
performance overhead, as shown in Figure 9b, the average event
execution time for each strategy is roughly similar, ranging from
227 to 296 milliseconds.

claims.text: The 169 real-world segmentation failures are grouped into custom views, SurfaceView/TextureView components, and dynamically generated components with weak or unavailable semantic/layout information.
claims.quote:
While GPT-Monkey achieved 95 % segmentation accuracy across
3337 real-world application functions, segmentation still failed in
169 of them.

claims.text: The authors judge segmentation failures to have limited overall detection impact because they concern less critical or less frequently used functions; no impact measurement is reported.
claims.quote:
However, these failure cases involve less critical
functions or less frequently used modules, so their impact on
the overall detection performance is relatively limited.

claims.text: GPT-Monkey's generated Themis event distribution is 69.3% clicks, 24.7% swipes and 6.0% other events.
claims.quote:
Swipe events account for 24.7 %, demonstrating that GPT-
Monkey also effectively utilizes swipes when navigating interface
content.

claims.text: The authors interpret event-type preferences as evidence that GPT-Monkey is context-aware and chooses appropriate testing actions for app state.
claims.quote:
These results further dem-
onstrate that GPT-Monkey possesses contextual awareness in
automatic event parameter generation and selects the most appro-
priate test method based on the app ’s state.

claims.text: Real-world crash categories comprise 174 NullPointerException, 117 IllegalStateException, 66 IllegalArgumentException, 23 IndexOutOfBoundsException, 13 UnsupportedOperationException and 4 InflateException observations.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, we performed an in-depth attribution analysis of
the crashes caused by application logic bugs discovered by GPT-
Monkey.

claims.text: The authors infer that complete contextual input is crucial for LLM semantic understanding and complex interaction-path judgment.
claims.quote:
In summary, complete
contextual information is crucial for LLM-driven analysis strategies,
especially in function semantic understanding and complex interac-
tion path judgment.

claims.text: Although not significant against Monkey, ComboDroid and APE, GPT-Monkey exclusively detects 7, 9 and 6 crashes those tools miss, versus 1, 2 and 2 crashes only they detect, which the authors read as a practical advantage.

metrics.name: Exclusively detected known crashes (McNemar discordant counts)

evidence.detail: McNemar exact tests are non-significant for these three comparisons (p=0.0703, 0.0654, 0.2891).

claims.quote: GPT-Monkey exclusively detects 7, 9, and 6 crashes missed by Monkey, ComboDroid, and APE, respectively, whereas these baselines only detect 1, 2, and 2 crashes that GPT-Monkey misses

claims.text: The authors conclude every module is indispensable and improves entry-area accuracy, segmentation, crash detection and efficiency; Table 15 shows removing log feedback leaves entry-area and segmentation accuracy at 100%.

metrics.name: Entry-area accuracy, segmentation rate, crash detection rate, time-to-crash across module ablations

claims.quote: Overall, the effectiveness of GPT-Monkey relies on the synergy among modules, with each module being indispensable.

claims.text: From the TextFocus comparison the authors infer that GPT-Monkey's advantage comes from LLM-driven segmentation, parameter tailoring and dual feedback rather than merely shrinking the testing scope.

metrics.name: FS-Acc, detection rate and time-to-crash versus Monkey-TextFocus

claims.quote: GPT-Monkey’s core advantage is not merely shrinking the testing scope, but the function segmentation obtained through global interface association, cross-modal alignment, and LLM reasoning

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Permitted event types: all versus clicks only
matched_comparisons.metric: Known crashes; mean event execution time
matched_comparisons.quote:
The
Click-Only strategy, despite using only click actions, still detects

claims.quote:

Hard, with only slight drops in line coverage (−0.01) and mutation score (−0.02), indicating robustness to increasing
problem difficulty.

claims.text: On correct code, replacing CANDOR prefixes with EvoSuite prefixes slightly reduces oracle correctness: 0.910/0.930/0.894 versus 0.874/0.922/0.857.
claims.quote:

still outperforms TOGLL by a large margin, with a minimum of 0.255 (0.857− 0.602) on Leetcode-Hard.

experiments, we observed serious hallucinations during the panel discussion; in over 70 % of the cases, thePanelists’

claims.text: In direct DeepSeek evaluation, correct oracles were often identified early before continued self-questioning.
claims.quote: In fact, we observed that DeepSeek often identified correct oracles early.

claims.text: Without the Planner, generated tests usually explore easy paths and lack a coherent strategy for untested paths.
claims.quote:
In our experiments, we observe that without thePlanner,
CANDOR generates tests exploring easy code paths in most cases, lacking a coherent strategy to explore untested code
paths.

claims.text: Separating complex subtasks among specialized agents prevents the planning/generation interference observed in the single-LLM condition and improves test generation.
claims.quote:
By decomposing
complex tasks and assigning each sub-task to a specialized LLM agent, we prevent this interference and improve the
effectiveness of CANDOR in unit test generation.

claims.text: Panel reasoning mitigates hallucination and is more robust than simple majority voting in producing accurate oracles.

evidence.detail: The paper describes Panelists confusing maximum with minimum, with Curator cross-checking their reasoning; inspection procedure and sample size not_reported.

However, the
Curatorcan correct these errors by cross-checking the reasoning logic, inputs, and outputs of eachPanelistrather than
relying solely on majority voting.

statistically significant (𝑝𝑣𝑎𝑙𝑢𝑒< 1𝑒− 2).

claims.quote:
This design ensures that incorrect or inconsistent outputs are identified and corrected,
making the panel discussion more robust than simple majority voting in producing accurate oracles.

claims.text: The dual-LLM pipeline preserves the benefit of deep reasoning; no direct oracle-quality comparison against untruncated direct DeepSeek is reported.

keeping outputs concise.

claims.text: Truncating DeepSeek at 2,000 tokens and extracting its answer with a basic LLM keeps oracle-evaluation output concise, whereas direct DeepSeek sometimes exceeds 10,000 tokens.
claims.quote:
To prevent this “overthinking”, we truncate DeepSeek’s output at2,000 tokens and use a basic LLM to
extract the correct oracle from its reasoning.

claims.quote:

which allows CANDOR to generalize well across programs of varying complexity in this context.

expressed in natural language or in weakly typed languages like Python in LLMs’ pretraining corpora.

claims.text: HieraTest is claimed to improve compilation success over EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatUniTest, ChatTester, HITS and TestBench; reported rates are 87.53%/88.07% for RQ1 and 95.19% for RQ2, while RQ1 traditional tools attain 100%.

In contrast,
HieraTest, by integrating global dependency information,
correctly resolves external class references and produces an
executable, high-quality test case (i.e., Figure 4(c)).

claims.quote:
Experiments on
Defects4J and HieraTest-Bench show that our approach sub-
stantially improves compilation success, coverage, and bug
detection over traditional and recent LLM-based baselines.

claims.text: The abstract claims consistently improved execution reliability over EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatUniTest, ChatTester, HITS and TestBench; Table II reports HieraTest success rates of 81.99%/73.12%, below several comparators.

evidence.description: Figure 4 inspects dependency use and executability in the build() example; this is an author case analysis, not independent reproduction.

In contrast,
HieraTest, by integrating global dependency information,
correctly resolves external class references and produces an
executable, high-quality test case (i.e., Figure 4(c)).

claims.quote:
Experimental results demonstrate that HieraTest consistently
outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of compilation
success, execution reliability, code coverage, and bug detection
capability.

claims.text: HieraTest achieves the highest structural coverage over EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatUniTest, ChatTester, HITS and TestBench: class/method/branch/line coverage is 96.00/79.93/87.95/64.10% on HieraTest-Bench and 92.63/81.93/85.30/73.97% on Defects4J.
claims.quote:
On Defects4J, HieraTest again delivers compet-
itive results, with class coverage (92.63%), method cover-
age (81.93%), branch coverage (85.30%), and line coverage
(73.97%), ranking among the top-performing methods.

claims.text: HieraTest generates semantically meaningful, dependency-consistent tests; the build() example correctly resolves FunctionItem references where ChatUniTest makes invalid mocking assumptions.

evidence.description: Figure 4 inspects dependency use and executability in the build() example; this is an author case analysis, not independent reproduction.
evidence.quote:
In contrast,
HieraTest, by integrating global dependency information,
correctly resolves external class references and produces an
executable, high-quality test case (i.e., Figure 4(c)).

claims.quote:
These
findings confirm that HieraTest can generate high-coverage,
semantically meaningful, and executable tests across diverse
projects, reflecting its robustness and generalizability.

claims.text: HieraTest detects 10.21% of the Defects4J bugs, exceeding ChatUniTest (5.67%), ChatTester (2.83%), HITS (2.15%) and TestBench (1.12%).

evidence.description: The Chart example examines the null-check defect and the generated dependency context in addition to reporting the aggregate detection rate.
evidence.quote:
As
shown in Figure 5(c), HieraTest successfully constructs a
valid execution context by mocking the CategoryPlot
dependency (line 6-13).

claims.quote:
HieraTest demonstrates strong bug detection capability,
achieving a detection rate of 10.21%, substantially outper-
forming ChatUniTest (5.67%), ChatTester (2.83%), HITS
(2.15%), and TestBench (1.12%).

claims.text: HieraTest improves bug detection over traditional baselines EvoSuite and Randoop; this is the conclusion's blanket claim, whereas Table III reports HieraTest 10.21%, EvoSuite 17.00% and Randoop 9.96%.
claims.quote:
Experiments on
Defects4J and HieraTest-Bench show that our approach sub-
stantially improves compilation success, coverage, and bug
detection over traditional and recent LLM-based baselines.

claims.text: Local dependency analysis improves test coverage on both benchmarks; removing it reduces HieraTest-Bench line coverage from 64.10% to 56.88% and Defects4J line coverage from 73.97% to 65.53%.
claims.quote:
On HieraTest-Bench, removing local dependency analysis or
global dependency analysis causes significant drops in line
coverage (from 64.10% to 56.88% and 55.80%, respectively),
demonstrating their importance in generating executable, com-
prehensive tests.

claims.text: Global dependency analysis is claimed to improve test coverage on both benchmarks; removing it reduces HieraTest-Bench line coverage from 64.10% to 55.80%, but Table IV shows Defects4J line coverage increases from 73.97% to 74.77%.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table IV, HieraTest consistently outperforms
all variants on both benchmarks, confirming the complementary
value of hierarchical dependency modeling and repair strategies.

claims.text: Framework-related generation and repair strategies improve all four coverage metrics on both benchmarks compared with the w/o framework ablation.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table IV, HieraTest consistently outperforms
all variants on both benchmarks, confirming the complementary
value of hierarchical dependency modeling and repair strategies.

claims.text: Increasing compile-time repair iterations generally improves coverage, with gains claimed to plateau beyond four; on Defects4J the multi-iteration settings approach but do not exceed the five-iteration configuration.
claims.quote:
Table V shows that increasing repair iterations generally
improves coverage, though gains plateau beyond four iterations.

claims.text: Multiple compile-time repair iterations are essential for robust performance.
claims.quote:
Overall, multiple iterations
are essential for robust performance.

claims.text: Five compile-time repair iterations offer the best trade-off between repair cost and coverage gains, although repair cost is not_reported.
claims.quote:
The full five-iteration
strategy offers the best trade-off between repair cost and
coverage gains.

claims.text: HieraTest's results across diverse projects demonstrate robustness, adaptability and generalizability within the evaluated Java/DeepSeek-V3 setting.
claims.quote:
These
findings confirm that HieraTest can generate high-coverage,
semantically meaningful, and executable tests across diverse
projects, reflecting its robustness and generalizability.

claims.text: Adding local dependency information yields richer assertions than ChatUniTest in the qualitative build() comparison.
claims.quote:
Moreover,
by incorporating local dependency information, HieraTest
generates richer assertions and broader coverage, enhancing
both bug detection capability and overall test quality relative
to existing baselines.

claims.text: On HieraTest-Bench, four repair iterations attain the highest class coverage (96.38% versus five iterations' 96.00%), while five iterations achieve higher method, branch and line coverage.
claims.quote:
On HieraTest-Bench, the four-iteration variant achieves the
highest class coverage (96.38%) but remains slightly below
HieraTest in method (79.93%) and line coverage (64.10%).

claims.text: In the Chart null-check example, HieraTest's test fails on the buggy version and passes on the fixed version; ChatUniTest's test instead raises NullPointerException on both.
claims.quote:
This test case precisely targets the
defect: it triggers an assertion failure in the buggy version
by exposing the incorrect null check, while passing in the
fixed version.

claims.text: HieraTest's highest overall coverage relative to EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatUniTest, ChatTester, HITS and TestBench indicates superior semantic reasoning.
claims.quote:
Notably, HieraTest
achieves the highest overall coverage, indicating superior
adaptability and semantic reasoning in understanding diverse
testing contexts.

claims.text: Local dependency information enhances HieraTest's bug-detection capability relative to ChatUniTest, as inferred from the richer assertions and coverage in the qualitative comparison.
claims.quote:
Moreover,
by incorporating local dependency information, HieraTest
generates richer assertions and broader coverage, enhancing
both bug detection capability and overall test quality relative
to existing baselines.

claims.text: Dependency modeling is especially important in complex, real-world, bug-prone settings, with global dependency analysis claimed to contribute most.
claims.quote:
Overall, both
local dependency modeling and global dependency analysis
mechanisms are indispensable for achieving high-quality test
generation, with global dependency analysis contributing most
in complex, real-world settings.

claims.text: The larger repair-related improvement on Defects4J suggests more complex dependency and compilation problems requiring additional repair cycles.
claims.quote:
The larger
improvement on Defects4J suggests that real-world projects
exhibit more complex dependency and compilation issues,
requiring additional repair cycles.

claims.text: For bug-prone projects such as Defects4J, the semantic richness and bug localization delivered by dependency/path guidance outweigh stability trade-offs against EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatUniTest, ChatTester, HITS and TestBench.
claims.quote:
These results suggest that hierarchical dependency modeling
and path-constraint analysis effectively enhance test quality,
particularly in real-world, bug-prone projects such as those
in Defects4J, where semantic richness and bug localization
outweigh stability trade-offs.

claims.text: HieraTest's coverage gains over the baselines (on Defects4J +19.11% class, +33.94% method, +22.91% branch, +45.41% line; on HieraTest-Bench +22.79%/+38.41%/+22.36%/+34.58%) come with only moderate declines in compilation and execution success rates.
claims.quote:
Compared with baseline methods, it improves class
coverage by 19.11%, method coverage by 33.94%, branch
coverage by 22.91%, and line coverage by 45.41%, with only
moderate declines in compilation and execution success rates.

claims.text: Iteratively refined context improves the functional validity of generated bug reproduction tests.
claims.quote:
We
show that providing iteratively refined, high-quality context significantly improves the accuracy
and validity of the generated tests.

claims.text: iCoRe's performance advantage generalizes across closed-source and open-source models, with Qwen3-32B achieving performance similar to the much larger DeepSeek-V3.
claims.quote:
In addition, this superiority generalizes to different models: whether paired
with DeepSeek-V3 or Qwen3-32B,iCoReconsistently maintains its lead over the baselines on both
datasets.

claims.text: iCoRe provides compact context: 2,603 tokens on SWT-bench Lite and 2,468 on TDD-bench Verified, reducing context burden versus BM25 and the specified LLM retrievers, although SWT context is longer and input cost higher than Otter's.
claims.quote:
Moreover,iCoReoffers more
concise context, averaging∼2,500 tokens, which is 12.6–89.0% shorter than other methods.

claims.text: With GPT-4o and the basic generator, iCoRe surpasses the compared end-to-end systems, including e-Otter++, in F→P@1: 42.0% versus 40.2% on SWT-bench Lite and 52.8% versus 51.4% on TDD-bench Verified.
claims.quote:
It surpasses all existing approaches, including the SOTA method e-Otter++
with GPT-4o (40.2% and 51.4%).

claims.text: On SWT-bench Lite, iCoRe with GPT-4o achieves 52.4% patch coverage, comparable to Amazon Q's 52.7%.
claims.quote:
In terms of Patch Coverage on SWT-bench Lite(Δ𝐶), our approach
achieves 52.4%, which is on par with the record held by the commercial, closed-source tool Amazon
Q (52.7%).

claims.text: On TDD-bench Verified, iCoRe with GPT-4o achieves 76.2% patch coverage, exceeding e-Otter++'s 70.3% by 5.9 percentage points.
claims.quote:
On TDD-bench, our approach achieves a high Patch Coverage of 76.2%, outperforming
e-Otter++ (70.3%) by 5.9 percentage points.

claims.text: iCoRe with GPT-4o costs $0.28/$0.26 per instance on SWT-bench Lite/TDD-bench Verified; the paper reports 6.4-fold lower cost than GPT-4o e-Otter++ and 3.4-fold lower cost than AssertFlip, and SWT cost is 9.8-fold below Claude-3.7 e-Otter++.
claims.quote:
The average cost per instance ofiCoRe+ basic generator is merely $0.26–$0.28, far below the
state-of-the-art approaches.

claims.text: Removing test retrieval lowers F→P@1/@5 from 42.0%/46.7% to 33.7%/40.6% on SWT-bench Lite and from 52.8%/55.2% to 35.2%/39.9% on TDD-bench Verified.
claims.quote:
Removing test
case retrieval (w/o Test) leads to the most severe performance degradation across both benchmarks.

claims.text: Removing production-code retrieval lowers F→P@1/@5 to 36.6%/41.7% on SWT-bench Lite and 40.8%/46.8% on TDD-bench Verified, relative drops of 12.9%/10.7% and 22.7%/15.2%.
claims.quote:
Removing code retrieval
(w/o Code) also results in a significant drop of F→P(@1/@5) by 12.9% and 10.7% on SWT-bench
Lite, and by 22.7% and 15.2% on TDD-bench Verified.

claims.text: Disabling sketch-driven iterative refinement lowers F→P@1/@5 to 37.0%/41.7% on SWT-bench Lite and 44.5%/49.2% on TDD-bench Verified; F→P@1 falls relatively by 11.9%/15.7%.
claims.quote:
When the iterative process is disabled (w/o Iteration), the F→P(@1) performance drops by 11.9%
on SWT-bench and 15.7% on TDD-bench.

claims.text: Removing function-call similarity lowers F→P@1/@5 to 39.5%/44.6% on SWT-bench Lite and 46.5%/52.1% on TDD-bench Verified; F→P@1 falls relatively by 6.0%/11.9%.
claims.quote:
Removing the function-call similarity component (w/o Function-Call Similarity) results in a
6.0% and 11.9% F→P(@1) performance drop on two benchmarks.

claims.text: Retrieved tests contribute more to bug reproduction performance than retrieved production code, as removing tests causes larger success-rate reductions on both benchmarks.

metrics.name: Relative F→P@1 decrease under module removal
Relative F→P@5 decrease under module removal

claims.quote:
These results indicate that both test cases
and production code play a critical role in BRT generation, but the former provides more critical
guidance.

claims.text: iCoRe retrieves developer-modified target tests more accurately than BM25, AEGIS's retriever, Otter's retriever and its evaluated ablations across reported file/function metrics; file MAP is 0.699/0.747 and function MAP is 0.466/0.438.
claims.quote:
Across all metrics at both the file and function levels,
iCoResignificantly surpasses that of all baseline methods and its ablated versions.

claims.text: Iterative refinement improves target-test retrieval; removing it lowers function MAP from 0.466 to 0.344 on SWT-bench Lite and from 0.438 to 0.316 on TDD-bench Verified, relative declines of 26.2%/27.9%.
claims.quote:
The function-level MAP decreases by 26.2% on SWT-bench Lite and 27.9% on TDD-
bench Verified.

claims.text: Function-call similarity improves target-test retrieval; removing it lowers function MAP to 0.449/0.418, relative decreases of 3.6%/4.6% on SWT-bench Lite/TDD-bench Verified.
claims.quote:
Removing the function-call similarity analysis (w/o Function-Call Similarity) decreases
function-level MAP by 3.6% and 4.6% on the two benchmarks, respectively.

claims.text: The LLM reranker preserves most target tests, filtering out only 4% of target tests supplied to it.

metrics.name: Percentage of input target tests filtered out

claims.quote:
By comparing the tests fed into the reranker with its final output, we
found that only 4% of target tests were filtered out by the LLM.

claims.text: Increasing sketch-feedback iterations improves bug reproduction over zero iterations; F→P@1 peaks at 42.0% after three cycles and performance largely stabilizes thereafter.
claims.quote:
The F→P(@1) rate peaks at 42.0% at the third
iteration.

claims.text: Five context tests give the best F→P@1: 42.0%, versus 34.4% with one and 41.3% with ten; ten tests slightly improve F→P@5 to 47.1% from 46.7%.
claims.quote:
Table 6 shows that
providing five tests yields the best performance on
F→P(@1).

claims.text: iCoRe is relatively insensitive to the function-similarity base weight over α=0.1–0.4, with reported F→P@1 mean 41.3% and standard deviation 0.45%.

metrics.name: Standard deviation of F→P@1 across α values

claims.quote:
As detailed in Table 7, the F→P(@1) rate
fluctuates minimally (Mean: 41.3%, Std: 0.45%) with different base weights, demonstrating the
robustness ofiCoReto these configurations.

claims.text: The default α=0.1 achieves the best tested F→P@1, 42.0%, compared with 40.9%, 41.3% and 40.9% for α=0.2, 0.3 and 0.4.
claims.quote:
In addition, 𝛼= 0.1yields optimal performance in our
experiments.

claims.text: iCoRe identifies more relevant and useful context for bug reproduction than the compared retrievers.

evidence.quote:
Accordingly, we extracted these
target tests from both datasets to serve as the ground truth for evaluating retrieval accuracy.

claims.quote:
These results underscore the effectiveness ofiCoRein identifying more relevant and
useful contexts for the BRT generator.

claims.text: Three refinement cycles offer a favorable balance between performance and efficiency.
claims.quote: Therefore, the default setting of three iterations is justified, balancing performance and efficiency.

claims.text: Selecting five context tests offers a favorable balance of context completeness, model focus and cost-effectiveness.
claims.quote:
Consequently, using five tests strikes the
optimal balance between providing comprehensive context and maintaining model focus and
cost-effectiveness.

claims.text: High-quality retrieved context reduces the need for multiple expensive LLM calls.
claims.quote:
This indicates that by
providing high-quality context,iCoReeffectively reduces the need for multiple calls to expensive
LLMs, achieving high performance through a basic prompt-then-generate process.

claims.text: Performance across TDD-bench issue-creation years 2017–2023 remains relatively stable, with reported mean 57.16% and standard deviation 11.75%.
claims.quote:
Performance across these issue creation
years remains relatively stable (Mean: 57.16%, SD: 11.75%), suggesting that the model does not
disproportionately favor older, potentially memorized issues.

claims.text: For 90% of evaluated instances, normalized Levenshtein similarity between generated tests and existing repository tests is below 0.56.
claims.quote: We found that for 90% of the instances, the similarity score remains below 0.56.

claims.text: Data contamination has a limited impact on the reported results.

metrics.name: Normalized Levenshtein similarity to repository tests

claims.quote:
These
findings confirm that the generator primarily relies on reasoning based on retrieved context rather
than memorization, indicating that the impact of data contamination is limited.

claims.text: The generator primarily reasons from retrieved context rather than memorizing tests.

metrics.name: Normalized Levenshtein similarity to repository tests

claims.quote:
These
findings confirm that the generator primarily relies on reasoning based on retrieved context rather
than memorization, indicating that the impact of data contamination is limited.

claims.text: Generator limitations despite sufficient context account for most manually sampled failures: 58% on SWT-bench Lite and 84% on TDD-bench Verified.

metrics.name: Manually classified generator-limitation share of sampled failures

claims.quote:
The majority of failures occurred when the retrieved context was sufficient, but the generator
failed to output a correct BRT.

claims.text: Failure to select a generated correct candidate as top-1 accounts for 18%/10% of sampled SWT-bench Lite/TDD-bench Verified failures.

metrics.name: Manually classified selection-failure share of sampled failures

claims.quote:
In these cases, the generator produced a correct BRT within the candidate list, but the selection
module failed to rank it as the top-1 choice.

claims.text: Ambiguous issue descriptions account for 14% of sampled SWT-bench Lite failures and none of the sampled TDD-bench Verified failures.

metrics.name: Manually classified ambiguous-description share of sampled failures

claims.quote: Some failures stem from the quality of the issue description itself rather than the generator.

claims.text: Missing critical retrieved context accounts for a minority of sampled failures: 10% on SWT-bench Lite and 6% on TDD-bench Verified.

metrics.name: Manually classified context-deficiency share of sampled failures

claims.quote: In a minority of cases, the retrieval module failed to locate the critical context.

ping to 17.92%.

hcs.quote:

of compilation checks in RepGen reduced the success rate in bug

sis feedback and runtime behaviour approximation had significant

hcs.name: RepGen without runtime feedback
hcs.removed: LLM runtime-behaviour approximation and symptom-based refinement feedback
hcs.page: 9, §4.6.2, Table 2; prose reverses the static/runtime percentages
hcs.quote:

sis feedback and runtime behaviour approximation had significant
impacts, reducing success rates in bug reproduction to 46.23% and
