hcs.name: RepGen without ANN retrieval
hcs.removed: ANN semantic retrieval
hcs.quote:
Disabling BM25 search, which captures exact lexical
matches, reduced RepGen’s success rate to 24.53%, while removing
ANN search, responsible for retrieving semantically related code,
resulted in a 26.42% success rate.

hcs.name: RepGen without BM25 retrieval
hcs.removed: BM25 lexical retrieval
hcs.quote:
Disabling BM25 search, which captures exact lexical
matches, reduced RepGen’s success rate to 24.53%, while removing
ANN search, responsible for retrieving semantically related code,
resulted in a 26.42% success rate.

hcs.name: RepGen without dependency extraction
hcs.removed: AST-based dependency extraction
hcs.quote:
Finally, omitting dependency extraction, re-
sponsible for capturing imports, helper functions, and referenced
variables, reduced RepGen’s success rate to 34.91%, highlighting
the need for a complete and executable context.

hcs.name: RepGen without module partitioning
hcs.removed: Module-centric partitioning and prioritization
hcs.quote:
omitting module partitioning reduced the success rate to 23.58%,
highlighting that prioritizing modules (e.g., components or classes)
based on the relevance of the code snippets rather than the sheer
number of snippets is essential for building an informative con-
text.

hcs.name: RepGen without snippet reranking
hcs.removed: Cross-encoder reranking of retrieved code snippets
hcs.quote:
Removing reranking, which refines
the relevance of retrieved snippets, decreased success to 30.19%,
showing that careful prioritization of candidate code is important
for context quality.

hcs.name: RepGen without training-loop extraction
hcs.removed: AST-driven training-loop extraction
hcs.quote:
Removal of the
training loop extraction component lowered RepGen’s performance
to 28.30%, indicating that incomplete loops without core training
logic can weaken the context.

hcs.name: RepGen without training-loop ranking
hcs.removed: Training-loop relevance ranking and selection
hcs.quote:
Removal of the training loop ranking component caused
the largest performance drop, reducing the success rate to 20.75%.

tively.

hcs.name: RepGen context supplied to standalone generation
hcs.removed: Planning, report restructuring, and full reproduction-agent validation/refinement
hcs.quote:
Using RepGen’s plan alone and context alone,
DeepSeek-R1-685B reproduced 63.21% and 68.87% of bugs, respec-
tively.

hcs.name: RepGen context and plan supplied to standalone generation
hcs.removed: Report restructuring and full reproduction-agent validation/refinement
hcs.quote:
Combining the learning-enhanced context with the plan
increased this to 71.70%.

hcs.name: RepGen restructured report, context, and plan supplied to standalone generation
hcs.removed: Full reproduction-agent validation/refinement
hcs.quote:
Similarly, when DeepSeek-R1-685B was
provided a restructured bug report along with the context and plan,
it achieved 65.04%.

hcs.name: RepGen artifacts with lightweight AST/PyLint agentic feedback
hcs.removed: Full relevance and runtime-symptom feedback replaced by lightweight AST/PyLint feedback
hcs.quote:
This performance further improved to 72.64%
when run with an agentic setup that enhances the context, plan,
and restructured report with lightweight PyLint and AST feedback.

claims.text: Reducer generation yields syntactically valid scripts for all 200 evaluated buggy codes.
claims.quote:
Using the prompt template in Listing 1,
Qwen2.5-Plus produced a syntactically valid reducer.py for all
200 buggy codes.

claims.text: ReduceFix successfully reduces 95.0% of LFTBench bugs, versus 40.0% for Pure LLM and 35.5% for the external ddmin-only comparator.
claims.quote:
Tables 3 and 4 show that
the LLM-generated reducers succeed on 95.0% of the 200 buggy
codes.

claims.text: Successful ReduceFix reductions remove 89.1% of input bytes on average; median compression is 100.0%, rounded.

metrics.name: Mean compression rate among successful reductions
Median compression rate among successful reductions

claims.quote:
OnLFTBench,ReduceFixwith Qwen2.5-Plus gen-
erates syntactically correct reducers for all the 200 bugs, and 95.0%
of those reducers successfully shrink the failure-inducing input by
an average of 89.1%.

claims.text: ReduceFix reduces reduction-stage API cost from $0.632 for Pure LLM to $0.017; the paper describes this as a 98% saving.
claims.quote:
At current API prices,
this comparison translates to $0.632 versus $0.017, 98% saving.

claims.text: Reduced Test improves overall pass@10 over both author controls for all four models; the abstract reports gains up to 53.8% over Origin Test and 17.6% over omitting tests.

evidence.detail: §5.3 reports a two-sided MWW p-value <0.05 for Reduced Test versus Origin Test based on four LLMs; no corresponding independent test is reported for the no-test comparison.

claims.quote:
Across all 4 evaluated LLMs, provid-
ing the reduced failure-inducing input consistently raises repair
accuracy.

claims.text: With Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-instruct, ReduceFix exceeds the end-to-end ddmin-replacement variant: pass@1/5/10 is 6.3/17.9/25.5% versus 5.7/16.1/22.0%; the pass@10 gap is reported significant.

evidence.detail: Two-sided MWW test for the pass@10 gap, p<0.05.

claims.quote:
We also evaluate an end-to-
end ddmin-only baseline that uses the reduced input when ddmin
succeeds and otherwise falls back to the original failing test, with
all other settings unchanged.

claims.text: On Python bugs, Reduced Test reaches 75.0% overall pass@10 versus 70.0% without tests and 60.0% with original tests; the paper calls the improvement significant without reporting a Python-specific significance test.
claims.quote:
OnLFTBench-Pywith Qwen2.5-Plus, Reduced Test lifts overall
pass@10 to 75.0% versus 70.0% for Baseline and 60.0% for Origin,
with the strongest gains on Medium tasks (Table 7).

claims.text: Reduced Test has the best overall prompt-composition results: pass@10 25.5%, versus 20.0% for Diff Lines and 19.0% for Reduced + Origin.
claims.quote:
Across the full 200-bug benchmark,
Reduced Testdelivers the best outcomes, reaching 25.5% pass@10.

claims.text: The paper attributes the benefit to the conjunction of compact prompts and complete counterexample evidence, claiming either alone is insufficient.
claims.quote:
The conjunction
of compact length and complete counter-example information is
therefore essential; either ingredient alone is insufficient.

claims.text: ChatRepair + ReduceFix improves over external ChatRepair across reported difficulty groups and sampling cutoffs; overall pass@10 rises from 30.5% to 37.0%, a 21.3% relative gain.
claims.quote:
The overall pass@10
rises from 30.5% to 37.0%, an absolute gain of 6.5 percentage points
and a relative gain of 21.3%.

claims.text: CREF + ReduceFix improves over external CREF overall: pass@1/5/10 increases from 13.9/31.6/39.0% to 14.7/32.7/40.0%; the pass@10 relative gain is 2.6%.
claims.quote:
Likewise,
CREF benefits fromReduceFix: overall pass@10 rises from 39.0%
to 40.0%, with pass@5 from 31.6% to 32.7% and pass@1 from 13.9%
to 14.7% onLFTBench(Table 11).

claims.text: ReduceFix is presented as a lightweight, portable add-on requiring no changes to existing APR conversation logic; engineering effort itself is not measured.
claims.quote:
These results demonstrate that
reducing the supplied failure-inducing test yields a measurable im-
provement without requiring any other adjustments to existing
APR systems.

claims.text: On OSS-Fuzz, ReduceFix achieves 91.7% crash-preserving reduction success, versus 75.0% for external ddmin-only and 0% for Pure LLM.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 12 and Table 13,
on 12 OSS-Fuzz crashes spanning FFmpeg, Poppler, PHP-src, and
MuPDF,ReduceFixpreserved the crash during reduction in 91.7%
of cases versus 75.0% forddmin-only, a +22.3% relative gain and an
absolute +16.7 points.

claims.text: On OSS-Fuzz, ReduceFix mean compression is 56.4% versus 51.8% for external ddmin-only, an 8.9% reported relative gain.
claims.quote:
Mean compression rose from 51.8% to 56.4%,
a +8.9% relative gain.

claims.text: On OSS-Fuzz, Reduced Test improves micro-average pass@1/5/10 to 19.2/29.2/41.7%, versus 17.5/25.0/25.0% without tests and 9.2/14.8/16.7% with original tests.
claims.quote:
On the 12-sample micro
average, pass@1 rose from 17.5% to 19.2% (+9.7% relative), pass@5
from 25.0% to 29.2% (+16.8% relative), and pass@10 from 25.0% to
41.7% (+66.8% relative).

claims.text: The authors claim applicability to realistic repository-level repair across the evaluated projects and languages; the reported scope is 12 selected single-file-patch instances.
claims.quote:
The evaluation demonstrates the effective-
ness ofReduceFixin real-world repository-level repair scenarios.

claims.text: Supplying the unreduced failing input often lowers repair success relative to omitting it, including overall GLM pass@10 8.5→6.5% and DeepSeek 66.5→63.0%.
claims.quote:
GLM-4-9B-chat’s overall pass@10 falls from 8.5%
with no test case to 6.5% when the complete input is added, while
DeepSeek-V3 drops from 66.5% to 63.0% under the same switch.

claims.text: The paper claims Reduced Test is consistently better than Origin Test across every model and difficulty group; Table 6 includes ties and some pass@1 reversals, so strict superiority across all reported outcomes is unsupported.

evidence.detail: MWW p<0.05 is reported for the overall Reduced-versus-Origin comparison based on four models, not every subgroup or cutoff.

claims.quote:
ReduceFixis consistently bet-
ter than Origin Test across all LLMs and difficulty groups, and
it also outperforms the Baseline in every overall comparison.

claims.text: The authors interpret the prompt intervention as showing that excessive input length dilutes model attention; attention is not measured directly.
claims.quote:
First, inserting the entire failure-
inducing input without reduction inflates the prompt by roughly
30 KB and consistently depresses success, confirming that exces-
sive length dilutes attention.

claims.text: The Python evaluation is interpreted as evidence of cross-language robustness.

metrics.name: Python pass@1/5/10 relative to author controls

claims.quote:
When evaluating onLFTBench-Py, the improvement ofReduce-
Fixis significant, indicating its cross-language robustness.

claims.text: Reduction success varies by difficulty: ReduceFix achieves 100.0/96.2/88.3% on C/D/E&F, versus Pure LLM 63.3/36.2/21.7%; external ddmin-only achieves 30.0/17.5/65.0%.
claims.quote:
All submissions of C-difficulty tasks are successfully reduced,
while D-difficulty tasks and E & F-difficulty tasks reach 96.2% and
88.3% success, respectively.

claims.text: ReduceFix succeeds across all six input families: 97.5/100.0/85.0/90.0/95.0/100.0% for single/multiple/dependent sequences, matrices, graphs and strings; corresponding Pure LLM rates are 36.2/50.0/22.5/0/65.0/90.0%.
claims.quote:
This pure LLM baseline succeeds on
only 40.0% of the bugs overall and 36.2% of the D-difficulty tasks,
and by input typeReduceFixremains robust on graph and string
cases whereddmin-only fails.

claims.text: Successful reductions have near-total median compression across difficulties; mean ReduceFix compression is 84.5/97.0/83.0% on C/D/E&F, lower than Pure LLM's 100.0/100.0/99.1% among its successful cases.
claims.quote:
Tasks in the C-difficulty and D-difficulty
groups achieve even larger average removals of 84.5% and 97.0%,
respectively.

claims.text: ReduceFix uses 94,217 input tokens versus 5,687,356 for Pure LLM on the 20-problem cost comparison.
claims.quote:
TheReduceFixrequires only 0.094
million input tokens for the same dataset.

claims.text: ReduceFix generates more output tokens than Pure LLM in the cost comparison: 20,270 versus 1,268, a 15.99-fold ratio.
claims.quote:
Table 5 compares the input/output token usage of two reduction
strategies onLFTBench.

claims.text: Ten of 200 ReduceFix cases fall back to the original input because search fails to produce a shorter candidate before the time limit, rather than because reducer code is syntactically invalid.
claims.quote:
10 of 200 forwarded the unreduced case
to the repair phase, and in all 10 cases, theddminloop did not yield
a shorter candidate before the time limit.

claims.text: The strongest repair gains are reported on D tasks: Qwen2.5-Coder pass@10 rises 25.0→36.2% and GLM 13.8→20.0%, reported as 44.8% and 44.9% relative gains.
claims.quote:
On D-difficulty tasks,
the Reduced Test prompt lifts Qwen2.5’s pass@10 by 44.8% and
pushes GLM-4-9B-chat up by 44.9%.

claims.text: On E&F tasks, Reduced Test improves over Origin Test for Qwen2.5-Plus, 51.7→55.0% pass@10, and DeepSeek-V3, 51.7→56.7%.
claims.quote:
Tasks with difficulties E&F see
Qwen2.5-Plus rise from 51.7% to 55.0%, and DeepSeek-V3 recover
part of the loss incurred by the origin test input, moving from 51.7%
to 56.7%.

claims.text: ReduceFix reduction succeeds on 18 of 20 Python cases, or 90%.
claims.quote:
In addition, for cross-language valida-
tion, we evaluate Qwen2.5-Plus onLFTBench-Pyunder the same
protocol; the reducer succeeds on 18 of 20 Python cases (90%).

claims.text: Mean prompt sizes are 3.2KB for Baseline and Diff Lines, 6.6KB for Reduced Test, 30.5KB for Origin Test and 36.4KB for Reduced + Origin; corresponding mean lines are 130.1, 132.6, 514.0, 2381.4 and 2637.7.
claims.quote:
Table 8 confirms that the five prompt
variants span more than an order of magnitude in length, from
roughly 3 KB forBaselineandDiff Linesto 36 KB forReduced + Ori-
gin.

claims.text: Prompt-composition advantages are larger on harder groups: Reduced Test reaches 36.2% pass@10 on D versus Diff Lines 25.0% and Origin 23.8%; on E&F it reaches 11.7% versus Diff Lines 6.7% and Reduced + Origin 3.3%.
claims.quote:
On the hardest
E&F-difficulty, it records 11.7% pass@10, almost doubling the 6.7%
achieved byDiff Linesand more than tripling the 3.3% scored by
Reduced + Origin.

claims.text: The paper claims Diff Lines is consistently superior to Reduced + Origin, especially on C tasks; Table 9 supports the overall and C/E&F comparisons but reverses D pass@5 and pass@10.
claims.quote:
Diff Lines is consistently superior to Reduced + Origin; the gap
is most pronounced on C-difficulty tasks, where pass@10 reaches
26.7% versus 23.3%.

claims.text: OSS-Fuzz reduction success is 100% on FFmpeg, ImageMagick, MuPDF and PHP-src and 75% on Poppler; Pure LLM fails on every project, while external ddmin-only fails on FFmpeg and achieves 50% on Poppler.
claims.quote:
The pure-LLM approach fails to reduce
any of the failure-inducing test inputs, mainly because these inputs
are long (exceeding 1 KB) and structurally complex (e.g., binary
file), which LLMs cannot effectively simplify.

claims.text: OSS-Fuzz compression is 35.4/5.0/87.4/97.7/25.4% on FFmpeg/ImageMagick/MuPDF/PHP-src/Poppler; external ddmin-only has no successful FFmpeg reduction and 4.6/88.1/85.6/22.8% on the other four, so MuPDF is a small regression.
claims.quote:
On MuPDF,
both preserved the crash, and compression was comparable (-0.8%
relative forReduceFix).

claims.text: OSS-Fuzz repair gains vary by project: FFmpeg pass@10 reaches 100% from 0%, MuPDF reaches 40% from 20%, and PHP-src pass@1 reaches 100% from 60% without tests; Poppler pass@10 stays 25% and ImageMagick remains unsolved.
claims.quote:
By project,
FFmpeg reached 100.0% pass@10 from 0%; MuPDF doubled pass@10
from 20.0% to 40.0%; PHP-src raised pass@1 from 60.0% to 100.0%;
Poppler stayed at 25.0%; ImageMagick remained unsolved.

claims.text: The paper claims repository-level reduced tests are more interpretable; no human interpretability assessment is reported.
claims.quote:
By combining semantic-aware LLM reasoning with traditional
reduction techniques,ReduceFixreliably preserves failure be-
havior while producing more concise and interpretable test cases.

claims.text: The ABC372E failure analysis attributes an unsuccessful reduction to renumbering vertices, which hides a defect dependent on absolute identifier magnitude.
claims.quote:
Because the defect depends on the absolute magnitude of vertex
identifiers, this renumbering masked the failure, the interestingness
predicate became false, andddminstopped without shrinking the
input.

claims.text: The FFmpeg analysis attributes successful ReduceFix reduction to structure-preserving transformations and adaptive chunking that retain container invariants before ddmin.
claims.quote:
In contrast, the LLM-generated reducer applies structure-
preserving transformations with adaptive chunking to maintain
those invariants before driving ddmin, which preserves the crash
and still reduces the input.

claims.text: The largest OSS-Fuzz pass@k improvements occur on projects where ddmin-only fails or compresses poorly, namely FFmpeg and PHP-src.
claims.quote:
The largest improvements in pass@k occur when
ddmin-only fails or compresses poorly, including in FFmpeg and
PHP-src.

claims.text: The authors conclude that combining an LLM-generated reducer with systematic ddmin search is both essential and efficient for reduction.
claims.quote:
These
results validate the core design ofReduceFix: leveraging LLM to
generate a reducer and then driving a systematic ddmin search is
both essential and efficient.

hcs.name: DROID FILLER: standalone text-input generation
hcs.quote:
DROID FILLER
instead adopts the function call-based context retrieval, which
allows the model to selectively and dynamically refer to the
external information sources when generating text contents.

hcs.name: DROID FILLER -Reasoning
hcs.removed: Separate reasoning stage/template; retain dynamic function calls, argument checking and retries
hcs.quote:
The ablation settings are as follows: -Reasoning
removes the reasoning step template from the prompt and
directly asks the model to either generate the text content or
invoke a function call.

hcs.name: DROID FILLER -FunctionCall
hcs.removed: Function-call context retrieval, including its function interface, argument checking and retry loop; retain reasoning-then-generation stages
hcs.quote:
-FunctionCall removes the function call-
based context retrieval so it has a reasoning step but does not
aware of any functions that can provide additional information.

hcs.name: Single-call GUI-context control: -Reasoning-FunctionCall and basic LLM prompting (LLM_Base)
hcs.removed: Reasoning stage and function-call context retrieval; basic LLM control uses local GUI prompting
hcs.quote:
-Reasoning-FunctionCall removes both the reasoning step
template and the function call-based context retrieval.

hcs.name: STEM integrated with DROID FILLER
hcs.quote:
We implement
DROID FILLER as a separate module that can be plugged into
the existing STEM framework, and the module is activated
when STEM generates a SetText event.

ecs.protocol: Post-hoc input-validity analysis and qualitative URL/search/date-input observations; 857/981 valid; precise validity rubric, evaluator, sample selection, repetitions and budget for this analysis not_reported

Analysis of 981 text inputs generated for 12 apps reveals
that 857 of them (87.4%) are valid.

claims.text: DroidFiller produces realistic inputs for 118/120 fields (98.3%), versus 111/120 (92.5%) for basic LLM prompting and 78/120 (65%) for the external category-matching comparator.
claims.quote:
Based on human labelling of whether the
generated input is semantically relevant or not, DROID FILLER
outperforms both baselines.

claims.text: On third-party fields, DroidFiller and basic LLM prompting perform similarly overall, although DroidFiller succeeds on some fields where basic prompting fails.
claims.quote:
For textfields from 3rd party apps, DROID FILLER and basic
LLM prompting show similar performances, but DROID FILLER
generates meaningful contents where the basic LLM prompting
does not.

claims.text: The separate reasoning stage improves realistic inputs from 112/120 to 118/120.
claims.quote:
The result implies that both the reasoning step
template and the function call-based context retrieval contribute
to the overall text generation quality, but the reasoning step
template seems to be a more crucial component on generating
better quality text contents.

claims.text: Function-call context retrieval improves realistic inputs from 116/120 to 118/120.
claims.quote:
The result implies that both the reasoning step
template and the function call-based context retrieval contribute
to the overall text generation quality, but the reasoning step
template seems to be a more crucial component on generating
better quality text contents.

claims.text: Removing both reasoning and function-call retrieval reduces realistic inputs from 118/120 to 111/120.
claims.quote:
The result implies that both the reasoning step
template and the function call-based context retrieval contribute
to the overall text generation quality, but the reasoning step
template seems to be a more crucial component on generating
better quality text contents.

claims.text: Reasoning contributes more to realistic-input quality than function-call retrieval in this benchmark.
claims.quote:
The result implies that both the reasoning step
template and the function call-based context retrieval contribute
to the overall text generation quality, but the reasoning step
template seems to be a more crucial component on generating
better quality text contents.

claims.text: Friend-profile invocation has precision 0.31, recall 0.65 and F1 0.42, with many unnecessary calls.
claims.quote:
The relatively low precision for the functions “get friend
profile” and “get samsung product info” indicates that there
are significant number of textfields that unnecessarily invoked
those functions.

claims.text: Samsung-product-information invocation has precision 0.14, recall 1.00 and F1 0.25, with many unnecessary calls despite detecting all labelled needs.
claims.quote:
The relatively low precision for the functions “get friend
profile” and “get samsung product info” indicates that there
are significant number of textfields that unnecessarily invoked
those functions.

claims.text: Coupon-code invocation is perfectly classified in this benchmark: precision, recall and F1 are all 1.00.
claims.quote:
We treat this as a ternary classification
problem and report the accuracy of function calling in Table VI.

claims.text: Overall function-call classification has micro precision/recall/F1 of 0.27/0.71/0.39 and macro scores of 0.48/0.88/0.56; recall exceeds precision.
claims.quote:
In contrast,
the recall is relatively high, which highlights the capability of
DROID FILLER detecting a necessity of additional information
for the target textfield and the overall screen state.

claims.text: For every field with an irrelevant function call, DroidFiller eventually generates at least one correct input; the Friends show-title example illustrates recovery.

metrics.name: Fields eventually receiving at least one correct input after an irrelevant call

claims.quote:
For example,
although DROID FILLER attempts to call “get friend profile”
on the textfield that requires a TV show name to be inputted,
it finally generates a correct show title, “Friends”.

claims.text: Some incorrect function calls also lead to incorrect text inputs.

metrics.name: Qualitatively observed incorrect inputs following incorrect function calls

claims.quote:
However, we also observe several cases that the incorrect
function calling leads to an incorrect text input as well;

claims.text: DroidFiller retrieves and outputs predefined valid Galaxy Store coupon codes; basic LLM prompting fails, while the external category-matching comparator also succeeds.

metrics.name: Qualitative agreement with the predefined valid coupon codes

claims.quote:
DROID FILLER correctly invokes the function and outputs the
predefined coupon codes based on the returned result of the
function.

claims.quote:
Overall, we observe partial improvements in testing effective-

claims.quote:
DROID FILLER , on the other hand,
generates an appropriate URL using the provided functions.

claims.text: In the illustrated budget-planner app, DroidFiller generates a search query that yields an expense-category list, while external original STEM fails.

metrics.name: Observed search results for the generated query

claims.quote:
Figure 8 shows that DROID FILLER successfully fills in the
search boxes within a budget planner app, with a valid search
query that yields the available expense category list, whereas
the original STEM fails to do so.

claims.text: DroidFiller adapts date strings to placeholder-indicated formats; external original STEM's fixed 2021-01-01 value is rejected in the illustrated case.
claims.quote:
On the other hand,
DROID FILLER can flexibly adapt the data to the desired format.

claims.text: Of 981 generated inputs across 12 apps, 857 (87.4%) are valid.

Analysis of 981 text inputs generated for 12 apps reveals

claims.text: Invalid integrated-run inputs commonly reflect misunderstanding of a field's intended use, such as supplying a dollar sign where only numbers are expected.

metrics.name: Qualitative inspection of invalid input causes

claims.quote:
The remaining invalid
inputs typically due to the misunderstanding of the intended
use of the text field.

claims.text: Missing broader context, including previously visited screens, is another observed cause of problematic input generation.
claims.quote:
Another common cause is that DROID FILLER
misses the larger context, such as the previously visited screens.

claims.text: STEM sometimes requests repeated generation for the same field because minor screen changes are mistaken for a new screen.

metrics.name: Qualitatively observed repeated same-field generation requests

claims.quote:
First, STEM sometimes makes repeated requests to
DROID FILLER to generate inputs for the same textfield.

claims.text: Even after fields are filled, an unsuitable subsequent STEM action can prevent progress or discard the entered text.

metrics.name: Qualitatively observed post-input failure to progress

claims.quote:
Second, even after
filling in all the required textfields, the app might not progress
if the subsequent event generated by STEM does not process
the entered texts.

claims.text: Minor UI variations, such as calendar-picker states, can inflate unique-state counts and weaken their interpretation as exploration diversity.

metrics.name: Qualitative examination of minor GUI-state variations

claims.quote:
Additionally, we note
that the number of unique states discovered can be significantly
inflated by UI components that introduce minor variations, such
as calendar pickers.

claims.text: The Settings search-field example suggests that enforced reasoning helps DroidFiller attend to relevant information in a long GUI prompt, while basic LLM prompting generates irrelevant general searches.

metrics.name: Qualitative relevance of generated Settings search queries

claims.quote:
Although
the app name, “Settings” is provided as a prompting context
both for DROID FILLER and LLM base, the result implies that
enforcing proper reasoning steps help refer to the relevant
information in the long prompting context.

claims.text: Without reasoning, DroidFiller struggles to generate valid queries for the illustrated AOL news/mail/video search field; full DroidFiller generates relevant topics.

metrics.name: Qualitative validity of AOL search-query examples

claims.quote: Fig. 5. Example text generations from different ablation settings.

claims.text: Without function-call retrieval, DroidFiller fails to produce the required product serial number in the illustrated registration field; the full system retrieves it.

metrics.name: Qualitative validity of the product-registration serial number

claims.quote:
DROID FILLER without function call-
based context retrieval fails to generate a valid serial number
for the target product, which is only given as an additional
context delivered by the result of function call (specifically,
get_samsung_product_info function).

claims.text: The authors expect DroidFiller to generalise to other commonly used apps because it relies on common LLM knowledge rather than app-specific analysis.
claims.quote:
since DROID FILLER
is drawing from common knowledge found in LLMs and not
any app specific analysis, we expect its ability to generalise to
other target apps as long as they are common apps used by the
majority of users.

claims.text: The partial coverage gains are interpreted as showing that integrating an LLM-based input generator into an automated GUI testing tool requires careful orchestration.
claims.quote: The results suggest that a careful orchestration is needed when integrating LLM-based input generator to automated GUI testing tools.

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Unnamed messaging/simple chat application; app identity, version and benchmark not_reported
ecs.protocol: Qualitative multi-account scenario demonstration; custom goal of testing multiple user interactions; persona credentials and synthesised second-account credentials; demonstration-specific model, run count and time budget not_reported.
ecs.quote: We demonstrate the potential of applying D ROID AGENT on testing multi-user interactions in Figure 10, which contains testing scenarios generated by DROID AGENT with a custom goal of “testing multiple user interactions”.

claims.text: DroidAgent achieves 60.7% mean activity coverage versus Humanoid's 51.4%, with significantly more covered activities; Table II reports 133 covered activities overall.

evidence.detail: Wilcoxon signed rank test against Humanoid, p < 0.045.
evidence.quote: A Wilcoxon signed rank test indicated that the number of activities cov- ered by D ROID AGENT was statistically significantly higher than those covered by Humanoid ( p < 0.045).

claims.quote: On average, D ROID AGENT achieves an activity coverage of 60.7%, slightly exceeding the best baseline, Hu- manoid, with an average coverage of 51.4%.

claims.text: DroidAgent covers more functional features than Humanoid across every subject, averaging 13.9 versus 7.3, including subjects where Humanoid has higher activity coverage.

evidence.detail: Wilcoxon signed rank test against Humanoid, p < 0.0008.
evidence.quote: A Wilcoxon signed rank test indicated that the number of features covered by DROID AGENT was statistically significantly higher than those covered by Humanoid ( p <0.0008).

claims.quote: D ROID AGENT consistently covers a significantly larger number of features than Humanoid (D ROID AGENT average: 13.9, Humanoid average: 7.3) across all subjects; this holds even where Humanoid has higher activity coverage.

claims.text: DroidAgent finds five crashes, compared with Humanoid's four, Monkey's four, DroidBot's three and GPTDroid's one, supporting crash-finding capability at least comparable to these baselines.

evidence.detail: One of DroidAgent's five detected crashes had previously been reported.
evidence.quote: D ROID AGENT finds five crashes in total (one of them had been reported as a past GitHub issue), while Humanoid finds four crashes in total (one of them had been reported).

claims.quote: Nevertheless, DROID AGENT still shows crash finding capa- bility on par with other baselines, suggesting its potential as a viable GUI testing technique.

claims.text: Manual assessment judges 85% of 374 unique generated tasks viable for their apps; the abstract reports 317 realistic and relevant tasks.

metrics.name: Number of realistic and relevant tasks

claims.quote: Figure 6 shows that, among all 374 unique tasks generated for 15 applications, we deemed 85% as viable, and 59% as completed by D ROID AGENT .

claims.text: DroidAgent successfully completes 59% of the 374 unique generated tasks according to manual assessment.
claims.quote: Figure 6 shows that, among all 374 unique tasks generated for 15 applications, we deemed 85% as viable, and 59% as completed by D ROID AGENT .

claims.text: The Reflector's task-success classifications achieve precision 0.72, recall 0.77 and F1 0.74 against manual completion labels.
claims.quote: Based on this manual labelling, we report that the Reflector achieves a relatively high level of accuracy in task result assessment, with precision of 0.72, recall of 0.77, and F1 score of 0.74.

claims.text: Knowledge retrievers appear to improve exploration breadth in the five-app ablation study; numerical Figure 8 bar values are not_reported in the supplied text.
claims.quote: Both the presence of knowledge retrievers and self-critique module seem to positively enhance D ROID AGENT ’s effectiveness in exploring the broader parts of the application.

claims.text: Actor self-critique appears to improve exploration breadth in the five-app ablation study; numerical Figure 8 bar values are not_reported in the supplied text.
claims.quote: Both the presence of knowledge retrievers and self-critique module seem to positively enhance D ROID AGENT ’s effectiveness in exploring the broader parts of the application.

claims.text: A two-hour DroidAgent exploration costs $13–$22 per application, averaging $18.1 across the evaluated apps.

metrics.name: API monetary cost per two-hour exploration
GPT-3.5/GPT-4 prompt and completion token counts

claims.quote: Accordingly, the present-time cost for running D ROID AGENT on a single application with a two-hour budget ranges between $13 to $22, summing up the cost from both the GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 models, averaging $18.1.

claims.text: DroidAgent plans and executes an average of 36 tasks per application, with standard deviation 8.8.

metrics.name: Number of planned and executed tasks per application
Across-application standard deviation of task count

claims.quote: DROID AGENT planned and ex- ecuted on average 36 tasks (standard deviation: 8.8) per AUT.

claims.text: Average task lengths vary from 7.4 to 11.2 actions across applications, with mean 8.9, below the 13-action maximum because Actor can stop early.
claims.quote: Although we set 13 as a maximum number of actions per task, the average task lengths vary across applications (min: 7.4, max: 11.2, mean: 8.9), as the Actor of D ROID AGENT can end the task earlier.

claims.text: The authors associate DroidAgent's coverage advantage with intuitive app functionality and identify weaker exploration on interfaces lacking widget text or containing distinct subregions within one view, including Scarlet-Notes and osmeditor4android.
claims.quote: For those applications that D ROID AGENT discovers significantly more activities than other baselines, the functionalities supported by the applications are relatively intuitive and follow the common sense.

claims.text: On AnkiDroid, DroidAgent and the compared exploration techniques reach a similar degree of activity coverage after two hours.
claims.quote: We observe the trend on the AnkiDroid app as a representative, in which the techniques including D ROID AGENT show a similar degree of activity coverage after two hours.

claims.text: On AnkiDroid, Humanoid initially increases activity coverage faster than DroidAgent and the other techniques during the first 30 minutes, before plateauing.

metrics.name: Activity coverage over elapsed exploration time

claims.quote: Humanoid shows a relatively higher growth rate in the first 30 minutes compared to others, but it fails to discover more activities afterwards.

claims.text: DroidAgent constructs dependent multi-task scenarios by reusing app data created in earlier tasks, demonstrated by ActivityDiary searches and subsequent AnkiDroid flashcard use.

metrics.name: Successful cross-task reuse of generated app data, qualitative cases

claims.quote: D ROID AGENT tries to search for a specific activity and successfully inputs a valid query, “Gym Workout”, which is an activity name created during a previous task.

claims.text: With account credentials in its persona profile, DroidAgent autonomously signs into commons and MaterialFB without startup login scripts.

metrics.name: Successful autonomous startup login in two apps, qualitative observation

claims.quote: Conversely, DROID A- GENT can autonomously sign into both apps without these scripts when provided with the relevant account credentials in its persona profile, making the sign-in process seamlessly integrates into its exploration routine.

claims.text: DroidAgent handles a redirected login encountered during AnkiDroid data synchronisation, rather than requiring advance scripting of that login path.

metrics.name: Successful handling of a redirected login, qualitative case

claims.quote: D ROID AGENT also exhibits adaptability in handling the app’s “hidden” login features, like the redirected login screen encountered during data synchronisation as previously highlighted (Figure 2).

claims.text: Adaptive retries are reported to help DroidAgent handle flaky login actions; no retry success rate or controlled robustness evaluation is reported.

metrics.name: Adaptive retry behaviour in login examples

claims.quote: D ROID AGENT can address such flakiness by adaptively retrying the failed action (e.g., re-clicking the login button), making it more resilient.

claims.text: The authors argue that associating a crash with a meaningful task makes it easier for developers to understand, illustrated by the commons image-upload cancellation crash.
claims.quote: For instance, in the “commons” app, the application crashes when one attempts to upload a picture and then cancels the process mid-upload.

claims.text: The authors believe that supplying the commons crash with its image-upload task description can help developers reproduce the issue more effectively.
claims.quote: The crash can be presented to a developer along with a task description of image uploading, which we believe aids in more effectively reproducing the issue.

claims.text: DroidAgent demonstrates autonomous multi-account social workflows, including creating a second account and adding the first account as a friend; the custom-goal chat demonstration also generates an interaction between accounts.
claims.quote: For example, when testing a messaging app, D ROID AGENT created a second account and added a first account as a friend, testing a realistic use case, without human intervention.

claims.text: During second-account creation, DroidAgent recovers from an email-field length restriction by using a shorter email address.

metrics.name: Successful adaptation to email truncation, qualitative case

claims.quote: Moreover, while creating the second account, DROID AGENT encounters a truncated email address due to the length limit of the textfield, but later it successfully works around the issue by using a shorter email address.

claims.text: DroidAgent's fixed external-app interaction limit sometimes prematurely terminates interactions needed for the tested workflow; the affected applications are not_reported.

metrics.name: Observed premature termination of essential external-app interactions, qualitative cases

claims.quote: However, we observe some cases that D ROID AGENT prematurely terminated essential interactions in the external app due to this limit.

Accordingly, ITeM extracts the test intentions from the
test script on the source app and then fulfills these intentions on the target app, thus completing
the migration of test scripts.

combination of action type and widget information as input, a common structured format used
in scripts [4, 16, 27].

in the prompt (see Table 2).

hcs.name: DSrepair
hcs.quote:
If the code fails to pass the test cases, DSrepair con-
structs a repair prompt and requests LLM to regenerate the
code (see Section III-B for details).

hcs.name: DSrepair w/o API
hcs.removed: API knowledge omitted from repair prompt
hcs.quote:
‘DSrepair w/o
API&Bug’ is for prompt without API and bug knowledge,
‘DSrepair w/o Bug’ is for prompt without bug knowledge, and
‘DSrepair w/o API’ refers to prompt without API knowledge.

hcs.name: DSrepair w/o Bug
hcs.removed: Enriched AST-node bug knowledge omitted from repair prompt
hcs.quote:
‘DSrepair w/o
API&Bug’ is for prompt without API and bug knowledge,
‘DSrepair w/o Bug’ is for prompt without bug knowledge, and
‘DSrepair w/o API’ refers to prompt without API knowledge.

hcs.name: DSrepair w/o API&Bug
hcs.removed: API knowledge and enriched bug knowledge omitted from repair prompt
hcs.quote:
‘DSrepair w/o
API&Bug’ is for prompt without API and bug knowledge,
‘DSrepair w/o Bug’ is for prompt without bug knowledge, and

hcs.name: DSrepair with plain-text retrieval
hcs.removed: DS-KG/SPARQL retrieval replaced by API-keyword plain-text retrieval, with a 50-token window per keyword
hcs.quote:
The API knowledge is
retrieved as a window of text encompassing 50 tokens per
keyword.

hcs.name: DSrepair+explanation
hcs.quote:
To explore the potential bene-
fits of this enriched API knowledge, we design experi-
ments with different richness levels of API information:
DSrepair+explanation, DSrepair+parameter&return, and DSre-
pair+explanation+parameter&return.

hcs.name: DSrepair+parameter&return
hcs.quote:
DSrepair+parameter&return adds informa-
tion about the function’s parameters and returns.

hcs.name: DSrepair+explanation+parameter&return
hcs.quote:
DSre-
pair+explanation+parameter&return combines both types of
information into the API knowledge.

claims.text: Across the four models, DSrepair repairs 104/145/164/140 programs (FR 18.51/25.80/29.18/24.91%), outperforming Code-Search, Chat-Repair, Self-Debugging-S, Self-Debugging-E and Self-Repair, with improvements of 44.4/14.2/20.6/32.1% over the second-best method.

evidence.quote:

correctness of the patches to make sure that the reported fixes
are not overfitted.

claims.quote:
We can observe that DSrepair significantly outperforms all
the baselines in terms of ANF and FR across all four LLMs
we study.

claims.text: DSrepair has the best repair performance for most library/model subsets, including NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib and PyTorch with GPT-3.5-turbo, and NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib and PyTorch with Codestral.

purposes.

seconds in the median, which is 3.50 times, 4.22 times,
and 19.11 times faster than that of COFUZZ, INTRIGUER,
and QSYM, respectively.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ solves an average 411.4 roadblocks per campaign versus COFUZZ 212.4, INTRIGUER 181.6 and QSYM 144.3; the accompanying every-subject superiority assertion has a Table III exception: curl 76.3 versus COFUZZ 89.0.
claims.quote:
On average,
HYLLFUZZsolved 411.4 roadblocks, while the baselines
solved 212.4, 181.6, and 144.3 roadblocks, respectively.

claims.text: Across subjects, larger numbers of solved roadblocks are reported to correlate positively with greater coverage improvement; no correlation coefficient or significance test is reported.
claims.quote:
These results demonstrate a positive
correlation between the number of roadblocks solved and the
improvement in code coverage.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ generates 2,828 concolic inputs in 24 hours on average, versus COFUZZ 2,494, INTRIGUER 2,154 and QSYM 1,475; its throughput advantage is large over QSYM but modest over the other two.

metrics.name: Mean concolic inputs generated per 24 hours

claims.quote:
On
average, HYLLFUZZgenerated 2828 inputs, while COFUZZ,
INTRIGUER, and QSYM generated 2494, 2154, and 1475
inputs, respectively.

claims.text: Fast LLM-based concolic execution is claimed to contribute to higher coverage, while not fully explaining the gain because COFUZZ and INTRIGUER generate comparable input counts.
claims.quote:
This result indicates that fast concolic execution con-
tributes to improved code coverage.

claims.text: Higher coverage is attributed to LLM solving rather than roadblock selection: on the same selected roadblocks, HYLLFUZZ solves php 837.1 in prose (827.1 in Table IV), jq 44.0, bc 200.0 and calc 880.1, versus best modified external engines 205.3, 9.0, 117.0 and 369.0.

evidence.detail: Inspection of uniquely covered branches traces successful PHP keyword completion to semantic reasoning; illustrative rather than comprehensive causal isolation.
evidence.quote:
After
interpreting the input “tr”, HYLLFUZZinferred the code se-
mantics and correctly generated the missing letter “y” to solve
the condition on line 13, generating a syntactically valid input
and achieving global optima.

claims.quote:
These results indicate that the improvement of
HYLLFUZZin code coverage stems from its LLM-based
solving ability rather than from the use of a different roadlock-
selection strategy.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ exceeds NAUTILUS branch coverage by 66.07% on average over libxml2, Lua, MuJS and php, and SUPERION by 127.04% over its supported libxml2 and MuJS subjects.
claims.quote:
Specifically,
compared to NAUTILUSand SUPERION, HYLLFUZZcovered
66.07% and 127.04% more branches, respectively.

claims.text: Coverage gains over grammar-aware fuzzers are interpreted as evidence that deeper path-constraint reasoning contributes beyond generating structurally valid inputs.
claims.quote:
These re-
sults indicate that to achieve this code coverage improvement,
only handling the input structures is not sufficient, and the
deeper reasoning over path constraints plays a significant role
in this improvement.

claims.text: The sliced-constraint hybrid architecture is claimed necessary for higher coverage than HF0: gains are 36.44% in php, 2.61% in jq, 16.71% in bc and 41.41% in calc, averaging 24.29%.
claims.quote:
From this result, we could see that the
hybrid architecture is necessary, as it significantly improves
the code coverage.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ's sliced-constraint hybrid architecture uses approximately 3.5× fewer LLM tokens than HF0.
claims.quote:
In addition, HYLLFUZZalso reduces the
LLM token usage by approximately 3.5×compared to HF0.

claims.text: The hybrid architecture is claimed to lower monetary cost relative to HF0, based on reduced token use; no comparative dollar amount is reported.
claims.quote:
Therefore, this hybrid architecture not only improves coverage
but also lowers monetary costs.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ solves over 60% of selected roadblocks; reported unsolved rates are php 26.26%, jq 39.64%, bc 16.04% and calc 19.34%.

metrics.name: Counts of selected and unsolved roadblocks

claims.quote:
HYLLFUZZfailed to solve approximately 16.04% to
39.64% of the selected roadblocks.

claims.text: Manual analysis attributes most remaining unsolved roadblocks, up to 80%, to input-unsatisfiable branches controlled by configuration or execution environment rather than fuzzed data.

metrics.name: Manually classified unsatisfiable fraction of unsolved roadblocks

claims.quote:
Instead, the majority of the roadblocks (up to 80%)
left unsolved by HYLLFUZZare in fact unsatisfiable, as the
corresponding branches are controlled by their configurations
and program environments rather than by the fuzzed inputs.

claims.text: More than half of eventually solved roadblocks are solved in one attempt; Figure 7 reports 50.59%.

metrics.name: Percentage of solved roadblocks requiring one attempt

claims.quote:
We
observe that more than 50% of the roadblocks are solved with
a single solving attempt, and that using fewer than five solving
attempts is sufficient to solve 94% of all solvable roadblocks.

claims.text: The text claims that fewer than five attempts solve 94% of solvable roadblocks; Figure 7 instead totals about 93.93% through five attempts, versus 86.03% through four.

metrics.name: Cumulative percentage of eventually solved roadblocks by attempt count

claims.quote:
We
observe that more than 50% of the roadblocks are solved with
a single solving attempt, and that using fewer than five solving
attempts is sufficient to solve 94% of all solvable roadblocks.

claims.text: Increasing solving attempts helps up to about five attempts, while additional attempts produce little further improvement.

metrics.name: Distribution of required attempts among solved roadblocks

claims.quote:
These results indicate that the LLM responses are relatively
stable, and that increasing the number of solving attempts up to
five can improve the success rate; however, additional attempts
beyond five yield little further improvement.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ uniquely covers substantially more branches than the external hybrid-fuzzer baselines.

metrics.name: Branches uniquely covered by HYLLFUZZ versus baseline fuzzers

claims.quote:
As
expected, HYLLFUZZuniquely covered substantially more
branches, reflecting its significant coverage improvement.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ nevertheless misses branches uniquely reached by the external baselines: 8 in bc, 144 in calc, 0 in jq and 556 in php.
claims.quote:
In contrast, the three baselines COFUZZ, INTRIGUER, and
QSYM also uniquely covered a small number of branches
in the subjects: 8 branches inbc, 144 branches incalc, 0
branches injq, and 556 branches inphp.

claims.text: Manual analysis attributes most baseline-only branches to switch-case/disjunct target choice, rather than inability of the LLM-based engine to solve the relevant constraints.

metrics.name: Manual classification of missed branches and target-selection causes

claims.quote:
As a result, some branches are missed,
because HYLLFUZZchooses one constraint to satisfy while
the baselines solve a different path constraint.

claims.text: The Jazzer-integrated Java variant exposes the seeded AIxCC Jenkins bug by overcoming request-mocking and hash-check roadblocks, whereas traditional concolic engines are reported unable to expose it; the case was released after the gpt-4o snapshot.

metrics.name: Seeded Jenkins vulnerability exposed / vulnerable location reached

claims.quote:
Subsequently, HYLLFUZZwas iteratively involved in reaching
deeper and deeper code locations, and finally exposed the
bug.

claims.text: The Jenkins/Jazzer case study is presented as evidence that HYLLFUZZ can be extended effectively to another implementation language.

metrics.name: Successful bug exposure in one Java/Jazzer case study

claims.quote:
HYLLFUZZcan be effectively extended to test programs
implemented in a different programming language.

claims.text: Avoiding heavy symbolic-execution infrastructure and manual environment/system-call modeling is claimed to improve usability and lower the adoption barrier; no user study or effort measurement is reported.
claims.quote:
Moreover, HYLLFUZZavoids the combination
of a heavy symbolic execution infrastructure and reduces the
manual effort involved in environment modeling and system
call support, which naturally enhances the usability of hybrid
fuzzing and lowers the barrier to its adoption.

claims.text: The low number of attempts needed for most solved roadblocks is interpreted as evidence that LLM responses are relatively stable.

metrics.name: Distribution of attempts required among eventually solved roadblocks

claims.quote:
These results indicate that the LLM responses are relatively
stable, and that increasing the number of solving attempts up to
five can improve the success rate; however, additional attempts
beyond five yield little further improvement.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ consistently outperforms each hybrid baseline in branch coverage across all evaluated runs, with Vargha–Delaney A12=1 for every subject.
claims.quote:
In all subjects, ˆA12 = 1(that is,
ˆA12 ≥0.70), indicating that HYLLFUZZconsistently achieved
higher branch coverage in all runs than each baseline.

claims.text: Running HYLLFUZZ costs only US$0.40 per subject-hour on average in the reported experiments.
claims.quote:
It is
worth noting that the monetary cost is relatively low: in our
experiments, running a subject for one hour only cost 0.40
USD on average.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ uses a modest prompt context: 1,570 tokens on average and a maximum observed 3,020 tokens in php.
claims.quote:
The average token count per prompt was 1,570, with the
maximum observed being 3,020 tokens inphpcontaining
millions of code lines.

claims.text: No generated code slice exceeds the model context window in the evaluated campaigns.
claims.quote:
We did not encounter cases where the
generated code slices exceeded the LLM’s context window
limit.

claims.text: Reported low monetary cost and modest token use are taken to demonstrate HYLLFUZZ's practical utility.
claims.quote:
These results further demonstrated the practical utility
of HYLLFUZZ.

claims.text: HYLLFUZZ incurs additional remote LLM/GPU resource consumption compared with locally CPU-executed traditional hybrid fuzzers; the resource difference is not quantified.
claims.quote:
Existing hybrid fuzzers execute locally on CPU-based hard-
ware, whereas HYLLFUZZrelies on a remotely hosted LLM
service with asymmetric computational resources (e.g., GPUs).

claims.text: In a manually examined PHP example, HYLLFUZZ completes 'tr' as the syntactically valid keyword 'try', while traditional solvers choose 'trz'.

metrics.name: Manually observed syntactic validity of the generated keyword

claims.quote:
After
interpreting the input “tr”, HYLLFUZZinferred the code se-
mantics and correctly generated the missing letter “y” to solve
the condition on line 13, generating a syntactically valid input
and achieving global optima.

claims.text: The larger PHP coverage gain and smaller jq gain are qualitatively attributed to stronger benefits of semantic reasoning for complex keyword structures than for simpler JSON structures.

metrics.name: Manual examples of keyword/JSON input structures

claims.quote:
Conversely, thejqinputs are
JSONfiles with relatively simple structures; for example,
“{}” represents key-value pairs and “[]” represents arrays.

claims.text: The extra bugs exposed by HYLLFUZZ lie behind complex paths: cxxfilt cases require 13 and 16 function calls, and an additional PHP case requires a valid function declaration that the external solvers only partially construct.

metrics.name: Manual path analysis of additional bug-triggering inputs

claims.quote:
Upon closer investigation, we found that the missed bugs
were hidden behind complex path constraints.

hcs.name: LlamaRestTest: adaptive REST API testing with LlamaREST-IPD and LlamaREST-EX
hcs.quote: When repeated failures occur (e.g., multiple 4xx responses), LlamaREST-IPD and LlamaREST-EX are activated.

hcs.name: LlamaRestTest without parameter-description analysis
hcs.removed: Parameter-description analysis
hcs.quote:
Removing the parameter description feature resulted in a noticeable
drop, with method coverage decreasing by 5.9 percentage points, branch coverage by 1.4 percentage
points, and line coverage by 4.5 percentage points.

hcs.name: LlamaRestTest without server-response analysis
hcs.removed: Server-response-message analysis by the language models
hcs.quote:
Interestingly, excluding the server response feature caused an even more significant drop,
particularly in method coverage, which fell by 6.1 percentage points, followed by branch and line
coverage, which decreased by 4.4 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively.

hcs.name: LlamaRestTest without LlamaREST-IPD
hcs.removed: LlamaREST-IPD dependency-identification model
hcs.quote:
The removal of LlamaREST-IPD had the most substantial impact on performance, reducing
method coverage by 9.2 percentage points, branch coverage by 6.2 percentage points, and line
coverage by 8.4 percentage points.

hcs.name: LlamaRestTest without LlamaREST-EX
hcs.removed: LlamaREST-EX parameter-value-generation model
hcs.quote:
Finally, excluding LlamaREST-EX resulted in moderate reductions in coverage, with method, branch,
and line coverage decreasing by 3.7, 4.5, and 3.0 percentage points, respectively.

hcs.removed: not_reported
hcs.quote:

services from the RESTGPT benchmark, whereas the evaluation of IPD rule extraction is based on
three of the services.

claims.text: Fine-tuned LlamaREST-EX improves mean semantic-validity precision to 72.44%, versus 22.94% for the base model in Table 3 and 68.82% for RESTGPT.

metrics.name: Semantic-validity precision assessed by two external developers

claims.quote:
LlamaREST-EX, especially its FT version, shows substantial gains over Llama3-8B, achieving an
average accuracy of 72.44%.

claims.text: Fine-tuned LlamaREST-IPD identifies 12 correct dependency rules, exceeding RESTGPT's nine and the base model's two.

metrics.name: Number of correctly generated IPD rules against extracted ground truth

claims.quote:
The FT variant of LlamaREST-
IPD identifies 12 correct IPD rules, compared to nine by RESTGPT, highlighting its ability to
capture more complex relationships.

claims.text: The 4-bit and 8-bit EX models retain reasonable semantic precision of 60.21% and 66.12%, respectively, below the unquantized model's 72.44%.
claims.quote:
Even the quantized versions of LlamaREST-EX (4-bit and 8-bit) show reasonable
performance, with 60.21% and 66.12% precision, respectively.

claims.text: IPD quantization yields six correct rules at 4-bit and seven at 8-bit, above the base model's two but below full precision's 12; 2-bit degrades to one.

metrics.name: Number of correctly generated IPD rules

claims.quote:
Moreover, with 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, the fine-tuned model remains
competitive with RESTGPT, while still performing considerably better than the base model.

claims.text: Fine-tuning alone modestly improves mean method, branch and line coverage from 49.21/23.24/48.51% to 50.11/23.55/49.91%.
claims.quote: The results show that fine-tuning alone produced modest improvements over the base model.

claims.text: Fine-tuning alone increases the summed mean number of processed closed-source operations from 23.0 to 24.5.

metrics.name: Number of successfully processed API operations

claims.quote:
LlamaRestTest with fine-tuning alone
processed 24.5 operations, which is 1.5 operations more than the base model’s 23 operations.

claims.text: Quantization improves average code coverage beyond the base and full-precision fine-tuned settings; 8-bit is best at 55.8/28.3/55.3% method/branch/line coverage, followed by 4-bit at 54.0/27.9/53.5% and 2-bit at 52.9/25.7/52.6%.
claims.quote:
LlamaRestTest with 8-bit quantization exhibited 6.6 percentage points improvement in method
coverage compared to the base model, reaching 55.8% coverage on average.

claims.text: Quantized models process more closed-source operations than the base model: 37.5 at 8-bit, 34.4 at 4-bit and 25.4 at 2-bit, versus 23.0.

metrics.name: Number of successfully processed API operations

claims.quote:
Finally, the 2-bit version was also more effective than the
base model, processing 25.4 operations (2.4 operations more than the base model).

claims.text: Quantization lowers mean IPD inference time from 48.9 seconds at full precision to 36.9, 26.2 and 26.1 seconds at 8-, 4- and 2-bit.
claims.quote:
For example, for IPD rule extraction (RQ1), the
fine-tuned model required 48.9 seconds per IPD on average, whereas the 8-bit quantized version
reduced the inference time to 36.9 seconds.

claims.text: With enhanced specifications, LlamaRestTest exceeds MoRest, RESTler, ARAT-RL and EvoMaster in average method/branch/line coverage, by 10.0–22.7, 9.2–18.7 and 10.0–22.1 percentage points.
claims.quote:
The results show that LlamaRestTest
consistently outperforms all other tools in method, branch, and line coverage.

claims.text: LlamaRestTest processes a summed mean 37.5 closed-source operations, versus MoRest 9.9, RESTler 10.6, ARAT-RL 11.6 and EvoMaster 11.2.

metrics.name: Number of successfully processed API operations

claims.quote:
Like the results on code coverage, LlamaRestTest
outperformed the other tools by a wide margin, successfully processing 37.5 operations overall.

claims.text: LlamaRestTest has higher reported fault-detection ability, with 204 deduplicated HTTP 500 observations over ten runs, versus MoRest 140, RESTler 130, ARAT-RL 160 and EvoMaster 130.

metrics.name: HTTP 500 counts, deduplicated by operation and response message

evidence.type: Qualitative analysis of a Spotify failure sequence
evidence.quote: This sequence exposes a hidden dependency conflict, which causes an Internal Server Error.

claims.quote:
LlamaRestTest demonstrated the highest fault-detection ability, discovering 204 faults in 10 runs
on the services in our benchmark.

claims.text: On Ohsome, only LlamaRestTest detects the reported server errors: 36 observations over ten runs versus zero for each comparator.

metrics.name: Deduplicated HTTP 500 count over ten runs

claims.quote:
For Ohsome, Lla-
maRestTest was the only tool to detect faults, identifying 36 errors where all other tools failed.

claims.text: On Spotify, only LlamaRestTest detects the reported server errors: eight observations over ten runs versus zero for each comparator.

metrics.name: Deduplicated HTTP 500 count over ten runs

evidence.type: Qualitative analysis of a Spotify failure sequence
evidence.quote:
This sequence exposes a hidden dependency conflict, which
causes an Internal Server Error.

claims.quote:
Similarly, LlamaRestTest was the only tool to find faults in Spotify, detecting 8 errors where all
others found none.

claims.text: Parameter-description analysis improves method/branch/line coverage by 5.9/1.4/4.5 percentage points relative to its removal.
claims.quote:
Removing the parameter description feature resulted in a noticeable
drop, with method coverage decreasing by 5.9 percentage points, branch coverage by 1.4 percentage
points, and line coverage by 4.5 percentage points.

claims.text: Server-response analysis improves method/branch/line coverage by 6.1/4.4/6.3 percentage points relative to its removal.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, excluding the server response feature caused an even more significant drop,
particularly in method coverage, which fell by 6.1 percentage points, followed by branch and line
coverage, which decreased by 4.4 and 6.3 percentage points, respectively.

claims.text: Including LlamaREST-IPD improves method/branch/line coverage by 9.2/6.2/8.4 percentage points relative to its removal.
claims.quote:
The removal of LlamaREST-IPD had the most substantial impact on performance, reducing
method coverage by 9.2 percentage points, branch coverage by 6.2 percentage points, and line
coverage by 8.4 percentage points.

claims.text: Including LlamaREST-EX improves method/branch/line coverage by 3.7/4.5/3.0 percentage points relative to its removal.
claims.quote:
Finally, excluding LlamaREST-EX resulted in moderate reductions in coverage, with method, branch,
and line coverage decreasing by 3.7, 4.5, and 3.0 percentage points, respectively.

claims.text: The conclusion claims that quantization preserves accuracy without substantial loss.

metrics.name: Number of correctly generated IPD rules

claims.quote:
Quantization further improves the model’s efficiency without substantial loss in accuracy,
making LlamaRestTest both powerful and practical for real-world use.

claims.text: Coverage improvements from fine-tuning and quantization are especially pronounced on Language-Tool and YouTube.
claims.quote:
The fine-tuned and quantized versions
generally exhibited higher coverage compared to the base model, with significant gains observed
for the Language-Tool and YouTube services in particular.

claims.text: Fine-tuned EX underperforms RESTGPT on Language-Tool and FDIC: 69.23% versus 82.98%, and 54.69% versus 70.42% semantic precision.
claims.quote:
LlamaREST-EX generally performs well, but there are two cases where it is less effective than
RESTGPT: Language-Tool and FDIC.

claims.text: Fine-tuned EX exceeds RESTGPT on Ohsome and Genome-Nexus: 92.16% versus 76.83%, and 57.02% versus 36.25% semantic precision.
claims.quote:
For example, on the Ohsome API, the FT version of LlamaREST-EX
reaches 92.16%, outperforming RESTGPT’s 76.83%; similarly, on Genome-Nexus, it scores 57.02%,
achieving considerably higher precision than RESTGPT (36.25%).

claims.text: The base model has particularly poor semantic validity on Spotify and Ohsome, with precision of 0% and 2.78%.
claims.quote:
It struggles significantly on APIs such as Spotify (0%) and Ohsome (2.78%),
underscoring its limitations in generating semantically valid values.

claims.text: The 2-bit model can underperform the full-precision model on domain-specific services such as Genome-Nexus and Spotify.
claims.quote:
Specifically, for services,
such as Genome-Nexus and Spotify, that rely heavily on domain-specific knowledge, the 2-bit
quantized model often generated incorrect outputs, leading to lower code coverage.

claims.text: The 4-bit and 8-bit models maintain better testing performance than full precision even in the described challenging domain-specific cases.
claims.quote:
However, the 4-bit and 8-bit quantized models
consistently outperformed the non-quantized models, even in these challenging cases.

claims.text: The ablation study identifies server-response analysis and IPD modeling as the most critical contributors overall, with IPD removal producing the largest coverage losses.
claims.quote:
The ablation on key components of LlamaRestTest shows that, while each component
contributes to the overall performance of LlamaRestTest, server response analysis and
inter-parameter dependency modeling are the more critical components, with their removal
causing larger drops in code coverage than the other components.

claims.text: LlamaREST-EX generates valid Spotify playlist IDs that enable successful execution of the playlist-tracks operation.

metrics.name: Successful execution of the playlist-tracks operation

claims.quote:
While many tools fail
to generate valid IDs, LlamaREST-EX, due to its fine-tuning, accurately retrieved and generated
valid Spotify playlist IDs.

claims.text: The Spotify interaction sequence reusing a retrieved ISRC as a user_id exposes a dependency conflict and triggers an internal server error.

metrics.name: HTTP 500 response from the described interaction sequence

claims.quote:
This sequence exposes a hidden dependency conflict, which
causes an Internal Server Error.

claims.text: Quantization makes LlamaRestTest practical for real-world deployment.
claims.quote:
Quantization further improves the model’s efficiency without substantial loss in accuracy,
making LlamaRestTest both powerful and practical for real-world use.

claims.text: Language-Tool's lower precision is attributed to difficulty handling complex, region-specific parameter formats.
claims.quote:
For Language-Tool, the low performance is primarily
due to LlamaREST-EX’s difficulty in handling complex parameter constraints, particularly for
region-specific formats.

claims.text: FDIC's lower precision is attributed to specialized financial knowledge missing from fine-tuning.
claims.quote:
In the case of FDIC, the lower
performance came from the specialized nature of the API, which requires more domain-specific
financial knowledge that our fine-tuning process did not fully capture.

claims.text: LlamaRestTest may be less effective on APIs whose response messages provide little useful feedback; the paper does not separately evaluate this condition.
claims.quote:
Conversely, LlamaRestTest may be less effective on services that provide minimal or
poor server feedback.

claims.text: Quantization may improve generalization through a regularization effect rather than memorization.
claims.quote:
Second, quantization introduces a regularization effect that may help the model
generalize better with various answers rather than memorizing specific examples [25].

claims.text: Faster quantized inference is proposed as a cause of improved testing effectiveness through more efficient server-response processing.
claims.quote:
The smaller models benefit from faster inference,
which enhances the effectiveness of REST API testing via more efficient processing of server
response messages.

claims.text: Small fine-tuned language models perform as well as or better than large language models (RESTGPT on GPT-3.5) in REST API testing tasks, balancing effectiveness and efficiency.

claims.text: Panta has higher line coverage than external comparator SymPrompt on every project, averaging 70.18% versus 43.91%, approximately 26.3 percentage points higher.
claims.quote:
On average, Panta achieves 26.3% higher line coverage and
22.7% higher branch coverage than SymPrompt.

claims.text: Panta has higher branch coverage than external comparator SymPrompt on every project, averaging 60.83% versus 38.17%, approximately 22.7 percentage points higher.
claims.quote:
On average, Panta achieves 26.3% higher line coverage and
22.7% higher branch coverage than SymPrompt.

claims.text: Panta reaches the high-branch-coverage threshold in 45 of 130 classes, compared with 16 for external comparator SymPrompt; HCC is defined as branch coverage of at least 75%.
claims.quote:
Regarding high
coverage count (HCC), 45 out of 130 classes achieve branch coverage
above 75%, compared to only 16 for SymPrompt.

claims.text: Panta's average pass rate is 55.92%, compared with 32.83% for external comparator SymPrompt, a difference of approximately 23.1 percentage points.
claims.quote:
The pass rate
of SymPrompt is, on average, 23.1% lower than Panta.

claims.text: Panta has a higher average mutation score than external comparator SymPrompt: 43.79% versus 31.30%.
claims.quote:
In terms
of mutation score, Pantaachieves a higher average score (43.8%)
than SymPrompt (31.3%), aligning with its superior code coverage
results.

claims.text: The iterative Panta_basic framework raises average line coverage from the single-pass baseline's 32.69% to 60.34%, a 27.65-point increase.
claims.quote:
For line and branch coverage, we observe a substantial improve-
ment when comparing Panta_basic to the baseline, with line cov-
erage increasing by 27.65% and branch coverage by 25.77%.

claims.text: The iterative Panta_basic framework raises average branch coverage from the single-pass baseline's 24.87% to 50.64%, a 25.77-point increase.
claims.quote:
For line and branch coverage, we observe a substantial improve-
ment when comparing Panta_basic to the baseline, with line cov-
erage increasing by 27.65% and branch coverage by 25.77%.

claims.text: Panta_cov has similar but slightly lower average line coverage than Panta_basic: 58.59% versus 60.34%.

evidence.description: A paired t-test reports no statistically significant coverage difference; p-values and equivalence bounds are not_reported.
evidence.quote:
A Paired T-test [19] confirms that the difference between them is
not statistically significant across all subjects.

claims.quote:
While Panta_cov achieves similar coverage,
its average coverage is slightly lower than that of Panta_basic.

claims.text: Panta_cov has similar but slightly lower average branch coverage than Panta_basic: 50.08% versus 50.64%.

evidence.description: A paired t-test reports no statistically significant coverage difference; p-values and equivalence bounds are not_reported.
evidence.quote:
A Paired T-test [19] confirms that the difference between them is
not statistically significant across all subjects.

claims.quote:
While Panta_cov achieves similar coverage,
its average coverage is slightly lower than that of Panta_basic.

claims.text: The coverage difference between Panta_cov and Panta_basic is reported as statistically non-significant across the subjects.

metrics.name: paired t-test significance for coverage differences; p-values not_reported

claims.quote:
A Paired T-test [19] confirms that the difference between them is
not statistically significant across all subjects.

claims.text: Hybrid coverage-driven path selection raises average line coverage to 70.18%, versus 60.34% for Panta_basic and 58.59% for Panta_cov.
claims.quote:
By integrating code coverage-driven path selection (Algorithm 2),
Pantafurther improves line and branch coverage by approximately
10% compared to the other two Pantavariants.

claims.text: Hybrid coverage-driven path selection raises average branch coverage to 60.83%, versus 50.64% for Panta_basic and 50.08% for Panta_cov.
claims.quote:
By integrating code coverage-driven path selection (Algorithm 2),
Pantafurther improves line and branch coverage by approximately
10% compared to the other two Pantavariants.

claims.text: Panta's coverage is nearly stable across the two complexity subsets: line coverage 70.37% versus 69.42%, and branch coverage 61.09% versus 59.81%.
claims.quote:
In contrast, Panta
maintains nearly consistent coverage across both complexity levels,
with only a 1 percentage point difference.

claims.text: The baseline, Panta_basic and Panta_cov lose approximately 6–9 coverage points on the higher-complexity subset, unlike full Panta.
claims.quote:
When analyzing
coverage across complexity categories, we observe a notable drop
of 6% to 9% for highly complex subjects ( CYC𝑚𝑎𝑥 > 20) in the
baseline, Panta_basic, and Panta_cov variants.

claims.text: Panta_basic improves average pass rate by approximately 6 points over the single-pass baseline, from 52.45% to 58.40%; the paper attributes this to repair.
claims.quote:
Panta_basic achieves
a 6% higher pass rate than the baseline, attributed to the test repair
phase incorporated in our framework.

claims.text: Adding program-analysis guidance yields slightly lower pass rates than Panta_basic: 55.92% for Panta and 55.81% for Panta_cov versus 58.40%.
claims.quote:
However, after integrating
program analysis information into the prompt, the overall pass rate
is slightly lower than Panta_basic, with only a 3.5% improvement
over the baseline.

claims.text: For Panta, average line coverage ranks Claude > Llama > Mistral > GPT: 73.20%, 70.18%, 56.60%, 54.05%.
claims.quote:
Thus, the ranking for code coverage is Claude > Llama > Mistral >
GPT.

claims.text: For Panta, average branch coverage ranks Claude > Llama > Mistral > GPT: 66.52%, 60.83%, 49.85%, 46.77%.
claims.quote:
Thus, the ranking for code coverage is Claude > Llama > Mistral >
GPT.

claims.text: For Panta, HCC ranks Claude > Llama > Mistral > GPT, with 62, 45, 34 and 22 classes respectively reaching the 75% branch-coverage threshold.
claims.quote:
For code coverage metrics, Claude performs the best, achieving
73.2% line coverage, 66.5% branch coverage, and 62 out of 130 classes
surpassing 75% branch coverage.

claims.text: For Panta, average mutation score ranks Claude > Llama > Mistral > GPT: 47.92%, 43.79%, 36.60%, 34.86%.

achieves the highest score, followed by Llama, Mistral, and GPT.

Claude > Llama > GPT > Mistral for pass rate.

comparable to Claude while being open-source, making it a more

claims.text: Runtime varies with class complexity, method count and project characteristics; the paper associates large utility classes with longer generation times.
claims.quote:
Runtime varies with class complexity, method count, and project
characteristics.

claims.text: Across models, repair is observed to handle compilation errors better than runtime errors such as failed assertions; error-specific success rates are not_reported.
claims.quote:
In contrast, LLMs
perform better in resolving compilation errors.

claims.text: The paper interprets runtime-repair difficulties as limited understanding of project-specific execution logic and expected outcomes.
claims.quote:
This indicates that
LLMs lack the capability to fully understand project-specific execu-
tion logic, as they struggle to infer runtime behaviors and expected
outcomes.

claims.text: The paper attributes Panta's weaker results in large utility classes to long class-level prompts that make complete test generation harder.
claims.quote:
For large classes, this results in
long prompts, increasing the difficulty for the LLM to generate com-
plete tests.

claims.text: Coverage-location information alone (Panta_cov) helps on low-complexity subjects such as Cli but is insufficient to improve coverage on more complex projects.
claims.quote: This suggests that for less complex subjects, code coverage information alone can be beneficial, but for more complex projects, it is insufficient to drive meaningful improvements in coverage.
