claims.text: NullRepair fully resolves 696/1,119 individual target errors (62%), versus SinglePrompt's 777 (69%) and external mini-SWE-agent's 853 (76%).

metrics.name: Per-patch full resolutions R: target removed, compilable, no new unresolved nullability errors

claims.quote: C1:NullRepairpatches compile and fully resolve the target errors in 62% of cases.

claims.text: Combined application resolves 704/1,119 errors (63%) for NullRepair, versus 802 (72%) for SinglePrompt and 878 (78%) for external mini-SWE-agent.
claims.quote: InCombinedthe baselines achieve a higher overall percentage of resolved errors (SinglePrompt 72% and mini-SWE-agent 78% in aggregate) compared toNullRepair(63% in aggregate).

claims.text: NullRepair largely preserves program semantics: 10/12 projects remain test-clean and 35/15,003 tests fail overall, versus SinglePrompt's 2,822 failures and external mini-SWE-agent's 1,233; each comparator fails tests in 8/12 projects.

metrics.name: Existing held-out unit-test failure counts/rates and test-clean project count

evidence.description: A separate source-blinded author review of 75 shared repaired cases evaluates semantic alignment and acceptability; it corroborates relative quality on a limited subset, with 40% of NullRepair patches still rated likely unacceptable.
evidence.quote: When reviewers prefer patches produced byNullRepair, it is due to their semantic precision and alignment with the program’s intent.

claims.quote: C2:NullRepairproducestest-cleanpatches in all but two benchmarks, whereas both baselines introduce at least one failing test in all but four benchmarks.

claims.text: NullRepair patches are rated likely acceptable without changes more often: 29/75 (39%) versus SinglePrompt's 16/75 (21%) and external mini-SWE-agent's 18/75 (24%), reported as a 61–81% relative increase.
claims.quote: Further, a manual assessment of patch quality shows thatNullRepair’s patches are more likely to be acceptable to developers without changes (61-81% more likely) and less likely to be completely unacceptable (23-33% less likely).

claims.text: NullRepair produces fewer patches rated likely unacceptable: 30/75 (40%) versus SinglePrompt's 45/75 (60%) and external mini-SWE-agent's 39/75 (52%), a reported 23–33% relative decrease.
claims.quote: Further, a manual assessment of patch quality shows thatNullRepair’s patches are more likely to be acceptable to developers without changes (61-81% more likely) and less likely to be completely unacceptable (23-33% less likely).

claims.text: NullRepair averages 1.2 minutes per error and 113 minutes per project; external mini-SWE-agent averages 1.4/133 minutes and SinglePrompt 0.3/24 minutes.

metrics.name: Mean wall-clock execution time per error/project

claims.quote: Per error the average execution time is 1.2 minutes.

claims.text: NullRepair costs about $0.05 per error/$4.23 per project, comparable to external mini-SWE-agent's $0.04/$4.05 and above SinglePrompt's $0.003/$0.32.
claims.quote: Based on current API pricing, this translates to a cost of $0.05 per error.

claims.text: NullRepair has significantly fewer compilation failures than SinglePrompt (63/1,119, 5.63%, versus 120/1,119, 10.72%) and is similar to external mini-SWE-agent (64/1,119, 5.72%); statistical significance testing is not_reported.

metrics.name: Non-compiling patches CE and compilation-failure rate

claims.quote: On average, for only 5.63% of errorsNullRepair produces patches that fail to compile, compared to 10.72% for SinglePrompt.

hcs.name: Locus patch-to-canary generation, evaluated independently of downstream fuzzing
hcs.removed: not_reported

promptLocusto automate the generation of a canary condition
(Magma relies on manual analysis), such that the unpatched version
satisfies the generated canary, while the patched version violates it.

we employ a self-reflection strategy that enables the agent to vali-
date the semantic correctness of generated predicates.

claims.text: On FrUITeR, LogiDroid successfully tests 40% of requirements, exceeding AppAgent (32%) and AutoDroid (27%); the reported improvement over the strongest comparator is 25%.
claims.quote: On the FrUITeR dataset, LogiDroid demonstrates a significant advantage.

claims.text: On FrUITeR, 20% of LogiDroid tests exactly match reference tests, versus AppAgent's 9% and AutoDroid's 15%.
claims.quote:
Specifically, 40% of the
generated test cases successfully verified target functions, and 20% are perfectly identical to the
ground-truth.

claims.text: Including assertions, LogiDroid successfully tests 57% of Lin requirements.

evidence.description: A separate WALLMauer assessment of 18 instrumentable Lin apps finds 96.5% overlap with reference-covered methods; this supports exercising relevant implementation logic, rather than independently confirming functional success.
evidence.quote:
On average, LogiDroid reaches 96.5% of the method coverage achieved by the ground-
truth test cases, whereas AutoDroid reaches only 86.0%.

claims.quote:
LogiDroid achieved a 57% success-rate, with 41% of test cases being perfectly identical to the ground-
truth.

claims.text: Including assertions, 41% of LogiDroid's Lin tests exactly match reference tests.
claims.quote:
LogiDroid achieved a 57% success-rate, with 41% of test cases being perfectly identical to the ground-
truth.

claims.text: With assertions excluded from scoring, Lin success-rate is 65%, exceeding AppAgent (42%) and AutoDroid (27%); the paper reports over 55% improvement over baselines.
claims.quote:
In this setting, LogiDroid* achieved a 65%
success-rate and a 48% perfect-rate.

claims.text: With assertions excluded from scoring, Lin perfect-rate is 48%, versus AppAgent's 21% and AutoDroid's 10%; the paper reports over 129% improvement over baselines.
claims.quote:
This outperforms baseline methods by over 55% in success-rate
and over 129% in perfect-rate.

claims.text: LogiDroid generates functional tests containing verification assertions, whereas AppAgent and AutoDroid only generate operation sequences.
claims.quote: Third, unlike existing approaches, LogiDroid can generate assertions.

claims.text: Semantic retrieval improves functional test generation: removing it lowers success-rate from 70% to 40% and perfect-rate from 30% to 10% on the sampled Lin apps.
claims.quote:
The results demonstrate that the Semantic-Retrieval, Knowledge-Fusion, and Decision-Generation
agents are all critical to the effectiveness of LogiDroid.

claims.text: Knowledge fusion improves functional test generation: removing it lowers success-rate from 70% to 20% and perfect-rate from 30% to 5%.
claims.quote:
Similarly, removing the Knowledge-Fusion Agent and the Decision-
Generation Agent leads to success-rate declines to 20% and 30%, respectively.

claims.text: Specialized decision generation improves functional test generation: replacing it with direct LLM decisions lowers success-rate from 70% to 30% and perfect-rate from 30% to 10%.
claims.quote:
Similarly, removing the Knowledge-Fusion Agent and the Decision-
Generation Agent leads to success-rate declines to 20% and 30%, respectively.

claims.text: The authors claim model robustness: GPT-5 to Gemini-2.5 changes full-test success/perfect rates from 70%/30% to 60%/20%, and event-only rates from 75%/50% to 75%/25%, while retaining an advantage over AppAgent and AutoDroid.
claims.quote:
Replacing the underlying LLM from GPT-5 with Gemini-2.5 does not compromise LogiDroid’s
performance advantage over baseline approaches.

claims.text: With Gemini-2.5 and event-only scoring, LogiDroid achieves 75% success-rate, exceeding AppAgent (25%) and AutoDroid (10%); the prose claims over 67% improvement.
claims.quote:
Compared to the baselines, LogiDroid improves the success-rate
by over 67%, and the perfect-rate by over 200%.

claims.text: For Gemini-2.5 event-only scoring, the prose claims over 200% perfect-rate improvement; Table 7 instead gives 25% versus AppAgent's 15% and AutoDroid's 10%, contradicting that bound against either comparator.
claims.quote:
Compared to the baselines, LogiDroid improves the success-rate
by over 67%, and the perfect-rate by over 200%.

claims.text: LogiDroid's mean generation runtime is 6 minutes per test: 25% lower than AppAgent's 8 minutes and 20% higher than AutoDroid's 5 minutes.
claims.quote:
Compared with AppAgent, LogiDroid
reduces runtime by 25% and token consumption by 9%.

claims.text: LogiDroid uses 31,796 tokens per test on average: about 9% fewer than AppAgent (34,936) and 73% more than AutoDroid (18,374).
claims.quote:
Compared with AutoDroid, LogiDroid
increases runtime by 20% and token consumption by 73%.

claims.text: LogiDroid generalizes to previously unseen TEM applications with 70% success-rate, exceeding AppAgent (50%) and AutoDroid (30%).
claims.quote:
Even on new
applications, LogiDroid still achieves strong performance, further demonstrating its ability to reuse
and adapt business logic across different applications.

claims.text: On TEM, LogiDroid's perfect-rate is 40%, exceeding AppAgent (20%) and AutoDroid (10%).
claims.quote:
LogiDroid achieves a perfect-rate of 40% and a success-rate of 70%, outperforming AppAgent (20%
and 50%, respectively) and AutoDroid (10% and 30%, respectively).

claims.text: The conclusion presents LogiDroid as a practical solution for large-scale industrial deployment; the reported evidence consists of benchmark outcomes rather than deployment or practitioner-utility measurements.
claims.quote:
Notably,
LogiDroid also exhibits advantages in generating test cases with complete verification assertions
for diverse functionalities, providing a practical solution for large-scale industrial deployment.

claims.text: The authors judge LogiDroid's runtime acceptable given its testing-accuracy gains; no separate human acceptability assessment is reported.
claims.quote:
Although there is room
for optimization in runtime efficiency, the current efficiency level remains acceptable considering
the significant improvements in testing accuracy (as shown in Section 4.2).

claims.text: On 18 instrumentable Lin apps, LogiDroid reproduces 96.5% of reference-covered methods on average versus AutoDroid's 86.0%; its mean 3,255 covered methods is also closer to the reference's 3,274 than AutoDroid's 2,933.
claims.quote:
On average, LogiDroid reaches 96.5% of the method coverage achieved by the ground-
truth test cases, whereas AutoDroid reaches only 86.0%.

claims.text: Failure inspection finds that incomplete extracted business logic can omit necessary steps and yield incomplete tests.
claims.quote:
First, the extracted business logic may fail to cover all necessary test steps for the target function-
ality, which leads to incomplete generated test cases.

claims.text: Failure inspection finds incorrect instruction-generation events, including confusion among semantically related GUI widgets.
claims.quote:
Second, the instruction generation component may produce incorrect events for the given test
steps, resulting in a generated test case with incorrect interactions.

claims.text: Failure inspection finds that incorrect step selection in hierarchical states can divert execution away from the intended functionality.
claims.quote:
Third, the step selection component may choose an incorrect step in a hierarchical state, causing
the generated test case to deviate from the intended functionality.

claims.text: The discussion asserts that the existing hallucination-mitigation mechanism maintains structural correctness and rule compliance; no separate validity rate is reported.
claims.quote:
While the current hallucination
mitigation mechanism effectively maintains structural correctness and rule compliance, an impor-
tant complementary aspect is the consideration of semantic inconsistencies.

claims.text: Format-compliant outputs can still omit critical interactions or contain assertions that misrepresent expected outcomes.
claims.quote:
In practice, even when
generated outputs satisfy predefined formatting constraints, they may still exhibit deviations from
the intended functionality, such as omitting critical interaction steps, and generating assertions
that do not faithfully reflect the expected outcomes.

claims.text: The authors argue that category-based narrowing and using a small relevant candidate set make substantially larger knowledge repositories feasible, although evaluation uses only 294 repository test cases.
claims.quote:
Looking toward real-world deployment with substantially larger repos-
itories, the scalability of LogiDroid remains feasible for two main reasons.

claims.text: The discussion argues that structured summaries plus multi-case retrieval and fusion preserve accurate knowledge identification despite omitted summary details; no retrieval-accuracy assessment is reported.
claims.page: 26, §5, Effect of semantic summaries on retrieval accuracy
claims.quote:
As a result, even if an individual
summary misses certain details, the subsequent multi-case retrieval and fusion process still provides
a robust basis for accurate knowledge identification in large-scale repositories.

claims.text: More available similar cases are associated with generally better effectiveness: success-rates for 0/1/2/3/≥4 cases are 17%/75%/33%/44%/49%, and perfect-rates are 0%/50%/33%/22%/30%; the pattern is not monotonic.
claims.quote:
The results show that, as the number of similar test
cases increases, the effectiveness of LogiDroid generally improves.

claims.text: The 75% success-rate with one similar case is less stable because that cohort has only four target cases; the authors also note its concentration in highly similar email apps.
claims.page: 27, §5, Influence of the number of similar test cases
claims.quote: However, this result is based on only four cases, which makes the statistics less stable.

claims.text: Even with no similar historical case available, LogiDroid retains some functional-test generation capability, achieving 17% success-rate.
claims.quote: When the number of similar test cases is zero, LogiDroid still achieves a success-rate of 17%.

claims.text: LogiDroid's perfect-rate advantage over AppAgent (122% on FrUITeR, 129% on Lin) is attributed to knowledge retrieval and alignment from historical test cases.
claims.quote: This advantage primarily stems from LogiDroid’s knowledge retrieval and alignment mechanism.

claims.text: LogiDroid's success-rate advantage over AutoDroid (48% on FrUITeR, 141% on Lin) is attributed to context-aware generation using multimodal GUI information and progressive decision-making.
claims.quote: This performance boost is mainly attributed to LogiDroid’s context-aware test generation mechanism.

claims.text: LogiDroid's relatively high token consumption is attributed to the multi-round progressive decision-making of the Decision-Generation Agent.
claims.quote: Deep analysis reveals that the relatively high token consumption of LogiDroid primarily stems from the progressive decision-making mechanism of Decision-Generation Agent.

claims.text: Across complete benchmark suites, LPR takes 10.77%, 34.88% and 36.96% less user-perceived elapsed time than external comparator Vulcan on C, Rust and JavaScript.
claims.quote:
For efficiency perceived
by users, LPR is more efficient when reducing large and complex
programs, taking 10.77%, 34.88%, 36.96% less time than Vulcan to
finish all the benchmarks in C, Rust and JavaScript, separately.

claims.text: Averaging per-benchmark percentage timing differences on Benchmark-C, LPR requires 45.83% more time than external comparator Vulcan.
claims.quote:
However, in terms of the average percentage difference of each
benchmark, LPR requires 45.83% more time compared to Vulcan
in Benchmark-C.

claims.text: LPR is more efficient than external comparator Vulcan on longer-running C and Rust cases: when both exceed one hour, it requires 4.15% and 21.69% less time, respectively.
claims.quote:
If
we only keep benchmarks where both tools take longer than one
hour, LPR requires 4.15% and 21.69% less time compared to Vulcan.

claims.text: External comparator Vulcan reduces simpler, shorter C/Rust programs faster than LPR.
claims.quote:
RQ2: From the perspective of users, LPR is more efficient than
Vulcan on more complex programs with longer processing time,
while Vulcan reduces faster than LPR on simpler and shorter
programs.

claims.text: All five transformations followed by Perses decrease program size on average on Benchmark-C: Function Inlining −25.5, Loop Unrolling −1.1, Data Type Elimination −6.3, Data Type Simplification −2.4 and Variable Elimination −5.9 tokens per iteration.

metrics.name: Mean per-iteration token change after transformation plus Perses

claims.quote:
RQ3: In Benchmark-C, all proposed transformations contribute
to the further reduction by either shrinking the programs directly
or providing reduction opportunities to Perses.

claims.text: Function Inlining, Data Type Elimination and Variable Elimination directly shrink Benchmark-C programs by mean 13.2, 4.7 and 4.3 tokens per iteration, respectively.

metrics.name: Mean per-iteration token change after transformation alone

claims.quote:
First,
Function Inlining, Data Type Elimination and Variable Elimination
are more likely to reduce the program size by themselves, with an
average size change -13.2, -4.7 and -4.3, separately.

claims.text: Loop Unrolling and Data Type Simplification directly increase Benchmark-C program sizes by mean 14.9 and 1.3 tokens per iteration, respectively.

metrics.name: Mean per-iteration token change after transformation alone

claims.quote:
However, for
the rest two transformations, i.e., Loop Unrolling and Data Type
Simplification, most of the program sizes increase instead, with
an average of 14.9 and 1.3 respectively.

claims.text: Transformation-attributed reductions on Benchmark-C are Function Inlining 88.2 tokens/62.12%, Data Type Elimination 20.8/14.62%, Variable Elimination 20.4/14.41%, Data Type Simplification 7.8/5.50%, and Loop Unrolling 4.8/3.35%; Function Inlining contributes most.

metrics.name: Mean total tokens removed per transformation across 100 runs
Share of total attributed token reduction

claims.quote:
Specifically, while Func-
tion Inlining is responsible for a reduction of 88.2 tokens on average,
contributing 62.12% to the overall decrease.

claims.text: Transformation impact prevalence differs across Benchmark-C: Data Type Elimination affects all 20 cases; Figure 6 reports Variable Elimination 17.4±0.5, Function Inlining 15.4±0.5, Data Type Simplification 12.4±2.3, and Loop Unrolling 6.6±1.9 cases; prose reports Loop Unrolling as 6.

metrics.name: Number of benchmarks with a size decrease attributable to each transformation, mean±SD

prompting approach results in 155.0± 8.7 tokens, which is far less
effective than results from the multi-level prompting approach, i.e.,
105.8±4.4 tokens.

claims.text: LspRag increases line coverage over CodeQA, RAG, SymPrompt and supported DraCo settings across all six projects and three models; reported relative gains over the best baseline span 91.4–174.55% for Go, 27.79–213.31% for Java and 16.87–31.57% for Python.

evidence.quote:
Our
statistical analysis confirms that these improvements are significant,
with all p-values being less than 0.05, thus supporting the𝐻1.

claims.quote:
The overall results, presented in Table 3, show that
LspRagconsistently improves line coverage across all projects, re-
gardless of the programming language or the underlying LLM.

claims.text: Reported syntactic-validity gains over baselines reach 242.86% for Go, 251.91% for Java and 20.16% for Python; Table 3 includes an exception to general superiority for Tornado/GPT-4o versus DraCo (84.53% versus 85.03%).
claims.quote:
Similarly, the valid rate of generated tests in-
creased by up to 242.86% for Golang projects, 251.91% for Java
projects, and 20.16% for Python projects.

claims.text: Adding LSP-guided context to Naive improves line coverage across all project/model settings: 26–1528% for Go, 82–490% for Java and 34–106% for Python.
claims.quote:
Specifically,LspRag− improved
line coverage by 26% to 1528% for Golang, 82% to 490% for Java,
and 34% to 106% for Python.

claims.text: Adding real-time fixing to retrieval-only LspRag− further improves line coverage: 45–162% for Go, 3–49% for Java and 1–13% for Python.
claims.quote:
By adding the fixing module,LspRagimproved line coverage
by an additional 45% to 162% for Golang, 3% to 49% for Java, and
1% to 13% for Python overLspRag−.

claims.text: Adding real-time fixing increases syntactic-validity rates: 59–273% for Go, 67–121% for Java and 0.5–10% for Python, with smaller benefits in Python.
claims.quote:
More importantly, it increased
the valid rate by 59% to 273% for Golang, 67% to 121% for Java,
and 0.5% to 10% for Python.

claims.text: Mean end-to-end generation/refinement latency is 28.27 seconds per focal method with GPT-4o.
claims.quote:
On average, our tool requires 28.27 seconds and 4,497 tokens
per focal method to generate and refine a unit test.

claims.text: Mean GPT-4o token consumption is 4,497 per focal method, with a reported breakdown of 2,732 for generation and 1,832 for fixing.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 4,LspRagaveragely uses 2,732 tokens for
the initial generation and 1,832 for fixing.

claims.text: Compared with CodeQA, LspRag uses 39% fewer tokens in the GPT-4o experiment.
claims.quote:
For instance, compared toCodeQA,
LspRaguses 39% fewer tokens while achieving a 135% improvement
in coverage.

claims.text: Compared with CodeQA, LspRag reports a 135% coverage improvement in the GPT-4o experiment.
claims.quote:

LspRaguses 39% fewer tokens while achieving a 135% improvement
in coverage.

claims.text: Compared with DraCo on Python, LspRag reports 9.6% more generation tokens and 24% more fixing tokens.
claims.quote:
When measured againstDraCo,LspRaguses 9.6%
more tokens for generation and 24% more for fixing, but these
increases yield coverage improvements of 30% and an additional
6%, respectively.

claims.text: Compared with DraCo on Python, LspRag reports 30% coverage improvement from generation and a further 6% from fixing.
claims.quote:

more tokens for generation and 24% more for fixing, but these
increases yield coverage improvements of 30% and an additional

claims.text: LLM API queries account for approximately 70% of LspRag latency.

metrics.name: fraction of elapsed time spent querying LLM APIs

claims.quote:
As detailed
in 6, the majority of this time (approximately 70%) is spent on LLM
API querying for generation and refinement.

claims.text: Key-token extraction and LSP context retrieval account for approximately five seconds per focal method.
claims.quote:
Our retrieval strategy,
which includes key token extraction and leveraging the LSP for
reference and definition providers, accounts for about 5 seconds of
the total time.

claims.text: Refinement accounts for over 30% of generation time.

metrics.name: fraction of elapsed time spent in refinement

claims.quote:
While the refinement stage constitutes over 30% of
the generation time, we consider this a necessary and acceptable
trade-off for the improvements it yields in both line coverage and
the rate of valid tests.

claims.text: The authors judge refinement overhead acceptable for interactive use given its coverage and validity gains.
claims.quote:
While the refinement stage constitutes over 30% of
the generation time, we consider this a necessary and acceptable
trade-off for the improvements it yields in both line coverage and
the rate of valid tests.

claims.text: LSP-guided context can reduce syntactic validity: Commons-CLI/GPT-4o falls from 32.61% to 28.59%, and Logrus/Deepseek-V3 from 22.50% to 17.05%, despite higher coverage.
claims.quote:
For instance, with
a complex project like Commons-CLI, the large volume of context
can distract the LLM, leading to syntactically incorrect code and a
lower valid rate forLspRag−.

claims.text: LspRag detects more injected faults than SymPrompt, CodeQA, StandardRAG and supported DraCo settings across the twelve Python/Java model/project settings; its mutation scores range from 19.01% to 58.50%.
claims.quote: As summarized in Table 6, LspRag consistently outperforms the baselines, suggesting that its accurate context retrieval not only boosts coverage but also enhances fault detection.

claims.text: The authors describe coverage as comparable to EvoSuite: LspRag is lower on Commons-CLI (37.72% versus 56.33%) and higher on Commons-CSV (83.20% versus 69.70%).
claims.quote:
Nevertheless, the result demonstrates thatLspRag
still delivers coverage results that are comparable toEvoSuite.

claims.text: LspRag has lower syntactic-validity rates than EvoSuite on both Java projects: 60.52% and 90.95%, versus EvoSuite's 100%.
claims.quote:
This design choice involves a trade-off,
where we sacrifice a guaranteed valid rate for broader applicability
and scalability.

claims.text: The seven-person majority assessment judges 47/62 explanations (75.8%) aligned with expert ground truth.

50.

claims.quote:
Participants thought that 75.8% (47 out of 62)
of explanations generated by Malo could be aligned with the

believed that fault explanations offer signiﬁcant insights and
enhance user comprehension of the localization results.

claims.text: Participants perceived rapid fault finding as a benefit of explainable localization; six of seven endorsed rapid localization, but developer task-completion time was not measured.

claims.quote:

of participants, speciﬁcally 6 out of 7, reported that fault lo-
calization is effective in rapidly ﬁnding faults.

claims.text: Malo successfully explains four of five DApp faults selected after the reported October 2023 GPT-4o mini knowledge cutoff.

and found that Malo successfully generated explanations for
four of them.

claims.text: P@K decreases as K increases; the authors interpret this, together with MRR=0.79 for GPT-4o mini, as ranking more relevant explanations higher.

evidence.detail: Authors reviewed the GPT-4o mini judge's reasons and decisions; per-condition agreement statistics not_reported.

reasons and results provided by GPT-4o mini for its evaluations,

claims.text: GPT-4o mini has the second-lowest reported cost, $0.003/function; costs are DeepSeek-V3 $0.002, DeepSeek-R1 $0.01, Doubao $0.012, GPT-3.5 $0.02, and Qwen $0.04.

with a processing cost of 0.003 per function.

that the explanations generated by Malo exhibit confusing

claims.text: Five of seven participants wanted fault-localization tools to provide repair suggestions.

constrained its ability toprocess complex inputs.

negatively affect the performance of the LLM [35].

performs Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, the leading LLM for code, by 51%.

best LLM baseline) generates 35 plausible patches for these bugs,
FLAMES (with RepairLLama as the base LLM) can generate 59
plausible patches, demonstrating 68% improvement over the best
baseline.

ments ranging from 23% to 68%.

significantly reduce VRAM usage in LLMs, successfully
minimizing average VRAM usage by up to 83% and reduc-
ing peak VRAM requirements from 80 GB to as low as 12.7

examined numbers of generated patches, with p values between
0.002 and 0.013 and effect sizes between 0.22 and 0.37, indicating
thatFLAMESis more time efficient than beam search.

claims.quote:
FLAMESreduce time by approximately 11.44 seconds and by 39.52
seconds with 10 and 200 generated patches.

claims.text: The paper reports significant timing benefits for RepairLLama at all five settings, but mean times favor FLAMES only at 10 and 200 patches: 44.40/57.55 and 98.42/101.35 seconds; means are higher for FLAMES at 25, 50 and 100 patches.

metrics.name: average time to find plausible patches in seconds

evidence.detail: All five comparisons have p=0.001–0.027, but absolute effect sizes omit direction and average times favor beam search in three settings.
evidence.quote:
The RepairLlama model also supports the hypothesis with p-
values between 0.001 and 0.027 across all examined numbers of
generated patches, confirming the time efficiency ofFLAMESover
the beam search, although the effect sizes range from negligible
to small.

claims.quote:
Consequently,FLAMESshows lower average running
times with 10 and 200 generated patches.

claims.text: InCoder-1B timing benefits are mixed: FLAMES is faster on average at 10, 50, 100 and 200 patches, slower at 25, and statistically significant only at 10 patches.

metrics.name: average time to find plausible patches in seconds

evidence.detail: Table 6 reports p=0.001 at 10 patches and p=0.195, 0.081, 0.059 and 0.178 at 25, 50, 100 and 200 patches.
evidence.quote:
The most favorable performance forFLAMESis observed with 10
generated patches, where it significantly outperforms the beam
search (p-value 0.001).

claims.quote:
AlthoughFLAMEStends to generate
patches faster at higher numbers of generated patches (50, 100,
and 200), it performs worse than BS with 25 generated patches.

claims.text: Semantic reward feedback increases the plausible-patch count from 150 to 210, a 40% improvement over probability-only guidance.
claims.quote: Our experimental results show that incorporating a semantic reward function can lead to a 40% increase, from 150 to 210, in plausible patches.

claims.text: Increasing expansion k from 3 to 10 raises the plausible-patch count from 190 to 210.
claims.quote:
Our findings show that as𝑘
increased from 3 to 10, the number of plausible patches increased
from 190 to 210.

claims.text: Further expansion-size increases up to k=30 yield 202–204 plausible patches, providing no improvement over the reported 210 at k=10.
claims.quote:
Unfortunately, a further increase of𝑘 to up to 30
showed minimal gains, with plausible patches ranging from 202 to
204.

claims.text: Variable P-UCB produces the most plausible patches: 210 versus 179 for UCB and 188 for Fixed P-UCB, reported improvements of 17% and 11%.
claims.quote:
This policy algorithm outperforms UCB and
Fixed P-UCB by 17% (179 plausible patches) and 11% (188 plausible
patches), respectively.

claims.text: FLAMES's repair-effectiveness advantage generalizes across the three evaluated Java benchmarks.

metrics.name: correct-patch count and relative improvement across benchmarks

claims.quote:
These re-
sults demonstrate the generalizability ofFLAMESacross various
evaluation benchmarks, highlighting its effectiveness in generating
correct fixes in different data sets.

claims.text: FLAMES's effectiveness generalizes across the six evaluated LLMs with different architectures and sizes.

metrics.name: correct-patch count and improvement across LLMs

claims.quote:
Therefore, we believe that FLAMES is capable of generalizing
effectively to different LLMs.

claims.text: On single-hunk Defects4J, FLAMES produces 211 plausible patches versus 170 for RepairLLama with beam search and 151 with multiple sampling.
claims.quote:
#Correct and #Plausible denotes
the number of correct and plausible patches generated by
each tool.

claims.text: On HumanEval-Java, FLAMES produces plausible patches for 133 bugs versus RepairLLama's 118.

metrics.name: number of bugs with plausible patches

claims.quote:
The
results are displayed as x/y, with x, y denotes the number of
bugs with correct and plausible patches, respectively.

claims.text: On TransformedD4J, FLAMES produces plausible patches for 776 bugs versus RepairLLama's 581.

metrics.name: number of bugs with plausible patches

claims.quote:
The
results are displayed as x/y, with x, y denotes the number of
bugs with correct and plausible patches, respectively.

claims.text: FLAMES's patch precision is 0.63, below RepairLLama with beam search at 0.66 but above multiple sampling at 0.59 and the other listed LLM-based comparators.

metrics.name: precision: correct patches divided by plausible patches

claims.quote:
Although this approach
slightly reduces the precision from 0.66 to 0.63, this trade-off is
justified by a 19% increase in repair success.

claims.text: Among FLAMES, RepairLLama, KNOD and FitRepair, FLAMES contributes the most unique fixes: 14 versus 6, 5 and 9 respectively.

metrics.name: number of unique correctly repaired bugs

claims.quote: FLAMES can fix 14 unique bugs.

claims.text: FLAMES complements existing APR methods; combining all evaluated techniques yields correct fixes for 299 bugs.

metrics.name: union of correctly repaired bugs across techniques

claims.quote:
By
combining all the techniques, we can successfully fix 299 bugs.

claims.text: Relative to original RepairLLama alone, FLAMES correctly repairs 42 bugs that RepairLLama misses.

metrics.name: number of correct fixes unique to FLAMES relative to RepairLLama

claims.quote:
First, while our approach,FLAMES, correctly fixes 21 more bugs
and 42 unique bugs compared to the original RepairLlama, there
are 21 bugs that the original model could repair butFLAMEScould
not.

claims.text: FLAMES fails on 21 bugs that original RepairLLama can correctly repair.

metrics.name: number of RepairLLama-repaired bugs missed by FLAMES

claims.quote:
First, while our approach,FLAMES, correctly fixes 21 more bugs
and 42 unique bugs compared to the original RepairLlama, there
are 21 bugs that the original model could repair butFLAMEScould
not.

claims.text: FLAMES achieves its reported repair success with a configured budget of 200 validated patches and 30 minutes per bug, compared with 1,000–5,000 patches and five hours for FitRepair and KNOD.
claims.quote:
Notably,FLAMESachieves this performance
with a budget of only 200 validated patches and a 30-minute pause
per bug, while FitRepair and KNOD require 1,000–5,000 validated
patches and a pause of 5-hours per bug.

claims.text: FLAMES produces plausible patches for 65%, 69% and 62% of bugs in the <60%, 60–80% and >80% test-suite line-coverage groups respectively.

metrics.name: percentage of bugs with plausible patches

claims.quote:
FLAMES produced plausible
patches for 65%, 69%, and 62% of bugs in these groups, and correct
patches for 40%, 42%, and 40%, respectively.

claims.text: FLAMES correctly repairs 40%, 42% and 40% of bugs in the <60%, 60–80% and >80% test-suite line-coverage groups respectively.

metrics.name: percentage of bugs with correct patches

claims.quote:
FLAMES produced plausible
patches for 65%, 69%, and 62% of bugs in these groups, and correct
patches for 40%, 42%, and 40%, respectively.

claims.text: Patch precision is slightly lower in the lower-coverage groups: 0.61 and 0.62 versus 0.64 above 80% coverage.

metrics.name: precision: correct patches divided by plausible patches

claims.quote:
However, the precision
for the >80% coverage group was slightly higher at 0.64, compared
to 0.61 and 0.62 in the lower coverage groups.

claims.text: The authors interpret the coverage-stratified results as consistent performance across test-suite quality, with a slight precision decrease on lower-coverage suites.

metrics.name: test-suite line coverage as a proxy for test-suite quality

claims.quote:
These results suggest
that FLAMES performs consistently across varying test suite quality,
with a slight decrease in precision on lower coverage suites.

claims.text: The authors report consistent trends between correct- and plausible-patch counts in comparisons of variants, without reporting a quantitative agreement analysis.

metrics.name: qualitative agreement between correct- and plausible-patch trends

claims.quote:
To minimize this risk, we only
utilized this metric when comparing different variants of the same
APR techniques, where we observed consistent trends between
correct patches and plausible patches.

claims.text: The authors hypothesize that test-validation feedback explains FLAMES's advantage over multiple sampling.

metrics.name: number of correct patches in comparison with multiple sampling
number of plausible patches in semantic-reward ablation

evidence.detail: A separate reward-feedback ablation reports 210 versus 150 plausible patches, supporting a feedback benefit but not isolating every difference from multiple sampling across all models.
evidence.quote: Our experimental results show that incorporating a semantic reward function can lead to a 40% increase, from 150 to 210, in plausible patches.

claims.quote:
We hypothesize that this perfor-
mance gap arises becauseFLAMESleverages feedback from test
validation to guide patch generation, whereas multiple sampling
relies solely on random sampling from the model’s output.

claims.text: The authors attribute FLAMES's beam-search effectiveness advantage to efficient GPU-resource use enabling more thorough patch-space exploration.

evidence.detail: The separate memory experiment reports lower VRAM and zero OOM errors for FLAMES; search-space thoroughness itself is not measured.
evidence.quote:
Additionally,FLAMESeliminates OOM errors, while the baselines
witness OOMs in up to 86.6% of the data points.

claims.quote:
This is due toFLAMES’s effective use of GPU resources which
allows for a more thorough exploration of the large patch space.

claims.text: The authors explain the limited benefit of larger k as a broader but shallower search that favors exploration over exploitation.

metrics.name: number of plausible patches across expansion sizes

claims.quote:
This is due to the broader, yet shallower search at higher k,
which favors exploration over the exploitation needed for certain
bugs.

claims.text: Variable P-UCB's advantage is attributed to dynamically balancing exploration and exploitation.

metrics.name: number of plausible patches across selection policies

claims.quote:
The performance of Variable P-UCB likely
stems from its ability to dynamically adjust the balance between
exploration and exploitation during the search process, thereby
optimizing the discovery of plausible patches.

claims.text: Inspection of the 21 RepairLLama-fixed bugs missed by FLAMES often finds a need for entirely new code segments, but similar patterns also occur among FLAMES-only fixes.

metrics.name: qualitative code-change patterns among uniquely repaired and missed bugs

claims.quote:
In an in-depth analysis on the 21 bugs that FLAMES cannot
repair, we observed that the frequent pattern that these bugs most
often require entirely new code segments.

claims.text: The authors hypothesize that FLAMES misses some RepairLLama-fixed bugs because its expansion size is 10 rather than RepairLLama beam search's scope of up to 25 tokens.

metrics.name: number of RepairLLama-fixed bugs missed by FLAMES

evidence.detail: Pattern inspection finds new-code-segment requirements in both missed and FLAMES-only repairs, weakening a bug-type explanation but not directly establishing expansion size as the cause.
evidence.quote:
However, we also notice
that these patterns appear in bugs that can be successfully repaired
by FLAMES but cannot be repaired by RepairLlama.

claims.quote:
Specifically, FLAMES’s failure to repair these bugs can
possibly be attributed to FLAMES’s smaller expansion size of 10.

claims.text: The multi-location results suggest that FLAMES can operate with coarse-grained bug regions when its base model supports them, reducing dependence on perfect fault localization in that setting.

metrics.name: number of correct multi-location repairs under coarse-grained localization

claims.quote:
These
results suggest that FLAMES may operate without perfect fault
localization, provided that its base models support such flexibility.

claims.text: The authors caution that increases in plausible patches do not necessarily yield proportional increases in correct patches.

metrics.name: number of correct patches, not_reported for the reward-feedback ablation

note that a substantial increase in plausible patches does not al-
ways result in a proportionally large increase in correct patches.

of 4.95% (from 48.51% to 53.46%).

method achieved an increase in target coverage of 47.72 percentage
points (from 9.82% to 57.54%).

claims.text: Numerous OS and PS API pairs occur within and across the four frameworks; TensorFlow→PyTorch has 2408 OS/737 PS pairs and the reverse has 2509 OS/609 PS pairs.

metrics.name: matched operation-similar and parameter-similar API-pair counts

claims.quote:
For example,
TensorFlow has 2408 #OS and 737 #PS API pairs in PyTorch,
while PyTorch has 2509 and 609 in TensorFlow.

claims.text: Threshold supplementation improves labelled-pair recall over Top-k alone: within-framework mean 86.29% versus 76.12%, cross-framework mean 86.05% versus 80.07%; every reported framework/scope condition improves.

metrics.name: coverage/recall of manually labelled OS API pairs

claims.quote:
As shown in Table V, the default setting “Matcher w/
optimization” achieves average matching coverage rates of
86.29% within frameworks and 86.05% across frameworks,
outperforming the “Matcher w/o optimization” setting.

claims.text: Few-shot CoT raises overall JSON/syntax validity from 50.00% to 65.00% for CodeLlama, 73.33% to 88.33% for CodeGemma, and 96.67% to 100% for Qwen; Qwen reaches 100% on both OS and PS subsets.
claims.quote:
This means that the generated code passes both JSON
parsing and Python syntax checks.

claims.text: Few-shot CoT raises overall known-bug reproduction from 35% to 50% for CodeLlama, 50% to 65% for CodeGemma, and 65% to 85% for Qwen; Qwen reproduces 10/10 OS and 7/10 PS bugs, although its PS result declines from zero-shot's 8/10.
claims.quote:
Moreover, it successfully
reproduces 17 shared bugs, achieving a 100% success rate
for #OS APIs, outperforming both the baseline and other
models.

claims.text: MirrorFuzz reports 315 bugs, including 262 previously unknown: TensorFlow 118/83, PyTorch 48/47, OneFlow 86/77 and Jittor 63/55 (total/unknown).

evidence.detail: 180 previously unknown reports confirmed, 80 fixed, and nine reports rejected; confirmation covers a subset of reported discoveries.
evidence.quote:
Among these, 180 are confirmed by
developers, 80 are fixed, and 9 are rejected.

evidence.detail: 52 bugs assigned CNVD IDs.
evidence.quote:
Furthermore, 52 bugs are
assigned CNVD IDs, and 5 bugs are marked as high-priority
by PyTorch developers for urgent resolution.

claims.quote:
Overall, MirrorFuzz detects 315 bugs, of which 262 are
previously unknown.

claims.text: Reported failures comprise 39 segmentation faults, 13 floating-point exceptions, 197 aborts and 66 other failures; Jittor contributes 56 other failures among its 63 reports.
claims.quote:
Across all
bug types, we observe 39 segmentation faults, 13 floating-point
exceptions, 197 program aborts, and 66 framework internal
errors.

claims.text: ASAN identifies nine NULL-pointer dereferences and one heap overflow in TensorFlow; in PyTorch it identifies eight NULL-pointer dereferences, 13 heap overflows, one container overflow and one stack overflow.
claims.quote:
We further evaluate bug detection capability by enabling
AddressSanitizer (ASAN) [68] on TensorFlow and PyTorch,
while builds for OneFlow and Jittor fail due to compilation
issues.

claims.text: OS relationships are the main reported bug source, while PS relationships cover gaps OS misses; Table VIII records 393 OS and 119 PS source associations, rather than unique incremental bug counts.
claims.quote:
Additionally,
#OS APIs are the primary source of bugs, while #PS APIs
supplement gaps that #OS APIs cannot cover.

claims.text: API coverage reaches 3995/4403 TensorFlow APIs and 1868/1992 PyTorch APIs; against Orion's 4037 and 1751, TensorFlow coverage is comparable and PyTorch improves 6.68%.
claims.quote:
MirrorFuzz demonstrates compre-
hensive coverage, supporting 3995 APIs in TensorFlow and
1868 APIs in PyTorch.

claims.text: Python-line coverage is 129663 lines (45.57%) for TensorFlow and 77707 (28.17%) for PyTorch, exceeding TitanFuzz's 92670 and 39207 by 39.92% and 98.20%.
claims.quote:
In terms of code coverage, MirrorFuzz significantly
outperforms the best baseline, TitanFuzz, with a 39.92% im-
provement for TensorFlow and a substantial 98.20% increase
for PyTorch.

claims.text: On MoCo-supported subsets, MirrorFuzz covers more APIs than MoCo: TensorFlow 145 versus 95, PyTorch 142 versus 72, and Jittor 68 versus 66.
claims.quote:
In terms of API and code coverage, MirrorFuzz
outperforms MoCo in both aspects.

claims.text: On MoCo-supported subsets, MirrorFuzz covers more Python lines than MoCo: TensorFlow 83875 versus 74756, PyTorch 67322 versus 26271, and Jittor 4841 versus 3955.
claims.quote:
In terms of API and code coverage, MirrorFuzz
outperforms MoCo in both aspects.

claims.text: Under the five-hour campaign limit, MirrorFuzz tests 385/400 TensorFlow APIs and all 400 PyTorch APIs, finishing PyTorch in 4h23min44s; Orion tests 148/172 and TitanFuzz 287/231 APIs in five hours.
claims.quote:
As shown
in Table XI, within the same time budget, MirrorFuzz tests
385 APIs in TensorFlow and completes testing all 400 APIs
in PyTorch, outperforming other baselines.

claims.text: The 400-API campaigns find 27 TensorFlow and 11 PyTorch unique bugs, exceeding Orion's 14/6 and TitanFuzz's 2/2.
claims.quote:
MirrorFuzz also reports the most unique
bugs, finding 27 in TensorFlow and 11 in PyTorch.

claims.text: MirrorFuzz achieves better crash-discovery time efficiency than Orion and TitanFuzz during the five-hour campaigns.

metrics.name: unique bugs over elapsed testing time

claims.quote:
This
demonstrates the advantage of MirrorFuzz in terms of bug
detection efficiency.

claims.text: MirrorFuzz finds the most crashes across older/current releases: PyTorch 39/31 and TensorFlow 142/115; the older PyTorch release is inconsistently printed as 1.13.1/1.31.1.

metrics.name: unique crash bugs by framework version

claims.quote:
MirrorFuzz detects 39 and 31 bugs in PyTorch
versions 1.13.1 and 2.4.1, respectively, and identifies 142
and 115 bugs in TensorFlow versions 2.10.0 and 2.17.0.

claims.text: In OneFlow's few-shot condition, removing the title yields the highest parameter accuracy, 78.60%, versus 75.50% with full context.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, we observe that in OneFlow, “#Issue w/o T”
achieves the highest accuracy in bug-causing parameter recog-
nition, while “#Issue w/o D” excels in buggy API recognition.

claims.text: In OneFlow's few-shot condition, removing the description yields the highest API accuracy, 94.20%, versus 92.40% with full context.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, we observe that in OneFlow, “#Issue w/o T”
achieves the highest accuracy in bug-causing parameter recog-
nition, while “#Issue w/o D” excels in buggy API recognition.

claims.text: In Jittor's few-shot condition, removing the description yields the highest parameter accuracy, 94.70%, versus 90.00% with full context.
claims.quote:
In Jittor, “#Issue w/o D” achieves the highest accuracy in bug-
causing parameter recognition.

claims.text: Most manually traced bug-source associations originate in TensorFlow and PyTorch; the authors attribute this to their larger API and historical-issue inventories.
claims.quote:
We
observe that bugs in these frameworks affect each other, and
most of these bugs are influenced by flaws in TensorFlow
and PyTorch.

claims.text: Shared-bug relationships also run from smaller OneFlow/Jittor frameworks to TensorFlow/PyTorch.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, bugs in Jittor and OneFlow can
also impact TensorFlow and PyTorch, despite having fewer
APIs and known issues.

claims.text: Some target bugs can be triggered through shared-bug information from multiple frameworks.
claims.quote:
Moreover,
we find that some bugs are repeatedly triggered by shared
bugs across different frameworks, possibly because developers
make the same mistakes when implementing these features.

claims.text: Qwen is claimed to possess superior code understanding, inferred from synthesis outcomes without a separate understanding measure.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, Qwen2.5-
Coder exhibits superior code understanding and generation
capabilities, further enhancing its performance.

claims.text: Developers confirm 180 previously unknown reports: TensorFlow 83, PyTorch 45, OneFlow 28 and Jittor 24.
claims.quote:

claims.text: Sanitisation and refinement increased generators producing manually judged valid data from 169/256 (66.01%) to 197/256 (76.95%).

metrics.name: Number and percentage of generators producing manually judged valid data

claims.quote:
The sanitisation and re-
ﬁnement steps improved the total number for generators
that produced valid data from 169 to 197 i.e. from 66.01%
to 76.95% for the 256 generator programs.

claims.text: Validator-based ranking effectively identifies invalid-data generators, with reported recall of 86.21% before and 77.9% after sanitisation/refinement.
claims.quote:
The high recall
number before and after sanitisation and reﬁnement is a
good indicator of the eﬀectiveness of ranking generators
with LLM synthesized validators.

claims.text: For the two selected contexts, the 50-output samples have high pairwise dissimilarity and variability.
claims.quote:
Both
the heatmaps are hot indicating a high distance between
the strings, which conﬁrms that the strings are dissimilar
to each other.

claims.text: The 10000-output samples for the two selected contexts show approximately uniform KDE distributions and good spread.

DOB respectively, which the original generator could not
produce.

claims.text: After the generator prompt, 122/256 generators were good by four-validator consensus.
claims.quote:
We found that 122 out of 256 generator programs
were already good after the generator prompt.

claims.text: Sanitisation/refinement changed 18 initially bad generators into good generators by validator ranking.
claims.quote:
Another
18 out of 256 generators were bad after the generator
step, but became good after sanitisation and reﬁnement.

claims.text: Twenty-three initially bad generators improved in rank after all refinements without reaching good status.
claims.quote:
There were 23 generator programs, which were bad
initially but became better after all reﬁnements were
applied, but did not become good.

claims.text: Eighty-six generators remained bad with unchanged rank after sanitisation/refinement.

metrics.name: Initially bad generators with unchanged final rank

claims.quote:
Finally, 86 generators were bad after the generator step
and remained bad, with the same rank after sanitisation
and reﬁnement.

claims.text: Seven initially bad generators became worse in rank after sanitisation/refinement.
claims.quote:
There were another 7 bad generators that
became worse, with a lower rank after sanitisation and
reﬁnements.

claims.text: Sanitisation made 15 generators good by validator ranking.
claims.quote:
A further breakdown revealed that 15
of these 18 generators, became good after sanitisation, 3
after length reﬁnement and 0 after data-type reﬁnement.

claims.text: Sanitisation improved the rank of 18 other generators that remained bad.

metrics.name: Generators becoming better but not good after sanitisation

claims.quote:
Again, a breakdown
shows that 18 became better after sanitisation, 5 became
better after the length reﬁnement and 0 became better
after the data-type reﬁnement.

claims.text: Length refinement made three generators good by validator ranking.

metrics.name: Generators becoming good after length refinement

claims.quote:
A further breakdown revealed that 15
of these 18 generators, became good after sanitisation, 3
after length reﬁnement and 0 after data-type reﬁnement.

claims.text: Length refinement improved the rank of five other generators that remained bad.

metrics.name: Generators becoming better but not good after length refinement

claims.quote:
Again, a breakdown
shows that 18 became better after sanitisation, 5 became
better after the length reﬁnement and 0 became better
after the data-type reﬁnement.

claims.text: Data-type refinement made no generators good or better by validator ranking.

metrics.name: Generators becoming good or better after data-type refinement

claims.quote:
Again, a breakdown
shows that 18 became better after sanitisation, 5 became
better after the length reﬁnement and 0 became better
after the data-type reﬁnement.

claims.text: Sanitisation lowered the rank of five generators.
claims.quote:
Of these 7 generators, 5 became worse after
sanitisation and 2 became worse after length reﬁnement.

claims.text: Data-type refinement did not worsen any generator's rank.

metrics.name: Generators becoming worse after data-type refinement

The data-type reﬁnement did not cause any generator
program to become worse.

claims.text: Ranking accuracy was 72.27% before and 67.57% after sanitisation/refinement.

metrics.name: Accuracy against manually judged generated-data validity

claims.quote:
After sanitisation and
reﬁnement, the accuracy of the ranking based strategy for
generator programs became 127+46/256=67.57%, while
the precision and recall became 46/(46+70)=39.65% and
46/(46+13)=77.9% respectively.

claims.text: Ranking precision fell from 55.97% before sanitisation/refinement to 39.65% afterward.
claims.quote:
After sanitisation and
reﬁnement, the accuracy of the ranking based strategy for
generator programs became 127+46/256=67.57%, while
the precision and recall became 46/(46+70)=39.65% and
46/(46+13)=77.9% respectively.

claims.text: False positives and low ranking precision arise because synthesized validators can reject valid data.
claims.quote:
The high number of false
positives and low precision is a result of the fact that the
LLM synthesized validators are not perfect and can fail on
valid data.

claims.text: The two 50-output KDE plots resemble a normal distribution, suggesting a possible bias toward the mean.

metrics.name: Kernel density estimate (KDE) of integer-valued or hashed outputs

claims.quote:
The 50 sample plots for the two contexts
resemble the normal distribution, signaling perhaps a bias
towards data near the mean.

claims.text: NCD heatmaps retain high pairwise dissimilarity at 10000 samples and beyond in the selected contexts.

metrics.name: NCD heatmap distances across sample counts

claims.quote:
We note that the maps remain hot even
as the number of samples increase to 10000 and beyond,
indicating that the strings are well diversiﬁed and have a
high variability.

claims.text: Ambiguous or incomplete descriptions can cause hallucinated structural constraints absent from the specification.
claims.quote:
When the textual descrip-
tion of the test data was ambiguous or incomplete, the
LLM tends to hallucinate [25] and produce structural
constraints that were not in the original speciﬁcation.

claims.text: Refinement failed to correct the erroneous alphanumeric interpretation in the E-Gift Voucher example.
claims.quote:
This test input
failed on a subset of validators and none of the reﬁnement
techniques was able to ﬁx the generator program for the
erroneous assumption that the voucher number should be
alphanumeric.

claims.text: The generated NPI provider-number program used a checksum computation differing from the required Luhn algorithm.
claims.quote:
This computation diﬀers from the Luhn
checksum algorithm actually used in the NPI provider
number.

claims.text: Refinement can turn an initially correct generator into an incorrect one, as illustrated by the hyphenated account-number example.
claims.quote:
Another behavior that we
observed was that the LLM synthesized generators that
were correct for either the initial or rephrased context,
but failed after reﬁnement.

claims.text: A generator encoding mobile number and DOB as constants produced valid but narrowly spread statement-password data.
claims.quote:
Thus, even though the generator
produced test data that was correct, the spread of the test
data was limited.

claims.text: Widening may introduce invalid generated data.
claims.quote:
Although our solution is a preliminary one, we
note that a simple widening of this kind can in turn lead
to invalid data being generated and may lead to multiple,
and even potentially unbounded, iterations of reﬁnement.

claims.text: Widening may require multiple, potentially unbounded refinement iterations.
claims.quote:
Although our solution is a preliminary one, we
note that a simple widening of this kind can in turn lead
to invalid data being generated and may lead to multiple,
and even potentially unbounded, iterations of reﬁnement.

claims.text: Synthesized generator programs occasionally enter infinite loops.
claims.quote:
In rare cases, the LLM synthesized
generators get stuck in an inﬁnite loop.

claims.text: Diversified generated data has potential to achieve high application coverage, although application coverage was not measured.
claims.page: p. 9, §III-D; coverage limitation in p. 8, §III-D and p. 10, §V-A
claims.quote:
Thus, we believe that the test data
generated by TestReﬁneGen has good potential to achieve
high coverage in the challenging no-box testing setting.

claims.text: Sanitisation is a simple yet powerful step for improving generator rank, contributing more rank improvements (15 to good, 18 to better) than length (3, 5) or data-type refinement (0, 0).

metrics.name: Validator-rank transitions attributed to each post-processing step

claims.quote: Thus, sanitisation turns out to be a simple yet powerful technique that can be used to improve the rank of a generator program.

hcs.name: JUnitGenie
hcs.quote:
With the distilled context knowledge, JUnitGenie generates
unit tests via an iterative pipeline where structured prompts
are submitted to an LLM, and the outputs are refined through
error checking until valid and runnable tests are obtained.

(w/o CKD+CKE) retains only test case refinement, using error
messages to repair tests without any contextual input.

hcs.removed: Context knowledge distillation; raw extracted context replaces distilled guidance
hcs.quote:
The third
(w/o CKD) includes both context extraction and refinement but
omits distillation, presenting raw context without structured
guidance.

claims.text: JUnitGenie generates 20,305 tests, the largest volume among EvoSuite, Randoop, ChatTester, CoverUp and HITS.
claims.quote:
From these paths, JUnitGenie generates 20,305 test
cases.

claims.text: 14,190 of 20,305 generated tests compile and reach the focal method (69.88%); this success rate exceeds ChatTester, CoverUp and HITS but trails EvoSuite and Randoop.
claims.quote:
After compilation and execution, 14,190 are identified
as valid (i.e., 6,115 of them are invalid), giving a success
rate of 69.88% in generating valid test cases.

claims.text: JUnitGenie produces more valid tests than all five external comparators; its per-project median is 1,355 and upper quartile 1,633.
claims.quote:
Compared to
other LLM-based tools, JUnitGenie achieves both the highest
number of valid test cases and the highest success rate.

claims.text: JUnitGenie averages 56.86% branch and 61.45% line coverage, exceeding all five external comparators; the abstract reports average gains equivalent to 29.60 and 31.00 percentage points.
claims.quote:
The
results show that JUnitGenie generates valid tests and improves
branch and line coverage by 29.60% and 31.00% on average over
both heuristic and LLM-based baselines.

claims.text: At 60 seconds, JUnitGenie has lower branch coverage than EvoSuite (39.33% versus 40.84%) but higher line coverage (43.72% versus 41.37%).
claims.quote:
With a 60s timeout, EvoSuite achieves slightly higher
branch coverage (40.84%) and comparable line coverage
(41.37%) to JUnitGenie (39.33% branch coverage, 43.72%
line coverage), while other tools perform noticeably lower.

claims.text: At 300 and 600 seconds per method, JUnitGenie exceeds every external comparator in branch and line coverage.
claims.quote:
This situation is dramatically changed when the timeout
is extended to 300s and 600s, where JUnitGenie begins to
outperform all baselines on both branch and line coverage.

claims.text: At 1,200 seconds, JUnitGenie leads all external comparators with 54.30% branch and 59.00% line coverage.
claims.quote:
When
the timeout is extended to 1,200s, the improvements of all
tools gradually converge and JUnitGenie still achieves the
highest coverage on both metrics (54.30% branch coverage and
59.00% line coverage), highlighting its better performance.

claims.text: Removing extraction, distillation and refinement gives the lowest ablation coverage: 24.74% branch and 27.84% line.
claims.quote:
Thew/o
(CKD+CKE+TCR)setting performs the worst, achieving only
24.74% branch coverage and 27.84% line coverage.

claims.text: Adding refinement to basic prompting raises branch coverage from 24.74% to 37.65% and line coverage from 27.84% to 42.97%.
claims.quote:
Adding test case refinement (w/o CKD+CKE) improves
coverage by 12–15%, as it repairs syntactically invalid yet
semantically meaningful tests through iterative refinement of
compiler error messages.

claims.text: Refinement without extracted context increases executable-test rate from 33.49% to 65.81% across five iterations.
claims.quote:
As illustrated by the red line in
Fig. 6, refinement raises the executable test rate from 33.49%
to 65.81% over five iterations.

claims.text: Across five refinement rounds, full JUnitGenie improves executable-test rate from 45.60% to 69.88%, and the undistilled-context ablation from 20.32% to 63.44%.
claims.quote:
Other variants show substantial
gains over five rounds, withJUnitGenieimproving from
45.60% to 69.88%, andw/o (CKD)from 20.32% to 63.44%.

claims.text: Adding raw extracted context to refinement reduces average branch coverage by 3.21 and line coverage by 4.27 percentage points.
claims.quote:
Notably, enabling context extraction without distillation
(w/o CKD) results in a slight performance drop, with branch
coverage decreasing by 3.21% and line coverage by 4.27%
compared to using refinement alone.

claims.text: Distillation raises branch/line coverage from 34.44%/38.70% to 56.86%/61.45%, gains of 22.42/22.75 percentage points.
claims.quote:
JUnitGenie attains 56.86% branch
coverage and 61.45% line coverage, representing gains of
22.42% and 22.75% overw/o CKD, respectively.

claims.text: Full JUnitGenie has the highest final executable-test rate: 69.88%, versus 65.81% with refinement only and 63.44% with raw context.
claims.quote:
In comparison,w/o (CKD+CKE)andw/o (CKD)
plateau at 65.81% and 63.44%, respectively.

claims.text: The full workflow improves branch and line coverage over Basic Prompting across all four evaluated models.
claims.quote:
The results show that our
method consistently outperforms the basic setting on all
models.

claims.text: Among open models, full JUnitGenie ranks Qwen2.5-Coder first (56.38%/60.68% branch/line), DeepSeek-Coder second (49.31%/53.92%), and CodeLlama third (44.91%/50.67%).
claims.quote:
Among the three open-source models evaluated with our
approach, Qwen2.5-Coder achieves the best overall results
with 56.38% branch and 60.68% line coverage, followed
by DeepSeek-Coder and CodeLlama.

claims.text: Open-model validity rates rank Qwen2.5-Coder 46.03%, DeepSeek-Coder 36.67%, and CodeLlama 34.95%.
claims.quote:
Qwen2.5-Coder also
produces the most valid tests and achieves the highest success
rate, with 7,247 valid tests at 46.03%, while DeepSeek-
Coder generates 5,443 valid tests at 36.67%, and CodeLlama
generates 3,961 valid tests at 34.95%.

claims.text: Qwen2.5-Coder produces 7,247 valid tests, exceeding DeepSeek-Coder's 5,443 and CodeLlama's 3,961.
claims.quote:
Qwen2.5-Coder also
produces the most valid tests and achieves the highest success
rate, with 7,247 valid tests at 46.03%, while DeepSeek-
Coder generates 5,443 valid tests at 36.67%, and CodeLlama
generates 3,961 valid tests at 34.95%.

claims.text: CodeLlama obtains the largest coverage gains from the full workflow: 34.60 branch and 38.40 line percentage points over Basic Prompting.
claims.quote:
At the same time, we observe
that CodeLlama benefits the most from JUnitGenie (34.60%
branch coverage increase and 38.40% line coverage increase).

claims.text: Generated tests reveal eight candidate issues, including four developer-confirmed and fixed major bugs: three in commons-codec and one in commons-lang.

evidence.description: CODEC-328/330/331 were fixed in da16f36/c4d8365/59929c3; LANG-1771 was fixed in 5a15ccb; all four are labelled Major.
evidence.quote:
Development teams have reacted to all these issues
and four of them are confirmed as real bugs and have been
fixed.

claims.quote:
Development teams have reacted to all these issues
and four of them are confirmed as real bugs and have been
fixed.

claims.text: High coverage on Lang (87.10%/92.41%) and CSV (76.57%/85.98%) is interpreted as exercising diverse, deep execution paths.
claims.quote:
It delivers particularly strong results on complex projects such
asLang(87.10% branch coverage, 92.41% line coverage)
andCSV(76.57% branch coverage, 85.98% line coverage),
demonstrating its ability to generate tests that exercise diverse
and deep execution paths.

claims.text: JUnitGenie's comparative coverage advantage grows with longer testing budgets.

metrics.name: coverage as a function of per-method timeout

claims.quote:
In addition, its advantage becomes more
pronounced with longer budgets, indicating that JUnitGenie
scales more effectively with extended testing time and achieves
higher overall coverage across real-world projects.

claims.text: Stronger models are better at following instructions, leading to higher validity and coverage.
claims.quote:
These results indicate
that stronger models are better at following instructions to
generate valid tests and achieve higher success rates, thereby
yielding greater coverage.

claims.text: The full workflow narrows coverage differences between weaker and stronger models.
claims.quote:
Hence, JUnitGenie not
only improves strong models but also substantially boosts
weaker ones, narrowing the performance gap.

claims.text: Qwen2.5-Coder with JUnitGenie performs comparably to GPT-4o-Mini (56.38%/60.68% versus 56.86%/61.45% branch/line).
claims.quote:
Interestingly, Qwen2.5-Coder performs on par with GPT-
4o-Mini.

claims.text: With Basic Prompting, Qwen2.5-Coder exceeds GPT-4o-Mini in average branch/line coverage (29.83%/32.03% versus 24.74%/27.84%).
claims.quote:
Under basic prompting, it slightly exceeds GPT-4o-
Mini in average coverage.

claims.text: The narrative reports Qwen2.5-Coder leading branch coverage on four projects and line coverage on three; Table V actually shows five branch wins.
claims.quote:
Under our setting, it achieves the
highest branch coverage in four out of 10 projects and the
highest line coverage in three.

claims.text: JUnitGenie requires about 13.68 hours per project on average and 12.80 hours median; its median is below ChatTester, CoverUp and HITS, while heuristic tools are faster.

metrics.name: mean and median generation time per project

claims.quote:
In terms of median generation
time, ChatTester, CoverUp, and HITS take 15.40, 13.35, and
17.85 hours, respectively, while JUnitGenie requires 12.80
hours.

claims.text: Code refinement accounts for over 60% of JUnitGenie's generation time and is its main bottleneck.

metrics.name: refinement share of total generation time

claims.quote:
The main
bottleneck lies in the code refinement phase, which accounts
for over 60% of the total time.

claims.text: JUnitGenie is claimed to offer a practical balance between efficiency and effectiveness.
claims.quote:
The fact that JUnitGenie spends relatively less time than
other LLM-based tools suggests that it achieves a practical
balance between efficiency and effectiveness, while producing
the highest number of valid tests among all methods.

claims.text: JUnitGenie identifies 14,132 CFG paths across 2,258 methods, averaging 6.26 paths per method.
claims.quote:
Across 2,258 focal methods, JUnitGenie identifies
and analyzes 14,132 CFG paths, with an average of 6.26 per
method.

claims.text: JUnitGenie can still fail on methods with complex control or data dependencies.
claims.quote:
Like most other SOTA approaches,
JUnitGenie may fail on focal methods with complex control or
data dependencies.

claims.text: 99% of benchmark methods have fewer than 100 CFG paths; under 1% show severe path explosion.
claims.quote:
Our analysis shows 99% of
methods in our dataset have fewer than 100 CFG paths, while
under 1% suffer severe path explosion.

claims.text: Highly branching control flow is JUnitGenie's main scalability limitation.
claims.quote:
The main limitation of JUnitGenie is scalability on highly
branching control flow.

claims.text: Some generated tests remain invalid after diagnostic-based refinement because of version-incompatible APIs or unavailable libraries.
claims.quote:
WhileFeedback Loop Refinementrepairs many cases
using diagnostics, some remain invalid since error messages
cannot resolve version mismatches or missing dependencies.

claims.text: Reaching the focal method does not establish correct test oracles; later exceptions can be false positives.
claims.quote:
A later exception may indicate a real bug or
an incorrect oracle, risking false positives.

claims.text: Unknown-bug discoveries are taken as evidence that path-sensitive context can yield useful test oracles.

evidence.description: Four discovered bugs were confirmed and fixed; this supports useful failures but does not establish general oracle accuracy.
evidence.quote:
Development teams have reacted to all these issues
and four of them are confirmed as real bugs and have been
fixed.

claims.quote:
Nevertheless, our
path-sensitive context enables the LLM to infer useful ora-
cles, demonstrated by discovering unknown real-world bugs.

claims.text: The paper claims robustness to stochasticity from coverage rankings under four timeouts; repeated-run variability is not reported, and its all-budgets superiority statement conflicts with the 60-second branch result.

metrics.name: coverage ranking across different time budgets

claims.quote:
Across all budgets, JUnitGe-
nie consistently achieves the highest branch and line coverage,
demonstrating robustness to stochasticity.

claims.text: Strong open-source models with JUnitGenie are claimed to provide a cost-effective alternative to closed-source models; model costs are not measured.
claims.quote:
These results show that with
proper enhancement, strong open-source models can match or
even surpass closed-source models, offering a cost-effective
solution for large-scale automated test generation.

claims.text: Compiler-feedback refinement is described as recovering syntactically invalid but semantically meaningful tests.
claims.quote:
Adding test case refinement (w/o CKD+CKE) improves
coverage by 12–15%, as it repairs syntactically invalid yet
semantically meaningful tests through iterative refinement of
compiler error messages.

claims.text: For Joda-Time withZone(DateTimeZone), 9,489 tokens of undistilled context accompany generation failure and zero coverage, attributed to context overload.
claims.quote:
The excessive
volume of undistilled context hinders the model’s ability
to isolate and leverage relevant information, leading to test
generation failure and zero coverage for the method.

claims.text: Rapid fixes after reports suggest generated failures and accompanying details help developers diagnose and resolve bugs efficiently.

evidence.description: Developers confirmed and fixed the four bugs; no measured debugging effort or quantitative resolution time is reported.
evidence.quote:
Development teams have reacted to all these issues
and four of them are confirmed as real bugs and have been
fixed.

claims.quote:
We also noted that several of the confirmed bugs were
fixed shortly after our reports were submitted, suggesting that
test failures and accompanying details provided by JUnitGenie
are useful in helping developers identify and resolve real
bugs efficiently.

Figure 2 illustrates the overall architecture of N ¨UWA, which
comprises three main components: test generation, adaptive
mutation, and a feedback loop.

The N ¨UWA-Gen
variant disables the adaptive mutation module, solely generat-
ing N seeds via the two-phase process, whereas N ¨UWA-Mut
disables the generation module, which produces N seeds by
applying mutations to test suite cases.

hcs.name: Nüwa-Mut
hcs.removed: Two-phase generation module; mutation operates on test-suite cases
hcs.quote:
The N ¨UWA-Gen
variant disables the adaptive mutation module, solely generat-
ing N seeds via the two-phase process, whereas N ¨UWA-Mut
disables the generation module, which produces N seeds by
applying mutations to test suite cases.

hcs.name: Nüwa-direct
hcs.removed: Single-operation generation stage; operation specifications feed direct multi-operation generation
hcs.quote:
In N ¨UWA-
direct variant, we directly generate multi-OP IRs from opera-
tion specifications, bypassing the single-op IR generation step
in the two-phase process.

Additionally, we design three N ¨UWA

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: MLIR commit bab01ae; previously unknown crash bugs
ecs.protocol: RQ1; default 24-hour experiments, five repetitions; error-message deduplication, compilation commands/backtraces, issue reporting and maintainer confirmation/fixes
ecs.quote:
To address RQ1, N ¨UWA is executed to fuzz the latest

claims.text: Nüwa reported 55 crash bugs on the latest MLIR revision; maintainers confirmed 18 and fixed 16.

evidence.detail: Project maintainers confirmed 18 reported bugs, including 16 fixed bugs; remaining reports awaited responses.

claims.quote:
Among the bugs we found, 18/16 have
been confirmed/fixed by project maintainers.

claims.text: In the controlled comparison, Nüwa detected more bugs than MLIRSmith, MLIRod and NNSmith: 56 versus 16, 18 and 26.
claims.quote:
As shown, N ¨UWA detects significantly more bugs
than the other techniques.

claims.text: Nüwa achieved broader input coverage than MLIRSmith, MLIRod and NNSmith: 43 dialects and 734 operations versus 12/172, 21/343 and 23/278.
claims.quote:
Moreover, N ¨UWA
achieves broader coverage by exercising 2.58× and 1.55×
more dialects than MLIRSmith and MLIRod, respectively, as
well as 3.68× and 1.81× more operations.

claims.text: Nüwa reached 83,202 covered source lines, reported as 1.53 times the line coverage of MLIRSmith and MLIRod.

metrics.name: Covered source lines measured with llvm-cov/gcov

claims.quote:
In total, N ¨UWA achieves a final line coverage of
83,202, which is 1.53× higher than that of MLIRSmith and
MLIRod, and a final branch coverage of 49,245, corresponding
to a 1.6× improvement relative to the other techniques.

claims.text: Nüwa reached 49,245 covered branches, reported as a 1.6-fold improvement over the compared techniques.
claims.quote:
In total, N ¨UWA achieves a final line coverage of
83,202, which is 1.53× higher than that of MLIRSmith and
MLIRod, and a final branch coverage of 49,245, corresponding
to a 1.6× improvement relative to the other techniques.

claims.text: Nüwa continued increasing coverage throughout the 24-hour campaign while existing techniques saturated early.

metrics.name: Reported coverage contributions: 86% in the first eight hours and 5%, 3%, 5% in subsequent four-hour windows

claims.quote:
Although existing techniques rapidly reach coverage satura-
tion, N ¨UWA is able to continuously maintain coverage growth
throughout the 24-hour period.

claims.text: The complete system detected more bugs than either module-removal ablation: 56 versus 38 for Nüwa-Gen and 47 for Nüwa-Mut.

metrics.name: Detected bugs within the shared 24-hour budget

claims.quote:
Specifically, compared
to N ¨UWA-Gen and N ¨UWA-Mut, N ¨UWA detects 1.47× and
1.2× more bugs, covers 1.27× and 1.2× more dialects as
well as 1.17× and 1.4× more operations.

claims.text: Combining generation and mutation increased input coverage to 43 dialects and 734 operations, versus 34/625 for generation alone and 36/520 for mutation alone.
claims.quote:
Specifically, compared
to N ¨UWA-Gen and N ¨UWA-Mut, N ¨UWA detects 1.47× and
1.2× more bugs, covers 1.27× and 1.2× more dialects as
well as 1.17× and 1.4× more operations.

claims.text: The complete system maintained higher line and branch coverage growth than either Nüwa-Gen or Nüwa-Mut.
claims.quote:
This demonstrates that N ¨UWA
consistently outperforms N ¨UWA-Mut and N ¨UWA-Gen in terms
of code coverage growth and the efficiency in detecting bugs.

claims.text: Both Nüwa-Gen and Nüwa-Mut exceeded MLIRSmith and MLIRod in bug detection.

metrics.name: Detected bugs: Nüwa-Gen 38, Nüwa-Mut 47; MLIRSmith 16, MLIRod 18

claims.quote:
In particular, from Figure 9, we can see that both N ¨UWA-
Gen and N ¨UWA-Mut significantly surpass MLIRSmith and
MLIRod in terms of code coverage and bug detection capacity.

claims.text: Both module-removal ablations exceeded MLIRSmith and MLIRod in source-code coverage.
claims.quote:
In particular, from Figure 9, we can see that both N ¨UWA-
Gen and N ¨UWA-Mut significantly surpass MLIRSmith and
MLIRod in terms of code coverage and bug detection capacity.

than the two-phase generation algorithm, and it experiences a
multiplicative increase in failures.

accuracy and efficiency of both generation and mutation.

investigated 16 fixed bugs and found that 8 bugs are introduced

drastically affect the reproduction process.

claims.quote:

triggered by other actions that ReActDroid does not support,

system settings (e.g., turning off Bluetooth).

claims.quote:

scenarios.

be biased due to varying degrees of familiarity with the app

claims.text: The paper attributes correctly ordered compound-action interactions to LLM reasoning with exploration history; action-order accuracy is not separately quantified.

ReActDroid effectively performs interactions involved in the
compound action in the proper order.

claims.text: For long exploration sequences or intricate reasoning, common sense alone is claimed insufficient and identified crash-page guidance is pivotal.
claims.quote:
However, for re-
ports that involve long exploration sequences or intricate logical
reasoning for reproduction, it becomes prohibitive for the LLM
to infer the reproduction steps solely based on common sense.

claims.text: ORFuzz achieves the highest mean over-refusal generation rate, 6.98%, versus Direct/Naive 0.40%, external OR-Bench 1.91% and external GPTFuzz 0.58%, beating all three on every target and exceeding twice their mean rates.

evidence.description: Separate OR-Judge evaluation against aggregated human labels supports oracle alignment, but does not independently validate the generated over-refusal cases.
evidence.quote:
This
indicates superior alignment with human consensus in both
continuous and categorical assessments.

claims.quote:
It achieves the highest average Over-Refusal Rate (ORR) of
6.98% across all target LLMs, significantly outperforming the
Naive method (0.40% avg).

claims.text: ORFuzz has competitive semantic diversity: mean MSS 0.308, compared with external OR-Bench 0.263, external GPTFuzz 0.353 and Direct/Naive 0.708; lower MSS is better.
claims.quote:
