average MSS (0.308) is competitive with the OR-Bench
Method (0.263) and notably better than GPTFuzz (0.353)
and Naive (0.708).

claims.text: ORFuzz and all four ablations cover all eight safety categories; the full system has broader category coverage than Direct/Naive (3), external OR-Bench (6) and external GPTFuzz (5).
claims.quote:
All
variants successfully covered all 8 safety categories.

claims.text: The full system has the top mean ORR (6.98%) and highest or second-highest ORR per target; every component removal lowers mean ORR (6.22% without seed sampling, 4.36% without seed selection, 5.11% without mutator selection, 3.16% without refinement in Table IV).

claims.text: ORFuzz produces transferable over-refusal tests; Phi-3.5- and Mistral-v0.3-targeted outputs transfer relatively well to other models, whereas Llama-3.1- and Gemma-2-targeted outputs transfer less well.

claims.quote:
Conversely, samples generated
specifically for Llama-3.1 and Gemma-2 exhibit lower cross-
model transferability.

claims.text: ORFuzzSet's 1,786 selected queries achieve a reported mean ORR of 57.37% across 14 LLMs and outperform XSTest, OR-Bench and COR in the benchmark comparison.

achieves the highest average ORR (57.37%) across all 14
models, significantly outperforming prior benchmarks and
validating its broad effectiveness.

claims.text: ORFuzzSet covers all eight defined safety categories.

results show that ORF UZZ SET covers all 8 safety categories.

claims.text: ORFuzz and ORFuzzSet are presented as a robust framework and useful resource for rigorous over-refusal evaluation; practical deployment or downstream dependability improvement is not evaluated.
claims.quote:
ORF UZZ
and ORF UZZ SET provide a robust automated testing frame-
work and a key resource for enhancing LLM dependability
through rigorous over-refusal assessment.

claims.text: The paper describes Llama-3.1 as having the highest ORR and Phi-3.5 the lowest irrespective of generation method; Table IV contains exceptions, so the universal wording is not supported across all controls.
claims.quote:
This observation suggests varying degrees
of over-conservatism in their safety guardrails and reinforces
the importance of model-specific testing strategies.

claims.text: Target models exhibit different safety-category sensitivities: Gemma-2 is reported as more prone to over-refuse physical/mental-health queries and Llama-3.1 crime/illegal-activity queries.

claims.quote:
This suggests that various LLMs, owing to varia-
tions in training data and safety mechanisms, exhibit distinct
sensitivities to over-refusal samples across safety categories.

claims.text: Increasing Qwen model size does not strictly increase ORFuzzSet ORR: Qwen2.5-7B and 14B both score 70.94%, above 3B's 51.10%.

metrics.name: ORFuzzSet ORR by Qwen parameter size

claims.quote:
Interestingly, within the
Qwen series, over-refusal propensity (on ORF UZZ SET) did
not strictly correlate with model size: Qwen2.5-7B (70.94%
ORR) was comparable to Qwen2.5-14B (also 70.94% ORR)
and notably higher than Qwen2.5-3B (51.10% ORR).

claims.text: Reasoning models o3, o3-mini and o4-mini have lower ORFuzzSet ORR than GPT-4o; the authors suggest reasoning may mitigate over-refusal, without isolating reasoning as the causal factor.

claims.quote:

interesting observation is that reasoning models (e.g., o3, o3-
mini, o4-mini) exhibit lower ORR on ORF UZZ SET compared
to their base counterparts (GPT-4o), suggesting that enhanced
reasoning capabilities may help mitigate over-refusal tenden-
cies.

claims.text: PALM is claimed to consistently have the highest compilation pass rate among RUG, SymPrompt and ChatTester; hashbrown reaches 41.19% versus SymPrompt's 6.63%.
claims.quote:
It consistently achieves
the highest compilation pass rate in this category, while
maintaining a high and stable execution pass rate that is com-
petitive with or superior to other LLM baselines across most
projects.

claims.text: PALM's execution pass rate is competitive with or better than the LLM baselines RUG, SymPrompt and ChatTester across most projects.
claims.quote:
It consistently achieves
the highest compilation pass rate in this category, while
maintaining a high and stable execution pass rate that is com-
petitive with or superior to other LLM baselines across most
projects.

claims.text: PALM substantially exceeds RustyUnit, RuMono, RUG, SymPrompt and ChatTester in coverage across nearly every project; http line coverage is 74.75% versus SymPrompt's 29.07%.
claims.quote:
It substantially surpasses all other baselines,
both classic and LLM-based, across nearly every project.

claims.text: PALM achieves 72.30% mean line coverage versus developer tests' 70.94%, exceeding developer line coverage in roughly half of the crates.
claims.quote:
In
comparison, tests generated by PALM surpassed the line
coverage of the original tests in almost half of the evaluated
projects, achieving an average of 72.30%.

claims.text: PALM averages 69.49% branch coverage versus developer tests' 66.47%, outperforming them in 10 of 15 crates.
claims.quote:
PALM demonstrated higher branch coverage in 10 out
of the 15 crates, further underscoring its practical utility in
software testing workflows.

claims.text: Basic and context-only prompts generally generate fewer tests than condition-chain-only prompts.
claims.quote:
Basic and
context-only prompts generally produced fewer tests than
condition chains-only prompts.

claims.text: Context-only prompts generally improve compilation success over condition-chain-only prompts, with the paper naming indexmap and strsim-rs as exceptions.
claims.quote:
Context-only prompts typically
yielded higher compilation success rates (except on indexmap
and strsim-rs) and better test pass rates (except on once cell
and rand).

claims.text: Context-only prompts generally improve execution pass rates over condition-chain-only prompts, with the paper naming once_cell and rand as exceptions.
claims.quote:
Context-only prompts typically
yielded higher compilation success rates (except on indexmap
and strsim-rs) and better test pass rates (except on once cell
and rand).

claims.text: Coverage generally ranks context-only above condition-chains-only above Basic Prompt, with some Basic Prompt exceptions.
claims.quote:
For code coverage, the general trend was context-
only>condition chains-only>basic prompts, though basic
prompts occasionally surpassed condition chains-only on some
projects.

claims.text: Combining context and condition chains generally gives higher coverage than either alone.
claims.quote:
Notably, prompts combining both context and con-
dition chains generally achieved higher coverage than either
component in isolation.

claims.text: Adding iterative repair improves compilation pass rates for every crate, with relative improvements exceeding 100% in some cases.
claims.quote:
The efficacy of model self-iteration
for repair was evident when comparing configurations with
and without this feature, showing universal improvements in
compilation rates–exceeding 100% in some instances–which
consequently boosted test pass rates and coverage.

claims.text: Adding iterative repair generally boosts execution pass rates.
claims.quote:
The efficacy of model self-iteration
for repair was evident when comparing configurations with
and without this feature, showing universal improvements in
compilation rates–exceeding 100% in some instances–which
consequently boosted test pass rates and coverage.

claims.text: Adding iterative repair improves test-suite coverage.
claims.quote:
The efficacy of model self-iteration
for repair was evident when comparing configurations with
and without this feature, showing universal improvements in
compilation rates–exceeding 100% in some instances–which
consequently boosted test pass rates and coverage.

claims.text: The paper claims full PALM attains the highest compilation rates among all ablations.
claims.quote:
Ultimately,
the full PALM methodology demonstrated superior perfor-
mance, achieving the highest compilation rates and crucially,
attaining the highest coverage across all evaluated projects.

claims.text: Full PALM attains the highest coverage across all evaluated projects among the ablations.
claims.quote:
Ultimately,
the full PALM methodology demonstrated superior perfor-
mance, achieving the highest compilation rates and crucially,
attaining the highest coverage across all evaluated projects.

claims.text: PALM supplies coverage-increasing tests to eight mature projects despite their existing developer tests.
claims.quote:
Despite this high baseline,
PALM successfully generated tests that increased coverage in
8 of these projects.

claims.text: Of 91 selected submitted tests, 80 were accepted and merged, five rejected and six pending: 87.91% merged overall and 94.12% among reviewed tests.

metrics.name: Accepted/merged, rejected and pending test counts
Merge rate among all submitted/reviewed tests (%)

claims.quote:
Of these, 80 were accepted and merged, 5
were rejected, and 6 are currently awaiting developer feedback.

claims.text: PALM's execution success is described as stable across projects.
claims.quote:
It consistently achieves
the highest compilation pass rate in this category, while
maintaining a high and stable execution pass rate that is com-
petitive with or superior to other LLM baselines across most
projects.

claims.text: PALM has lower compilation success than the classic tools RustyUnit and RuMono.
claims.quote:
A noteworthy observation is PALM’s compilation pass rate,
which is lower than that of classic tools like RustyUnit and
RuMono.

claims.text: PALM yields a substantially larger volume of tests than the classic tools RustyUnit and RuMono.
claims.quote:
This ultimately results in a substantial pool of
valid test cases, providing the breadth needed to achieve high
coverage.

claims.text: LLM-generated tests, including PALM's, are shorter and commonly target a single input condition compared with RustyUnit's longer tests.
claims.quote:
The distinct test generation philosophies in-
fluence output characteristics: RustyUnit (SBST) produces
comprehensive, longer unit tests, while LLM-based tools gen-
erate shorter tests, often targeting single input conditions.

claims.text: PALM is included among LLM tools completing generation in roughly two to three hours, contrasting with RuMono's prolonged execution.
claims.quote:
We
observed that, unlike the prolonged execution of RuMono,
LLM-based tools typically complete test generation in 2-
3 hours, varying with project scale and code complexity.

claims.text: Static-analysis targeting together with compilation success lets PALM generate tests for a broader set of project functions.
claims.quote:
PALM’s strategy of integrating static analysis for
comprehensive function targeting, combined with its higher
compilation success rates, allows it to generate tests for a
broader set of functions within a project.

claims.text: Projects where PALM fails to beat developer line coverage are predominantly affected by extensive macro use.

evidence.detail: Authors investigated projects lacking coverage-increasing tests and observed extensive macro use; inspection protocol/counts not_reported.
evidence.quote:
For projects
where PALM did not identify coverage-enhancing tests, our
investigation revealed extensive use of macros, a feature for
which PALM currently lacks specialized handling, thus limit-
ing its effectiveness in these specific contexts.

claims.quote:
Instances where PALM did not
attain superior line coverage were predominantly attributed to
the extensive use of macros within those projects, which posed
challenges for effective test generation.

claims.text: Most developers are receptive to PALM's generated tests when they are meaningful and increase coverage, despite some caution about LLM code.
claims.quote:
Developer interactions during the PR process indicated
that while some expressed caution towards LLM-generated
code, most were receptive, provided the tests were meaningful
and demonstrably increased coverage.

claims.text: Five rejections mainly reflect perceived redundancy or a demand for value beyond coverage gains.
claims.quote:
The 5 rejected tests
were primarily due to developers seeking additional value
beyond mere coverage improvement or perceiving the tests
as redundant.

claims.text: Some generated tests require developer-requested style, description or usage revisions before merging.
claims.quote:
Several tests were merged after incorporating
developer feedback regarding code style, test descriptions, or
usage patterns.

claims.text: An average generated test consumes approximately 1500 input and 300 output tokens.
claims.quote:
On average,
generating a single unit test required approximately 1500
input tokens and 300 output tokens.

claims.text: Each triggered repair round uses about 800 additional tokens on average.

metrics.name: Mean additional tokens per repair round

claims.quote:
When the iterative repair
mechanism was triggered, each repair round consumed an
additional 800 tokens on average.

claims.text: The full 15-project campaign including ablations reportedly consumes about 800 million tokens and costs about $300 for around 65,000 generated tests.
claims.quote:
For the entire evaluation
across all 15 projects, which involved analyzing approximately
40,000 lines of code and generating around 65,000 test cases
(including the full ablation study), the total consumption was
approximately 800 million tokens.

claims.text: PALM can generate tests for a concurrency-primitive function such as wait.
claims.page: p.10, §VI; pp.3,6, motivating example and Fig.4
claims.quote:
For instance, as shown in our motivating example
(Section III), PALM successfully generates tests for func-
tions involving concurrency primitives, which are notoriously
difficult for concolic engines to handle without specialized,
manually-crafted models.

claims.text: A qualitative failure mode is uncompilable tests that misuse Rust language semantics, especially ownership.
claims.quote:
We identified two primary failure pat-
terns: compilation failures due to misunderstanding language-
specific semantics, and path constraint satisfaction failures due
to a lack of causal reasoning.

claims.text: Stateful path constraints can remain unsatisfied because the LLM misses that an earlier API call must modify the state checked later.
claims.quote:
The
LLM often fails here because it cannot infer this non-local,
causal dependency between an action (advance()) and its
future consequence on an internal state check, highlighting a
fundamental gap in reasoning about stateful object lifecycles.

claims.text: PALM's measured costs are judged manageable for academic studies and potentially viable in industrial pipelines when used selectively.
claims.quote:
This analysis demonstrates that while not trivial, the cost is
manageable for comprehensive academic studies and could be
viable for integration into industrial pipelines, especially when
applied selectively to critical or complex code modules.

claims.text: PALM is argued to handle real-world semantic and environmental complexity better than formal constraint-solving approaches.

evidence.detail: Positive feedback on selected contributed tests is invoked as corroboration of semantic capability; no controlled formal-solver comparison is reported.
evidence.quote:
The high compilation
success rates and positive developer feedback (Section V-C)
from our study underscore this unique capability.

claims.quote:
However, PALM’s advantages
emerge precisely where formal methods often falter: in han-
dling thesemantic and environmental complexitiesof real-
world code.

claims.text: Path minimization is claimed to improve scalability by mitigating path explosion.
claims.quote:
It directly mitigates the path
explosion problem, a key limitation of concolic execution,
through its path minimization technique (Section IV-B2).

claims.text: PALM is argued to require less engineering effort than constructing and maintaining a symbolic-execution engine.
claims.quote:
This, combined with a significantlylower engineering over-
headcompared to developing and maintaining a symbolic
execution engine, positions PALM as a more pragmatic and
readily adaptable alternative.

claims.text: PALM increases the ratio of compilable tests by up to 20% and coverage by up to 50%; the comparison reference is not specified.
claims.quote:
Our GPT-4o mini-based proto-
type increased the ratio of correctly generated, compilable
tests by up to 20% and improved coverage by up to 50%.

claims.text: DS3.1 PAGENT generates 86 successful PoCs, with a reported 42.3% success rate, exceeding every evaluated Cybergym agent by at least 53%; reported gains over GPT-5, GPT-4.1, Claude-4 and Claude-3.7 are 53.57%, 309.5%, 56.36% and 126.36%.

metrics.name: PoC success rate and relative improvement

claims.quote:
Compared to GPT-5, GPT-4.1, Claude-4, and Claude-3.7 based
agents, DS3.1 based PAGENT showcases 53.57%, 309.5% 56.36%, 126.36% improvement respectively.

claims.text: DS3.2 PAGENT generates 130 successful PoCs, with a separately reported 64.6% success rate; it exceeds all evaluated Cybergym agents by at least 132% and also exceeds reimplemented PoCGen and Faultline, which generate 68 and 56 PoCs.

metrics.name: PoC success rate and relative improvement

claims.quote:
The DeepSeek3.2-based PAGENT further outperforms all cybergym agent baselines by at least
132%.

claims.text: Static-analysis guidance increases PoC success for both models: SA-only versus no guidance is 33.9% versus 14.6% for DS3.1 and 45.1% versus 28.6% for DS3.2, with reported relative gains of 132.9% and 57.69%; adding SA to DA-only also increases success.

metrics.name: Relative success improvement from static analysis

claims.quote:
Specifically, the static
analysis component provides improvements of 132.9% and 57.69% over the non-guided variant
across both DS3.1 and DS3.2 models, respectively.

claims.text: Dynamic-analysis guidance increases PoC success for both models: DA-only versus no guidance is 28.7% versus 14.6% for DS3.1 and 36.7% versus 28.6% for DS3.2; full versus SA-only is 42.3% versus 33.9% and 64.6% versus 45.1%, while the prose reports approximately 25% and 42% fewer PoCs when DA is removed.

metrics.name: Reported relative reduction after removing dynamic analysis

claims.quote:
Removing the dynamic analysis component from
PAGENT reduces the number of PoCs found by approximately 25% and 42% across both DS3.1 and
DS3.2 models, respectively.

claims.text: Static and dynamic analysis are claimed to contribute almost equally to PAGENT's PoC success.

metrics.name: PoC success rates across guidance ablations

claims.quote:
Figure 7 demonstrates that both the static and dynamic analysis components
almost equally improve the PoC generation success rate of the PAGENT.

claims.text: DS3.1 PAGENT generates 23 exclusive PoCs, exceeding every plotted single Cybergym agent or combination of the top three agents.
claims.quote:
Notice that the number of PoCs generated by
PAGENT with Deepseek3.1 alone exceeds that of any combination of the top-3 cybergym agents.

claims.text: DS3.2 PAGENT generates 40 exclusive PoCs, claimed to be at least twice the success of the other plotted agents or their combinations in the exclusive-PoC analysis.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, the PAGENT
approach with DeepSeek-3.2 achieves twice the PoC generation success rate as other agents or
their combinations.

claims.text: PAGENT produces 20 post-patch crashing PoCs with DS3.1 and 32 with DS3.2, compared with 7–8 for the plotted baseline agents; the DS3.2 result is presented as a fourfold improvement over the best baseline.

metrics.name: PoCs still crashing patched program versions

claims.quote:
PAGENT generates
almost 3 times as many post-patch PoCs as any other baseline agent.

claims.text: PAGENT is claimed to be scalable for automated PoC generation; the evaluation spans ten projects with reported sizes of approximately 66K–3762K lines of code, without a reported scaling-time or resource-consumption study.
claims.quote:
In this paper, we present a novel approach calledProgram Analysis Guided proof of concept
generation agENT (PAGENT)that is scalable and significantly improves the success rate of automated
PoC generation compared to prior results.

claims.text: The DeepSeek models used by PAGENT have a cited output-token API price of $0.42 per million tokens versus $14 for GPT-5/Sonnet-4, presented as approximately 32–33 times cheaper per output token.

metrics.name: API price per million output tokens

claims.quote:
For example,
the cost of output tokens for the API access with DeepSeek is almost 33 times (0.42$ vs 14.00$ per
million tokens) lower than closed-sourced LLMs such as GPT-5, Sonnet-4.

claims.text: PSearch with GPT-3.5 and 32 candidates repairs 201/835 Defects4J bugs (106 v1.2, 95 v2), exceeding all 12 APR comparators and D4C by 21 overall.
claims.quote:
On the Defects4J dataset,PSearchobtains the highest 201 bug-
fixes, fixing 21 more bugs than the second-place D4C.

claims.text: PSearch obtains 280 plausible Defects4J fixes at 32 candidates, 70 more than D4C.
claims.quote:
Specifically,PSearchobtains a total of 280
plausible fixes, 70 more plausible fixes than that of D4C.

claims.text: PSearch repairs all 40 Java QuixBugs bugs, reported for GPT-3.5 at 16/32 candidates and GPT-4o-mini at 16.
claims.quote:
The results show thatPSearchis capable of
fixing all the bugs in QuixBugs.

claims.text: At 16 candidates, PSearch improves correct repairs over vanilla for all seven backbones; GPT-3.5 rises 132→159 and GPT-4o-mini 128→158.
claims.quote:
Results show that the repair capabilities of all seven LLMs
generally improve after applyingPSearch.

claims.text: PSearch is particularly advantageous for complex single-function bugs: gains include +12 GPT-4o-mini, +8 GPT-3.5, +14 Yi-Coder-9B, +8 Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and +4 Qwen2.5-Coder-3B.
claims.quote:
It
indicates thatPSearchhas a particular advantage in fixing complex
bugs.

claims.text: Supplying test information improves correct repairs for all seven LLM-only controls by 8–21 bugs.
claims.quote:
The results
show that test information consistently improves the effectiveness
of all seven evaluated LLMs.

claims.text: CoT improves correct fixes for six of seven models versus vanilla in Table 5; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B is unchanged there but improves 79→99 in Table 6.
claims.quote:
Compared with
Vanilla prompting, most LLMs achieve better repair performance
with CoT.

claims.text: CoT increases plausible fixes over vanilla by 32 for Yi-Coder-9B and 10 for GPT-3.5.
claims.quote:
Yi-Coder-9B and GPT-3.5 show the largest gains, with CF
improving by 31 and 7, and PF improving by 32 and 10, respectively.

claims.text: ToT has inconsistent effects versus vanilla, reducing correct fixes by 7 for GPT-4o-mini, 19 for Llama-3.1-8B and 2 for Stable-Code-3B.
claims.quote:
In contrast, ToT does not consistently improve performance and
even reduces CF for GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Stable-Code-
3B by 7, 19, and 2, respectively.

claims.text: CoT outperforms ToT on most evaluated models.
claims.quote:
Overall, CoT outperforms ToT on
most evaluated LLMs.

claims.text: At 16 candidates, PSearch's combined search/evaluation improves all seven models over CoT; gains include +20 GPT-3.5, +27 GPT-4o-mini and +6 Yi-Coder-9B.
claims.quote:
In particular, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o-mini, and Yi-Coder-9B withPSearch
fix 20, 27, and 6 more bugs than their CoT counterparts, respectively.

claims.text: Stronger models are claimed to assess patch quality more accurately and guide search better; reported evidence measures repaired bugs rather than evaluator accuracy.
claims.quote:
This suggests that stronger models can provide more
accurate patch evaluation, which in turn guides the search more
effectively.

claims.text: For Qwen2.5-Coder-3B and Llama-3.1-8B, PSearch becomes more competitive with CoT as patch size grows, eventually surpassing it.
claims.quote:
For Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-
Coder-3B,PSearchis initially comparable to or slightly worse
than CoT at small patch sizes, but gradually matches and then sur-
passes CoT as the patch size grows.

claims.text: Increasing GPT-3.5 PSearch's patch budget 16→32 yields 42 additional correct fixes, 159→201.
claims.quote:
When the patch size increases to 32, GPT-3.5 withPSearchfixes
42 additional bugs.

claims.text: Increasing GPT-3.5 PSearch's patch budget 32→500 yields 11 additional correct fixes.
claims.quote:
It can be observed that a
larger patch size (500) leads to more plausible fixes (16) and correct
fixes (11).

claims.text: Increasing GPT-3.5 PSearch's patch budget 32→500 yields 16 additional plausible fixes.
claims.quote:
It can be observed that a
larger patch size (500) leads to more plausible fixes (16) and correct
fixes (11).

claims.text: At 48 candidates PSearch achieves 204 ConDefects correct fixes; prose claims +39 over ChatRepair, but Table 8 gives ChatRepair 241 and vanilla GPT-3.5 165.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 8, when patch size = 48 (16 iterations,
3 patches per iteration),PSearchobtains 211 plausible fixes and 204
correct fixes, which is 40 more plausible fixes and 39 more correct
fixes than ChatRepair.

claims.text: At 48 candidates PSearch achieves 211 ConDefects plausible fixes; prose claims +40 over ChatRepair, but Table 8 gives ChatRepair 249 and vanilla GPT-3.5 171.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 8, when patch size = 48 (16 iterations,
3 patches per iteration),PSearchobtains 211 plausible fixes and 204
correct fixes, which is 40 more plausible fixes and 39 more correct
fixes than ChatRepair.

claims.text: At 96 candidates PSearch reaches 264 ConDefects correct fixes, 23 above ChatRepair and 60 above PSearch at 48 candidates.
claims.quote:
When we increase search iteration to 32 and set patch size
to 96, we find that the performance ofPSearchis further enhanced,
with 287 plausible fixes and 264 correct fixes, which surpasses
ChatRepair by 23/38 correct/plausible fixes.

claims.text: At 96 candidates PSearch reaches 287 ConDefects plausible fixes, 38 above ChatRepair and 76 above PSearch at 48 candidates.
claims.quote:
When we increase search iteration to 32 and set patch size
to 96, we find that the performance ofPSearchis further enhanced,
with 287 plausible fixes and 264 correct fixes, which surpasses
ChatRepair by 23/38 correct/plausible fixes.

claims.text: Test-as-Judge is claimed to improve patch-search efficiency by guiding refinement from simple to complex tests; a corresponding search-efficiency control measurement is not_reported.
claims.quote:
Compared to allowing the model to search patches without
evaluation, Test-as-Judge guides LLMs in the right direction for
repairs, improving the efficiency of patch search.

claims.text: With perfect localization, PSearch resolves 164/300 SWE-Bench-Lite issues, 54.67%, +51 versus vanilla and +35 versus ChatRepair; it exceeds KGCompass/OpenHands and ranks behind Refact.ai Agent/SWE-agent.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table 9, compared with vanilla
LLMs,PSearchhelps Qwen3-Coder-480B fix 51 more bugs.

claims.text: PSearch demonstrates repair capability across the evaluated Java/Python and repository/competition bug settings.
claims.quote:
The above experimental results demonstrate thatPSearchhas
significant advantages over previous methods and vanilla LLMs in
repairing bugs across multiple languages (Java/Python) and multi-
ple types (Repository/Competition).

claims.text: PSearch repairs 27/79 VUL4J vulnerabilities, 34.17%, exceeding all reported comparators and ChatRepair by 12.
claims.quote:
When using the same
base model (GPT-3.5),PSearchfixes 12 more vulnerabilities than
ChatRepair, demonstrating its superiority in vulnerability repair.

claims.text: PSearch costs $0.03/bug at 16 candidates and $0.06 at 32, versus $0.14 for ChatRepair/RepairAgent at the paper's comparison prices; the 32-candidate cost is 43% of either comparator.
claims.quote:
The cost ofPSearchis $0.06 per bug, which
is 43% of ChatRepair ($0.14) and RepairAgent ($0.14).

claims.text: PSearch is claimed to be faster than existing APR tools; at 32 candidates it reports 50 min/bug versus ChatRepair's ≤5 h, but Table 11 also gives RepairAgent only 920 s.
claims.quote:
With the patch size set to 32, which is the smallest among
all three baselines,PSearchspends an average of 50 minutes per
bug, shorter than that of ChatRepair.

claims.text: PSearch uses 20,000 tokens/bug at 16 candidates and 40,000 at 32; the latter is 19% of ChatRepair's 210,000 and 14.8% of RepairAgent's 270,000.
claims.quote:
Moreover,PSearchalso has
a significant advantage in terms of the average number of tokens
spent and monetary cost per bug, which is only 19% of the 210,000
tokens reported by ChatRepair and 14.8% of the 270,000 tokens
reported by RepairAgent.

claims.text: PSearch uses 16 or 32 candidates per Defects4J bug versus ChatRepair's 500 and RepairAgent's 117.
claims.quote: Table 11: Cost analysis on Defects4J.

claims.text: On Defects4J-v1.2, 32-candidate PSearch fixes eight fewer bugs than ChatRepair, while testing far fewer candidates.
claims.quote:
AlthoughPSearchfixes 8 fewer bugs than ChatRepair on Defects4J-
v1.2, it is acceptable given the differencesof patch size setting.

claims.text: The five compared methods show broadly consistent project-level repair distributions.
claims.quote:
When comparing
PSearchagainst baseline methods, we find that the bug-fix distri-
bution among the five methods shows considerable consistency.

claims.text: Prose claims PSearch beats all four selected comparators on Compress, JacksonDatabind and Jsoup, although Table 2 gives JacksonDatabind PSearch 18 versus D4C 24.
claims.quote:
PSearchsignificantly outperforms the other four baselines on Com-
press, JacksonDataBind, and Jsoup.

claims.text: PSearch uniquely fixes 10 Defects4J-v1.2 and 12 v2 bugs missed by D4C, GiantRepair, ChatRepair and RepairAgent.
claims.quote:
In particular,PSearchuniquely fixes 10 bugs on
Defects4J-v1.2 and 12 bugs on Defects4J-v2 that are not repaired
by any of the other four methods, demonstrating thatPSearchcan
substantially complement existing repair approaches.

claims.text: PSearch and the four selected comparators share 20 repaired v1.2 bugs and 13 repaired v2 bugs, suggesting overlapping repair patterns.
claims.quote:
Meanwhile,
the five methods still share a non-trivial overlap, with 20 commonly
fixed bugs on Defects4J-v1.2 and 13 on Defects4J-v2, indicating
that they capture some common repair patterns while retaining
different strengths.

claims.text: PSearch also repairs Gson_15 and Lang_16, previously described as ChatRepair-specific fixes.
claims.quote:
PSearchcan fix both Gson_15
and Lang_16 which ChatRepair [41] mentions as unique fixes.

claims.text: PSearch repairs the multi-location function-level bug Cli_19, which the compared baselines cannot fix.
claims.quote:
Instead, fixing this bug requires modifying the function in multiple
places, thus bringing much difficulty to APR and no baselines can
fix it.

claims.text: The generated Cli_19 patch differs textually from the developer patch but is semantically equivalent.
claims.quote:
As shown in Figure 3,PSearcharrives at a correct patch that is
different from the developer patch but semantically equivalent.

claims.text: Repair success is claimed higher for single-line and single-hunk bugs than single-function bugs; Table 3 reports counts without subtype denominators.
claims.quote:
In terms of buggy types, the success rate for fixing single-line
(SL) and single-hunk (SH) bugs is significantly higher than that for
single-function (SF) bugs.

claims.text: GPT-3.5 PSearch with 32 candidates fixes 69 more Defects4J bugs than vanilla GPT-3.5 with 16 candidates, 201 versus 132.
claims.quote:
Moreover, with the patch size set to 32,
GPT-3.5 (PSearch) can fix 201 bugs, which is 69 more bug-fixes
than vanilla GPT-3.5.

claims.text: Four repaired VUL4J vulnerabilities require changes across multiple methods.
claims.quote:
PSearchsuccessfully fixes a total of 27 vulnerabilities, including
4 multi-method vulnerabilities, surpassing all baseline methods,
achieving a repair success rate of 34.17%.

claims.text: Diminishing additional repairs at 500 candidates are interpreted as PSearch approaching its repair ceiling.
claims.quote:
This indicates thatPSearchhas
already approached its upper limit.

claims.text: The motivational Jsoup_54 experiment succeeds after eight PSearch attempts, whereas direct sampling, single-path iteration and genetic search fail under the stated limited budget.
claims.quote: After eight attempts, the model successfully fixes Jsoup_54.

claims.text: The authors report no strong evidence of data leakage from training-data, benchmark-origin and generated/developer-patch overlap checks, while acknowledging contamination remains possible.
claims.quote:
Although
we do not observe strong evidence of leakage, we cannot fully rule
out subtle contamination due to the scale of modern pretraining
corpora.

claims.text: For GPT-4o-mini and GPT-3.5 at 16 candidates, 90% (27/30) and 74% (20/27) of PSearch's improvement over vanilla is attributable to search and evaluation, i.e. the gain over CoT.

hcs.name: RAT: hybrid retrieval-augmented and RFC-based CRL differential testing
hcs.quote: Building on these foundations, RAT integrates LLM-driven retrieval, intelligently guided test case generation, and cross-implementation differential testing to expose concealed parsing and validation inconsistencies.

claims.text: End-to-end identification and updating achieves 60.16% update accuracy, exceeding KNN (8.51%), NMT (19.83%) and CEPROT (31.62%), with reported relative gains of 607%, 203% and 90%.

evidence.description: Reference-code similarity also favors ReAccept; CodeBLEU is a distinct comparison procedure but does not establish executable correctness.
evidence.quote:
Regarding the
CodeBLUE metric, ReAccept also outperforms other approaches with a score of 82.03%.

claims.quote:
ReAccept achieves
an update accuracy of 60.16% on correctly identifying the obsolete test code, surpassing KNN’s
8.51%, NMT’s 19.83%, and CEPROT’s 31.62% by 607%, 203%, and 90%, respectively.

claims.text: ReAccept obtains 82.03% CodeBLEU, above KNN (37.63%), NMT (32.35%) and CEPROT (63.11%); the paper reports relative improvements of 118.7%, 154.4% and 30.4%.
claims.quote:
Regarding the
CodeBLUE metric, ReAccept also outperforms other approaches with a score of 82.03%.

claims.text: Identification achieves 98.13% accuracy, positive precision/recall/F1 of 95.57/96.49/96.01%, and negative precision/recall/F1 of 98.92/98.63/98.77%; it outperforms RG, KNN, NMT and SITAR, marginally exceeds CHOSEN, and is comparable to CEPROT.
claims.quote:
It can be observed that ReAccept signifi-
cantly outperforms RG, KNN, NMT, and SITAR, marginally outperforms CHOSEN, and shows
comparable performance to CEPROT.

claims.text: The RQ1 narrative states that ReAccept identifies more obsolete tests than KNN, NMT and CHOSEN; Table 4 instead gives CHOSEN slightly higher positive recall (96.69% versus 96.49%).
claims.quote:
Specifically, in the identification phase, ReAccept identifies more obsolete test code compared
to KNN, NMT, and CHOSEN classifiers.

claims.text: The RQ1 narrative states that CEPROT surpasses ReAccept in obsolete-test identification, without specifying the identification metric for that comparison.
claims.quote:
Although CEPROT surpasses ReAccept in the obsolete
test identification phase, ReAccept demonstrates significantly better performance in the obsolete
test update phase, ultimately securing a notable overall advantage.

claims.text: ReAccept's updated tests compile at 85.44%, above the strongest external baseline CEPROT at 49.52%.
claims.quote:
The CSR ofReAccept is 85.44%, which is
substantially higher than the best baseline’s 49.52%.

claims.text: ReAccept's updated tests pass at 74.76%, above KNN (31.07%), NMT (24.27%) and CEPROT (39.82%).
claims.quote:
We can observe thatReAccept significantly
outperforms all the baselines, in terms of all three metrics.

claims.text: ReAccept successfully updates tests that run, pass and cover changed production statements in 71.84% of cases, versus KNN 7.77%, NMT 22.33% and CEPROT 35.92%; reported gains are 825%, 222% and 100%.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, the updated test code generated
by ReAccept have a 71.84% chance of covering the updated product code, considerably higher than
the best baseline’s 35.92%.

claims.text: Most ReAccept-generated updates are claimed to appropriately validate production-code changes, beyond being syntactically correct.
claims.quote:
These results indicate that most of the test code generated by ReAccept
are not only syntactically correct but also appropriately validate the production code changes,
while existing techniques struggle to effectively update the test code.

claims.text: Model choice affects compilation: CSR is 76.70% for GPT-3.5, 85.44% for GPT-4 preview, 83.50% for GPT-4 turbo and 82.52% for GPT-4o; GPT-4 preview exceeds GPT-3.5 by 8.74 percentage points.

claims.quote:

claims.quote:

and 13.59% over gpt-3.5-turbo-0125.

Overall, these results
demonstrate that both scrolling and expansion are complementary: neither alone is sufficient, and

claims.text: ReFLAIR maintained consistent effectiveness on the 36-webpage, 28-domain extended dataset: 84.62% precision and 93.32% recall, respectively 4.13 percentage points higher and 1.99 points lower than on Dp.

Recall across primary and extended datasets

claims.quote:
ReFLAIR
maintains robust performance with precision increased by 4.13% and recall decreased by 1.99%,
indicating consistent effectiveness across diverse domains.

claims.text: Token and monetary costs increased modestly on De, supporting practical cost scalability: 603K tokens and $1.27 per webpage, both reported as 1.07 times Dp, while mean widget count increased by 1.20 times.

The
average token usage is 603K, corresponding to 1.07x of the 562K tokens required for𝐷𝑝, with a
per-page cost of $1.27, representing 1.07x of the $1.18 cost per page for𝐷𝑝.

claims.text: Runtime remained practically scalable on the more complex De pages, averaging 4.54 hours per webpage versus 3.23 hours on Dp, a reported 1.41-fold increase.
claims.quote:
In comparison, the sequential runtime under the same configuration
for𝐷𝑝 is 3.23 hours, corresponding to an increase by a factor of 1.41x due to complex pages.

claims.text: Similar informative-widget, actionable-widget and overall scores supported robustness across the two semantic widget roles.

These results closely
align with the overall performance and further validate the robustness of our approach.

claims.text: Prompt engineering improved the direct GPT-4.1 control's precision from 6.67% for Base to 57.82% for PE.
claims.quote:
Through prompt engineering strategy (i.e., GPT-4.1-PE), we found that the LLM’s effectiveness
in detecting reflow issues improved significantly.

claims.text: Prompt engineering improved the direct GPT-4.1 control's recall from 0.47% for Base to 39.91% for PE.
claims.quote:
Through prompt engineering strategy (i.e., GPT-4.1-PE), we found that the LLM’s effectiveness
in detecting reflow issues improved significantly.

claims.text: The direct GPT-4.1 controls demonstrated knowledge of reflow concepts despite their weak detection performance.
claims.quote:
During our evaluation of two GPT-4.1-related baselines (i.e., GPT-4.1-Base and GPT-4.1-PE), we
observed that GPT-4.1 possesses knowledge of reflow concepts.

claims.text: GPT-4.1-Base often gave overly optimistic assessments claiming no reflow issues despite observable information or functionality loss.
claims.quote:
The reflowed
(mobile) version of the webpage is well-implemented, with no reflow issues.

claims.text: ReFLAIR detected the Mailinator reflow issue illustrated by missing FAQ and API navigation options.
claims.quote:
For instance, consider the reflow issues affecting the Mailinator website, illustrated
in Fig. 1.

claims.text: ReFLAIR detected the disappearance of ESPN's social-media follow panel after reflow.
claims.quote:
Similarly,ReFLAIRdetected issues with the social media follow panel on the ESPN website,
shown in Fig. 7.

claims.text: ReFLAIR detected the NIH content-presentation issue in which an informative mouse-brain image disappeared after reflow.
claims.quote:
ReFLAIRalso successfully identified content presentation issues, as demon-
strated in Fig. 8.

claims.text: Insufficient multi-step exploration can prevent ReFLAIR from revealing widgets hidden behind nested menus, as illustrated by USGS and ESPN.
claims.quote:
First, insufficient exploration can miss information that requires multi-step
interactions, causingReFLAIRto fail in revealing the corresponding widgets on the reflowed page.

claims.text: Magnetic snapping in carousels can cause false reflow alarms when temporarily exposed text disappears after the gesture ends.
claims.quote:
Second, false alarms may arise in scenarios where sliding windows employ magnetic snapping
behavior.

claims.text: Automatically moving banners can cause timing-dependent false alarms when an existing logo is temporarily outside the visible region.
claims.quote:
In that case, the system
fails to find the Sony logo and incorrectly reports it as a reflow issue, even though the logo is
present but temporarily out of view.

claims.text: Token usage varied substantially and was skewed by expensive webpages: total tokens had mean 561,590, median 252,294, minimum 13,557 and maximum 2,682,072.

metrics.name: Total tokens per webpage: mean, median, minimum and maximum

claims.quote: The statistics in Table 3 show that token usage per subject varies considerably.

claims.text: Prompt tokens dominated computational cost, averaging 552,514 tokens versus 9,076 completion tokens per webpage.
claims.quote:
Overall, the results indicate that prompt tokens account for the
majority of the cost, whereas completion tokens contribute only marginally.

claims.text: Widget and functionality extraction were the runtime bottleneck, consuming 73.19% of runtime; exploration consumed 23.39%, and widget matching only 3.43%.
claims.quote:
Widget extraction and functionality extraction dominate the overall execution time, consuming
73.19% of the total runtime when considering both the original page (41.50%, 4,819s) and reflow page
(31.69%, 3,679s) processing stages.

claims.text: Complex booking webpages were cost outliers: booking.com exceeded 2.6 million tokens in a run, and booking-platform processing was reported to cost approximately $4.99 averaged across three runs.

metrics.name: Mean API cost across three runs

claims.quote:
The substantial difference between the median ($0.54) and mean
($1.18) indicates that the average cost is skewed by computationally intensive webpages, such as
booking platforms, which require approximately $4.99 on average across three experimental runs.

claims.text: The supplementary lazy-loading inspection found successful Stage 1 extraction of four sampled widgets; the fifth sampled widget was outside scope because it was a non-actionable image without alternative text.

The implemented mechanisms therefore
cover most responsive patterns observed.

claims.text: ReFLAIR remained effective with Gemini-3-Pro on Dxconf: precision and recall were both 94.85%, compared with GPT-4.1's 96.20% precision and 91.24% recall.
claims.quote:
Specifically, Gemini-3-Pro achieved a precision of 94.85% and a recall of 94.85%, which
corresponds to a marginal decrease of 1.35% in precision and a slight increase of 3.61% in recall.

claims.text: ReFLAIR maintained strong effectiveness at the tablet viewport, achieving 92.50% precision and 91.36% recall, supporting adaptability beyond the default 320-CSS-pixel layout.
claims.quote:
These results provide evidence thatReFLAIRmaintains strong performance
beyond the 320-CSS-pixel layout and does not overfit to that specific viewport configuration.

claims.text: The authors estimated that parallelizing original/reflow extraction and scrolling/expansion could reduce mean runtime from 3.23 hours to 7,333 seconds, or 2.04 hours; this was a projection from component timings.

metrics.name: Parallel runtime estimated from measured sequential component times

claims.quote:
With this strategy, the average
runtime decreases to 7,333 seconds (2.04 hours).

claims.text: The authors projected that finer-grained parallelization could reduce runtime by 79.82% to approximately 39.05 minutes; no evaluated parallel harness configuration was reported.

metrics.name: Projected runtime reduction from component-level timing analysis

claims.quote:
With full parallelization, however, 79.82% of the
runtime could be reduced, cutting the total processing time to approximately 39.05 minutes.

claims.text: RTED has the highest accuracy: 0.70 on BugsInPy versus CHATTESTER's 0.50, and 0.67 on TypeBugs versus SymPrompt's 0.50, reported improvements of 40% and 34%.

RTED outperforms both static and
dynamic baselines in detecting Python type errors,
achieving the highest precision, recall, F1-score, and
accuracy across two benchmarks.

claims.text: RTED reaches F1=0.61 on both benchmarks, exceeding the best external baselines, CHATTESTER=0.17 on BugsInPy and HITS=0.33 on TypeBugs.

dynamic baselines in detecting Python type errors,
achieving the highest precision, recall, F1-score, and
accuracy across two benchmarks.

claims.quote:
Moreover, to
detect those bugs, Pyinder, CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, and
HITS produces 21, 19, 14, 35 false positives respectively,
whileRTED only produces 13 false positives, achieving an
improvement of 173.9%∼245.9% in precision.

claims.text: RTED detects 34 benchmarked type errors versus Pyinder=5, CHATTESTER=7, SymPrompt=3 and HITS=12, with highest recall at 0.50/0.54; the abstract/conclusion summarize its advantage as 22–29 additional bugs.
claims.quote:
From the figure,RTED successfully detects 34
bugs, while Pyinder, CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, and HITS
detect only 5, 7, 3, and 12 bugs, respectively.

claims.text: RTED produces 13 false positives, fewer than Pyinder=21, CHATTESTER=19, SymPrompt=14 and HITS=35.

detect those bugs, Pyinder, CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, and
HITS produces 21, 19, 14, 35 false positives respectively,
whileRTED only produces 13 false positives, achieving an
improvement of 173.9%∼245.9% in precision.

hcs.name: ReinFix (ReinFixDP): agentic program repair with dependency-based internal search and root-cause-aware external retrieval
hcs.quote:
To coordinate these processes,
we implement our approach on the basis of the Reasoning and Act-
ing framework [52], empowering the LLM to autonomously plan,
analyze, and invoke the appropriate repair ingredients search tools
as needed.

hcs.name: ReinFixNN: neither ingredient search
hcs.removed: Both internal ingredient search and external ingredient search removed
hcs.quote:
We removed two key components from
the original ReinFix implementation to establish a basic baseline
that represents the fundamental repair capabilities of ChatGPT.

hcs.name: ReinFixDN: dependency-based internal search only
hcs.removed: External pattern-matching ingredient search removed
hcs.quote:
Only the internal ingredient
search component is used for contextual code search, assisting
LLMs in better analyzing the root cause of the bugs.

hcs.name: ReinFixNP: root-cause-aware external search only
hcs.removed: Dependency-based internal ingredient search removed
hcs.quote:
Only the external ingredient search component is
used for bug pattern retrieval, assisting LLMs in better identifying
repair behaviors to generate patches.

hcs.name: ReinFixFP: FitRepair-style internal retrieval plus ReinFix external retrieval
hcs.removed: Dependency-based internal search replaced by FitRepair's similarity-based identifier retrieval
hcs.quote:
The original internal ingredient search com-
ponent of ReinFix is replaced with FitRepair’s repair ingredient
retrieval scheme to observe the impact of using different contex-
tual code search strategies on the repair results.

hcs.name: ReinFixDR: ReinFix internal search plus RAP-Gen-style external retrieval
hcs.removed: Root-cause-aware external retrieval replaced by RAP-Gen's code-similarity retrieval
hcs.quote:
To explore the advantages of ReinFix’s pattern-matching-based
external ingredient search approach over the retrieval schemes
used in recent work [42], we replaced ReinFix’s original external
ingredients search component with RAP-Gen’s repair ingredient
retrieval scheme.

Project counts: Chart 11, Cli 8, Closure 27, Codec 9, Collections 1, Compress 10, Csv 6, Gson 3, JacksonCore 5, Jacksondatabind 11, JacksonXml 1, Jsoup 18, JxPath 0, Lang 17, Math 29, Mockito 6, Time 2.
claims.quote:
RepairAgent generates
correct ﬁxes for 164 bugs, where 116 are exactly as ﬁxed
by the developers and 48 are semantically consistent
with the developer-provided patches.

claims.text: RepairAgent produces 186 test-passing plausible fixes: v1.2/v2 counts 96/90; project counts Chart 14, Cli 9, Closure 27, Codec 10, Collections 1, Compress 10, Csv 6, Gson 3, JacksonCore 5, Jacksondatabind 18, JacksonXml 1, Jsoup 18, JxPath 0, Lang 17, Math 29, Mockito 6, Time 3.

The approach generates plausible ﬁxes for
186 bugs.

claims.text: Correct Defects4J repairs comprise 115 single-line, 46 multi-line/single-file and 3 multi-file bugs, demonstrating repair of 49 bugs requiring more than one line.
claims.quote:
Speciﬁcally, as shown in Table IV,
the approach ﬁxes 115 single-line bugs, 46 multi-line
(single-ﬁle) bugs, and 3 multi-ﬁle bugs.

claims.text: RepairAgent's 164 correct repairs are comparable to ChatRepair's 162, and exceed ITER's 57 and SelfAPR's 110.
claims.quote:
RepairAgent achieves a comparable record by ﬁxing
a total of 164 bugs.

claims.text: RepairAgent repairs 90 Defects4J-v2 bugs versus ChatRepair's 48.
claims.quote:
Our work particularly excels in
Defects4Jv2, where RepairAgent ﬁxes 90 bugs, while
ChatRepair only ﬁxes 48 bugs.

claims.text: RepairAgent repairs 39 bugs unrepaired by ChatRepair, ITER or SelfAPR: 18 single-line, 20 multi-line and one multi-file.

metrics.name: Correct repairs unique relative to the three baselines

claims.quote:
In particular, RepairAgent ﬁxes 39 bugs
that were not ﬁxed by any of the three baselines.

claims.text: RepairAgent outperforms ChatRepair, ITER and SelfAPR on repairs requiring more than one line; its multi-line count is 46 versus 29, 14 and 24, respectively.

of the bug ﬁxes, as shown on the right-hand side of
Table IV, RepairAgent particularly outperforms other
tools for bugs that require more than a single-line ﬁx.

can generalize to code bases of multiple domains.

claims.text: RFCAUDIT finds 47 unique bugs: 40 new and 7 previously reported; Babel/BFD/NHRP/RIPng/DHCP/IGMP contribute 10/14/10/2/4/7.

evidence.detail: 20 of 47 unique bugs confirmed or patches approved/merged; subset corroboration, not all reports.
evidence.quote:
To date, 20 out of 47
unique bugs have been confirmed or their patches have been
approved or merged by the developers.

claims.quote:
Grouping
related bug reports, we uncovered 47 unique bugs, including
40 new bugs and 7 already reported ones.

claims.text: Manual review finds 68 true-positive reports among 83, giving 81.9% precision; per-protocol precision is 75.0/93.3/83.3/66.7/66.7/80.0%.

evidence.detail: 20 of 47 unique bugs confirmed or patches approved/merged; subset corroboration, not all reports.
evidence.quote:
To date, 20 out of 47
unique bugs have been confirmed or their patches have been
approved or merged by the developers.

claims.quote:
As shown in Table II, RFCAUDITgenerates a total
of 83 bug reports across six protocols, of which 68 are true
positives, yielding an overall precision of 81.9%.

claims.text: Detected bugs span seven semantic categories: State 15, Parsing 11, Routing 7, Timer 7, Config 3, Err Handle 2 and Demultiplex 2.
claims.quote:
To better understand the diversity
of functional bugs detected by RFCAUDIT, we categorize
the 47 unique bugs into seven categories, namelyParsing,
Config,Routing,Err Handle,State,Timer, andDemultiplex.

claims.text: On 131 sampled properties, retrieval raises function recall from 71.3% to 95.1%; final type and macro recall are 77.8% and 75.0%, versus 0.0% initially.
claims.quote:
More
importantly, recall improves significantly—95.1% (136 of 143)
for functions, 77.8% (7 of 9) for types, and 75.0% (6 of 8)
for macros—with only one bug missed overall, caused by
code misinterpretation rather than missing context.

claims.text: Final retrieval precision is 56.0% for functions, 87.5% for types and 100.0% for macros; function precision was 59.3% after localization.
claims.quote:
After theretrieval
stage, precision is 56.0% for functions (136 of 243), 87.5%
for types (7 of 8), and 100.0% for macros (7 of 7).

claims.text: Table III reports function F1 improving from 65.6% to 70.5%, with final type F1 82.4% and macro F1 100.0%; the latter is inconsistent with the reported 75.0% macro recall.
claims.quote:
Table III reports the context retrieval accuracy
across protocols.

claims.text: Only one bug is missed in the sampled retrieval assessment, attributed to code misinterpretation rather than missing context.

metrics.name: bugs missed because of incomplete context

claims.quote:
More
importantly, recall improves significantly—95.1% (136 of 143)
for functions, 77.8% (7 of 9) for types, and 75.0% (6 of 8)
for macros—with only one bug missed overall, caused by
code misinterpretation rather than missing context.

claims.text: RFCAUDIT finds more unique bugs than Copilot with Claude 3.7, Claude 3.5 or GPT-4o: 47 versus 37, 26 and 16; new bugs are 40 versus 29, 21 and 13. It has the highest per-protocol bug counts, including ties.
claims.quote:
In
contrast, RFCAUDITachieves 81.9% precision and discovers
47 bugs in total (40 new) with far less manual effort (Table
II).

claims.text: RFCAUDIT's 81.9% precision exceeds Copilot with Claude 3.7/Claude 3.5/GPT-4o at 36.3/19.9/11.4%; it has the lowest false-positive rate across protocols.
claims.quote:
RFCAUDITconsistently reports the lowest false-positive
rates and the highest bug counts across all protocols.

claims.text: RFCAUDIT is claimed to require far less manual validation effort than Copilot; it produces 83 reports versus 215, 538 and 1,315, but validation time is not_reported.
claims.quote:
In
contrast, RFCAUDITachieves 81.9% precision and discovers
47 bugs in total (40 new) with far less manual effort (Table
II).

claims.text: RFCAUDIT redetects 12 of LTL-Fuzzer's 15 previously reported bugs: 7 in TinyDTLS and 5 in Contiki-Telnet.
claims.quote:
RFCAUDITsuccessfully detected 12 of the 15
zero-days originally reported by LTL-Fuzzer, without requir-
ing manual property construction or predicate-to-location map-
ping.

claims.text: RFCAUDIT covers a broader range of functional properties than LTL-Fuzzer: only 11 of its 47 violated properties could be encoded for LTL-Fuzzer; 36 could not.

metrics.name: RFCAUDIT-detected violated properties expressible for LTL-Fuzzer
properties requiring constraints beyond plain LTL or lacking predicate locations

claims.quote:
In contrast, when we attempted to encode the 47 violated
properties from our dataset as LTL-Fuzzer properties, only
11 could be expressed; the remaining 36 required constraints
beyond plain LTL or lacked precise predicate locations.

claims.text: RFCAUDIT detects temporal violations without the manual property construction or predicate-to-code mapping required by LTL-Fuzzer.

metrics.name: requirement for manual property construction and predicate mapping

claims.quote:
RFCAUDITsuccessfully detected 12 of the 15
zero-days originally reported by LTL-Fuzzer, without requir-
ing manual property construction or predicate-to-location map-
ping.

of 1123K input and 90K output tokens, costs $5.03, and
completes each protocol analysis in 81 minutes.

claims.quote:
As shown in Table V, RFCAUDITuses an average
of 1123K input and 90K output tokens, costs $5.03, and
completes each protocol analysis in 81 minutes.

claims.quote:
As shown in Table V, RFCAUDITuses an average
of 1123K input and 90K output tokens, costs $5.03, and
completes each protocol analysis in 81 minutes.

claims.text: Removing semantic summaries lowers overall precision from 81.9% to 51.4%.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table VI, removing semantic index-
ing drops precision from 81.9% to 51.4% and reduces detected
bugs from 47 to 26.

claims.text: Removing semantic summaries lowers unique bugs from 47 to 26 (18 new, 8 known).
claims.quote:
As shown in Table VI, removing semantic index-
ing drops precision from 81.9% to 51.4% and reduces detected
bugs from 47 to 26.

claims.text: Removing all demand-driven retrieval tools lowers overall precision from 81.9% to 47.1%.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table VI, this results in a sharp drop in precision
(from 81.9% to 47.1%) and fewer detected bugs (from 47 to
36).

claims.text: Removing all demand-driven retrieval tools lowers unique bugs from 47 to 36 (26 new, 10 known); Babel is a local exception, with 12 versus the full system's 10.
claims.page: 10, §IV-E, Ablation Study 2, Table VI; 7, Table II
claims.quote:
As shown in Table VI, this results in a sharp drop in precision
(from 81.9% to 47.1%) and fewer detected bugs (from 47 to
36).

claims.text: Removing Query, Query_Callee or Query_Caller lowers precision from 81.9% to 50.0%, 47.7% or 47.3%, respectively.
claims.quote:
As
shown in Table VII, removing any single tool sharply reduces
precision from 81.9% with full retrieval to about 47–50%,
with little difference across tools.

claims.text: Removing Query, Query_Callee or Query_Caller yields 41, 45 or 39 unique bugs instead of 47; Query_Caller removal causes the largest coverage loss.
claims.quote:
However, the number of
detected bugs varies, with the largest drop occurring when
Query_Calleris removed (from 47 to 39), suggesting it
contributes the most to overall bug coverage.

claims.text: Self-critique reduces false-positive rate from 63.9% to 18.1%, a reported relative reduction of 71.7%; corresponding precision is 36.1% versus 81.9%.
claims.quote:
This leads to a higher false positive rate (18.1% to 63.9%)
and fewer bugs (47 to 45), emphasizing its crucial role in
enhancing detection precision and finding overlooked bugs.

claims.text: Self-critique raises aggregate unique bugs from 45 to 47, although full-system bug counts fall on Babel (14 to 10) and BFD (15 to 14).
claims.page: 10, §IV-E, Ablation Study 3, Table VI; 7, Table II
claims.quote:
This leads to a higher false positive rate (18.1% to 63.9%)
and fewer bugs (47 to 45), emphasizing its crucial role in
enhancing detection precision and finding overlooked bugs.

claims.text: Developers have confirmed 20 of the 47 unique bugs or approved/merged their patches; every bug report receiving a developer response was confirmed.
claims.quote:
We further validated our results by reporting
newly discovered bugs to protocol developers, where all bug
reports that received a response have been confirmed as true
positives.

claims.text: The 15 false positives are attributed to incomplete context (3), RFC misinterpretation (6), code misinterpretation (5) and intentional implementation choice (1); RFC errors are the largest group.

metrics.name: false positives by manually classified root cause

claims.quote:
We analyze the 15 false posi-
tives reported by RFCAUDITto understand their root causes.

claims.text: Without semantic summaries, false positives caused by incomplete context increase from 3 to 14 and become the dominant cause.

metrics.name: false positives attributed to incomplete context

claims.quote:
We observe that false positives
due to(i) incomplete context retrievalrise significantly (from
3 to 14), making it the main source of false positives in
this setting.

claims.text: On BFD, RFCAUDIT with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 detects 11 and 13 true bugs, respectively.
claims.quote:
RFCAUDIT
detected 11 and 13 true bugs with the precision of 71.4% and
70.3%, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness across
models.

claims.text: On BFD, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 configurations achieve 71.4% and 70.3% precision, respectively.
claims.quote:
RFCAUDIT
detected 11 and 13 true bugs with the precision of 71.4% and
70.3%, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness across
models.

claims.text: The authors interpret successful BFD audits with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 as effectiveness across models; broader cross-model stability is not directly measured.
claims.quote:
RFCAUDIT
detected 11 and 13 true bugs with the precision of 71.4% and
70.3%, respectively, demonstrating the effectiveness across
models.

claims.text: On industry-scale stacks, RFCAUDIT finds 12 unique aws-c-http bugs from 18 reports and one true-positive Linux TCP/IP report from three.
claims.quote:
On aws-c-http, RFCAUDITdetected 18 inconsistencies,
of which 12 were confirmed as true positives, yielding 12
unique bugs.

claims.text: The industry-scale evaluation is described as high precision, although the reported counts imply 12/18 for aws-c-http and 1/3 for Linux TCP/IP.
claims.quote:
These results demonstrate that
RFCAUDITscales to industry-scale codebases and can expose
real specification violations with high precision.

claims.text: Successful audits of 74K-LoC aws-c-http and approximately 190K-LoC Linux TCP/IP are presented as scalability to industry-scale codebases; runtime and cost at this scale are not_reported.
claims.quote:
These results demonstrate that
RFCAUDITscales to industry-scale codebases and can expose
real specification violations with high precision.

claims.text: The Babel case study identifies request forwarding that chooses a non-feasible route without first trying a feasible route; the corrective patch was merged.

evidence.detail: Developers merged the forwarding-order fix.
evidence.quote:
We submitted a fix to prioritize
feasible routes, which has been merged by the developers.

claims.quote:
As shown in Figure 9(a),
FRRouting ignored this ordering and always chose a non-
feasible route.

claims.text: The NHRP case study identifies missing loop detection for a Responder Address Extension; developers confirmed the bug.

evidence.detail: Developers confirmed the missing-loop-detection bug.
evidence.quote:
The bug was
confirmed by the developers.

claims.quote:
As shown in Figure 9(b), FRRouting
omitted this check, allowing persistent forwarding loops that
consume resources and delay address resolution.

claims.text: RippleGUItester found 119 deduplicated previously unknown bugs across 111 PRs: Firefox 29, Zettlr 63, JabRef 17 and Godot 10.

evidence.description: Among the 26 findings persisting in latest versions, 16 were fixed and two confirmed; this validates only a subset of the 119 findings.
evidence.quote:
After reporting these bugs to the corresponding develop-
ment teams, 16 bugs have already been fixed, two have
been confirmed, six remain under discussion, and two
were marked as working as intended.

claims.quote:

RippleGUItester detected 119 unique bugs.

saintcan generate tests for applications without Ope-

Also, with

coverage compared to bigger models such as GPT-o1.

forms EvoMaster for Feature-service and Genome-Nexus (+50.5%
and +22.0% in line coverage).

forms EvoMaster for Feature-service and Genome-Nexus (+50.5%

claims.text: With the same Gemini models, Sakura increases compilability over external comparator Gemini CLI by 50–78% (30–43 percentage points); rates are 97.3% with Pro and 91.3% with Flash.
claims.quote:
Sakuraachieves substantially higher compilability than Gemini CLI, with improve-
ments of 50–78% (30–43 percentage points) depending on the underlying model.

claims.text: Open-source Sakura models compile more tests than proprietary-model Gemini CLI; Devstral Small 2 reaches 85.4% versus Gemini CLI/Pro's 54.6%.
claims.quote: EvenSakura with smaller models like Devstral Small 2 (85.4%) outperforms Gemini CLI using Gemini 2.5 Pro (54.6%) by 56.3% (30.7 percentage points).

claims.text: Using the same Gemini models, Sakura improves coverage overlap over Gemini CLI by 38–66% (18–31 percentage points).

metrics.name: Class, method, line and branch coverage overlap with ground truth

claims.quote: With the same models,Sakuraachieves 38–66% (18–31 percentage points) higher coverage overlap than Gemini CLI.

claims.text: Open-source Sakura models exceed Gemini CLI/Pro's branch overlap: approximately 73% for Qwen3-Coder and 64% for Devstral versus 46% for Gemini CLI/Pro.

metrics.name: Branch coverage overlap with ground truth

claims.quote: Sakurawith open-source models (73% branch coverage for Qwen3-Coder, 64% for Devstral Small 2) outperforms Gemini CLI with Gemini 2.5 Pro (46%), demonstrating that agentic architecture can compensate for model capacity.

claims.text: With identical Gemini models, Sakura improves structural recall over Gemini CLI by 31–72% (14–36 percentage points) across all four structural properties.

metrics.name: Recall of instantiated types, assertion types, method calls and focal methods

claims.quote: Sakuraimproves structural recall by 31–72% (14–36 percentage points) over Gemini CLI with the same models, with consistent gains across all four properties, including focal method identification (70% vs. 42% using Gemini 2.5 Pro).

claims.text: Open-source Sakura models have greater structural recall than proprietary-model Gemini CLI; Qwen3-Coder reaches 65–79%.

metrics.name: Recall of instantiated types, assertion types, method calls and focal methods

claims.quote: Open-source models underSakurastill surpass the proprietary baseline, with Qwen3-Coder reaching 65–79% recall.

claims.text: Sakura's structural recall and coverage overlap decline as description abstraction increases.
claims.quote: Nevertheless, performance at high abstraction remains substantially below that of low-abstraction inputs, suggesting room for improvement.

claims.text: Sakura retains a structural-recall advantage over Gemini CLI at every abstraction level; at high abstraction Pro retains 45.5% focal-method recall versus 18.2% for Gemini CLI/Pro.

metrics.name: Recall of instantiated types, assertion types, method calls and focal methods

claims.quote: All approaches degrade as abstraction increases, butSakuramaintains a substantial advantage at every level.

claims.text: At high abstraction, Sakura maintains 58–71% coverage overlap versus Gemini CLI's 28–38%; Pro's average overlap is 110.5% (33.2 percentage points) higher than Gemini CLI/Pro.

metrics.name: Class, method, line and branch coverage overlap with ground truth

claims.quote: Coverage overlap trends are similar, with Sakuramaintaining 58–71% overlap at high abstraction versus 28–38% for the baseline.

claims.text: At high abstraction, open-source Sakura models still outperform proprietary Gemini CLI in focal-method recall; Qwen3-Coder reaches 40.6% versus Gemini CLI/Pro's 18.2%.
claims.quote: For focal-method recall at high abstraction, open-source models underSakurastill outperform the proprietary baseline (Qwen3-Coder: 40.6% vs. Gemini CLI with Pro: 18.2%).

claims.text: Under increasing abstraction, focal-method recall deteriorates most sharply, while assertion-type recall is relatively resilient.

metrics.name: Focal-method and assertion-type recall across abstraction levels

claims.quote: Among structural properties, focal methods degrade most sharply while assertion types remain robust, suggesting verification intent is more resilient to abstraction than behavioral localization.

claims.text: Sakura/Pro sustains 64–85% across coverage and structural metrics on >5-focal-method tests; its same-model advantage over Gemini CLI widens with complexity to 25–49 percentage points.

metrics.name: Recall of instantiated types, assertion types, method calls and focal methods

claims.text: ScenGen detects 106 scenario-specific crashes: Email 9, Music 6, Note 16, Photo 6, Translation 15, Shopping 9, Login 10, Calculation 9, Weather 18, Alarm-clock 8; aggregate totals exceed Monkey SCN 29, Stoat SCN 43, PIRLTest SCN 51, GPTDroid 63, ScenTest 71 and ASOT 89.

claims.text: ScenGen's operation sequences are described as longer and semantically coherent; quantitative sequence-length results are not_reported.

claims.text: Deeper scenario exploration is claimed to reveal bugs requiring multiple dependent interactions that traditional approaches miss; interaction depth is not quantified.
claims.quote: This deeper exploration enables the detection of complex bugs that only manifest after multiple dependent interactions, which are often missed by shorter or random sequences generated by traditional approaches.

claims.text: Localization correction provides fault tolerance under changing or cluttered interfaces.

evidence.detail: Visual occlusion and repeated icons are identified as common initial error contexts; no separately quantified stress condition is reported.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that most initial localization errors occur in cases where widgets are visually occluded (e.g.,drop-down or scrollable menus) or contain highly similar visual components (e.g.,repeated icons).

claims.quote: These results confirm that ScenGennot only maintains high localization precision in stable UI conditions but also exhibits strong fault tolerance under dynamically changing or visually cluttered interfaces.

claims.text: The paper claims generation time is stable across domains and varies less than the baselines; no dispersion statistic is reported, and Table8 does not show a uniformly smaller range than all baselines.

claims.text: Token demand grows with scenario complexity and interaction depth, especially for Shopping and Login versus Photo and Alarm-clock.
claims.quote: Complex testing scenarios such as “Shopping” and “Login” consume more tokens due to their intricate, multi-step interactions and the frequent involvement of the self-correction mechanism.

claims.text: GUI-state verification and completion verification dominate token use, averaging 15,377 and 11,388 tokens; logical decisions and self-correction average 5,232 and 1,458.
claims.quote: A closer examination of the six stages indicates that the app GUI state verification ( 𝑇4) and test completion verification (𝑇5) stages generally exhibit the highest token consumption.

claims.text: Structured visual inputs are claimed to improve semantic efficiency over purely textual representations while keeping token consumption manageable; no visual-versus-text author-harness ablation is evaluated.
claims.quote: Compared to purely text-based representations, this visual grounding strategy significantly improves semantic efficiency while maintaining manageable token consumption.

claims.text: Structured memory and stepwise context scoping are claimed to keep cost driven by scenario reasoning rather than uncontrolled history accumulation; context-growth measurements are not_reported.
claims.quote: This behavior is attributable to the structured memory mechanism and step-wise invocation strategy, which limit each LLM call to the necessary contextual information.

claims.text: Observed runtime is claimed to be practical for automated testing workflows; no practitioner assessment or acceptance threshold is reported.
claims.quote: Although the involvement of LLM calls introduces additional latency compared to purely heuristic-based tools, the observed runtime remains within a practical range for automated testing workflows.

claims.text: Long-horizon/context-window limitations did not cause an observed experimental bottleneck; task-horizon and context-limit measurements are not_reported.
claims.quote: In practice, long-horizon limitations have not posed a bottleneck in our experiments.

claims.text: Among 15 unsuccessful-generation cases, premature termination is the largest category (6; 40%); the other reported categories contain 3 completion-detection, 3 localization, 2 app-design and 1 unconventional-process cases.
claims.quote: Premature Termination is therefore the most dominant failure type, representing 40% of the observed failures.

claims.text: Initial localization errors predominantly involve occluded widgets or visually similar/repeated elements.
claims.quote: Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that most initial localization errors occur in cases where widgets are visually occluded (e.g.,drop-down or scrollable menus) or contain highly similar visual components (e.g.,repeated icons).

claims.text: The 12 final incorrect decisions comprise six premature terminations, two redundant continuations, two widget-semantic errors, one missing prerequisite and one rare alternative-path error.
claims.quote: A detailed examination of the 12 incorrect decisions reveals distinct error types.

claims.text: Across 187 Google Play apps, Trident detects 102 non-crash bugs in 74 apps.

evidence.detail: Developers fixed 31 and confirmed 12 of the 43 newly reported bugs; this corroborates a subset of the 102-bug yield.
evidence.quote: We submitted these 43 bugs to developers, and all of them have been fixed/confirmed so far (31 fixed and 12 confirmed, none of them rejected).

claims.quote: For the 187 apps, Trident detects 102 non-crash bugs in 74 apps, of which 43 bugs in 42 apps are never discovered before.

claims.text: Of the real-world findings, 43 bugs in 42 apps were previously undiscovered.

evidence.detail: Developers fixed or confirmed all 43 new reports, corroborating bug validity without independently establishing every novelty judgment.
evidence.quote: We submitted these 43 bugs to developers, and all of them have been fixed/confirmed so far (31 fixed and 12 confirmed, none of them rejected).

claims.quote: For the 187 apps, Trident detects 102 non-crash bugs in 74 apps, of which 43 bugs in 42 apps are never discovered before.

claims.text: Only 9 of Trident's 43 new bugs are detected by external comparators Genie and Odin.

metrics.name: overlap of new bugs with Genie/Odin detections

claims.quote: Furthermore, only 9 of these new bugs are detected by Genie [37] and Odin [26].

claims.text: All 43 submitted new bugs received developer acceptance: 31 fixed and 12 confirmed, with none rejected.
claims.page: p. 9, Section IV-C and Table III
claims.quote: We submitted these 43 bugs to developers, and all of them have been fixed/confirmed so far (31 fixed and 12 confirmed, none of them rejected).

claims.text: In the example-count sweep, bug detection improves up to four examples and then worsens as further examples are added.

metrics.name: bug detection rate; definition and numeric results not_reported

claims.quote: We can see that the non- crash bug detection performance increases with more exam- ples, reaching the highest bug detection rate with 4 examples.

claims.text: On the three known-bug datasets, Trident detects every bug detected by the best comparators Odin and NightHawk.
claims.quote: We also compare the similarities and differences of the bugs between the best baselines (Odin and NightHawk) and our approach, and the results show that all bugs detected by them are also detected by Trident.

claims.text: Trident reveals multiple bug types missed by baselines, including duplicated income records and incorrect navigation.
claims.page: pp. 8-9, Section IV-A and Figures 1 and 8
claims.quote: These bugs belong to different types and are not detected by the baseline method.

claims.text: Developer feedback identifies submitted bugs as affecting core functionality and deserving high priority.

evidence.detail: 31 new bugs were fixed, a practical outcome distinct from the qualitative priority feedback.
evidence.page: p. 9, Section IV-C and Table III
evidence.quote: We submitted these 43 bugs to developers, and all of them have been fixed/confirmed so far (31 fixed and 12 confirmed, none of them rejected).

claims.quote: This bug is crucial because it affects a core functionality that users frequently interact with.

claims.text: Higher coverage is interpreted as giving greater confidence in app quality and potentially exposing more bugs.
claims.quote: This indicates the effectiveness of Trident in covering more activities and codes, thus bringing higher confidence to app quality, potentially uncovering more bugs.

claims.text: Text-image alignment is interpreted as improving MLLM understanding of GUI structure and semantics and its judgments.
claims.quote: This further indicates that the alignment of text with images can help MLLM understand the structure and semantic information of GUI pages and make reasonable judgments.

claims.text: Testing history is interpreted as retaining knowledge and enabling a global view for reaching unvisited areas.
claims.quote: The history can help retain knowledge during testing and gain global viewpoints to reach uncovered areas.

claims.text: Similar bug examples are interpreted as helping the model understand what non-crash bugs should look like and produce the required output.
claims.quote: This indicates that by providing similar examples, the MLLM can quickly think out what should the non-crash bugs look like, which further indicates the demonstration can facilitate the MLLM in producing the required output.

claims.text: Functionality COT is interpreted as improving functional understanding through expected-path inference and comparison with the tested path.
claims.quote: This indicates that through COT, MLLM can infer the possible path of the functionality based on its description, and then judge the testing path, improving MLLM’s understanding of the functionality and bug detection performance.

claims.text: The downturn with too few or too many examples is attributed to insufficient information or noise in the supplied examples.
claims.quote: This indicates that too few or too many examples would damage the performance, because of the tiny information or the noise in the provided examples.

claims.text: GPT-4o GUIRepair resolves 157/517 issues (30.37%), exceeding all listed external systems: Globant 153, Zencoder 140, Agentless Lite with Claude 131 and with GPT-4o 127.

task instances than the best closed-source commercial system,
Globant Code Fixer Agent [70], and 17 more task instances
than Zencoder [71].

claims.text: Full GUIRepair repairs more test issues than either individual component or the base workflow: 157 versus 146 I2C, 148 C2I and 136 base; the full-versus-base gain is 21 issues (15.44%).

Table III, the full implementation, GUIRepair f ull, solves 157
instances, which is better than any other variant.

instances than GUIRepair base, achieving a 8.82% improvement.
