claims.text: SOAPFL localizes 175/395 bugs at Top-1, 46 more than LLMAOOchiai and 54 more than ChatGPTOchiai.
claims.quote:
Overall, S
OAPFL achieves reasonable performance: it
can localize 175 out of 395 bugs within Top-1, 46 more than
LLMAOOchiai and 54 more than ChatGPT Ochiai.

claims.text: SOAPFL's project-wise Top-1 performance exceeds the two adapted LLM baselines on nearly every project; on Closure, LLMAOOchiai localizes ten more bugs.
claims.quote:
When con-
sidering the Top-1 metric on the individual project, we observe
that SOAPFL signiﬁcantly outperforms the other two techniques
on nearly every project except Closure, where LLMAO Ochiai
localizes 10 more methods within Top-1.

claims.text: SOAPFL performs better than the adapted LLM baselines on aggregate Top-3/5 except that LLMAOOchiai exceeds its Top-5 count by 17, 253 versus 236.
claims.quote:
In terms of Top-3 and
Top-5 metrics, we found that S
OAPFL consistently performs
better except on Top-5, where LLMAOOchiai slightly exceeds
SOAPFL by localizing 17 more bugs.

claims.text: SOAPFL exceeds AutoFL and Agentless at all aggregate Top-N metrics: 175/232/236 versus 149/186/191 and 136/173/185.
claims.quote:
Overall, S OAPFL consistently outperforms the other
two systems across all three metrics, it localizes 26 and 39
more bugs than AutoFLand Agentless, respectively, within
Top-1, and 45 and 51 more within the Top-5.

claims.text: SOAPFL's aggregate Top-1 count exceeds Ochiai by 95 and FLUCCS by 15, but is one below DeepFLcov and 17 below GRACE.
claims.quote: As shown in Table III,S OAPFL does not outperform all of the STBFL approaches, as it localizes 175 of 395 bugs within Top-1, 95 more than Ochiai, 15 more than FLUCCS, 1 less than DeepFL

claims.text: Without Closure, SOAPFL localizes 143 bugs at Top-1, only two fewer than GRACE and 77/25/31 more than Ochiai/FLUCCS/DeepFLcov.
claims.quote: The last row of Table III presents the result without project Closure, S OAPFL reaches a similar level as GRACEin terms of Top-1

claims.text: On 226 additional Defects4J-V2.0.0 bugs, SOAPFL achieves 106/154/160 Top-1/3/5, exceeding all four statistic-based comparators; its Top-1 advantage is 21 over GRACE.
claims.quote: SOAPFL signiﬁcantly outperforms the other STBFL approaches by localizing 21 more bugs within Top-1 than GRACE, 63 more than DeepFL

claims.text: The cross-project results demonstrate stronger generalization than the statistic-based techniques.
claims.quote:
Such results demonstrate the stronger generalization of
the LLM-based FL systems.

claims.text: SOAPFL complements AutoFL, Agentless, DeepFLcov and GRACE by uniquely localizing ten bugs at Top-1.
claims.quote:
Speciﬁcally, 10 bugs can be uniquely local-
ized within Top-1 by S
OAPFL while the numbers for AutoFL,
Agentless, DeepFLcov, and GRACEare 9, 4, 27, and 12, respec-
tively.

claims.text: The union of SOAPFL, AutoFL and Agentless localizes 63 Top-1 bugs missed by both DeepFLcov and GRACE.
claims.quote:
Overall, AutoFL, Agentless, or SOAPFL localize 63 bugs
that cannot be localized by DeepFLcov or GRACEwithin Top-
1.

claims.text: Replacing the first two SOAPFL stages with GRACE Top-10 candidates improves Top-5 from 236 to 248.
claims.quote:
We refer to this variant approach as
SOAPFLG, whose performance on Defects4J-V1.2.0 is shown
in TableV.

claims.text: The GRACE-input variant loses 38 Top-1 and 15 Top-3 localizations versus SOAPFL, 137/217 versus 175/232, supporting the value of failure-analysis and navigation context.
claims.quote:
This phenomenon conﬁrms that the components in
S
OAPFL can provide LLM with richer fault-related context,
thereby improving the FL accurac y.

claims.text: Removing Test Behavior Analysis reduces aggregate Top-1/3/5 from 175/232/236 to 153/218/224.
claims.quote:
In comparison, when we abandon the Test Behavior Analysis
task in N-TBA, the performance of S
OAPFL declines more
slightly from 175 to 153 on Top-1.

claims.text: Removing Test Failure Analysis produces the largest aggregate ablation loss: 31/19/18 fewer Top-1/3/5 bugs, leaving 144/213/218.
claims.quote:
Among them,
N-TFA exhibits the worst performance, which localizes 31,
19, and 18 fewer bugs than S OAPFL within Top-1, Top-3, and
Top-5 metrics, respectively.

claims.text: Removing Method Doc Enhancement reduces aggregate Top-1/3/5 to 156/220/228, losses of 19/12/8.
claims.quote:
N-MDE shows relatively minimal
performance loss compared to S OAPFL, but still leads to an
effect decrease of 19, 12, and 8 in Top-1, Top-3, and Top-5
metrics, respectively.

claims.text: Withholding method comments reduces aggregate Top-1/3/5 to 147/209/224, supporting their contribution to localization.
claims.quote:
For T-MDE and T-MD, we observed that the presence of
code comments can effectively help S
OAPFL better understand
method functionality, ther eby enhancing the performance of
FL.

claims.text: Replacing multi-round Method Review with one batch reduces aggregate Top-1/3/5 to 156/217/226, losses of 19/15/10.
claims.quote:
Finally, the number of bugs that N-MMR localizes
within Top-1, Top-3, and Top-5 decreases by 19, 15, and 10,
respectively, which conﬁrms the effectiveness of the multi-
round dialogue strategy in Method Review tasks.

claims.text: The RQ2 summary identifies Test Behavior Analysis and method comments as the most influential designs.
claims.page: 12, V-B, Answer to RQ2; Table VI instead has the largest Top-1 loss for N-TFA
claims.quote:
Among them, the Test Behavior Analysis task and the
use of method comments exert the most signiﬁcant impact.

claims.text: Without rationales, participants localize approximately as many bugs within the time limit as SOAPFL's automatic Top-5 count.
claims.quote:
We observed
that in the Human-NR group where the rationale is unavailable
for the results, the number of bugs that participants were able
to pinpoint closely matched the number localized by S OAPFL
within Top-5.

claims.text: Providing rationales increases developers' successful localizations; Math and Closure exceed the automatic Top-5 counts by 13 and 16, respectively.
claims.quote:
Surprisingly, in the Human
group, the number of bugs found by participants showed a con-
siderable increase, especially in the Math and Closure projects,
where the localized bugs increased by 13 and 16 respectively
compared to the Top-5.

OAPFL offers affordable cost in terms

nodes represent states of the codebase and edges represent actions
(Search for code exploration, Plan for strategic reasoning, and
Edit for code modification).

cations exist.

exploration patterns and reduced fix accuracy.

unrelated to resolving the issue, which can distract the model and
reduce its ability to judge which chain is most likely to lead to a
correct fix.

claims.text: Superior localization is claimed to cause better issue resolution, with 41.4% Pass@1 versus external baselines' 23.0–38.8%.
claims.quote:
This superior localization performance directly translates to
better issue resolution, with SWE-Debate achieving 41.4% Pass@1
compared to baseline methods ranging from 23.0% to 38.8%.

claims.text: Graph traversal captures structural relationships missed by individual exploration, especially for issues spanning multiple files.
claims.quote:
The graph traversal strategy effectively captures
structural relationships that single-agent individual exploration
often misses, particularly for multi-file issues where traditional
methods frequently fail due to insufficient architectural understand-
ing.

claims.text: Localization chains containing numerous candidate files can cause excessive editing exploration time without convergence; no separate timing results are reported.
claims.quote:
Our experiments reveal that when the localization
chain contains numerous candidate files, the editing process be-
comes inefficient, with agents spending excessive exploration time
without converging on optimal solutions.

claims.text: SWE-Debate integrates with existing issue-resolution frameworks without major modifications, enabling practical adoption.
claims.quote:
Third, the framework integrates seamlessly with existing issue
resolution systems without requiring major modifications.

claims.text: Competitive debate is claimed to enhance specialized localization approaches, inferred from outperforming external LocAgent rather than evaluating a debate-augmented LocAgent.
claims.quote:
This shows that competitive multi-
agent debate can enhance even domain-specific approaches.

claims.text: Dependency-graph construction can be computationally expensive on large codebases and limit scalability.
claims.quote:
The graph construction
process can be computationally expensive for large codebases, lim-
iting scalability.

claims.text: The batch-processing workflow limits integration with real-time development workflows.
claims.quote:
The current batch processing approach limits
integration with real-time development workflows.

claims.text: For SymPy-13974, the selected localization chain is claimed to cover every modified function and identify the needed modification locations.

metrics.name: Qualitative inclusion of modified functions in the selected localization chain

claims.quote:
Notably, all modified functions
were covered by the selected localization chain, demonstrating the
accuracy and completeness of our code navigation strategy.

claims.text: In SymPy-13974, structured planning and debate are claimed to facilitate coordinated edits across multiple modules.
claims.quote:
The localization chain effectively surfaces
the relevant symbolic manipulation points, while the structured
planning and debate framework facilitates coordinated edits across
multiple modules.

claims.text: The SymPy-13974 patch is claimed to correctly handle TensorProduct powers and resolve the issue as expected.
claims.quote:
Together, they contribute to generating a valid
and verifiable patch that resolves the issue as expected.

claims.text: Outperforming the strongest same-model external baselines (OpenHands and SWE-Agent with DeepSeek-V3-0324, 38.8%) shows that the debate framework adds issue-resolution benefit beyond model selection.
claims.quote:
This demonstrates that our competitive multi-agent de-
bate framework provides substantial benefits beyond what can
be achieved through model selection alone.

claims.text: Gains over same-model baselines are taken as evidence that performance stems from reasoning rather than memorization of SWE-Bench data; no contamination-free evaluation is reported.
claims.quote:
The substantial improvements over base-
line methods using identical models provide evidence that perfor-
mance gains derive from enhanced reasoning capabilities rather
than memorization effects.

matched_comparisons.metric: Pass@1

claims.text: With GPT-3.5, TRACE repairs 187 Defects4J bugs, exceeding D4C by 21 bugs (12.7%) and ChatRepair, ThinkRepair and RepairAgent by 25, 26 and 23 bugs respectively.

metrics.name: Number of manually assessed correct patches

claims.quote: Notably, under the same condition of applying GPT-3.5 as the base LLM, TRACE still surpasses recently proposed approaches such as ChatRepair, ThinkRepair, RepairAgent, and D4C, repairing 25, 26, 23, and 21 more bugs, respectively.

claims.text: With GPT-4o, TRACE repairs 204 Defects4J bugs, 26 more than D4C (14.6%), achieving the best reported repair performance.

metrics.name: Number of manually assessed correct patches

claims.quote: TRACE successfully repairs 204 bugs in Defects4J, outperforming the best baseline APR approach by 14.6%.

claims.text: TRACE complements D4C, RepairAgent and ChatRepair by correctly repairing 33 bugs not repaired by those tools under the GPT-3.5 comparison.

metrics.name: Number of uniquely repaired bugs relative to three comparator tools

claims.quote: Compared to the best baseline tools built on the same base model, TRACE achieves 33 unique repair cases, outperforming all of these baselines.

claims.text: On DebugBench with GPT-3.5, TRACE obtains 512 verified patches versus D4C's 453, improving by 13.0% overall and 10.7%, 12.7% and 16.0% for C++, Java and Python.

metrics.name: Number of LeetCode-verified patches by language and overall

claims.quote: As shown in Table  6, TRACE achieved the highest number of verified patches across all programming languages and all base LLMs.

claims.text: On DebugBench with GPT-4o, TRACE obtains 570 verified patches versus D4C's 524, improving by 8.8% overall and 7.7%, 6.4% and 12.3% for C++, Java and Python.

metrics.name: Number of LeetCode-verified patches by language and overall

claims.quote: Similarly, when employing GPT-4o as the base model, TRACE achieves an 8.8% improvement in repair performance over D4C, with gains of 7.7%, 6.4%, and 12.3% in C++, Java, and Python, respectively.

claims.text: On DebugBench with Llama-3.1-70B, TRACE obtains 508 verified patches versus D4C's 434, improving by 17.1% overall and 15.8%, 19.9% and 15.5% for C++, Java and Python.

metrics.name: Number of LeetCode-verified patches by language and overall

claims.quote: When Llama-3.1 is used as the base model, the advantage grows even larger: TRACE exceeds D4C by 17.1% overall, with per-language improvements of 15.8% on C++, 19.9% on Java, and 15.5% on Python.

claims.text: The repair template repository improves repair effectiveness: full TRACE produces 25 more plausible Defects4J patches and 30 more verified DebugBench patches than TRACE_nt.
claims.quote: As presented in Table  7, TRACE𝑎𝑙𝑙 generates 25 more plausible patches than TRACE𝑛𝑡 on Defects4J.

claims.text: Execution feedback improves repair effectiveness: full TRACE produces 30 more plausible Defects4J patches and 32 more verified DebugBench patches than TRACE_nf at the same patch count.
claims.quote: As shown in Table  7, TRACE𝑎𝑙𝑙 fixes 30 and 32 more bugs than TRACE𝑛𝑓 on Defects4J and DebugBench, respectively, demonstrating that the design of execution feedback is also crucial for improving repair performance.

claims.text: TRACE's structured repair reasoning improves repair effectiveness over the author-constructed ThinkRepair-style few-shot variant, adding 22 plausible Defects4J patches and 26 verified DebugBench patches.
claims.quote: As shown in Table  7, TRACE𝑎𝑙𝑙 fixes 22 and 26 more bugs than TRACE𝑓 𝑠 on Defects4J and DebugBench, respectively, demonstrating that TRACE’s repair reasoning engine outperforms ThinkRepair’s few-shot selection strategy.

claims.text: Repair strategy planning improves repair effectiveness, adding 11 plausible Defects4J patches and 16 verified DebugBench patches relative to TRACE_np.
claims.quote: As shown in Table  7, TRACE𝑎𝑙𝑙 fixes 11 and 16 more bugs than TRACE𝑛𝑝 on Defects4J and DebugBench, respectively, indicating that the introduction of the planning step in the repair reasoning engine also improves repair performance.

claims.text: Full TRACE improves repair capability over repeated direct LLM generation with identical initial artifacts, adding 42 plausible Defects4J patches and 59 verified DebugBench patches.
claims.quote: As shown in Table  7, TRACE𝑎𝑙𝑙 fixes 42 and 59 more bugs than TRACE𝑑𝑔 on Defects4J and DebugBench, respectively.

claims.text: Increasing execution-feedback iterations from one toward three improves TRACE's repair performance on both sampled benchmarks; the one-iteration condition performs worst.

metrics.name: Number of repaired bugs versus iteration cap; numerical outcomes not_reported in supplied text

claims.quote: The results show that TRACE repairs the fewest bugs on both benchmarks when the iteration number is set to one.

claims.text: Repair-performance gains plateau at three feedback iterations, with only marginal improvements at larger caps.

metrics.name: Number of repaired bugs versus iteration cap; numerical outcomes not_reported in supplied text

claims.quote: However, once the iteration number reaches three, performance gains plateau with only marginal improvements thereafter.

claims.text: With GPT-3.5 on Defects4J, TRACE averages 426K tokens per bug: more than D4C's 158K and RepairAgent's 270K, but fewer than ChatRepair's 467K.
claims.quote: On average, TRACE consumes 426K tokens per bug, which is higher than RepairAgent and D4C, but lower than ChatRepair.

claims.text: TRACE is more cost-effective per successful Defects4J repair than ChatRepair: $0.51 versus $0.65 per fixed bug under the same token-to-USD conversion.
claims.quote: Therefore, TRACE achieves a lower cost per fixed bug than ChatRepair, indicating that despite higher absolute token usage partly due to structured reasoning, TRACE is more cost-effective per successful repair than sampling-heavy conversational repair in practice.

claims.text: TRACE is robust to moderately less-precise template wording: plausible patches decline from 254 to 247 on Defects4J and verified patches from 512 to 505 on DebugBench, with reported success-rate drops of 1.6 and 1.2 percentage points.

claims.quote: Although removing technical detail from the template descriptions introduces a slight performance degradation, the overall behavior remains stable and the key conclusions of our main experiments still hold.

claims.text: TRACE's explicit reasoning trajectory improves interpretability and helps developers understand and validate generated patches; no human interpretability assessment is reported.
claims.quote:
Thus, TRACE not only im-
proves repair effectiveness, but also contributes to more interpretable and reliable repair processes by providing a transparent reasoning trajectory, which helps developers better understand and validate the generated patches.

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Defects4J: all five projects, 8192 focal methods
ecs.protocol: Three-run mean; repair plus generation iteration and positive prompt injection, without coverage-guided feedback; common up-to-four-iteration policy; JUnit 4/OpenClover; Pass/TBC/TLC
ecs.quote: We conduct ablation experiments using three metrics on three incomplete and one complete TestART.

claims.text: On Defects4J, TestART reaches 78.55% Pass, exceeding initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5 by 28.64 percentage points, ChatGPT-4.0 by 18.80, external A3Test by 63.29 and external ChatUniTest by 18.50.
claims.quote: The total pass rate is 63.29% higher than A3Test, 28.64% higher than ChatGPT-3.5, 18.80% higher than ChatGPT-4.0, and 18.50% higher than ChatUniTest.

claims.text: TestART's Defects4J compilation-error rate is 12.43%, approximately 7 percentage points below initial-generation ChatGPT-4.0.
claims.quote: Compared with the second place in each indicator, TestART reduces the compilation error rate by 7.0% compared to ChatGPT-4.0 and was 8.0% lower than ChatUniTest in the running error rate.

claims.text: TestART's Defects4J runtime-error rate is 8.50%, approximately 8 percentage points below external ChatUniTest.
claims.quote: Compared with the second place in each indicator, TestART reduces the compilation error rate by 7.0% compared to ChatGPT-4.0 and was 8.0% lower than ChatUniTest in the running error rate.

claims.text: TestART repairs approximately 50% of the three common compilation-error categories on Defects4J: missing symbols, method-call errors and access denial.

metrics.name: Compilation-error repair success rate by category

claims.quote: The three most common compilation errors (“cannot find symbol”, “Method call error” and “Access denied”) can be repaired with about 50% success.

claims.text: TestART repairs approximately 75% of runtime errors on Defects4J.
claims.quote: The overall repair rate of runtime errors is as high as 75%.

claims.text: Template T2 repairs almost all errors in the reported Boolean-assertion categories.

metrics.name: T2 repair success rate by assertion-error category

claims.quote: T2 in TestART makes four error types (“AssertNull”, “AssertNotNull”, “AssertTrue” and “AssertNotNull”) almost 100% repaired.

claims.text: Template T3 repairs 65.37% of AssertEquals errors.
claims.quote: Due to complex parameter formats and data types, errors caused by “AssertEquals” and “Exceptions” can still be repaired by 65.37% and 82.03% based on T3 and T4, respectively.

claims.text: Template T4 repairs 82.03% of exception errors.
claims.quote: Due to complex parameter formats and data types, errors caused by “AssertEquals” and “Exceptions” can still be repaired by 65.37% and 82.03% based on T3 and T4, respectively.

claims.text: TestART achieves the highest Defects4J total coverage, with TBC 69.40% and TLC 68.17%, exceeding initial-generation ChatGPT-4.0 by 17.54 and 17.29 percentage points and outperforming external A3Test and ChatUniTest.
claims.quote: Compared to the second-ranked ChatGPT-4.0, TestART improves TBC by 17.54% and TLC by 17.29%.

claims.text: On focal methods successfully tested by TestART, its Defects4J branch/line coverage is 88.54%/90.96%, exceeding external EvoSuite by approximately 2.5/3.4 percentage points under that denominator.
claims.quote: TestART achieves 88.54% branch coverage and 90.96% line coverage rates, exceeding EvoSuite by 2.5% and 3.4%, respectively.

claims.text: Adding the repair strategy raises Defects4J Pass from 49.91% to 78.55%, a 28.64-percentage-point increase.
claims.quote: The most apparent core module for improvement is the repair strategy, which not only enhances the pass rate but also improves the coverage rate.

claims.text: Adding repair raises Defects4J TBC/TLC from 43.10%/42.58% to 62.13%/62.24%, so the pass-rate improvement is accompanied by increased coverage.
claims.quote: This validates that our fixed templates do not improve pass rate at the expense of coverage.

claims.text: Adding generation iteration with positive prompt injection to repair increases TBC/TLC from 62.13%/62.24% to 66.48%/64.49%; Pass remains 78.55%.
claims.quote: The iteration and coverage-guided testing feedback both contribute to the improvement of the coverage rate by about 3%.

claims.text: Adding coverage-guided feedback to repair plus iteration increases TBC/TLC from 66.48%/64.49% to 69.40%/68.17%; Pass remains 78.55%.
claims.quote: The iteration and coverage-guided testing feedback both contribute to the improvement of the coverage rate by about 3%.

claims.text: Positive prompt injection enables incremental convergence during generation loops; convergence itself is not separately measured.
claims.quote: In addition, positive prompt injection as a main part of iteration ensures that LLMs converge incrementally during loops.

claims.text: The paper attributes reduced LLM hallucination to TestART; hallucination incidence is not directly measured.
claims.quote: The evaluation results demonstrate that TestART can suppress the hallucination problem and generate high-quality test cases.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART increases aggregate Pass from 51.30% to 71.30% relative to initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5; the corresponding RUL/WIN/BPG rates are 59.39%/60.26%/77.48% versus 32.12%/27.56%/63.48%.
claims.quote: In terms of overall HITS dataset comparisons, TestART increases correctness by approximately 20% and surpasses ChatGPT-3.5 by 19% in both test branch coverage (TBC) and test line coverage (TLC).

claims.text: On HITS, TestART attains aggregate TBC/TLC of 69.74%/69.52%, versus 50.28%/50.61% for initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5, with higher total coverage in each project.
claims.quote: In terms of overall HITS dataset comparisons, TestART increases correctness by approximately 20% and surpasses ChatGPT-3.5 by 19% in both test branch coverage (TBC) and test line coverage (TLC).

claims.text: TestART repairs 41.08% of compilation errors on HITS.
claims.quote: We also analyze the repair results, finding that TestART successfully repaired 41.08% of compilation errors and 71.70% of runtime errors.

claims.text: TestART repairs 71.70% of runtime errors on HITS.
claims.quote: We also analyze the repair results, finding that TestART successfully repaired 41.08% of compilation errors and 71.70% of runtime errors.

claims.text: TestART generalizes to the evaluated unlearned HITS projects while retaining substantial performance improvements.
claims.quote: TestART demonstrates strong performance on the unlearned dataset, achieving a stable accuracy improvement while effectively generalizing to new data.

claims.text: On Defects4J, 68.58% of TestART generation tasks finish within one minute, 90.59% within two minutes and 99% within five minutes.

metrics.name: Generation time per focal method and cumulative completion proportions

claims.quote: As shown in the figure, 68.58% of the unit test generation tasks are completed within one minute, while 90.59% are finished within two minutes.

claims.text: The paper claims TestART is more efficient than external EvoSuite by comparing TestART's observed generation times with EvoSuite's configured ten-minute maximum search time.
claims.quote: The maximum search time we set when generating test cases using EvoSuite is 10 minutes, which means TestART is more efficient than EvoSuite.

claims.text: Reported API cost per 100 generations is lowest for Gson at approximately $0.20 and reaches approximately $0.45 for Lang; the RQ5 summary instead gives a $0.30 lower bound.

metrics.name: API monetary cost per 100 generations, calculated from prompt/completion token pricing

claims.quote: Gson has the lowest unit test generation cost, averaging approximately 0.2$ for 100 times unit test generation, while Lang requires about 0.45$.

claims.text: The paper judges TestART's time and monetary costs acceptable and controllable, without reporting a user assessment or an acceptance threshold.
claims.quote: TestART demonstrates acceptable and controllable time and money cost, with 90.59% of a single generation task completed within two minutes and the money cost for 100 generation tasks ranging from 0.3$-0.45$

claims.text: On the Huawei Internal dataset, TestART improves Pass over the ChatGPT-3.5 initial-generation control by about 20% as reported; exact numerical rates are not_reported in the supplied text.
claims.quote: Notably, TestART outperforms ChatGPT-3.5 across all three metrics, with significant improvements of about 20% on Internal dataset .

claims.text: On the Huawei Internal dataset, TestART improves total branch and line coverage over the ChatGPT-3.5 initial-generation control by about 20% as reported; exact numerical rates are not_reported in the supplied text.

metrics.name: Total branch coverage, called TBL in §6

claims.quote: Notably, TestART outperforms ChatGPT-3.5 across all three metrics, with significant improvements of about 20% on Internal dataset .

claims.text: Errors involving unimplemented abstract methods and instantiation of abstract classes have the lowest compilation-error repair rates.

metrics.name: Compilation-error repair rate by error category

claims.quote: The implementation and inheritance of the abstract method and class lead to the lowest compile error repair rate for “Abstract method not be implemented” and “Abstract class cannot be instantiated” errors.

claims.text: Syntax errors and missing-symbol errors have the highest compilation-error repair rates, attributed respectively to LLM repair and template T1.

metrics.name: Compilation-error repair rate by error category

claims.quote: The two errors with the highest compile repair rate are “Syntax error” and “Cannot find symbol”, which benefit from feedback error reports to LLMs for self-repair and T1 in TestART, respectively.

claims.text: The Fail and Others categories, handled by LLM repair, have relatively low repair rates.

metrics.name: Repair success rate for Fail and Others categories

claims.quote: Note that the errors of “Fail” and “Others” are repaired by LLMs, so the repair rates are relatively low.

claims.text: TestART produces approximately half as many Defects4J test cases as external EvoSuite: 12,359 versus 23,570.
claims.quote: It is noteworthy that the test cases generated by TestART are about half the number produced by EvoSuite (12,359 compared to 23,570), greatly reducing the execution costs.

claims.text: The paper infers lower execution cost than external EvoSuite from TestART's smaller generated suite; test-execution cost is not directly measured for this comparison.
claims.quote: It is noteworthy that the test cases generated by TestART are about half the number produced by EvoSuite (12,359 compared to 23,570), greatly reducing the execution costs.

claims.text: Against external EvoSuite on the passed-method coverage comparison, TestART wins on three Defects4J projects and trails on two by approximately 5% average coverage as reported; the text does not identify which projects form each group.
claims.quote: From Fig. 7, we observe that TestART outperforms EvoSuite in three projects, while in the remaining two, it trailed by an average coverage rate of only 5%.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART generates 1253 tests versus 1104 for initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5, approximately 13% more; the printed BPG count of 7109 is inconsistent with this total.
claims.quote: Additionally, TestART generates 1,253 test cases for 885 focal methods, only 13% more than ChatGPT-3.5.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART lowers aggregate compilation errors from 34.35% to 22.94% relative to initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5, with lower rates in every project.
claims.quote: TestART clearly achieves superior performance in each project.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART lowers aggregate runtime errors from 13.79% to 4.63% relative to initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5, with lower rates in every project.
claims.quote: TestART clearly achieves superior performance in each project.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART's aggregate passed-method branch/line coverage is 98.17%/98.24%, versus 97.43%/98.09% for initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5.
claims.quote: TestART clearly achieves superior performance in each project.

claims.text: Initial generation accounts for approximately half of API cost, with repair and iterative feedback together accounting for the remainder.

metrics.name: API monetary cost by workflow phase

claims.quote: Furthermore, the initial generation phase accounts for the largest proportion of the total cost, constituting approximately 50%.

claims.text: For Lang, repair costs exceed iteration costs.

metrics.name: API cost for repair versus iteration

claims.quote: In some projects, such as Lang, the repair cost is higher than the iteration cost.

claims.text: For Chart, iteration costs exceed repair costs.

metrics.name: API cost for iteration versus repair

claims.quote: In contrast, for the Chart project, the iteration cost exceeds the code repair cost.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART generates 1700 assertions versus 1131 for initial-generation ChatGPT-3.5, an increase of 569.
claims.quote: As shown in the last column of Table 5, the total number of assertions generated by TestART exceeds that of ChatGPT-3.5 by 569.

claims.text: The paper interprets TestART's substantial assertion count as ensuring comprehensive test validation; assertion correctness or completeness is not independently assessed.
claims.quote: This demonstrates that TestART not only improves the code coverage of test cases but also maintains a substantial number of assertions, ensuring comprehensive test validation.

claims.text: The paper attributes improved test quality and usability to repair, using executable-validity outcomes without a human usability evaluation.
claims.quote: The repair strategy effectively repairs main compile and runtime errors, improving the quality and usability of LLM-generated test cases.

claims.text: On HITS, TestART detects synthetic mutation errors with MC 53.11% and TS 79.20%; the paper reports approximately 20% better error detection than external EvoSuite.
claims.page: 17, Table 5; 19, §6, Potential of error detection capability
claims.quote: As shown in the MC and TS columns of Table 5, TestART achieves a total of 53.11% mutation coverage (MC) and 79.20% test strength (TS).

claims.text: The paper infers that data leakage does not significantly affect TestART from similar correctness and coverage results on Defects4J and HITS; contamination is not directly measured.
claims.quote: We also find that the correctness and coverage results on Defects4J and HITS dataset are almost indistinguishable, which suggests that the issue of data leakage does not significantly affect our method.

claims.text: The paper attributes Chart's greater iterative-feedback cost to complex, large focal methods requiring more iterations; a quantified complexity–cost analysis is not_reported.
claims.quote: This is attributed to the higher proportion of complex and large focal methods in this project, which often require multiple iterations to achieve high coverage, thereby increasing the cost of iterative feedback.

the approach has detected 19 regressions, out of which 13 had

claims.text: The default GPT-4o-mini multi-question classifier achieved 55% precision, 67% recall and 60% F1.
claims.quote:
The classifier that predicts whether a behavioral change is intended
is effective in practice, with a precision of 55% and a recall of 67%.

claims.text: Classifier results are described as relatively stable across the tested models and classifier variants.
claims.quote:
First, and perhaps
most importantly, the results are relatively stable across different
models and different variants of the classifier.

claims.text: No model is uniformly best: GPT-4o wins with the single-question classifier, whereas GPT-4o-mini and DeepSeek-R1 both exceed GPT-4o's F1 with the multi-question classifier.

metrics.name: F1 by model and classifier setting

claims.quote:
While the overall best configuration, in terms of F1-score, is
GPT-4o with the single-question classifier, both GPT-4o-mini and
DeepSeek-R1 outperform GPT-4o when using the multi-question
classifier.

claims.text: For GPT-4o, single-question classification has higher F1 than multi-question classification (71% versus 53%).
claims.quote:
The
single-question classifier outperforms the multi-question classifier
in terms of F1-score for GPT-4o, but the multi-question classifier
outperforms the single-question classifier for DeepSeek-R1.

claims.text: For DeepSeek-R1, multi-question classification has higher F1 than single-question classification (56% versus 47%).
claims.quote:
The
single-question classifier outperforms the multi-question classifier
in terms of F1-score for GPT-4o, but the multi-question classifier
outperforms the single-question classifier for DeepSeek-R1.

claims.text: For GPT-4o-mini, multi-question classification offers approximately the same F1 (60% versus 61%) and a better precision/recall balance, raising precision from 49% to 55% while lowering recall from 80% to 67%.

claims.text: TestTailor achieves the highest average coverage: 80.87% statement and 74.51% branch; gains are 5.01/4.17 percentage points over CoverUp and 12.23/12.54 over CODAMOSA-20min, with significant paired differences versus all three external baselines.

evidence.description: Repeated-measures ANOVA and paired project-level t-tests; every TestTailor-versus-baseline statement/branch comparison has p<0.001.
evidence.quote:
Pairwise paired𝑡-tests show thatTestTailorsignificantly outperforms each
baseline (𝑝< 0.001), including CoverUp, the strongest competing method.

evidence.description: Ten repeats on each of three projects reproduce the ranking in all 30 runs; corroboration covers that subset.
evidence.quote:
The results showed minimal variance (maximum standard
deviation of 3.98% in tqdm) and 100% ranking consistency, withTestTailoroutperforming all
baselines in all 30 runs.

claims.quote:
On average, it reaches 80.87% statement coverage and 74.51% branch coverage,
ranking consistently higher than all baselines.

claims.text: TestTailor has the highest statement and branch coverage simultaneously on 16 projects, versus four each for CoverUp and CODAMOSA-20min and three for TELPA.

metrics.name: Number of projects best on both coverage metrics

claims.quote:
When examining the number of projects where
each method attains the highest coverage on both metrics simultaneously,TestTailordominates
with 16 projects, followed by CoverUp and CODAMOSA-20min with 4, TELPA with 3.

claims.text: TestTailor yields especially large coverage gains on difficult, low-initial-coverage projects such as ansible, tqdm and dataclasses_json; tqdm branch coverage reaches 44.74% and dataclasses_json 60.85%, exceeding all external baselines.
claims.quote:
In difficult
projects such as ansible, tqdm and dataclasses_json, TestTailor consistently outperforms other
methods.

claims.text: TestTailor has the highest intended-target hit accuracy among successfully executing tests: 85.2%, versus 75.3% for CoverUp and 63.8% for TELPA.

metrics.name: Coverage accuracy / effective coverage hit rate (%)

claims.quote:
As shown in Table 3,
TestTailorachieves the highest accuracy of 85.2%, compared with 75.3% for CoverUp and 63.8% for
TELPA.

claims.text: Removing path-proximal tests and divergence analysis lowers coverage to 72.8% statement and 66.8% branch (8.1/7.7 points below full TestTailor); this loss is about three times the loss from removing constraints, making proximal guidance the dominant contributor.
claims.quote:
When disabling Path-Proximal Test + Divergence Analysis (TestTailorConstr), coverage drops
to 72.8% statement and 66.8% branch—decreases of 8.1% and 7.7% relative to the full system.

claims.text: Symbolic path constraints provide additional coverage benefit: removing them while retaining proximal guidance reduces statement and branch coverage by 2.7 and 2.3 percentage points.
claims.quote:
Both path-proximal guidance and path constraints contribute significantly toTestTailor’s
effectiveness.

claims.text: Removing both path-oriented component groups reduces statement coverage by 12.4 points and branch coverage by 12.1 points relative to full TestTailor.
claims.quote:
The results show
that the fullTestTailorconsistently outperforms its
simplified versions, highlighting the contribution of
each component.

claims.text: Path-proximal guidance and symbolic constraints contribute complementary coverage improvements; the combined removal penalty is roughly the sum of individual penalties.
claims.quote:
Together, the two
mechanisms explain the superior coverage reported in RQ1.

claims.text: TestTailor remains the highest-coverage method with GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3; the reported ranking is preserved and backend changes cause only 0–2 percentage-point coverage reductions.
claims.quote:
The ranking of all approaches is preserved
regardless of the underlying model: CODAMOSA-20min < TELPA < CoverUp <TestTailor.

claims.text: TestTailor costs $19.94 in API usage versus CoverUp's $51.90, approximately 40% as much (about 60% lower).
claims.quote:
In contrast, CoverUp andTestTailorexhibit comparable
success rates (0.29 and 0.31, respectively), butTestTailorachieves this with significantly lower
cost than CoverUp ($19.94 vs. $51.90).

claims.text: TestTailor's reported successful-call rate is 0.31, comparable to CoverUp's 0.29 and above TELPA's 0.14; §5.4 interprets success as improving coverage, while §4.2.4 describes executability.

metrics.name: LLM Calls Successful Rate (coverage improvement in §5.4; executability in §4.2.4)

claims.quote:
In contrast, CoverUp andTestTailorexhibit comparable
success rates (0.29 and 0.31, respectively), butTestTailorachieves this with significantly lower
cost than CoverUp ($19.94 vs. $51.90).

claims.text: On ansible, TestTailor delivers steeper and more sustained coverage growth per counted test-generation LLM call than TELPA and CoverUp.

metrics.name: Coverage growth versus generation-related LLM-call count

claims.quote:
Among them,TestTailorexhibits the steepest and most sustained
growth, consistently outperforming TELPA and CoverUp in coverage improvement per unit of
LLM usage.

claims.text: TestTailor offers the best reported balance between coverage gains and monetary cost among TestTailor, TELPA and CoverUp.
claims.quote: TestTailorachieves the best balance between cost and effectiveness.

claims.text: The paper claims superior scalability as the LLM-call budget increases, based on the ansible coverage-versus-call curves.
claims.quote:
This underscores thatTestTailordelivers not only higher cost-effectiveness but also
superior scalability as the budget of LLM calls increases.

claims.text: The extended ansible experiments indicate coverage convergence with little remaining improvement; TestTailor converges at a higher coverage level than TELPA and CoverUp.
claims.quote:
It generates more
coverage improvements per LLM call than TELPA and CoverUp, and reaches convergence at
a higher coverage level with moderate resource consumption, demonstrating both efficiency
and scalability.

claims.text: On easier projects with high initial coverage, TestTailor maintains coverage competitive with the strongest external baselines, with limited additional gains.
claims.quote:
It maintains
competitive performance on simpler projects with already high baseline coverage.

claims.text: Across ten repeats on each of tqdm, sanic and cookiecutter, coverage varies little (maximum reported standard deviation 3.98% on tqdm) and TestTailor outranks every external baseline in all 30 runs.
claims.quote:
The results showed minimal variance (maximum standard
deviation of 3.98% in tqdm) and 100% ranking consistency, withTestTailoroutperforming all
baselines in all 30 runs.

claims.text: On 17 projects with strong Claude-generated initial suites, TestTailor increases statement coverage from 88.6% to 96.6% and branch coverage from 78.3% to 92.3%.
claims.quote:
ApplyingTest-
Tailorfurther increased coverage to 96.6% and 92.3%, respectively.

claims.text: Using developer-written seed suites on 24 modules, TestTailor increases statement and branch coverage by 13.37 and 9.48 percentage points.
claims.quote:
TestTailorsuccessfully boosted
statement and branch coverage by 13.37 and 9.48 percentage points, respectively.

claims.text: The paper argues that improving already strong test suites makes TestTailor suitable for regression testing or CI/CD pipelines with mature suites.
claims.quote:
This shows thatTestTailor
is not only effective in low-coverage settings but also capable of uncovering residual paths when
the baseline is already strong—making it suitable for regression testing or CI/CD pipelines where
projects typically maintain mature test suites.

claims.text: The paper infers that harness guidance matters more for these coverage gains than raw model coding ability, allowing comparatively weaker models to improve stronger-model seed suites.

evidence.description: The paper invokes Claude's higher SWE-bench ranking than the default backend; this evaluates a different task and does not isolate guidance from model capability in test generation.
evidence.page: 18, §6, Robustness with Strong Baselines and footnote 11
evidence.quote: This comparison result was obtained from https://www.swebench.com/index.html.

claims.quote:
This indicates that even
comparatively weaker models can achieve substantial gains when properly constrained toward
coverage-relevant goals.

claims.text: The paper interprets developer-suite coverage gains as evidence that TestTailor identifies complex corner cases overlooked by human developers and improves mature real-world suites.
claims.quote:
This substantial
improvement indicates that our tool can identify and cover complex corner cases that human
developers overlook, demonstrating its practical value in enhancing mature, real-world test suites.

claims.text: In the pilot study, a fourth refinement iteration per unit yields less than 1% additional coverage over three iterations.
In the pilot study, a fourth refinement iteration significantly increases API cost relative to three iterations.

thatTestWeaveraccelerates code coverage growth and generates
more effective test cases than the state-of-the-art approaches.

dataset, it achieves 68% line coverage, outperformingCoverUpand

for branch coverage,TestWeaverreaches 54%, compared to 47%

egories.

hcs.name: InterDroid
hcs.quote:
InterDroid is implemented as a fully au-
tomated GUI testing tool, which uses or extends the following tools:
VirtualBox and the Python pyvbox [ 2] for running and Android
Debug Bridge (ADB) [1] for interacting with the app.

hcs.name: InterDroid w/o Knowledge Extraction
hcs.removed: Relevant-case retrieval replaced by random historical-case selection

we remove the retrieval process for relevant historical inter-app
test cases and replace it with a random selection strategy.

hcs.quote:
For
InterDroid w/o Memory Implanting , we remove the global and
local memory mechanisms, instead adopting a traditional RAG ap-
proach that directly inputs knowledge text into the model without
maintaining structured history contexts.

visual information.

pacts performance, confirming the effectiveness of InterDroid.

edge but without structured global memory.

memory results in a 52.9% drop in EM accuracy.

claims.text: Unified SWE-Reasoner resolves 46.00%, closely matching Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 (46.20%) and exceeding OpenAI o1 (45.60%) and DeepSeek-R1 (41.20%) under SWE-SynInfer+.
claims.quote:
This unified approach closely matches the performance of the signif-
icantly larger proprietary Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 model (46.20%) and
surpasses OpenAI-o1 (45.60%) and DeepSeek-R1 (41.20%), clearly
demonstrating the effectiveness of our unfied TTC strategies.

claims.text: At 46.00%, the method ranks highest among the reported ≤100B systems, including NebiusAI and Agentless Mini with Llama3-SWE-RL.
claims.quote:
Within the≤ 100B model-size category, our method achieves the
highest issue-resolution accuracy, establishing a new state-of-the-
art.

claims.text: Internal-TTC SWE-Reasoner 32B resolves 37.60%, surpassing Llama-3.1-Instruct 405B.
claims.quote:
This approach resolves 37.6%
of issues on SWE-bench Verified with trained 32B model, surpassing
Llama 3.1 405B [27].

claims.text: Adding external TTC at budget 8 raises SWE-Reasoner's resolution rate from 37.60% to 46.00%.
claims.quote:
Our experiments demonstrate that this development-
process-based search strategy significantly improves performance
with fixed model size, and when combined with our Internal TTC
approach, yields even greater performance gains.

claims.text: Long-CoT training improves resolution from the ShortCoT control's 28.80% to 37.60%.
claims.quote:
Upon removing the Long Chain-of-
Thought (Long CoT) component (-w/o. LongCoT), we observed a
significant reduction in issue resolution accuracy from 37.60% to
28.80%.

claims.text: Repository-aware rejection sampling improves resolution from 33.00% with unfiltered training trajectories to 37.60%.
claims.quote:
This decline under-
scores the importance of carefully curated, high-quality reasoning
trajectories for effective training.

claims.text: The complete internal-TTC training achieves 37.60% resolution versus 28.00% for the prompt-CoT, untrained-base control.
claims.quote:
Table 2: Ablation experiment of the Internal TTC method,
where Resolved is the issue resolution rate on SWE-bench
Verified, and Chunk, Func, and File are the fault location
success rates at three different levels.

claims.text: SWE-Reasoner has the highest chunk/function/file localization success: 51.00/54.49/72.19%, versus ShortCoT 49.05/51.68/69.18%, no-rejection 48.76/51.94/71.38%, and no-training 44.22/47.25/60.69%.
claims.quote:
Table 2: Ablation experiment of the Internal TTC method,
where Resolved is the issue resolution rate on SWE-bench
Verified, and Chunk, Func, and File are the fault location
success rates at three different levels.

claims.text: The paper claims both internalized Long- and Short-CoT consistently outperform prompt-CoT across difficulty buckets; Figure 6 nevertheless has ShortCoT below Prompt CoT at level 3 (0.38 versus 0.44).
claims.quote:
As shown in Figure 6, models employing internalized CoT (both
Long and Short) consistently outperform Prompt-CoT-based meth-
ods.

claims.text: On the hardest bucket, LongCoT resolves 24% versus ShortCoT's 4%, approximately a sixfold rate.
claims.quote:
Crucially, our internalized Long CoT approach significantly
surpasses Short CoT performance on the hardest bucket (level 5),
achieving an issue-resolution rate approximately six times higher.

claims.text: SWE-Reasoner and OpenAI o1 generate more reasoning tokens as issue difficulty increases.
claims.quote:
From
the figure, we observe that both SWE-Reasoner and OpenAI o1 con-
tinue to adaptively allocate more reasoning tokens to increasingly
challenging tasks, demonstrating a clear test-time computation scal-
ing phenomenon.

claims.text: Dev-Search obtains the highest issue-resolution rate at each tested rollout budget, compared with ORM_Exec, Exec and the external Agentless-derived Voting strategy.
claims.quote:
First, our proposed Dev-Search strategy consistently
achieves the highest resolution rate across all budget conditions,
clearly demonstrating its overall effectiveness.

claims.text: Dev-Search's resolution performance increases as the rollout budget grows from 1 to 2, 4 and 8.
claims.quote:
Moreover, a dis-
tinct test-time compute scaling phenomenon emerges, evidenced
by steadily improving performance as inference budgets increase.

claims.text: ORM_Exec improves resolution steadily as generation budgets increase.
claims.quote:
Importantly, incorporating the ORM-based tie-
breaking method in the ORM_Exec variant mitigates this issue,
achieving stable improvements with increased budgets.

claims.text: Larger external-search budgets improve or preserve resolution in difficulty levels 1–4, with notable gains at levels 3 and 4.

metrics.name: issue-resolution rate by difficulty and rollout budget

claims.quote:
As expected, increasing inference budgets consistently improved
issue-resolution performance for difficulty levels 1 through 4, par-
ticularly notable in difficulty levels 3 and 4.

claims.text: For difficulty 5, increasing rollouts from 1 to 2 or 8 reduces resolution from 21% to 16%.
claims.quote:
However,
at the highest difficulty level (bucket 5), we observed a slight reduc-
tion in resolution accuracy when using higher inference budgets.

claims.text: The method reaches competitive large-model performance with substantially lower computational demands.
claims.quote:
Importantly, our method achieves this performance with sub-
stantially lower computational demands, emphasizing that careful
inference-time computation strategies effectively leverage smaller
models to reach competitive results.

claims.text: Across the 12 repository subsets, unified SWE-Reasoner matches or exceeds DeepSeek-R1 in most repositories and approaches the larger closed-source models in numerous cases.
claims.quote:
Notably, SWE-Reasoner-32B (TTC) matches or surpasses
the performance of DeepSeek-R1 671B in the majority of reposito-
ries, and closely approaches the performance of larger closed-source
models in numerous instances.

claims.text: The cross-repository results indicate robust generalization and potential applicability across a wide range of real-world software engineering scenarios.
claims.quote:
This consistent cross-domain perfor-
mance underscores our method’s robust generalization capabilities,
highlighting its potential applicability and effectiveness across a
wide spectrum of real-world software engineering scenarios.

claims.text: Unified TTC uniquely resolves 17 issues that the compared Claude, o1, DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3 configurations fail to solve.
claims.quote:
The diagram reveals
that our unified TTC framework uniquely solves 17 issue instances
that other models fail to address, while also sharing a substantial
number of successfully resolved issues with major models.

claims.text: Claude 3.5 Sonnet v2 shows increasing output tokens with difficulty, whereas ShortCoT does not show the trend clearly.
claims.quote:
Interestingly, we also observed that Claude3.5
Sonnet v2, despite being a model not explicitly trained for inference-
intensive computation, exhibited a similar scaling trend, whereas
ShortCoT model did not show this behavior clearly.

claims.text: Exec's resolution rate falls at generation budget 8.
claims.quote:
Conversely, the Exec baseline exhibited an unexpected drop in per-
formance at the highest budget (budget=8).

claims.text: ORM-based tie-breaking mitigates the instability seen with random tie-breaking in Exec.
claims.quote:
Importantly, incorporating the ORM-based tie-
breaking method in the ORM_Exec variant mitigates this issue,
achieving stable improvements with increased budgets.

claims.text: Exec's high-budget decline may reflect false-positive verification caused by limited coverage or incomplete reproduction, amplified by random patch selection.
claims.quote:
A potential explanation
for this performance decline is that execution-based verification
alone (specifically, reproducing code functionality) might occasion-
ally yield false positives due to limited coverage and incomplete re-
producibility, leading to instability when randomly selecting among
candidate patches.

claims.text: The hardest-bucket decline suggests external-search gains may be limited by the underlying model's reasoning capability.
claims.quote:
This counterintuitive finding suggests that, for extremely challeng-
ing tasks, the effectiveness of external compute strategies may reach
inherent limitations imposed by the model’s reasoning capabilities.

claims.text: Additional external compute allows exploration of broader reasoning trajectories.
claims.quote:
This clearly indicates
that additional test-time compute can indeed enhance model perfor-
mance, allowing the agent to explore broader reasoning trajectories
and effectively handle moderately challenging problems.

If function pass all test

hcs.quote:
In addition, we build baseline
approaches, BaseChatGPT, BaseCodeLlama, BaseDeepSeek, and
BaseStarCoder, which utilize the basic LLMs to perform a repair (i.e.,
directly using existing bug-fixing data as examples) without any
Chains-of-Thoughts reasoning process and feedback information.

hcs.name: ThinkRepair-v1: no interaction feedback
hcs.removed: Interaction feedback and within-session feedback-driven revision removed; CoT collection, selection and candidate verification retained.
hcs.page: 9, §5.3 and Table 8; 3–5, retained collection and verification mechanisms
hcs.quote:
We build a variant of ThinkRepair without
interaction feedback as ThinkRepair-v1 and another variant with-
out CoT few-shot learning as ThinkRepair-v2.

hcs.name: ThinkRepair-v2: no CoT few-shot learning
hcs.removed: CoT knowledge collection, stored CoTs and automatic few-shot selection removed; ordinary bug-fix examples retained with interaction feedback.
hcs.quote:
We build a variant of ThinkRepair without
interaction feedback as ThinkRepair-v1 and another variant with-
out CoT few-shot learning as ThinkRepair-v2.

hcs.name: ThinkRepair with Semantic-based Selection
hcs.removed: Contrastively fine-tuned UniXcoder replaced by pretrained UniXcoder for semantic embedding; clustering and cosine selection retained.
hcs.quote:
During the fixing
phase, the most semantic similar examples are picked out from
each cluster based on cosine similarity.

hcs.name: ThinkRepair with IR-based Selection
hcs.removed: Contrastive semantic embedding, clustering and cosine selection replaced by indexed BM25 retrieval.
hcs.quote:
IR-based Selection builds indexes for code in the knowledge

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: The 98 correct patches from Defects4J V1.2, perfect-fault condition
ecs.protocol: Post-hoc lexical comparison with developer fixes; 24/98 lexical matches; remaining correct patches assessed as semantically equivalent; no new generation run.
ecs.quote:
We find that out of 98 correct patches, 24 of them lexically match the
ground-truth (24.5%), while the other patches semantically match
the ground-truth.

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Defects4J V1.2 correct-patch set after excluding 24 lexical matches
ecs.protocol: Post-hoc exclusion and overlap analysis against prior methods; 29 remaining uniquely repaired bugs; no new generation run.
ecs.quote:
Moreover, even
after excluding all the correct patches (24) that aligned with the ref-
erence developer patch, ThinkRepair is still capable of generating
the correct patch for 29 unique bugs, none of which could be fixed
by any previous methods.

claims.text: On Defects4J V1.2 with perfect fault information, ThinkRepair improves correct-fix totals over the corresponding basic LLMs by 59.1%–88.5%: 98/70/63/59 versus 52/44/39/37.
claims.quote:
In particular, the performance of ThinkRepair is
significantly better than Basic LLM with improvements ranging
from 59.1%∼88.5%.

claims.text: Improvement with ChatGPT, CodeLlama, DeepSeek and StarCoder supports the claimed LLM-agnostic applicability of ThinkRepair.

metrics.name: Correct-patch improvement across four backend LLMs

claims.quote:
This not only demonstrates the superiority of
our ThinkRepair approach, but also its universal applicability, as it
is not tailored for any specific LLM, but is suitable for various LLMs.

claims.text: ThinkRepair fixes 98 Defects4J V1.2 single-function bugs with perfect fault information, 22 more than external comparator ChatRepair, a 28.9% improvement.

metrics.name: Difference and relative improvement over ChatRepair

claims.quote:
With the perfect
fault information provided, ThinkRepair can auto-fix 98 bugs and
22 more bugs (28.9% improvements) than ChatRepair for single func-
tion bugs in Defects4J V1.2.

claims.text: With perfect fault information, ThinkRepair matches external comparator ChatRepair on QuixBugs, fixing 39 Java bugs and all 40 Python bugs.
claims.quote:
For the QuixBugs dataset, ThinkRepair
and ChatRepair can auto-fix the same number of bugs.

claims.text: ThinkRepair improves over BaseChatGPT across Defects4J V1.2 repair subsets: method-level gains are 122.2%, 128.6% and 120% for SF/SH/SL, and perfect-fault gains are 88.5%, 77.3% and 67.7%; project results also favor ThinkRepair, with Closure gains of 280% and 138.5%.

metrics.name: Correct patches by repair subset and project

claims.quote:
When provided with perfect fault information,
ThinkRepair can auto-fix 88.5%, 77.3%, and 67.7% more bugs for
single function, single hunk, and single line bugs in Defects4J V1.2.

claims.text: ThinkRepair also outperforms BaseChatGPT on Defects4J V2.0 across the reported fault-information conditions and SF/SH/SL subsets.
claims.quote:
Similarly, on Defects4J V2.0, ThinkRepair achieves an overwhelm-
ing better performance than BaseChatGPT.

claims.text: With perfect fault information, ThinkRepair fixes 31 more Defects4J V1.2 single-function bugs than external comparator AlphaRepair, a 46.3% improvement; its largest project gains are 8–9 bugs in Closure, Lang and Math.
claims.quote:
In particu-
lar, the performance of ThinkRepair is significantly better than
AlphaRepair in three projects (Closure, Lang, and Math), with im-
provements ranging from 8 to 9 bugs (40.9%∼72.7%).

claims.text: With method-level fault information, ThinkRepair fixes 80 Defects4J V1.2 single-function bugs versus external comparator Codex's 63, an improvement of 17 bugs or 27%.
claims.quote: (46.3%) than AlphaRepair with the perfect fault information provided, and auto-fix 17 (27%) and 62 (344.4%) more bugs than Codex and GPT-NeoX with only method-level fault information provided, respectively.

claims.text: With method-level fault information, ThinkRepair fixes 80 Defects4J V1.2 single-function bugs versus external comparator GPT-NeoX's 18, an improvement of 62 bugs or 344.4%.
claims.quote: auto-fix 17 (27%) and 62 (344.4%) more bugs than Codex and GPT-NeoX with only method-level fault information provided, respectively.

claims.text: ThinkRepair with CodeLlama can match or surpass external comparator AlphaRepair despite the basic CodeLlama control's weaker repair results.
claims.quote:
However, under our unsupervised setting,
CodeLlama (i.e., ThinkRepair*) can achieve performance on par
with or surpass supervised approach (i.e., AlphaRepair).

claims.text: ThinkRepair uniquely fixes 31 Defects4J V1.2 bugs that neither BaseChatGPT nor external comparator AlphaRepair fixes.

metrics.name: Number of uniquely correctly fixed bugs

claims.quote:
It is
noteworthy that ThinkRepair successfully fixes 31 unique bugs that
BaseChatGPT and AlphaRepair are unable to resolve.

claims.text: ThinkRepair outperforms the reported NMT-based comparators on Defects4J V1.2, fixing 98 bugs versus 37–67 and improving totals by 46.3%–164.9%; its project counts are highest or tied highest.
claims.quote:
With the perfect fault information, ThinkRe-
pair achieves the best overall performance with a total of 98 bug
fixes, representing a significant improvement over the NMT-based
baselines, in the range of 46.3% (67 of KNOD)∼164.9% (37 of DLFix).

claims.text: ThinkRepair with CodeLlama fixes 70 Defects4J V1.2 bugs, 3–33 more than the reported NMT-based comparators.
claims.quote:
Specifi-
cally, ThinkRepair* fixes 3∼33 more bugs than the SOTA APRs.

claims.text: ThinkRepair is claimed to offer good efficiency because it considers at most 125 candidate patches per bug, whereas some NMT comparators consider up to 10,000.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, ThinkRepair generates far fewer patches (≤ 125 in
total per bug) than the NMT-based approaches that may generate
up to 10,000 patches per bug [21, 40], which indicates ThinkRepair
can also ensure a good efficiency.

claims.text: ThinkRepair complements the NMT-based comparators by uniquely fixing 32 Defects4J V1.2 bugs, the largest unique-fix count in that comparison.

metrics.name: Number of uniquely correctly fixed bugs

claims.quote:
Overall, ThinkRepair has a more powerful ability
than baselines since it can auto-fix the most number of unique bugs
(i.e., 32) that other baselines can hardly fix.

claims.text: On Defects4J V2.0, ThinkRepair fixes 107 bugs, 60–65 more than the reported NMT-based comparators, an improvement of 127.7%–154.8%.
claims.quote:
ThinkRepair can auto-fix 107 bugs on Defects4J V2.0,
with 60∼65 (127.7%∼154.8%) more bugs than the current state-of-
the-art NMT-based APRs.

claims.text: On Defects4J V2.0, CodeLlama-backed ThinkRepair fixes 72 bugs and improves over the reported NMT comparators by 53.2%–71.4%.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, ThinkRepair* fixes 72 bugs
and improves baselines by 53.2%∼71.4%.

claims.text: ThinkRepair fixes 39 QuixBugs-Java bugs, 14–26 more than the reported NMT-based comparators.
claims.quote:
Additionally, ThinkRepair
has improved NMT-based baselines by fixing 14∼26 more bugs on
QuixBugs-Java and 19∼21 bugs on QuixBugs-Python.

claims.text: ThinkRepair fixes all 40 QuixBugs-Python bugs, 19–21 more than the reported NMT-based comparators.
claims.quote:
Additionally, ThinkRepair
has improved NMT-based baselines by fixing 14∼26 more bugs on
QuixBugs-Java and 19∼21 bugs on QuixBugs-Python.

claims.text: Adding CoT knowledge collection and few-shot selection without feedback raises correct fixes from the ordinary few-shot control's 36 to 57.
claims.quote:
The combination between“Knowledge
Collection” and “Few-Shot Selection” is effective for ThinkRepair,
which improves ChatGPT a lot (i.e., 36→57) and emphasizes the
importance of prompting ChatGPT by selecting high-quality of
examples.

claims.text: Adding interaction feedback without CoT few-shot learning raises correct fixes from 36 to 62.
claims.quote:
The “Interaction Feedback” seems to contribute the
performance of ThinkRepair, which brings ChatGPT with a large
improvement (i.e., 36→62).

claims.text: Combining CoT few-shot learning and feedback gives the best component-study result: 80 correct fixes versus 57 without feedback, 62 without CoT few-shot learning and 36 for the ordinary few-shot control.
claims.quote:
ThinkRepair is capable of generating 44 more correct fixes than
ChatGPT with a few-shot setting (i.e., 36→80).

claims.text: Increasing the interaction limit from one to five improves correct fixes from 57 to 80, with the largest increase at two interactions, which produces 75 fixes.

metrics.name: Correct patches by maximum interaction count

claims.quote:
Notice that
ThinkRepair has a big improvement when interacting twice with
ChatGPT (i.e., 57→75).

claims.text: Additional interactions have diminishing repair benefit: correct fixes rise only from 75 to 80 after the second interaction and remain 80 at limits five, six and seven.

metrics.name: Correct patches by maximum interaction count

claims.quote:
However, when continuously increasing
the number of interactions, the rate of performance improvement
decreases (i.e., 75→80) and meanwhile, the interaction cost with
ChatGPT is increasing.

claims.text: Semantic and contrastive example selection yield more correct fixes overall than BM25 and random selection: 235 and 249 versus 225 and 222; their gains over random selection are 13 and 27 bugs.

metrics.name: Correct patches by selection strategy and benchmark

claims.quote: (1) BothContrastive-based Selection and Semantic-based Selection help to generate more correct fixes than IR-based Selection and Randomly Selection, which indicates the importance of the semantic similarity among samples.

claims.text: Contrastive selection is the best-performing tested example-selection strategy overall, with 249 correct fixes versus semantic selection's 235.

metrics.name: Total correct patches across four benchmarks

claims.quote:
Overall, Contrastive-based Selection performs
the best and shows promising results in selecting high-quality ex-
amples, which may benefit from the well-trained semantic encoder
(i.e., UniXcoder) fine-tuned with contrastive learning.

claims.text: ThinkRepair repairs bugs beyond Defects4J and QuixBugs: ChatGPT-backed ThinkRepair fixes 19/44 RWB V1.0 bugs, and DeepSeek-backed ThinkRepair fixes 10/29 RWB V2.0 bugs.

metrics.name: Correct patches on newly collected real-world bugs

claims.quote:
According to
the results, we can conclude that ThinkRepair possesses the abil-
ity to fix bugs in real-world projects, not just limited to the bugs
present in the Defects4J dataset and QuixBugs dataset.

claims.text: Both RWB evaluations outperform external comparator AlphaRepair: 19 versus 9 correct fixes on V1.0 and 10 versus 6 on V2.0.
claims.quote:
Furthermore,
both ThinkRepair and ThinkRepair* outperform AlphaRepair, un-
derscoring the practicality and viability of our approach.

formance improvement is limited (i.e., 34→36).

claims.text: In the Mockito-29 case, ThinkRepair preserves intended functionality and correctly handles null, whereas BaseChatGPT changes an intended output string and fails to repair the bug correctly.

claims.quote:

accurately recognizes the importance of preserving the original

failing tests to directly guide the repair process.

claims.text: Increasing the allowed number of interactions increases communication cost, motivating the default limit of five as a cost-effectiveness compromise.

ment and the communication cost caused by ChatGPT, we adopt

hcs.name: TLR
hcs.quote:
Guided by a finite typestate automaton (FTA), we
use a debugger to execute the program step-by-step, extracting the error-propagation path from the
nearest related memory allocation to the error-triggering point.

hcs.name: TLR-F
hcs.removed: Typestate-guided error-trace retrieval replaced with the error report and implicated program-file context.
hcs.quote:
The first baseline,
TLR-F, incorporates the error report alongside program files directly implicated in the error-
triggering point.

hcs.name: TLR-M
hcs.removed: Typestate-guided error-trace retrieval replaced with the error report and functions identified in the error backtrace.
hcs.quote:
The second baseline,TLR-M, extends this approach by including all functions
identified in the error backtrace in addition to the error report.

hcs.name: TLR-NT
hcs.removed: Context trace omitted from prompts; error report, error-propagation path and other components retained.
hcs.quote:
TLR-NT omits the context trace in the prompts while maintaining all other
components unchanged (such as bug report and error-propagation path), allowing us to measure
the specific impact of typestate-guided context trace information.

evidence.detail: The Pylint example describes inspection of signatures and bodies in expand_modules.py.
evidence.quote:
It then analyzes the method signatures of this file
to confirm its relevance and inspects method bodies to uncover the failure-inducing logic.

claims.quote:
The performance improvement of GenLoc over GenLoc-NoEmbed and GenLoc-Naive indicates
that GenLoc goes beyond superficial cues (e.g., filenames or keywords) and performs deeper rea-
soning.

claims.text: NoEmbed and Naive obtain similar aggregate localization results: Accuracy@1 46.05% versus 46.31%, MAP@10 0.42 versus 0.43, and MRR@10 0.50 for both.
claims.quote:
Although GenLoc-NoEmbed and GenLoc-Naive obtain sim-
ilar results, the overlap analysis (Fig. 9) shows that they
capture distinct subsets of bugs.

claims.text: NoEmbed and Naive localize distinct subsets of bugs despite their similar aggregate scores.
claims.quote:
Although GenLoc-NoEmbed and GenLoc-Naive obtain sim-
ilar results, the overlap analysis (Fig. 9) shows that they
capture distinct subsets of bugs.

claims.text: Post-processing is said to correct erroneous fully qualified filenames, including omitted package segments; no separate path-validity rate is reported.
claims.quote:
Post-processing
corrects these errors and refines the final ranking, leading to more accurate localization results.

claims.text: GPT-4o-mini is presented as suitable for large-scale or budget-constrained use because it combines competitive localization performance with lower per-bug cost.
claims.quote:
Despite this cost difference, GPT-4o-mini delivers
competitive performance, making it suitable for large-scale or budget-constrained settings, whereas
GPT-5.1 is preferable when maximizing localization accuracy is the primary objective.

claims.text: GenLoc reportedly averages 47.7 seconds per bug across the experiments; dataset-specific timing and the timing aggregation procedure are not reported in the supplied text.
claims.quote:
GenLoc takes on average 47.7 seconds per bug in our experiments; detailed runtime and cost analyses are provided in the
replication package.

claims.text: The authors infer that combining all four non-retrieval exploration functions supports broader bug coverage from the distinct bug subsets found by NoEmbed and Naive.
claims.quote:
This demonstrates the im-
portance of combining all four functions, search_file(),
search_method(), get_method_signatures_of_a_file() and
get_method_body(), to achieve broader coverage.
