claims.text: Detailed prompts produce 2–6 semantically valid MRs per case study, compared with 0–2 for none prompts.

metrics.name: SEM: number of semantically valid MRs

claims.quote: The detailed configuration consistently achieves the best results, yielding between 2 and 6 semantically valid MRs per case study.

claims.text: The paper reports that removing prompt information generally reduces the number of syntactically valid inferred MRs.

metrics.name: SYN: number of syntactically valid MRs

claims.quote: This is reflected in a gradual decrease in the number of syntactically and semantically valid MRs, with semantic validity being the most affected.

claims.text: Semantic validity is more affected by removing prompt information than syntactic validity.

metrics.name: SEM: number of semantically valid MRs
SYN: number of syntactically valid MRs

claims.quote: This is reflected in a gradual decrease in the number of syntactically and semantically valid MRs, with semantic validity being the most affected.

claims.text: Removing original MRs harms semantic validity more than removing input features, with a larger drop in three of four cases.
claims.quote: Comparing configurations, removing the original MRs (noMR) has a stronger negative impact than removing the input features (noIF ), especially regarding semantic validity.

claims.text: The paper reports that including the fixed example specification increases the number of inferred MRs.
claims.quote: Including an example in the prompt has an effect, too: when it is removed (no-example), the assistant performance drops across all configurations, in terms of both the number of derived MRs and their validity.

claims.text: The paper reports that including the fixed example specification improves inferred-MR validity.
claims.quote: Including an example in the prompt has an effect, too: when it is removed (no-example), the assistant performance drops across all configurations, in terms of both the number of derived MRs and their validity.

claims.text: MR inference is fast within the evaluated scope: median times are 11.7–36.4 seconds and mean time per semantically valid MR is 9.97 seconds.

metrics.name: Median inference time over five executions
Mean seconds per semantically valid MR

claims.quote: As Table  3 shows, inference was fast, with median times between 11.7 and 36.4 s, and an average computation time of 9.97 s per semantically valid MR.

claims.text: Inferred MRs are largely diverse under the composite signatures; mean pairwise similarities are 0.247, 0.197, 0.286 and 0.179 for Data Centres, Autonomous Vehicles, Automata and Words.

metrics.name: Composite pairwise Jaccard similarity of footprint, signed and structural signatures

claims.quote: These results indicate that the inferred MRs are largely diverse, although a small subset exhibits moderate similarity (between 0.4 and 0.7).

claims.text: AI-inferred MRs tend to have lower structural complexity than human-designed reference MRs across all case studies.
claims.quote: We observe that the inferred MRs have comparable depth but tend to be simpler than human-designed MRs, as reflected by the smaller tree size, volume and effort in all case studies.

claims.text: Inferred and human-designed MRs have comparable nesting depth, typically around 3–4.
claims.quote: Depth remains in a narrow range for both inferred and human-designed MRs (typically 3–4), suggesting that the assistant preserves their characteristic nesting structure rather than producing oversimplified MRs.

claims.text: In Data Centres, the assistant recovers one human-designed MR exactly and two approximately similar variants.
claims.quote: In addition, in the data centres case study, the assistant generated an MR identical to one from the original work, and two others achieved approximately 70% similarity.

claims.text: For every evaluated MR, at least one LLM generates all requested follow-ups correctly.

metrics.name: Percentage of correct follow-ups per MR

claims.quote: We can observe that the assistive task generally obtained good results, since for every MR, at least one LLM correctly generated the number of requested follow-ups.

claims.text: Mean follow-up correctness is highest for Autonomous Vehicles at 95.4%, followed by Data Centres at 87.24%, Words at 83.3% and Automata at 78.6%.

metrics.name: Mean percentage of correct follow-ups by case study

claims.quote: The case study with the best results was autonomous vehicles (an average effectiveness of 95.4% for all LLMs), followed by data centres (87.24%), words (83.3%) and automata (78.6%).

claims.text: o4-mini and gpt-5-mini achieve the best reported overall correctness, 99.61% and 99.22%, with all follow-ups correct for eight and nine of the twelve MRs respectively.

metrics.name: Number of MRs with all requested follow-ups correct

claims.quote: We observe that the best overall LLMs for this task were o4-mini and gpt-5-mini, as they achieved correctness percentages of 99.61% and 99.22%.

claims.text: Most or all follow-ups generated with o4-mini and gpt-5-mini are different, at 99.9% and 100% respectively.
claims.quote: They also correctly generated all follow-ups for 8 and 9 MRs out of 12 (66.7% and 75%), and most or all generated follow-ups were different (99.9% and 100%).

claims.text: Repair feedback improves follow-up correctness overall; Table 11 reports mean gains of 12.2, 2.17, 34.57, 12.7 and 1.35 percentage points for the five LLMs, with the largest gain for gpt-4o-mini.

metrics.name: Correctness percentage-point improvement from repair loops

claims.quote: Table  7 shows the effect of the semantic loops: all case studies and LLMs benefited from them.

claims.text: Semantic repair has a larger effect on follow-up-generation effectiveness than syntactic repair.
claims.quote: We focus just on the ‘‘semantic’’ loop (i.e., checking if the generated model is a follow-up), as it had a much bigger impact on the overall effectiveness than the syntactic loop.

claims.text: Increasing source size reduces correctness in 60% of model/domain combinations; gpt-5-nano on Data Centres drops from 100% to 14%.

metrics.name: Correctness percentage-point difference between smallest and largest source cases
Fraction of model/domain conditions with degraded correctness

claims.quote: We can observe that size impacted most LLMs and domains, since in 60% of the cases, the performance with bigger source test cases was worse.

claims.text: Reasoning LLMs are more stable as source size increases: reported mean correctness changes are −1.08 points for o4-mini and +2.08 for gpt-5-mini, versus −46.5 for gpt-5-nano, −27 for gpt-4o-mini and −12.41 for gpt-4.1-mini.

metrics.name: Mean correctness change between smallest and largest source cases

claims.quote: The LLMs with better scalability were o4-mini and gpt-5-mini, while the least scalable was gpt-5-nano.

claims.text: Follow-up-generation time generally increases with source test case size.

metrics.name: Mean follow-up-generation time in seconds by source size

claims.quote: Finally, we observe that execution times tend to increase with source test case size.

claims.text: Repair loops add computational cost because every repair cycle incurs an additional LLM call; the paper characterises the overall cost impact as slight.
claims.quote: We report the number of cycles, since each cycle implies a call to the LLM, increasing the computational cost.

claims.text: gpt-4.1-mini is fastest in 17 of 20 domain/size conditions; o4-mini and gpt-5-mini win the remaining three larger-case conditions.

metrics.name: Number of domain/size conditions with fastest time

claims.quote: gpt-4.1-mini was the fastest LLM 17 out of 20 times.

claims.text: Reasoning LLMs have better time scalability: mean increases from smallest to largest source cases are 28.18 seconds for o4-mini and 36.25 for gpt-5-mini, compared with 50.79–123.33 for the other models.

metrics.name: Mean time increase from smallest to largest source test case

claims.quote: However, reasoning LLMs (o4-mini and gpt-5-mini) showed better time degradation with size than the other LLMs.

claims.text: The assistant produces MRs of human-plausible complexity, generally favouring simpler formulations.

metrics.name: AST size and depth relative to human-designed MRs

evidence.quote: In addition, in the data centres case study, the assistant generated an MR identical to one from the original work, and two others achieved approximately 70% similarity.

claims.quote: These results suggest that the assistant can infer MRs with a human-plausible complexity, although often tends towards simpler contexts.

claims.text: Across prompt conditions, the assistant generates 10, 14, 6 and 4 different MRs; 8, 12, 4 and 2 respectively are absent from the prompt examples, giving 26 new MRs.

metrics.name: Number of inferred MRs absent from prompt examples

claims.quote: Across configurations, the assistant generated 10, 14, 6 and 4 different MRs for data centres, autonomous vehicles, automata and words, respectively, of which 8, 12, 4 and 2 MRs were not included as examples in the prompt.

claims.text: The first semantic-repair iteration contributes the largest share of corrections: 58.6%, 78.1%, 100% and 71.2% by domain; the third contributes the least.

metrics.name: Iteration's share of total correctness improvement

claims.quote: On average, the iteration that achieved the greatest increase in correctness percentage (i.e., fixed the most errors) was the first one, with 58.6% for data centres, 78.1% for autonomous vehicles, 100% for automata, and 71.2% for words.

claims.text: Residual errors become harder to repair in later iterations, as unsuccessful-repair percentages generally increase.

metrics.name: Percentage of unsuccessful repair attempts by iteration

claims.quote: First, most fixes succeed in the first iteration (which is also observed in Table  7), and errors become more difficult to fix in subsequent iterations.

claims.text: Automata and Words are the hardest domains to repair, with unsuccessful-repair rates of 93.20% and 91.95%.

metrics.name: Aggregated percentage of unsuccessful repairs by domain

claims.quote: Second, the most difficult case studies to fix were automata and words, with unsuccessful rates of 93.20% and 91.95%.

claims.text: gpt-4.1-mini has the lowest overall unsuccessful-repair rate, 52.84%.

metrics.name: Overall percentage of unsuccessful repairs per LLM

claims.quote: Finally, the LLM with the lowest rate of unsuccessful fixes was gpt-4.1-mini.

claims.text: Syntactic repair is rarely needed: 1.3% of follow-ups trigger it, with 91.8% of those triggers attributed to gpt-5-nano, 6.6% to gpt-4o-mini and 1.6% to o4-mini.

metrics.name: Percentage of generated follow-ups triggering XMI repair

claims.quote: Specifically, the XMI fixer was triggered for a 1.3% of the generated follow-ups, and of those, a 91.8% was for gpt-5-nano, a 6.6% for gpt-4o-mini, and a 1.6% for o4-mini.

claims.text: Removing input-feature definitions tends to produce simpler MRs while preserving the original MR templates.
claims.quote: In  contrast, when removing input features (noIF ), the assistant still relies on these templates, but it tends to generate simpler MRs.

claims.text: The Data Centres inferred-MR collection contains redundancy: 28.2% of pairs have similarity in [0.5,0.7), and three MRs are equal.
claims.quote: However, a 28.2% of pairs lies in the [0.5, 0.7) range, indicating MR pairs moderately similar, and 3 MRs were found to be equal (similarity 1).

claims.text: Some Autonomous Vehicles inferred MRs exceed human-reference complexity despite lower averages; maximum Halstead effort is 66.44 versus 47.55.

metrics.name: Mean AST size and Halstead effort

claims.quote: The inferred MRs show slightly lower average tree size (13 vs 11.33) and effort (47.55 vs 37.35), though some reach or even surpass the effort of the human-designed MRs (maximum effort 47.55 vs 66.44).

claims.text: gpt-4o-mini's many repair cycles produce high overall generation times despite its token-generation speed.
claims.quote: The case of gpt-4o-mini is interesting, as it has good speed in tokens/s, but generally needs to perform many repair cycles, resulting in overall higher times than other LLMs (even reasoning ones).

claims.text: For gpt-5-mini on Words, six repairs make the smallest-size condition relatively slow.

metrics.name: Mean generation seconds by source size

claims.quote: This can be seen in the words case study for gpt-5-mini, in which one of the slowest times was with the smallest source test case (size 1), because it needed 6 repairs.

claims.text: The example setting has slightly lower MR-inference latency except for Words, but the difference is not statistically significant.

evidence.quote: In all case studies except words, inference latency was slightly lower in the example setting than in the no-example one, but the difference is not statistically significant according to the Wilcoxon test.

claims.quote: In all case studies except words, inference latency was slightly lower in the example setting than in the no-example one, but the difference is not statistically significant according to the Wilcoxon test.

claims.text: The observed trade-offs suggest using gpt-4.1-mini for small source cases and reasoning LLMs for larger or more complex cases.
claims.quote: Hence, considering all factors, using a fast LLM like gpt-4.1-mini is sufficient for small source test cases, whereas a reasoning LLM may pay off for large source test cases or complex domains.

claims.text: Automatically inferred MRs may reduce human MR-elicitation effort; actual effort reduction is not measured.

metrics.name: Number of valid and new inferred MRs

claims.quote: In practice, this means that the inferred MRs may reduce the effort of MR elicitation, but their fault-revealing effectiveness still requires dedicated assessment, for instance through mutation testing.

claims.text: The lower follow-up-generation success for Automata may be caused by its more complex graph structure.
claims.quote: This may be attributed to the fact that automata have the inputs with the most complex structure, with transitions connecting three different objects (the source and target states, and the symbol).

claims.text: Semantic improvement loops benefit Autonomous Vehicles most (up 119.2 points summed over LLMs), followed by Data Centres (86.3), Words (23.3) and Automata (23.2).

metrics.name: Summed correctness percentage-point gain from improvement iterations

claims.quote: The case study that benefited the most was autonomous vehicles (up by 119.2 percentual points), followed by data centres (up by 86.3 percentual points), words (up by 23.3 percentual points) and automata (up by 23.2 percentual points).

claims.text: TF-Pro generates correct option combinations for 85% of the 60-case benchmark, versus 45% for LLM_o and 50% for LLM_p.
claims.quote:
Trans ferFuzz-Pro successfu lly generated ideal op-
tion combinations for 85.0% of target binaries, signiﬁcantly
outperforming LLM
o and LLMp, which achieved 45.0% and
50.0%, respectively.

claims.text: Automated option generation takes under 90 seconds, compared with over 20 minutes per case for an expert performing the manual analysis required by external comparator TransferFuzz.
claims.quote:
As shown in Fig. 7, TF-Pro adds less
than 90 seconds for automated option generation.

claims.text: TF-Pro validates all 38 propagated target cases, giving recall 1.0 and expanding the affected-instance scope of 15 CVEs from 15 to 53; its recall exceeds OCTOPOCs, AFLGo, Windranger, SelectFuzz and DAFL.

metrics.name: Correctly validated propagated cases / affected-instance count

claims.quote:
As shown in Table IV, TransferFuzz-Pro achieves a pre-
cision of 1.0 and a recall of 1.0, successfully validating all
38 propagated vulnerability samp les.

claims.text: TF-Pro achieves precision 1.0 with no false positives and 108 true negatives, improving on LibAM's precision of 0.260 while matching the other verification methods' precision.
claims.quote:
As shown in Table IV, TransferFuzz-Pro achieves a pre-
cision of 1.0 and a recall of 1.0, successfully validating all
38 propagated vulnerability samp les.

claims.text: The source-instrumented TF-Pro fuzzing stage is reported to be 2.5–26.2 times faster than the compared directed fuzzers, including approximately 2.5 times faster than SelectFuzz.
claims.quote:
It veriﬁed more vul-
nerabilities than existing m ethods and achieved a speedup of
2.5x to 26.2x.

claims.text: Binary-instrumented TF-Pro generates PoCs for the vulnerable binaries in all eight listed Linux distribution/version settings, including settings unavailable to external comparator TransferFuzz because source code is missing.
claims.quote:
The results demonstrate that TransferFuzz-Pro
can generate PoCs for real-world binaries, even in the absence
of source code, by leveraging binary instrumentation.

claims.text: KBGM improves fuzzing efficiency, with especially large benefits on the complex Binutils vulnerability cases.
claims.quote:
In the absence of KBGM (No KBGM), TransferFuzz-Pro
showed a signiﬁcant drop in efﬁciency due to the lack of key-
byte traces from taint analysis, which are critical for bypassing
essential constraints.

claims.text: The authors claim that NSA improves efficiency across all tested vulnerabilities; Table VI nevertheless contains a tie and several reversals.
claims.quote:
A consistent reduction in efﬁciency was observed, as the NSA
module contributed to performance improvements across all
tested vulnerabilities.

claims.text: Without KBGM, Table VI reports no successful exposure for CVE-2016-4491 and CVE-2016-6131 on objdump, nm-new and addr2line, whereas the full configuration exposes them.
claims.page: 12, §V-F; 13, Table VI, CVE-2016-4491 and CVE-2016-6131 rows
claims.quote:
This performance degradation was par-
ticularly evident for vul nerabilities such as CVE-2016-4490,
CVE-2016-4491, CVE-2016-4492, and CVE-2016-6131.

claims.text: The binary-instrumented variant remains faster than existing verification methods despite its instrumentation overhead.
claims.quote:
TF-Pro_bin veriﬁcation speed
is slightly slower but s till exceeds existing methods.

claims.text: Successful source-instrumented verifications generally finish within 60 minutes; the discussion gives the stronger summary that verification finishes within two hours and over half of cases take under one minute.
claims.quote:
Despite these challenges,
TransferFuzz-Pro consistently completed vulnerability veriﬁca-
tions within two hours, with over half of the cases resolved in
under one minute.

claims.text: Without using base-binary PoCs as initial seeds, TransferFuzz-Pro fails to generate PoCs for CVE-2017-18267, CVE-2018-11102 and CVE-2018-20330, as do the external compared methods.
claims.quote:
However, without leveraging PoCs from the base binary, none
of the methods, including TransferFuzz-Pro, were able to gen-
erate PoCs for three vul nerabilities (CVE-2017-18267, CVE-
2018-11102, and CVE-2018-20330).

claims.text: TF-Pro preserves external comparator TransferFuzz's fuzzing performance because the fuzzing stage is unchanged.
claims.quote:
TF-Pro preserves the efﬁciency of
TransferFuzz, as it does not modify the fuzzing process.

claims.text: Binary instrumentation makes TF-Pro slightly slower than source instrumentation while retaining the same successful-run counts in Table V.
claims.quote:
TF-Pro matches TransferFuzz’s performance (no fuzzing
modiﬁcations), while TF-Pro
bin incurs minor slowdowns due
to binary instrumentation.

As illustrated in Fig. 8, the resource
consumption of TF/TF-Pro is comparable to AFLGo, Select-
Fuzz, and DAFL.

For TF-
Pro

sistent with other binary instrumentation-based fuzzing tools.

claims.text: The authors consider the measured resource consumption manageable for practical vulnerability verification.
claims.quote:
Despite this, the
resource consumption of all methods, including TransferFuzz-
Pro, remains manageable and doesnot hinder their applicability
for vulnerability veriﬁcation.

claims.text: The selected Claude3.5-Sonnet option-generation implementation costs approximately $0.30 per case.
claims.quote:
In our experiments, the cost per case was
approximately $0.3.

claims.text: GPT-4o and o1-preview provide no significant performance gains over the selected base model on the option-generation task; numerical results and statistical testing are not reported.
claims.quote:
More powerful
models, such as GPT-4o or o1-preview, provided no signiﬁcant
performance gains.

claims.text: The observed maximum number of option-generation iterations is seven.
claims.quote:
The maximum number of iterations for
TransferFuzz-Pro was 7.

claims.text: All evaluated numeric parameters with loose restrictions are successfully generated, including addr2line's address input.

metrics.name: Correct generation of loosely constrained numeric parameters

claims.quote:
In our evaluation, all the numbers with loose
restrictions were successfully generated.

claims.text: For objdump, LLM-driven debugging finds more vulnerability-triggering option combinations than prior manual analysis.
claims.quote:
For objdump, the LLM identiﬁed
more option combinations capable of triggering vulnerabilities
compared to prior manual analysis.

claims.text: Exact numeric requirements can defeat option generation: split's -C option is found, but the required value 1024 is not correctly supplied.
claims.quote:
Nonetheless, it can still generate the required
“-C” option except for the precise number, effectively reducing
manual effort.

claims.text: Option generation has difficulty when code lacks clear semantic cues, especially for niche projects lacking useful model knowledge.
claims.quote:
On the other hand, TransferFuzz-Pro encounters
difﬁculty when option selection lacks clear semantic cues in
the code.

claims.text: The direct-generation and code-input-only controls struggle with specific or complex option combinations.
claims.quote:
In contrast, the other two methods struggle with cases requir-
ing speciﬁc options or complex combinations.

claims.text: KBGM's contribution varies across cases; its impact is described as minimal for CVE-2017-11733.
claims.quote:
How-
ever, the impact on CVE-2017-11733 was minimal, indicating
that KBGM’s effectiveness in extracting key bytes is not uni-
form across all cases.

claims.text: The authors report that No KBGM remains faster than alternative external methods despite its degradation relative to full TF-Pro.
claims.quote:
Despite this limitation, No KBGM still
outperformed alternative methods in terms of speed.

claims.text: Removing NSA is reported to cause a less severe performance decline than removing KBGM.
claims.quote:
For No NSA, TransferFuzz-Pro also experienced a decline in
performance, though it was less severe compared to No KBGM.

claims.text: Key-byte traces cannot be extracted for every vulnerability, with CVE-2017-7303 given as an observed example.
claims.quote:
Not
all vulnerabilities allow for the extraction of key-byte traces, as
observed with CVE-2017-7303.

claims.text: The authors report that TF-Pro adds no static-analysis distance-calculation time relative to SelectFuzz; option-generation time is additional to the fuzzing-stage timings.
claims.quote:
Since TF and TF-Pro do not add
additional calculations, the static analysis time is the same as
Selectuzz, and the time of TF-Pro’s Option Generation process
is shown in Fig. 8.

claims.text: Automated option generation is claimed to make the system accessible to users without software-analysis or vulnerability expertise; no novice-user evaluation is reported.
claims.quote:
TransferFuzz-Pro is the ﬁrst work to automate processes
through option combination generation, making it accessible to
users without expertis e in software analys is or vulnerabilities.

claims.text: In the fuzzing-stage comparison, source-instrumented TF-Pro verifies all 35 Table V target cases (34 with 10/10 successful runs, objcopy with 6/10), including CVE-2016-4491 and CVE-2016-6131 cases that AFLGo, Windranger, SelectFuzz and DAFL never expose, so it verifies more vulnerabilities than these directed fuzzers.

metrics.name: Number of vulnerabilities exposed and successful runs out of 10

claims.quote:
Answering RQ3: TransferFuzz-Pro consistently out-
performs existing methods in terms of both speed and
the number of vulner abilities veriﬁed.

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Source-code versus binary instrumentation of the same TF-Pro workflow.
matched_comparisons.metric: Per-case mean time-to-exposure and successful runs in Table V.
matched_comparisons.result_a: Lower μTTE in all 35 paired rows; thumbnail/CVE-2016-10095: 56s; objdump/CVE-2016-4487: 5s; objcopy/CVE-2017-7303: 1h30m2s with 6/10 successes; all other rows have 10/10 successes.
matched_comparisons.result_b: Higher μTTE in all 35 paired rows; corresponding examples: 1m8s, 6s, and 1h52m with 6/10 successes; all other rows have 10/10 successes.
matched_comparisons.quote:
TF-Pro matches TransferFuzz’s performance (no fuzzing
modiﬁcations), while TF-Pro
bin incurs minor slowdowns due
to binary instrumentation.

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Presence of key-byte-trace-guided mutation.
matched_comparisons.metric: Mean time-to-exposure, N.A. exposure failures and successful-run counts in Table VI.
matched_comparisons.result_a: Faster in 34/35 rows; exposes all six CVE-2016-4491/6131 Binutils cases that are N.A. without KBGM. Costs: swftocxx/CVE-2018-8807 takes 20m2s versus 18m49s; objcopy/CVE-2017-7303 has 6 successes versus 7. For objdump/CVE-2016-4489, Table VI reports 54s, whereas Table V reports 4s.
matched_comparisons.result_b: Generally slower; six N.A. cases; addr2line/CVE-2016-4492 takes 1h18m3s with 5 successes versus full TF-Pro's 17s. Advantages: swftocxx/CVE-2018-8807 takes 18m49s; objcopy has 7 successes, although its μTTE is longer at 1h43m16s.
matched_comparisons.quote:
In the absence of KBGM (No KBGM), TransferFuzz-Pro
showed a signiﬁcant drop in efﬁciency due to the lack of key-
byte traces from taint analysis, which are critical for bypassing
essential constraints.

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Presence of Nested Simulated Annealing energy scheduling.
matched_comparisons.metric: Mean time-to-exposure and successful-run counts in Table VI.
matched_comparisons.result_a: Faster in 31/35 rows, tied in one and slower in three. Examples of gains: objdump/CVE-2016-4491 3m37s versus 6m19s; objcopy approximately 1h30m and 6 successes versus 2h14m and 4. Losses: objdump/CVE-2016-4492 32s versus 29s; swftoperl/CVE-2017-11733 52s versus 43s; swftotcl/CVE-2018-8962 46m16s versus 43m19s.
matched_comparisons.result_b: Generally slower, with 4 objcopy successes versus 6; faster on the three identified reversal cases. Equal to full TF-Pro at 4s for objdump/CVE-2016-4490.
matched_comparisons.quote:
For No NSA, TransferFuzz-Pro also experienced a decline in
performance, though it was less severe compared to No KBGM.

ecs.sut_or_benchmark: Six additional unnamed internal production repositories; MR versions; results pooled across repositories
ecs.protocol: One-week CI/CD deployment, triggered on MR opening; newly added/modified focal methods; prebuilt knowledge base; execute generated tests on MR revision; developer-confirmed requirement deviations count as bugs; bugs fixed and false-positive report proportion; repeated runs and per-repository results not_reported
ecs.quote:
Specifically, SeGa
was integrated into the CI/CD pipeline and automatically triggered when a merge request (MR)
was opened.

claims.text: SeGa detects 29/60 known bugs (recall 0.48), versus 7, 7, 6 and 4 for CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, HITS and RATester: 22–25 additional bugs.
claims.quote:
From the figure, SeGa iden-
tifies 29 bugs in total, while CHATTESTER, Sym-
Prompt, HITS, and RATester detect 7, 7, 6, and 4
bugs, respectively.

claims.text: SeGa achieves pooled precision 0.73 versus 0.54, 0.54, 0.55 and 0.57 for CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, HITS and RATester, a reported relative improvement of 26.9%–34.6%.
claims.quote:
Moreover, SeGa
attained a precision of 0.73, compared to 0.54, 0.54, 0.55, and 0.57 for CHATTESTER, SymPrompt,
HITS, and RATester, respectively.

claims.text: SeGa achieves the highest F1 on every subject (0.53, 0.75, 0.52, 1.00), with pooled F1 0.58 versus 0.19, 0.19, 0.17 and 0.12 for CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, HITS and RATester.
claims.quote:
From
this table, SeGa consistently outperforms all compared techniques across all projects, achieving
the highest F1-score in every case and substantially improving recall on business logic bugs while
maintaining higher precision.

claims.text: Semantic knowledge construction improves F1 and recall over using raw PRDs on Subjects 1–3; Subject 4 ties.
claims.quote:
This con-
firms that simply providing full PRDs is insufficient; the knowledge base is necessary to distill and
organize requirement information into usable functionality entries.

claims.text: Knowledge construction raises precision over the raw-PRD ablation on Subjects 1–3; the ablation has precision 0.23, 0.30 and 0.24, while Subject 4 ties at 1.00.
claims.quote:
As shown in
Table 3, SeGa𝑤/𝑜 𝑏𝑎𝑠𝑒 produces consistently low F1-scores on Subject-1 (0.24), Subject-2 (0.32), and
Subject-3 (0.27), with particularly low precision (0.23 on Subject-1 and 0.24 on Subject-3).

claims.text: Relevant-functionality retrieval improves F1 and recall over passing every functionality entry on all four subjects.
claims.quote:
This indicates that functionality retrieval is essential
to focus the agent on the subset of functionalities that matter for the focal method.

claims.text: Functionality retrieval improves precision over unfiltered functionality context on all subjects; unrelated functionalities otherwise cause many false positives.
claims.quote:
However, without relevance filtering, it is easily misled by unrelated
functionalities, leading to many false positives.

claims.text: Scenario derivation improves F1 and recall on Subjects 1–3, with Subject 4 tied; without it, Subject-3 recall is only 0.35.
claims.quote:
However, without explicit
preconditions, actions, and outcomes, the agent struggles to construct inputs that trigger subtle,
context-dependent bugs.

claims.text: Full SeGa has higher precision than the scenario-free ablation on Subjects 1–3 and ties on Subject 4.
claims.quote: Overall, the full SeGa performs the best in terms of all metrics across all subjects.

claims.text: Standalone compilation repair improves F1 and recall over repair by the generation agent on Subjects 1–3; Subject 4 ties.
claims.quote: This result confirms the benefit of standalone compilation repair.

claims.text: Standalone compilation repair raises precision over the in-agent-repair ablation on Subjects 1–3 and ties on Subject 4.
claims.quote: Overall, the full SeGa performs the best in terms of all metrics across all subjects.

claims.text: The one-week deployment finds 16 previously unknown business-logic bugs, all developer-confirmed and fixed; no compared baseline reports these issues, although the MRs had passed existing tests and local validation.

evidence.description: Subsequent developer fixes corroborate the detected bugs; initial developer confirmation was the primary acceptance criterion.
evidence.quote:
Across the production repositories, SeGa successfully detected 16 previously un-
known business logic bugs, all of which have been fixed by developers, while none of the baseline
techniques reported any of these issues.

claims.quote:
Across the production repositories, SeGa successfully detected 16 previously un-
known business logic bugs, all of which have been fixed by developers, while none of the baseline
techniques reported any of these issues.

claims.text: SeGa is claimed to produce fewer false-positive reports than CHATTESTER, SymPrompt, HITS and RATester.
claims.quote:
These results indicate that SeGa not only detects substantially
more business logic bugs, but also produces fewer false positives in industrial settings.

claims.text: SeGa is claimed to maintain low false-positive rates, although this benchmark contains only buggy methods and defines no true negatives.
claims.quote:
That is, it not only detects the most business
logic bugs, including many unique ones, but also maintains low false positive rates.

claims.text: SeGa remains effective on complex cross-module Subjects 1 and 3, detecting 5 and 16 bugs versus CHATTESTER's 1 and 4.
claims.quote:
Nevertheless, even under the challenging conditions,
SeGa detects 5 and 16 bugs on Subject-1 and Subject-3, respectively, whereas the strongest baseline,
CHATTESTER, detects only 1 and 4.

claims.text: SeGa covers nearly all bugs found by the external comparators, missing one unique to SymPrompt, and finds the largest set missed by every comparator.
claims.quote:
Notably, SeGa covers nearly all
bugs found by the other techniques (missing only
one uniquely detected by SymPrompt) and also dis-
covers the largest number of bugs that no baseline
can find.

claims.text: In deployment, intentional project-specific behaviors account for false-positive reports representing 30% of all reports.
claims.quote:
Regarding false
positives, SeGa occasionally reports behaviors that appear suspicious when evaluated solely against
requirement text but are intentional under project-specific conventions (30% of the total reports).

claims.text: Developers can quickly dismiss deployment false positives, so these reports do not overwhelm the practical usefulness of detected bugs.
claims.quote:
Importantly, developers were able to quickly dismiss
these reports, indicating that while false positives exist, they are generally explainable and do not
overwhelm the practical usefulness of the detected bugs.

claims.text: Developer feedback says generated tests help reveal subtle requirements that had previously remained implicit.
claims.quote:
Feedback from the participating developer
teams highlighted that the generated tests were not only accurate in exposing faulty behavior,
but also helped surface subtle requirements that were previously implicit.

claims.text: Previously unknown detected bugs span the major business-logic bug categories, including functional correctness and security examples.
claims.quote:
We further analyzed the detected bugs and found that
they span the major bug categories introduced earlier.

claims.text: Buggy code changes associated with newly detected bugs average 91.35 lines.

metrics.name: Mean lines in buggy code changes

claims.quote:
The corresponding buggy code changes
involve91.35lines on average and often implement the correct control flow yet violate documented
requirements due to mismatched conditions, states, or cross-component assumptions.

claims.text: SeGa averages 236.85 seconds per focal method, slower than CHATTESTER (139.91), SymPrompt (187.11) and HITS (134.74).
claims.quote:
On average, SeGa takes 236.85 seconds per focal method, with CHATTESTER re-
quiring 139.91 seconds, SymPrompt 187.11 seconds, and HITS 134.74 seconds per method.

claims.text: The paper judges SeGa's additional runtime justified by its improved business-logic bug detection.
claims.quote:
Given the high real-world cost of business logic bugs, the
overhead of SeGa is justified by its improved effectiveness.

claims.text: The retrospective study and additional deployment support generalization across projects, domains and development contexts within the reported single-company Go setting.

evidence.description: Subsequent developer fixes corroborate the detected bugs; initial developer confirmation was the primary acceptance criterion.
evidence.quote:
Across the production repositories, SeGa successfully detected 16 previously un-
known business logic bugs, all of which have been fixed by developers, while none of the baseline
techniques reported any of these issues.

claims.quote:
These results provide evidence
that SeGa generalizes across projects, domains, and development contexts, partially mitigating this
threat.

claims.text: The scenario-free ablation achieves relatively high precision among the ablations, including 0.59 on Subject 3.
claims.quote:
SeGa𝑤/𝑜 𝑠𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑜
achieves relatively higher precision but much lower recall.

claims.text: The paper attributes fewer false-positive reports in the scenario-free ablation to generic tests with weaker assertions.
claims.quote:
This tends to reduce false positives because, without scenario-level guidance, the generator
usually produces generic tests with weaker or incomplete assertions.

claims.text: Change-aware focal-method selection and relevant-scenario targeting are claimed to let CI/CD testing scale without overwhelming developers.
claims.quote:
Prioritizing focal methods affected by a change and generating a limited number of tests
by targeting only relevant business scenarios per method allows semantics-driven testing to scale
without overwhelming developers.

claims.text: Some SeGa false positives arise from implausible downstream-service or database failure assumptions.
claims.quote:
First, some
false positives arise when the model hypothesizes implausible failure scenarios that are unlikely
in deployed production systems.

claims.text: Ambiguous or underspecified PRDs can cause plausible but unintended test oracles and false positives.
claims.quote:
We observed that, in such cases, the generated
oracles sometimes reflect plausible but unintended behaviors, leading to false positives.

claims.text: Implicit team conventions and module responsibility boundaries cause context-dependent false positives that explicit PRDs do not resolve.
claims.quote:
This illustrates
that accurate business logic bug detection depends not only on explicit requirements, but also on
module responsibilities and project-specific practices that may not be fully captured in PRDs.

claims.text: Without scenario derivation, the generation agent tends to produce generic tests with weaker or incomplete assertions.
claims.quote:
This tends to reduce false positives because, without scenario-level guidance, the generator
usually produces generic tests with weaker or incomplete assertions.

claims.text: Without standalone repair, the generation agent spends many iterations resolving compilation errors and can exhaust its iteration budget.
claims.quote:
A major reason is that the agent spends many iterations handling compilation errors by
searching for missing context, rewriting tests, and repeatedly re-triggering new errors, until it
reaches the iteration budget.

claims.text: Partial visibility of cross-service requirements can yield incomplete or misleading interpretations in the observed cases.
claims.quote:
We observed cases where correct behavior depends on interactions across services, and partial
visibility can lead to incomplete or misleading interpretations of requirements.

claims.text: LANTERN improves DeepSeek-V3 repair across all 11 languages, especially Rust (+22.09%); reported gains also include Go 11.31%, PHP 9.33%, Kotlin 8.87%, C# 8.82%, and Ruby 8.33%.

evidence.detail: MWW p=0.0126; Cliff's delta=0.64 (large).
evidence.quote:
Our MWW tests [33, 49] further confirm
the improvements with a p-value of 0.0126 ( < 0.05) and a Cliff’s
Delta [10, 56] of 0.64 (large effect).

claims.quote:
It is worth noting
that Rust bugs benefit the most from translation-based repair, which
achieves an increment of 22.09%.

claims.text: Bug-specific reasoning produces successful repairs earlier than greedy or random language selection; first-iteration Kotlin and Ruby Pass@10 are 0.96 and 0.92, and JavaScript repairs appear immediately.
claims.quote:
Instead, a more tailored approach that analyzes
specific bugs to select the optimal target language leads to more ro-
bust repair performance.

claims.text: Reasoning achieves superior target-language ranking: MAP@k is 1.00 for the first three iterations, converges to 0.938 by iteration five, and averages 0.957.
claims.quote:
Figure 7 shows that the reasoning strategy maintains an𝑀𝐴𝑃 @𝑘
of 1.00 for the first three iterations and converges to 0.938 by the
fifth iteration, reflecting its consistent ability to identify optimal
languages.

claims.text: Reasoning ranks successful target languages earlier than greedy/random: NDCG@1 is 1.00, NDCG@k remains higher at every iteration, and its average is 0.954.
claims.quote:
Figure 8 exhibits that the reasoning strategy starts with
a𝑁𝐷𝐶𝐺 @𝑘 of 1.00 at the first iteration and consistently performs
better than the other strategies at each iteration, highlighting its
early advantages in the ranking.

claims.text: Reasoning has higher early Precision@k; all three strategies converge by iteration three.
claims.quote:
According to Figure 9a, the reasoning strategy remains higher
𝑃𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑖𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛 @𝑘 until all strategies converge to the same level at the
third iteration, demonstrating its early identification of valid fixes.

claims.text: Reasoning reaches full recall by iteration five, compared with iteration nine for greedy and the final iteration for random.
claims.quote:
Figure 9b shows that it achieves full recall with a 𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙 @𝑘 of
1.00 by the fifth iteration, ahead of greedy and random strategies,
which converge only at the ninth and final iterations, respectively.

claims.text: Reasoning has an early F1@k advantage over greedy and random language selection.
claims.quote:
Similarly, the𝐹 1@𝑘 scores in Figure 9c highlight its early advantage,
aligning with our previous𝑃𝑎𝑠𝑠@10observations.

claims.text: Reasoning uses the shortest mean translation path: 2.52 steps, versus random 2.69 and greedy 2.98.
claims.quote:
the reasoning strategy achieves the shortest av-
erage translation path length (2.52), outperforming both random
(2.69) and greedy (2.98) strategies, thereby minimizing resource
consumption throughout the iterative process as unfixed bugs must
propagate through all subsequent iterations.

claims.text: The shorter reasoning-guided translation paths minimize resource consumption during iterative repair.
claims.quote:
the reasoning strategy achieves the shortest av-
erage translation path length (2.52), outperforming both random
(2.69) and greedy (2.98) strategies, thereby minimizing resource
consumption throughout the iterative process as unfixed bugs must
propagate through all subsequent iterations.

claims.text: LANTERN leads repair performance in 9 of 11 languages against direct repair, ChatRepair, Self-Planning, and Self-Collaboration; gains over ChatRepair include Go 5.46%, Kotlin 4.91%, and PHP 6.76%.
claims.quote:
Fig-
ure 10 shows LANTERN achieves the highest𝑃𝑎𝑠𝑠 @10scores across
xCodeEval, leading in 9 out of 11 languages.

claims.text: Translation-based repair addresses harder bugs than initial direct repair: median difficulty is 500 higher for C# and 400 higher for Java, Kotlin, Ruby, and Rust.

metrics.name: Median Codeforces difficulty of repaired bugs

evidence.detail: Difficulty distributions differ: p=5.25E−48; Cliff's delta=0.37 (medium).
evidence.quote:
Our statistical analysis reveals a signifi-
cant difference in difficulty between bugs fixed via translation and
those initially fixed with a p-value of5.25𝐸− 48and Cliff’s delta of
0.37 (medium effect).

claims.quote:
We notice that the translation-based repair can fix bugs with
500 higher median difficulty for C#, while for Java, Kotlin, Ruby, and
Rust, it enables successful repair of a group of bugs with median
difficulty increased by 400.

claims.text: Translation generally preserves bug semantics: 20,750/32,277 coarse outcomes are unchanged, including 12,225 PASSED, 3,881/4,318 WRONG ANSWER, and all 3,021 TIME LIMIT EXCEEDED transitions.
claims.quote:
For the consistent transitions, we notice that a total of 20750 out
of all 32277 cases remain consistent in coarse-grained categories.

claims.text: Back-translation preserves semantics for most repaired code: 7.56% of fixed bugs are lost and 85.95% of correct samples remain; the reported sample-loss test is not significant.

evidence.detail: Before/after correct-sample comparison: p=0.39; Cliff's delta=0.22; this does not establish semantic equivalence.
evidence.quote:
Our statistical tests on correct samples before and
after back-translation yield a p-value of 0.39 (> 0.05) and a Cliff’s
Delta of 0.22, confirming that the loss caused by back-translation is
not significant.

claims.quote:
Back-translation preserves
semantic consistency for most repaired code, with an overall loss
of only 7.56% of fixed bugs while 85.95% of correct samples are
preserved.

claims.text: Cross-language translation outperforms repeated repair without translation, including Rust +16.55%, PHP +7.27%, Go +6.96%, and Ruby +5.71% in final Pass@10.

evidence.detail: Final Pass@10 gains: p=1.95E−03; Cliff's delta=0.42 (medium).
evidence.quote:
Our
statistical analysis of the final Pass@10 improvements confirms
that translation-based repair significantly outperforms direct repair
with a p-value of1.95𝐸− 03and Cliff’s Delta of 0.42 (medium effect).

claims.quote:
The bug translation component contributes
significantly to enhancing program repair effectiveness, with its
most substantial impact observed in Rust, achieving a 16.55%
improvement in Pass@10.

claims.text: Historical feedback improves early repair convergence; Rust first-iteration Pass@10 is 0.82 with feedback versus 0.74 without it.
claims.quote:
For example, in Rust, our approach
achieves a𝑃𝑎𝑠𝑠 @10of 0.82 in the first iteration compared to only
0.74 without historical feedback.

claims.text: Removing historical feedback leaves final Pass@10 similar once translation iterations are completed.
claims.quote:
We see that the final𝑃𝑎𝑠𝑠 @10
performance of the two remains similar, which is expected since
both are fundamentally translation-based repair like other strate-
gies.

claims.text: LANTERN fixes more Defects4J bugs than ChatRepair: 170 versus 141 on v1.2 and 60 versus 54 on v2.0.
claims.quote:
On
Defects4J 1.2, LANTERN resolves 170 bugs versus ChatRepair’s 141
(+29 bugs).

claims.text: On SWE-bench Lite, LANTERN resolves 110/300 issues (36.67%), exceeding AGENTLESS at 95/300 (31.67%).
claims.quote:
On SWE-Bench Lite, LANTERN achieves stronger results, re-
solving 110/300 instances (36.67%) versus AGENTLESS’s 95/300
(31.67%).

claims.text: With Claude 3.5 Sonnet, LANTERN improves Pass@10 in every language; highlighted gains are Kotlin 16.94%, PHP 17.95%, and Rust 18.30%.
claims.quote:
LANTERN elevates Claude’s perfor-
mance across every language, with massive boosts in Kotlin (+16.94%),
PHP (+17.95%), and Rust (+18.30%), demonstrating that even fron-
tier proprietary models benefit significantly from cross-language
translation.

claims.text: With Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, LANTERN improves repair across languages; highlighted gains are Rust 26.58%, C# 10.42%, Go 10.13%, and PHP 11.67%.
claims.quote:
LANTERN provides dramatic improvements on Rust
(+26.58%), C# (+10.42%), Go (+10.13%), and PHP (+11.67%), revealing
that LANTERN can elevate strong open-source models to achieve
performance competitive with or superior to highly-capable propri-
etary models.

claims.text: LANTERN's repair gains generalize across DeepSeek-V3, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct.
claims.quote:
LANTERN demon-
strates model-agnostic generalizability across different LLMs.

claims.text: LANTERN generalizes to real-world Java and repository-level Python defects, including issue resolution involving multiple files.
claims.quote:
LANTERN outperforms ChatRepair and
AGENTLESS on the challenging real-world benchmarks, which
demonstrates strong generalizability to real-world issue resolution,
revealing its cross-language translation paradigm is effective for
complex, real-world software defects, including those that require
understanding context across multiple files.

claims.text: Translation itself can repair defects, especially compilation errors, before a separate repair attempt; some compilation errors persist as other error categories. A small subset of WRONG ANSWER cases also becomes PASSED during translation.
claims.quote:
First, we notice that most bugs with COMPILATION ERROR can
be fixed early in the translation phase, or transformed into other
categories of bugs if minor additional issues remain within them.

claims.text: Improvement on less common languages suggests LANTERN generalizes beyond mainstream languages and reduces language-dependent repair disparities.
claims.quote:
Furthermore, our significant improvements
on less common languages like Rust suggest that the approach
generalizes beyond mainstream languages.

claims.text: Random language selection produces earlier repairs than greedy ordering: JavaScript is first repaired at iteration four versus nine; random achieves Go Pass@10 0.90 at iteration one and Rust 0.86 at iteration two.
claims.quote:
For example, JavaScript (JS) bugs are only
repaired in the ninth iteration after translation to C++, and PHP
bugs cannot be fixed until the second iteration.

claims.text: Reasoning preferentially selects particular target languages: first-iteration fixed-bug paths include C# 150, C++ 138, C 78, Java 68, and Python 59.

metrics.name: Successful translation-path counts by target language

claims.quote:
For example, the top-5
target languages in the first iteration, C#, C++, C, Java, and Python
account for 150, 138, 78, 68, and 59 bugs, respectively.

claims.text: Language-specific memory/time behavior contributes to inconsistent execution categories across translations.
claims.quote:
Sec-
ondly, language-specific differences such as memory and time usage
are also critical contributors to the transition inconsistency.

claims.text: Translation can fix semicolon-related compilation errors even when the target language also requires semicolons.
claims.quote:
Such compilation errors can be
fixed even when translating to languages that require semicolons,
revealing the inherent features of LLM-based code translation.

claims.text: Localized context windows provide scalability for resolving issues in large repositories without representing entire projects.
claims.quote:
This demon-
strates that complete semantic representation of entire projects is
unnecessary—focusing on relevant context maintains both scalabil-
ity and efficiency for large-scale codebases.

claims.text: Focusing on localized context preserves efficiency for large codebases.
claims.quote:
This demon-
strates that complete semantic representation of entire projects is
unnecessary—focusing on relevant context maintains both scalabil-
ity and efficiency for large-scale codebases.

claims.text: Qwen with LANTERN outperforms Claude's direct repair on Rust: Pass@10 72.00% versus 67.79%.
claims.quote:
For instance, QWen with LANTERN achieves 72.00%
on Rust, surpassing Claude’s direct repair score of 67.79%.

claims.text: Direct Qwen repair varies substantially across languages, struggling particularly on Rust (45.42%) and C# (69.50%).
claims.quote:
QWen’s baseline shows signifi-
cant variance, particularly struggling with languages requiring
strict compilation or complex type systems like Rust (45.42%) and
C# (69.50%).

claims.text: Back-translation losses vary by language: Java loses 11/91 fixed bugs, while correct-sample losses are greatest for C# (182) and least for Rust (six).

Java expe-
rienced the greatest loss with 11 out of 91 fixed bugs incorrectly
translated, which remains a small number of bugs compared to
its correctly translated bugs.

claims.text: LANTERN successfully addresses most bugs that resist direct LLM-based repair attempts.

metrics.name: Pass@10 improvement over initial direct repair

claims.text: GPT-3.5 SyzGPT reaches 87.84% SVR versus zero-shot 11.49%, fixed few-shot 26.83% and external Fuzz4All 16.74%; §3.3 instead prints 11.47% and 26.84% for zero/few-shot.
claims.quote:
The superiority of SyzGPT indicates that our prompting method significantly improves
the syntactic validity of seed generation.

claims.text: GPT-3.5 SyzGPT has the highest OER, 42.66%, versus zero-shot 0.70%, few-shot 7.80%, external Fuzz4All 12.16% and ECG 12.61%.
claims.quote:
By comparing methods using the same LLM, SyzGPT achieves the highest OER
(42.66% with GPT-3.5), validating its effectiveness.

claims.text: SyzGPT SVRs for GPT-3.5/GPT-4/Claude/CodeLlama/CodeLlama-syz/Llama-3/Vicuna are 87.84/72.48/73.17/82.11/87.84/68.81/48.85%.
claims.quote:
The results are shown in
Table 2, where our method demonstrates effectiveness and superiority.

claims.text: Claude has the highest effective-seed count, 261, and OER, 59.86%; other SyzGPT OERs are GPT-3.5 42.66%, GPT-4 55.05%, CodeLlama 33.71%, CodeLlama-syz 47.01%, Llama-3 43.58%, Vicuna 2.75%.
claims.quote:
The results in Table 2 highlight the effectiveness and diversity of the generated programs across
different models.

claims.text: Fine-tuning CodeLlama increases zero-shot SVR from 0% to 48.62% and SyzGPT SVR from 82.11% to 87.84%.
claims.quote:
Using fine-tuned CodeLlama-syz can improve SVR of Zero-shot from 0% to 48.62% and
SVR of SyzGPT from 82.11% to 87.84%.

claims.text: Fine-tuning raises SyzGPT OER from 33.71% to 47.01% and zero-shot OER from 0% to 21.33%.
claims.quote:
We also find fine-tuning CodeLlama with context effective programs can boost the generation
performance of SyzGPT and Zero-shot.

claims.text: Default GPT-3.5 generation is reported efficient and acceptable: 1769.33 tokens, 4.66 seconds and about $0.007 per program.
claims.quote:
In our method’s default configuration (GPT-3.5), a high-quality program can
be generated within a few seconds and fewer than 2k tokens (0.007$), which is quite efficient and
acceptable.

claims.text: Heuristic repair averages 5 milliseconds per program.
claims.quote:
For the cost of program repair, it takes an average of 5 milliseconds per program, which
is accurate and fast enough, eliminating the need to use LLM for repair.

claims.text: SyzGPT covers 184705/193758/174435 basic blocks on Linux 6.6/5.15/4.19, reporting 17.73% average improvement over seven external fuzzers; the conclusion instead prints 31.85%.
claims.quote:
Compared to Syzkaller, MoonShine, Healer, ACTOR, MOCK, ECG, and KernelGPT, SyzGPT achieves
15.83%, 15.70%, 28.03%, 42.76%, 5.21%, 9.05%, and 7.52% average coverage improvements.

claims.text: Unique-coverage finding ratios exceed external Syzkaller/MoonShine/ECG/KernelGPT by 4.28×/3.93×/2.22×/1.88×.
claims.quote:
Specifically,
SyzGPT shows significant gains in unique coverage finding ability over Syzkaller (4.28×), MoonShine
(3.93×), ECG (2.22×), and KernelGPT (1.88×).

claims.text: LFSC-exclusive coverage is 8295/10001/4897 blocks, exceeding every external comparator with available measurements.
claims.quote: According to Table 3, SyzGPT outperforms all state-of-the-art fuzzers across every metric.

claims.text: SyzGPT produces 36.27%/36.26%/14.24%/19.82% more valuable inputs than external Syzkaller/MoonShine/ECG/KernelGPT.
claims.quote:
It also surpasses these fuzzers in the number of valuable
inputs (𝑁𝑣𝑖) by 36.27%, 36.26%, 14.24%, and 19.82%, respectively.

claims.text: The paper claims 12.75/14.31/57.68/15.52/7.92/9.39/24.24% more covered syscalls than the seven external fuzzers; Table 3 supports higher normalized rates but fewer absolute calls than KernelGPT; the conclusion additionally labels 17.73% as LFS syscall coverage.
claims.quote:
In terms of syscalls metrics, SyzGPT
covers 12.75%, 14.31%, 57.68%, 15.52%, 7.92%, 9.39%, and 24.24% more syscalls compared with all
other fuzzers, with increases of 112.72%, 44.69%, 132.63%, 29.91%, 8.25%, 31.18%, and 46.60% in LFSC,
respectively.

claims.text: SyzGPT covers 588/645/571 LFSC, reporting 58.00% average improvement over seven external fuzzers.
claims.quote:
According to our evaluation, SyzGPT achieves improvements of 17.73% in code coverage,
58.00% in LFS coverage, and 323.22% in vulnerability detection across three LTS kernels.

claims.text: SyzGPT finds 115 crash-title-deduplicated vulnerabilities versus external Syzkaller 78, MoonShine 85, Healer 12, ACTOR 36, MOCK 11, ECG 65 and KernelGPT 64; reported average improvement is 323.22%.
claims.quote:
On three LTS kernels, SyzGPT found 115 vulnerabilities, while Syzkaller, MoonShine,
Healer, ACTOR, Mock, ECG, and KernelGPT found 78, 85, 12, 36, 11, 65, and 64, respectively.

claims.text: SyzGPT finds 27 vulnerabilities unique among the eight fuzzers versus external comparators' 9/14/2/10/5/9/13.
claims.quote:
And among all the vulnerabilities found on three kernels,
SyzGPT found 27 unique ones, while Syzkaller, MoonShine, Healer, ACTOR, Mock, ECG, and
KernelGPT only found 9, 14, 2, 10, 5, 9, and 13.

claims.text: SyzGPT finds 10 unique directly LFSC-induced vulnerabilities versus external Syzkaller/MoonShine/Healer/ACTOR/MOCK/ECG/KernelGPT's 2/4/6/1/4/4/4.
claims.quote:
On three kernels,
SyzGPT, Syzkaller, MoonShine, Healer, ACTOR, Mock, ECG, and KernelGPT discover 10, 2, 4, 6,
1, 4, 4, and 4 unique LFSC-introduced vulnerabilities, respectively.

claims.quote: Additionally, the overall accuracy decreases from 97% to 84%, underscoring the importance of traceability-assisted inconsistency identification in effectively distinguishing implementation errors from format extraction errors.

claims.text: Relevant-section diagnosis achieves 100% format-error accuracy versus 0% with the entire RFC.
claims.quote: Without traceability, the LLM fails to identify any Format Extraction Errors, causing accuracy in this category to drop from 100% to 0%.

claims.text: The full workflow finds 69 unique bugs versus four with whole-format generation and whole-RFC diagnosis.

evidence.details: 36 reported bugs confirmed; remaining reports pending review.
evidence.quote: We reported them to the developers, with 36 confirmed so far and others pending review.

claims.quote: In contrast, ParCleanse, using fine-grained testing, detected 75 logical inconsistencies and 4 crashes, with 69 unique bugs detected.

claims.text: The full workflow reports 75 logical inconsistencies versus 22 under the joint testing/traceability ablation.
claims.quote: In contrast, ParCleanse, using fine-grained testing, detected 75 logical inconsistencies and 4 crashes, with 69 unique bugs detected.

claims.text: Fine-grained generation is claimed to explore the input space more thoroughly than whole-format generation.
claims.quote: This demonstrates that fine-grained test generation enables thorough input space exploration, triggering more logical inconsistencies and unique bugs.

claims.text: The project demonstrates the potential to fully automate software validation from natural-language specifications.
claims.quote: The project also demonstrates the potential for fully automating software validation based on natural language specifications, a process previously considered predominantly manual due to the need to understand specification documents and derive expected outputs for test inputs.

claims.text: Seven protocols achieve 100% inconsistency-identification accuracy.
claims.quote: Our manual evaluation confirms that ParCleanse correctly identifies 87 inconsistencies: 76 (72 logical and 4 crash) of 79 Implementation Errors and all 11 Format Extraction Errors, achieving an overall 97% accuracy and 100% accuracy for seven protocols.

claims.text: 83 of 86 logical inconsistencies are classified correctly, approximately 97%.
claims.quote: Among 86 detected logical inconsistencies, 83 (72 logical Implementation Errors, 11 Format Extraction Errors) are accurately classified, achieving 97% accuracy, highlighting ParCleanse ’s effectiveness in distinguishing between implementation and format extraction errors.

claims.text: Crash identification accuracy is 100%, with crashes automatically considered implementation errors.
claims.quote: Since crashes are always Implementation Errors, the identification accuracy for crashes is 100%.

claims.text: Testing detects 90 raw inconsistencies: 86 logical and four crashes.
claims.quote: As shown in column “Detected Incons.”, ParCleanse detects a total of 90 (86 logical and 4 crash) inconsistencies across all protocols.

claims.text: Format refinement lowers dependent-constraint precision from 85% to 73%.
claims.quote: However, ParCleanse ’s precision of dependent constraints slightly decreases after refinement.

claims.text: Refinement identifies two additional missing dependent constraints.
claims.quote: After refinement, the model identifies two additional missing constraints but produces inaccurate formulas due to the complexity of dependencies, leading to a minor precision drop.

claims.text: The joint whole-format/whole-RFC ablation has only 4% logical-error identification accuracy versus 97% for ParCleanse.

metrics.name: Overall identification accuracy (90% as printed for the joint ablation)

claims.quote:
Without traceability-assisted inconsistency identification, accuracy in identifying real implementa-
tion errors drops sharply from 97% to 4%, highlighting that, without traceability, LLMs struggle to accurately detect logical inconsistencies due to hallucinations.

claims.text: Whole-format testing predominantly triggers crashes: 211 of 233 detected issues.
claims.quote: Without fine-grained property-level mutation, most detected issues are crashes (211 out of 233), with only 4 unique bugs identified.

claims.text: ParCleanse generates a proof of concept for every detected bug.
claims.quote: ParCleanse generated a PoC (Proof of Concept) for each bug.

claims.text: Of 36 confirmed bugs, 17 fixes are merged, 18 pull requests approved pending merge, and one remains unresolved.
claims.quote: Of the 36 confirmed bugs, 17 are fixed and merged, 18 have approved pull requests pending merge, and 1 remains unresolved.

claims.text: BFD extraction misses all dependent constraints, yielding 0% recall.
claims.quote:
For BFD, since the LLM-
extracted format contains no dependent constraints, its precision is denoted with “-”.

claims.text: ParCleanse exposes Babel's missing prohibition of all-zero/all-one RouterId values.

evidence.details: The motivating RouterId validation bug was confirmed and fixed.
evidence.quote: It is confirmed and now fixed as shown in Figure 1.

claims.quote: It is confirmed and now fixed as shown in Figure 1.

claims.text: TCP extraction accuracy suffers on implicit DataOffset/header-alignment and bit-offset relationships.
claims.quote: Among these protocols, TCP shows a drop in performance due to the handling of the DataOffset field, which involves header alignment and bit-level offsets.

claims.text: The experiments reveal no observed bugs in the RFC documents.
claims.quote: Additionally, in our experiments, we did not observe any document bugs.

claims.text: Dependent constraints are the most difficult element type to extract, with overall recall of 44% across the nine protocols.
claims.quote: Dependent constraints are particularly challenging, as they require understanding how different fields influence one another, often through implicit rules or cross-references within the protocol specification.

claims.text: The whole-document comparison is argued to show that the divide-and-conquer gains are not explained by GPT-4o having seen the RFC documents during pretraining.

metrics.name: Format-extraction precision/recall with versus without divide-and-conquer

claims.quote: To mitigate this, we compare with a baseline where the entire document is fed directly to GPT-4o (Section 5.5.2). These experiments validate the effectiveness of our divide-and-conquer design.

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Traceability-assisted Phase-3 format refinement versus the Phase-1 format
matched_comparisons.metric: Expert-ground-truth precision/recall (%), ordered message types; field names; field types; independent constraints; dependent constraints (E1–E9 versus E19)
matched_comparisons.quote: Overall, refinement improves the quality of extracted protocol formats, increasing the precision and recall of independent constraints (column “Indep. Constr.”) by 11% (88% to 98%) and 21% (68% to 82%).

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: DocTree divide-and-conquer extraction versus whole-RFC extraction, both before Phase-3 refinement
matched_comparisons.metric: Expert-ground-truth precision/recall (%), ordered message types; field names; field types; independent constraints; dependent constraints (E19 versus E20)
matched_comparisons.quote: For example, field name recall decreases from 94% to 54%, and field type recall drops from 89% to 37%.

matched_comparisons.changed_factor: Relevant RFC section versus entire RFC supplied for inconsistency diagnosis
matched_comparisons.metric: Logical / format-error / overall inconsistency-identification accuracy (E10–E18 versus E21)
matched_comparisons.quote: Additionally, the overall accuracy decreases from 97% to 84%, underscoring the importance of traceability-assisted inconsistency identification in effectively distinguishing implementation errors from format extraction errors.

claims.text: ESBMC VeriExploit achieves 85.60% overall reproduction success versus 11.80% for the baseline; the results prose instead states 83.23% for ESBMC.
claims.quote:
Experiments show
that VeriExploit is effective at automating bug reproduction,
achieving a success rate of 85.60% on our benchmark dataset.

claims.text: SolCMC VeriExploit achieves 64.60% overall reproduction success versus 11.80% for the baseline.
claims.quote: The LLM-Only baseline only reaches 11.80%.

claims.text: Both full pipelines reproduce all six evaluated vulnerability classes and outperform the baseline in every class; ESBMC/SolCMC/baseline reentrancy success is 80.00%/44.35%/7.83% in Table III, although the prose gives 11.80% for baseline reentrancy.
claims.quote:
The verification-assisted
methods succeed across all bug categories.

claims.text: ESBMC cumulative success increases over reflection rounds 1–5: 65.00%, 71.60%, 80.20%, 81.60%, 85.60%.
claims.quote:
As re-
flection iterations increase,ESBMC improves sharply in the
first three rounds (65.00% →71.60%→80.20%), then levels
off (81.60%→85.60%).

claims.text: SolCMC cumulative success increases over reflection rounds 1–5: 58.80%, 59.60%, 61.20%, 63.80%, 64.60%.
claims.quote:
SolCMCshows smaller, steady gains
across rounds (58.80%→64.60% by iteration 5).

claims.text: Small retry caps of approximately three rounds capture most benefits, with diminishing returns thereafter.
claims.quote:
This conver-
gence indicates that most benefits arrive early; small retry caps
(around three rounds) capture the bulk of improvements, with
diminishing returns thereafter for both backends.

claims.text: Manual inspection finds no self-contained exploit among 428 ESBMC and 323 SolCMC valid outputs, whereas 15 of the baseline's 59 valid outputs fail functional separation.
claims.quote:
As a comparison, among the 59 valid cases
from the Baseline, 15 failed to achieve functional separation.

claims.text: The generated interaction-separated exploits preserve structurally realistic attack patterns.

evidence.description: The separate Doftcoin case illustrates modular interactions and alternative attack orders; it does not measure user usefulness or realism across deployments.
evidence.quote:
The separated interaction
structure allows multiple valid attack paths.

claims.quote:
We prefer interaction-separated, since it helps
to reveal multiple attack paths and better matches real-world
patterns.

runtime (SolCMC: 25.41→73.88 s; ESBMC: 23.74→45.78 s).

claims.text: Without reflection, matched context improves overall success from 48.20% to 49.60% with ESBMC and from 33.00% to 48.40% with SolCMC; reentrancy success rises from 40.00% to 46.96% and from 0.87% to 46.96%, respectively.

claims.text: The authors identify self-reflection as the key driver of reproduction effectiveness.

improving results and handling complex vulnerabilities like

generation is likewise critical for overall success.

indicates that VeriExploitperforms on par with the state

ample is reported, even when multiple valid sequences exist.

claims.text: ViBR detects action boundaries with precision 0.87, recall 0.85 and F1 0.86, outperforming all compared methods; reported relative gains over GIFdroid are 7.4%, 1.2% and 4.9%.
claims.quote:
First,
we evaluate our approach in segmenting the action scenes from 75 GUI recordings that are widely-
studied in the prior studies, achieving up to 87%, 85%, and 86% in precision, recall, and F1-score,
respectively.

claims.text: ViBR's tap, scroll and input classification accuracies are 0.88, 0.93 and 1.00; the prose claims superiority over all baselines, although Table 2 ties GIFdroid on scroll and input.
claims.quote: Moreover, our approach achieves higher action-type classification accuracy than all baselines, reaching 0.88, 0.93, and 1.00 accuracy for tap, scroll, and input actions, respectively.

claims.text: ViBR's GUI consistency comparison reaches precision 0.86, recall 0.88 and F1 0.87, exceeding ABS, SIFT, SSIM and CLIP; reported improvements over SSIM are 43.3%, 37.5% and 40.3%.
claims.quote: It consistently outperforms all baselines, achieving a 43.3% improvement in precision, 37.5% in recall, and 40.3% in F1-score compared to the best-performing baseline, SSIM.

claims.text: Adding post-action context to the ungrounded comparator raises precision/recall/F1 from 0.65/0.60/0.62 to 0.73/0.71/0.72.
claims.quote: Incorporating the post-action frame improves the performance to 0.73 precision, 0.71 recall, and 0.72 F1-score, yielding gains of 8%, 11%, and 10%, respectively.

claims.text: Adding region grounding/attention guidance to the pre/post/current comparator raises precision/recall/F1 from 0.73/0.71/0.72 to 0.86/0.88/0.87, the best ablation-study result.
claims.quote: Overall, the full configuration of ViBR,Pre-action frame (GroundingDINO) + Post-action frame + Current GUI, achieves the best performance, further validating the effectiveness of region-guided prompting.

claims.text: Region-guided comparison remains functionally accurate under layout shifts and dynamic surrounding content that mislead the ungrounded ablations.

evidence.description: Fig. 7(e-f) illustrates shifted Fullscreen mode and dynamically surrounded Videos targets; no condition-specific quantitative results are reported.
evidence.quote: The ablation baselines fail to recognize these as functional consistent states due to reliance on holistic matching, whereas our region-guided prompt enables robust matching by reasoning over the local interaction semantics.

claims.quote: The ablation baselines fail to recognize these as functional consistent states due to reliance on holistic matching, whereas our region-guided prompt enables robust matching by reasoning over the local interaction semantics.

claims.text: Delayed resource rendering can cause ViBR to split one user action into multiple scenes.
claims.quote: First, over-segmentation may occur when there are delays in resource loading, e.g., one segment is produced for the GUI transition, and another for the delayed rendering of content triggered by the same user action.

claims.text: Dynamic ads or video playback can be falsely segmented as separate user actions.
claims.quote: Second, dynamic GUI elements such as advertisements or video playback can produce continuous frame differences that are mistakenly interpreted as separate user actions.

claims.text: Semantically uncorrelated successive screens can prevent ViBR from inferring the recorded action.
claims.quote: For instance, in Fig. 8(a), tapping the “Dropbox” button leads to a next screen with no clear semantic correlation with the original GUI, making it hard for the VLMs to infer the action.

claims.text: Masked PIN output can prevent ViBR from recovering the exact recorded input without intermediate-transition context.

claims.text: Direct GPT-4o's poor segmentation is attributed to insufficient frame-level granularity and ambiguous prompts/action-scene definitions.

claims.text: Post-action context is said to shift GUI comparison from superficial appearance toward reasoning about the expected interaction outcome.
claims.quote: This improvement occurs because the post-action frame provides critical context about the expected outcome of the user interaction, enabling the model to reason beyond static appearance matching.

claims.text: CLIP-based ViBR segmentation can capture semantic as well as structural changes that defeat GIFdroid's SSIM comparison in transient-overlay examples.
